News.title: Woman ‘sexually assaulted’ on packed train in horror broad daylight attack – as cops release CCTV in hunt for man
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

TRAIN 'ATTACK' Woman ‘sexually assaulted’ on packed train in horror broad daylight attack – as cops release CCTV in hunt for man







Next

COPS have launched a manhunt after a woman was allegedly sexually assaulted on a train.

British Transport Police have released an image of a man they want to question.

The woman was travelling on a rail service between Birmingham and Derby on September 21 at just after 9am.



During the journey a man sat next to her and repeatedly commented on her appearance before allegedly sexually assaulting her.



He got off the train at Derby station.

Detectives are keen to speak to the man in the image as he may have information that could assist their ongoing investigation.

Anyone who recognises him is asked to contact BTP by texting 61016 or calling 0800 40 50 40, quoting reference 76 of 22 September.



Information can also be given to Crimestoppers anonymously on 0800 555 111.

News.title: Heartbroken family pay tribute to ‘much-loved’ mum found dead in house – as woman, 26, arrested in murder probe
News.content:
'DEEPLY MISSED' Heartbroken family pay tribute to ‘much-loved’ mum found dead in house – as woman, 26, arrested in murder probe







Next

A HEARTBROKEN family have paid a touching tribute to a woman who was found dead inside a property, as cops arrest a woman as part of a murder probe.

The woman has been named as Yvonne Kemp, with her loved ones saying she was “known for her caring heart, strength and kindness”.



Her body was discovered at a home in Crondall Street, Manchester, with police also arresting a 26-year-old woman on suspicion of murder.

The suspect has also been detained under the Mental Health Act.



Yvonne’s family said: “Yvonne was a much-loved mum, Nana, sister and auntie, known for her caring heart, strength and kindness.

“She was the kind of person who would do anything for anyone, always putting others before herself.

“She leaves behind a family who love her dearly and memories that will be cherished forever.

“Yvonne will be deeply missed and forever loved by all who knew her.“

Officers were called to a disturbance at an address in Moss Side shortly before 1.30pm on October 19.

Emergency services attended and sadly found the body of a woman.



Detective Chief Inspector Louise Edwards said at the time: “We understand an incident of this nature will cause concern however we would like to reassure the public that we believe this is an isolated incident and there is no wider threat to the community.

“We would ask that people stay away from the scene and we’d like to thank the local community for their patience whilst officers undertake their work.

“If you have any information in relation to this incident, please get in touch via the reporting function on our website, Live Chat or by calling 101 quoting log 1631 of 19.10.26.

“Alternatively you can speak to Crimestoppers anonymously on 0800 555 111.”

A spokesperson for Greater Manchester Police said previously: “We were called to a disturbance at an address on Crondall Street, Manchester shortly before 1.30pm on Monday 19 October 2026.



“Emergency services attended and sadly found the body of a woman.

“A 26-year-old woman has been arrested on suspicion of murder and currently remains in custody for questioning.

“A scene is in place as officers conduct their enquiries as part of this investigation.”

News.title: ‘Ultra-left’ activist known to French terror cops accused of torching 143-yr-old town hall in ‘apocalyptic’ France riots
News.content:
Next

AN accused “ultra-left militant” has been arrested for torching the historic 143-year-old spire during the “apocalyptic” French riots.

Hodei Ciarra Docampo, 34, was hauled into custody by special forces and faces up to 20 years behind bars for the devastating arson attack.



Flames engulfed the listed Limoges town hall during Saturday’s rampant disorder, causing the building’s clock tower to collapse.

Shocking footage showed the ornate spire crumbling under intense hear before toppling in front of the baying crowds.



Heavily armed officers from the elite RAID counter-terrorism unit launched a dawn raid on Ciarra Docampo’s home in Val d’Issoire, a town 30 miles north of Limoges.

“They arrested him just after dawn,” said a prosecuting source.

“He has a record for attacking police, and for belonging to ultra-Left extremist groups, and was on a watchlist for these reasons.”

The groups were not named, but they are believed to be environmental ones linked with radical protest.

Ciarra Docampo comes from a Basque background, and is known to have family in both France and northern Spain.

Limoges prosecutors have opened an investigation into “destruction of property by dangerous means committed by an organised group.”



The offence which is punishable with two decades in prison, and a fine equivalent to around £130,000.

Ciarra Docampo is the “principal suspect” for starting the fire, according to the same prosecutors.

One said it is “unlikely that he acted alone”, and he is now in the hands of France’s anti-terrorist prosecutor’s office.



Guillaume Guérin, the Mayor of Limoges, said a “full reconstruction” of the 19th Century architectural gem is now necessary.

The cost is expected to be in line with the millions which were spent on restoring Notre Dame Cathedral in Paris, following a fire in 2019.

Up to half-a-million people took to the streets of France over the weekend to protest against the cost of living, rising fuel prices and declining public services.

A total of 2400 were arrested for a variety of offences, and some 149 of them have since been convicted and sentenced to prison for violence or property damage, following fast-track trials.

The Interior Ministry has now imposed curfews in parts of major cities, including Paris and Marseille, in a bid to halt the unrest.



Sébastien Lecornu, France’s Prime Minister, said the curfews had given France “a night of calm” overnight Monday to Tuesday.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

He refused to rule out implementing an official state of emergency if the chaos continued, but said curfews seemed adequate for the time being.

Lecornu said: “I’m absolutely determined to restore public order.”

News.title: Labour will FINALLY approve North Sea gas field after months of dithering as energy costs soar
News.content:
Next

A GAS field in the North Sea will finally be given the go-ahead tomorrow after months of Labour dithering, The Sun understands.

Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh was tonight expected to approve the licence for the Jackdaw project early Wednesday morning.



Her eco-obsessed predecessor Ed Miliband sat on the decision and instead doubled down on a Net Zero drive.

Supporters of the Jackdaw gas field insist it will safeguard energy security, generate billions in taxes and protect industry jobs.



Located 150 miles east of Scotland, the Shell-owned project was fiercely opposed by climate activists who successfully halted its progression in the High Court.

Since coming to power, Andy Burnham has pledged to take a “pragmatic” approach to North Sea oil and gas extraction.

The price of gas in the UK has soared as a result of the Iran war, with the energy price cap increasing by 4 per cent this month.

Jackdaw’s owner has insisted it would produce up to 6 per cent of all gas output when fully fired up.

Mr Burnham has come under pressure from some Labour MPs and trade unions to approve Jackdaw to create more gas supply.

But he has also been pulled the other way by Net Zero-supporting backbenchers as well as Green Party figures.



The PM is also facing a decision on the Rosebank oil field which has similarly been hotly contested.

Mr Burnham has committed to honour Labour’s election manifesto ban on any new North Sea drilling licences being issued.

Both Jackdaw and Rosebank were already granted licences before the election in 2022 but were bogged down by legal rows.

News.title: Mum and baby dolphin tragically put down after getting stuck in mud amid seven-hour Devon rescue
News.content:
Next

A DESPERATE battle to save a mother dolphin and her baby ended in heartbreak after both animals were put to sleep following a major seven-hour rescue operation.

The two dolphins got stranded in thick mud in the River Plym near Saltram, Devon, as the tide went out.



A major emergency response involving HM Coastguard, firefighters and volunteer divers was launched.

The animals got trapped in a hard-to-reach spot at the bottom of a steep riverbank.



A specialist fire team was called in to reach the stranded animals and allow a vet to carry out an urgent medical examination.

The footage shows a rescue team arriving and assessing the situation before attempting a rescue.



Large floats are put down first to stop rescuers getting stuck in the mud themselves.

Then attempts are made to put sheets under the mum and baby in an effort to lift them to safety.



But despite the rescue effort, the operation ended in tragedy when the vet determined that the most humane course of action was to euthanise both the mother and her calf.

Both dolphins were showing signs of extreme stress, with serious concerns that neither would survive the journey by road required to return them to the open sea.

In August 2023, beachgoers were left distraught after a failed attempt to rescue a young bottlenose dolphin in St Ives Harbour, Cornwall.

The year before, a pod of dolphins rescued a Brit swimmer from a 6ft shark lining up a deadly attack.

Adam Walker claims the heroic creatures formed a protective circle around him to fend off the underwater beast in New Zealand.

News.title: Iranian & British man, 25 & 24, re-arrested for ‘assisting Iran’ in connection with RAF Fairford ‘bomb’ plot probe
News.content:
'TERROR' PROBE Iranian & British man, 25 & 24, re-arrested for ‘assisting Iran’ in connection with RAF Fairford ‘bomb’ plot probe







Next

TWO men have been re-arrested on suspicion of aiding Iran as part of the RAF Fairford bomb plot investigation.

The security scare last month saw armed cops swoop in on three vans nearby to the military base.



A 24-year-old UK national and 25-year-old dual UK/Iranian national have now been re-arrested on suspicion of assisting a foreign intelligence service.

The first man, 24, was initially arrested on September 27, the same day of the reported activity at the guarded base.



The 25-year-old was arrested just a few days later on October 1.

They were then, amongst seven others, released on bail and under investigation.



All five other men initially arrested currently remain on police bail.

Police said petrol was recovered from the vans, but no improvised explosive devices were found.



Head of National Counter Terrorism Policing in the UK, Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, said: “Since the events at RAF Fairford on Sunday 27 September, our specialist teams have been working tirelessly to interrogate the many lines of enquiry involved in this hugely complex investigation.

“So far seven men have been arrested in connection with our investigation.

“As a result of the ongoing efforts of our officers, earlier today two of those men were re-arrested for offences relating to Section 3 of the National Security Act – assisting a foreign intelligence service.

“This is very much a live investigation, and our evidence gathering continues, but at this time our position remains the same; we consider it highly likely that there is Iranian state involvement. Our investigators are continuing to examine what that level of involvement was and the ambition behind it.

“From the outset our priority has been to uphold the integrity of this investigation and hold those who wish to do our country harm, accountable.



“We know the public have unanswered questions. I want to be as transparent as possible and when we are in the position to share more, we will.”

This comes after Prime Minister Andy Burnham revealed it is “highly likely” the incident was coordinated by Iran, and directed by the regime’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.

Donald Trump also confirmed that every American bomber – including at least 10 B-1 bombers – deployed to Fairford had been returned home a week after the incident.

According to US media reports, the withdrawal appears to be in response to fresh or renewed security concerns about safety on the base.

The Gloucestershire base has been used by US bombers to carry out strikes against Iran.



Iran has previously denied involvement.

News.title: Female police cadet, 23, who ‘sexually assaulted teen boy’ hides behind mask & sunglasses as she faces 15 years in jail
News.content:
DISGRACED CADET Female police cadet, 23, who ‘sexually assaulted teen boy’ hides behind mask & sunglasses as she faces 15 years in jail







Next

A TRAINEE cop accused of sexually abusing a teenage boy hid behind a mask and dark sunglasses as she appeared in court.

Laura Beatrice Richardson, 23, faces up to 15 years behind bars if convicted of two counts of unlawful sexual intercourse with an underage youth.



Prosecutors allege Richardson, from Williamstown near Adelaide, had sex with a boy under 17 at least twice in June.

Under South Australian law, a person must be aged 17 or older to consent to sexual activity.



The cadet allegedly abused the teenager in one of Adelaide’s northern suburbs while she was studying at the Fort Largs Police Academy.

She has since been suspended from duty on full taxpayer-funded pay, according to The Adelaide Advertiser.



Richardson appeared at Adelaide Magistrates Court on Tuesday, where prosecutors asked a judge for more time before the case could proceed.

They said they needed 12 weeks to gather crucial evidence – including DNA reports and phone data – before the accused can enter a plea.

Prosecutors told the court: “Your Honour, there are some outstanding materials… some DNA reports, some further SAPOL affidavits, a review of the accused’s phone and some Yarrow Place report.”

Yarrow Place is a specialist sexual assault support centre based in North Adelaide.



Richardson was granted police bail following her arrest and was remanded on continuing bail after Tuesday’s hearing.

The trainee and her legal team refused to answer questions from waiting reporters as she left the court building.

She is yet to enter a plea, with the case set to return to court in January.



The case comes after a court was told how a twisted teacher contacted a student on social media and asked him: “Do you like what you see?”

Tayla Brailey, 32, pleaded guilty to sex abuse charges relating to two teens, one aged 16 and one 17, in March.

Australia‘s NSW District Court was told how she targeted her victims on social media before ordering them “not to tell anyone”.

“The offender instigated the chat … by asking ‘Do you like what you see? I see you liking my photos’, to which [the younger student] said ‘Yeah I do’,” the prosecutor told the court during a sentence hearing last month.

During a phone call, Brailey told the boy she was planning to take a shower and then sent him a photo of a reflection of herself in the shower.



She then asked that he also send her a sexually explicit picture, to which she replied: “Yum”.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Brailey later admitted to having sexual intercourse with a 17-year-old, sexually touching the teen, and using a carriage service to access child abuse material (CAM).

She has also admitted to sexually touching a 16-year-old and transmitting child abuse material to herself via a carriage service.

News.title: NHS doc who wrote kids’ book praising stoning unmasked as man behind ‘Palestine poppy’ bid to ‘hijack’ Remembrance Day
News.content:
SYMBOL OF 'HATE' NHS doc who wrote kids’ book praising stoning unmasked as man behind ‘Palestine poppy’ bid to ‘hijack’ Remembrance Day







Next

AN NHS worker has been unmasked as the designer of a controversial “Palestine poppy” which sparked fury from veterans.

Abdul Qader Ismail, 41, who works as a trainee paediatrician, is selling a pin showing a 12-sided poppy surrounded by the colours of the Palestinian flag.



It is sold for £1.78 on eBay, and he says the profits are being donated to organisations and charities “working to end the occupation” of Palestinian territories.

On his Linkedin, he posted an eBay link and wrote: “In commemoration of the thousands of innocent Palestinian men, women and children killed, and the millions displaced during the Gazan Genocide of 2023, we created the ‘Palestine Poppy’.



“Our intention was for this to be worn as a symbol of unity with the beleaguered, oppressed and occupied people of Palestine.

“Their suffering is decades old, from before the Nakba of 1948, and for too long have they been robbed of their victimhood.



“Our intention is for the Palestine Poppy to become an anti-apartheid symbol, similar to the raised fist, to be worn until the people of Palestine have their freedom.”

Dr Ismail, from Birmingham, also penned a series of books that cover subjects including stoning.

He wrote in one: “These punishments are meant to serve as a deterrent… and any excuse is found not to apply them.”

There are concerns the divisive poppy pin could divert donations away from supporting war veterans.



Army veteran Trevor Coult told LBC: “The Palestinian poppy is just another way to cause division in the run-up to Remembrance Day.

“You’ve got people out there that just want to cause division and cause hurt.

“There’s no money from this poppy sale that goes toward helping any veterans.”

Former Army officer Lt Col Stuart Crawford also said the badge was an attempt to “ride on the coat-tails of the familiar red poppy”.

“The so-called ‘Palestine Poppy’ is about as far away from remembrance as it’s possible to be. It is unashamedly political, designed to divide rather than unite.”



Dr Ismail allegedly suggested Israelis were a disease in a now-deleted Facebook post, The Telegraph reported.

In a deleted YouTube video, he also appeared to defend Hamas’s October 7 attack as “armed resistance” that was legal under international law, the newspaper claimed.

British-Pakistani Dr Ismail graduated from the University of Oxford with a degree in medicine in 2010, according to his CV.



He then completed a PhD at the University of Leicester.

The Spectator reported he is a member of the Green Party, which has repeatedly come under fire for antisemitism allegations.

The news outlet also reported that he sponsored the “Zionism is Racism” motion at the Greens’ party conference that has been condemned.

Labour threatened to collapse power sharing with the Greens after Zack Polanski’s party adopted the Zionism Is Racism motion.

Councils will be forced to terminate deals with the Greens if local councillors do not condemn the motion in writing within one week.



Andy Burnham said the policy “is wrong, it is antisemitic and this side of the House will have nothing to do with it”.

The PM said Labour “cannot support a partnership with a party that holds a position that has recently been adopted”.

The party confirmed this position would hold at a national and local level.



Labour party chair Bridget Phillipson said she expected to make Greens reject the position and call on Mr Polanski to reconsider the position.

She said: “We have asked local Green groups to respond as a matter of urgency. Where they are unable to provide that assurance, Labour will bring any such local arrangement to an end.

“This isn’t an issue of party politics; it’s about doing what is right and upholding the values anyone holding public office should share.”

The ultimatum given by Labour will give the Greens an opportunity to strongly rebuke the motion.

The Green Party is also facing an investigation from the equalities watchdog after it adopted its controversial policy.



Polanski ducked the vote after claiming he was tied up campaigning in the Holborn and St Pancras by-election.

Former Green leader Caroline Lucas blasted Mr Polanski for not voting on the motion.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Ms Lucas told BBC Newsnight: “I would have hoped he would have been a very strong critic of this motion. The motion was flawed from top to bottom — in my view it is dangerous, it is divisive.”

The Sun has approached Dr Ismail for comment.

News.title: Heartbreaking tribute to 'caring' grandmother 'murdered' in her Manchester home as cops issue update
News.content:
Heartbreaking tribute to 'caring' grandmother 'murdered' in her Manchester home as cops issue update

Yvonne Kemp has been named as the woman found dead at a property in Moss Side, Manchester, with her family paying tribute to the grandma "who was loved by all who knew her"

View 2 Images Yvonne Kemp (r) and her partner Tom Grant (Image: MEN)

A woman found dead at her home in Manchester sparking a murder investigation was a "much loved" grandma says her family.

Emergency services rushed to the Moss Side area following reports of a disturbance at a property on Crondall Street just before 1.30pm on Monday.

A 26-year-old woman has been arrested on suspicion of murder and has been detained under the Mental Health Act.

In a heartfelt tribute to Yvonne, her family said: “Yvonne was a much-loved mum, Nana, sister and auntie, known for her caring heart, strength and kindness.

“She was the kind of person who would do anything for anyone, always putting others before herself. She leaves behind a family who love her dearly and memories that will be cherished forever.

“Yvonne will be deeply missed and forever loved by all who knew her.“

View 2 Images A police cordon was put in place in Moss Side (Image: Jason Roberts /Manchester Evening News)

Along with the tribute, the family have shared a photo of Yvonne and her beloved partner, Tom Grant, reported the Manchester Evening News.

A statement from Greater Manchester Police read: "Officers were called to a disturbance at an address on Crondall Street, Manchester shortly before 1.30pm on Monday 19 October 2026.

"Emergency services attended and sadly found the body of a woman. A 26-year-old woman has been arrested on suspicion of murder and has been detained under the Mental Health Act."

Detective Chief Inspector Louise Edwards from GMP's Major Incident Team previously said: “We understand an incident of this nature will cause concern however we would like to reassure the public that we believe this is an isolated incident and there is no wider threat to the community.

“We would ask that people stay away from the scene and we’d like to thank the local community for their patience whilst officers undertake their work.

Article continues below

News.title: Ebola virus confirmed in new country as epidemic behind 4,600 deaths spreads
News.content:
Ebola virus confirmed in new country as epidemic behind 4,600 deaths spreads

The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has now led to confirmed cases in four other countries with the latest being Nigeria

View Image Ebola has been found in Nigeria (Image: Getty Images/Science Photo Library RF)

The Democratic Republic of the Congo's fast moving Ebola outbreak has now led to a confirmed case in a fifth country - as the death toll rises to more than 4,600.

‌



‌



Nigeria confirmed an Ebola case in its capital, Abuja, today (Tuesday) after a patient who arrived from Uganda tested positive for the virus, the country's Health Ministry said.

‌



The patient was admitted to a private hospital in Abuja before being diagnosed with Ebola. Health Minister Muhammad Pate said authorities had begun tracing 44 people identified as contacts of the patient.

‌



Authorities in the DRC have confirmed 9,552 cases, according to latest figures, with 4,602 patients dying.

Kenya has had nine cases with one death and Uganda 20 with two while one case has been identified in France. Uganda was later declared free of the virus.

Article continues below

Ebola symptoms include bleeding from ears, eyes, nose or mouth. According to the NHS other symptoms include being sick, diarrhoea and tummy pain, a skin rash, yellowing of the skin and eyes and muscle pain.

News.title: Robert F Kennedy's granddaughter Kyle dies aged 42 six years after spinal cord injury left her paralysed
News.content:
Robert F Kennedy's granddaughter Kyle dies aged 42 six years after spinal cord injury left her paralysed

Kyle Kennedy, the granddaughter or Robert and Ethel Kennedy, died at her home aged 42. Her death came years after suffering a spinal cord injury that left her with long-term paralysis, it is not confirmed the cause of her death

View 4 Images The mum-of-three died at her home in Massachusetts (Image: Kyle Kennedy/Facebook)

The granddaughter of Robert F Kennedy and Ethel Kennedy has died aged just 42.

‌



‌



Kyle Kennedy died on September 21 at her home in Westwood, Massachusetts. Her death was announced in an online obituary, but the cause has not been revealed. The mum-of-three left behind sons Conor, 12, and Declan, 10. Her daughter Josephine died just days after she was born.

‌



In 2020, Kyle suffered a severe spinal cord injury that left her with long-term paralysis and other medical challenges. Her obituary said: “The years that followed brought struggles but Kyle fought to maintain her dry wit and determination through it all, trying to be the best possible mother to her sons and caring for her two beloved, ill-behaved Wheaten terriers.”

‌



To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

View 4 Images Kyle leaves behind sons Conor, 12, and Declan, 10 (Image: Kyle Kennedy/Facebook)

RAF Eurofighter Typhoon suddenly declares mid-air emergency near Manchester READ MORE :

Kyle was one of Robert F Kennedy, known as Bobby, and Ethel’s 34 grandchildren and the daughter of Michael Kennedy. She was also the niece of Robert F Kennedy Jr and great-niece of assassinated former president John F Kennedy. Her mother, Victoria Denise Gifford, was the daughter of NFL legend Frank Gifford.

‌



Kyle was just 13 when her father Michael died after hitting a tree while skiing with relatives in 1997. Years later, she suffered the loss of her baby daughter Josephine, known as Josie, who was Conor’s twin sister. Her family said she carried her daughter’s memory with her throughout her life.

Before her spinal injury, Kyle was a keen runner who completed the Boston Marathon in 2019 in driving rain. She beat her father’s time by 20 minutes. It is not confirmed how she suffered the injury the following year, but described the struggles she faced afterwards while raising her sons.

‌



View 4 Images Kyle was the granddaughter of Robert F Kennedy, who was assassinated in 1968 (Image: Bettmann Archive)

She later used her experience to speak up for others living with disabilities, giving evidence at the Massachusetts state house during a hearing about discrimination in disabled healthcare. Much of Kyle’s working life was spent trying to improve education for young children, particularly those from disadvantaged backgrounds.

‌



She began teaching in New York City’s public schools through Teach for America, spending two years in classrooms before moving into education reform. She later worked with technology companies on school curricula and helped coach teachers working with younger pupils.

View 4 Images After her injury, Kyle advocated for people living with disabilities (Image: Getty Images for Robert F. Kennedy Human Rights)

Article continues below

The obituary paid tribute to her and read: “Blessed with a formidable intellect, dry wit, and beauty, she will be remembered for her devotion to her children Conor, Josephine, and Declan, and her support for educational reform for disadvantaged children and for people living with disabilities.”

Her funeral was held privately.

News.title: Celebrity Traitors' Michael Sheen gave away 'pretty much all' of his money
News.content:
Celebrity Traitors' Michael Sheen gave away 'pretty much all' of his money

Michael Sheen has said he gave away "pretty much all" of his money, describing himself as a not-for-profit actor after using personal funds to clear strangers' debt

View 3 Images Michael Sheen says he gave away "pretty much all" of his money (Image: BBC/Studio Lambert/Euan Cherry)

Michael Sheen has referred to himself as a not-for-profit actor after saying that he has given "pretty much all" of his money away. He explained that his approach to his wealth started when he was a teenager.

‌



‌



Michael, 57, has appeared in huge films such as The Twilight Saga and Far From The Madding Crowd, as well as big TV shows such as Good Omens.

‌



Using his pay cheques from all his credits, the star, who is now on Celebrity Traitors, has used £100,000 of his personal funds to clear the debt of strangers, and sold property to finance a homelessness project.

‌



Talking to Saga Magazine, Michael shared that he "didn't care" about money when he was 18. "I wasn't living in poverty, but I made do with what I had," he said. "As with many things in my life, I've gone away and then come back home, back to the point where I started."

View 3 Images Michael Sheen on Celebrity Traitors

To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

‌



He added that he feels "very lucky" to earn a lot of money, but "either on purpose of accidentally, I've ended up giving pretty much all of it away".

Michael said he wanted to make sure his family - daughters Lily Mo, 27, Lyra, six, Mabli, four, and partner Anna Lundberg - is alright, but still feels the same way about money that he did 38 years ago.

‌



Back in 2021, Michael called himself a "not-for-profit actor". Whilst talking to the Big Issue, he shared that he sold his own houses to bankroll the 2019 Homeless World Cup after funding for the project fell through.

He said that moment was a turning point for him because he realised that he could do those kinds of things and "it's not going to ruin me".

‌



View 3 Images Michael Sheen has sold some of his properties to fund homelessness properties

He said: "There was something quite liberating about going, all right, I’ll put large amounts of money into this or that, because I’ll be able to earn it back again. I’ve essentially turned myself into a social enterprise, a not-for-profit actor.”

‌



Michael has also set up the End High Cost Credit Alliance, which helps people find affordable ways of borrowing money, and pledged £50,000 over five years to fund a bursary that would help Welsh students go to Oxford University.

The star also shared that making The Passion in his hometown of Port Talbot in 2011 also helped him figure out what he really wanted to do with his money. "I got to know people and organisations within my hometown that I didn’t know existed.

‌



"Little groups who were trying to help young carers, who had just enough funding to make a tiny difference to a kid’s life by putting on one night a week where they could get out and go bowling or watch a film and just be a kid. I would come back to visit three or four months later, and find out that funding had gone and that organisation didn’t exist anymore.”

Michael is currently appearing on Celebrity Traitors where he is playing for a prize of £100,000 to be donated to a charity of the winner's choice.

News.title: Nigel Farage could miss out on dozens of seats due to anti-Reform tactical voting at next election
News.content:
Nigel Farage could miss out on dozens of seats due to anti-Reform tactical voting at next election

EXCLUSIVE: Survey commissioned by Electoral Calculus also found anti-Reform sentiment had grown over the last 12 months - as the right-wing party faces scandals on multiple fronts

View 2 Images The survey commissioned by Electoral Calculus found anti-Reform sentiment had grown over the last 12 months (Image: Getty Images)

Nigel Farage could miss out on dozens of seats across the country at the next general election due to anti-Reform tactical voting, according to new research.

‌



‌



The survey commissioned by Electoral Calculus also found anti-Reform sentiment had grown over the last 12 months - as the right-wing party faces scandals on multiple fronts.

‌



It found 50% of Labour supporters in areas facing a two-way battle between Tories and Reform would be willing to hold their nose to vote Conservative and keep Mr Farage's candidates out of power.

‌



This is an increase of 12% since 2025 when Electoral Calculus last asked voters their intentions.

Researchers also found almost all Green voters would lend their support to Labour to defeat Reform if their constituency was a two-horse fight. But fewer than half of Reform supporters would vote Tory in an attempt to inflict defeat on Labour.

Martin Baxter, CEO of Electoral Calculus, said: "As Labour under Burnham rebuilds its base, left-of-centre voters are surprisingly willing to lend their votes to whomever can stop Reform, even if that means Labour supporters voting Conservative.

‌



Close Nigel Farage ally appears to admit £5million Brexit comment slip up in undercover footage READ MORE :

View 2 Images Andy Burnham's Labour could gain dozens extra seats under anti-Reform tactical voting (Image: POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

"Anti-reform tactical voting has grown over the past year and could cost Reform dozens of seats because the right is divided."

‌



The findings are based on a survey of over 10,000 voters from pollsters Find Out Now and show Reform could secure 127 seats at the next election on 22% of the vote share.

But with tactical voting, the number of seats Reform could win may fall by 44 to just 83.

‌



Meanwhile Andy Burnham's Labour would win an extra 35 seats under tactical voting with 287 in total - but still short of the 326 seats needed to form a majority in the House of Commons.

The research also contains a warning for Mr Burnham, who promised at last month's Labour conference to fight the next general election on a pledge to change the UK's voting system.

‌



Before becoming Prime Minister he supported moves towards a proportional representation (PR) model.

But Electoral Calculus found PR would not benefit Labour under the current circumstances, with the party dropping to 23% in the polls to tie with Reform for the top spot.

‌



The research adds: "We see that Labour performs best under FPTP [first-past-the-post] with tactical voting at 27pc, keeping a lead over Reform on 22% and the Conservatives on 19%.

"Under this system, tactical voting pushes both the Liberal Democrats and the Greens below 10%, while Restore sits on 8%."

‌



Mr Baxter added: "Interestingly, the first-past-the-post system, plus tactical voting, helps left-of-centre parties much more than proportional representation, which could put Nigel Farage and Rupert Lowe into Downing Street."

Tyron Surmon, Head of Research of Find Out Now, said: "At the peak of Reform's polling last summer, there was deep concern that despite only having a third of the vote, this would be enough for them to get a majority in Parliament.

Article continues below

"While this reawakened interest in changing the electoral system, our polling shows that such proposals are a double-edged sword. Thanks to a right-wing split between Reform and the Conservatives, and anti-Reform tactical voting, it may actually be Labour who benefits most from our current system. And any move away from it could be to their peril."

News.title: RAF Eurofighter Typhoon suddenly declares mid-air emergency near Manchester
News.content:
RAF Eurofighter Typhoon suddenly declares mid-air emergency near Manchester

A Eurofighter 2000 belonging to the RAF has issued a 7700 emergency code while flying at 15,000ft near Manchester

View Image A Eurofighter jet has declared an emergency over the UK (stock image) (Image: AFP/Getty Images)

An RAF fighter jet has declared a mid-air emergency over the UK.

‌



‌



The Eurofighter Typhoon 2000 issued the 7700 code while flying at 15,000ft near Manchester, with the reason currently unclear. The Mirror has contacted the Ministry of Defence for a statement.

‌



The plane was flying from RAF Coningsby when it got into difficulty according to flight tracking data.

‌



When a plane transmits a 7700 code, it indicates there is a general emergency. The pilot puts the four-digits into a transponder which immediately alerts air traffic control that the aircraft is in distress and requires priority handling.

Content cannot be displayed without consent

The exact nature of the incident is unclear as it acts as a "catch-all" for any emergency situation that isn't a hijacking (code 7500) or radio failure (7600). Data from Flightradar24 shows that the plane landed back at RAF Coningsby at 4.02pm.

‌



The Eurofighter Typhoon is a multi-role, high-performance combat aircraft that was developed alongside Germany, Italy, and Spain.

The latest distress call, comes after NATO fighter jets were sent out to inspect a British Airways plane travelling to London after both pilots reportedly failed to respond to air traffic controllers.

‌



The incident took place after the captain and first officer of flight BA899 are said to have failed to respond to calls for about half an hour. The Airbus A321, from Pafos in Cyprus to London Heathrow, was flying over Germany at the time.

It was Eurofighter Typhoons that were sent out by the German military to inspect the cockpit and ensure there was no threat.

‌



Meanwhile, British fighter jets are to be sent to help shoot down Houthi drones and missiles fired into Saudi Arabia, Defence Secretary Wes Streeting has said, as the UK extends its military support for the kingdom.

RAF Typhoons will fly defensive missions to help protect Saudi cities and critical infrastructure from escalating strikes from the Iran-backed militant group.

‌



This will be limited to a defensive role rather than supporting Saudi strikes against the Houthis, and the jets will not operate in Yemeni airspace, according to the Ministry of Defence.

The UK will also send military advisers and an Atlas A400M military transport aircraft to help move equipment within Saudi Arabia. The move comes after mounting Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia have killed hundreds, with the capital’s King Khalid International Airport repeatedly targeted this month.

Article continues below

Mr Streeting said the UK was acting to protect civilians and bring an end to a conflict that is adding to cost pressures on British households. The UK was already providing defensive air-to-air refuelling for Saudi jets, which has now been extended for a further 90 days.

News.title: 'Everyone but Trump knows he's lost Iran war - he will keep gambling with lives as Putin blatantly betrays him'
News.content:
It is nearly impossible to imagine the US-Iran war not exploding again. And yet the most sensible thing to happen would be for the war to end in a peace deal.

The problem is that everybody but US President Donald Trump knows America has lost the war. Even if he did know it, he would not have the heart to admit it.

He will keep upping the stakes, gambling with the lives of others, threatening more war, until perhaps the power to do so is removed from him, because Iran will not allow him to stop.

To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

‌



View 6 Images Donald Trump will keep upping the stakes with Iran until the power to do so is removed from him (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Britain at risk of more terror attacks as US-Iran war set to explode again READ MORE :

Tehran has outplayed him at every turn, correctly gambling on Trump being drawn into their trap and withstanding billions of pounds worth of airstrikes. It seems Tehran’s appetite for shaking off deadly US airstrikes grows with every Trump outburst and military action as the regime sacrifices its own people.

Why would Trump think Iran was going to give up and surrender, given its willingness to slaughter tens of thousands just for demonstrating?

‌



View 6 Images Fearsome fighters: The Yemeni Houthis (Image: HOUTHI MILITARY MEDIA CENTER HANDOUT/EPA/Shutterstock)

Iran looks set to react and escalate if the US attacks, deploying proxy forces such as the increasingly potent Yemeni Houthis, the Shia pro-Tehran Iraqi militia, even the vastly depleted Hezbollah. The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps has strangleholded the Strait of Hormuz and is able to attack merchant shipping at will, whilst deploying the Houthis to choke the Bab al-Mandab Strait on the other side of the Yemeni peninsula.

View 6 Images Houthi fighter attacking Saudi backed forces in Jawf Province, Yemen (Image: HOUTHI MILITARY MEDIA CENTER HANDOUT/EPA/Shutterstock)

Every ridiculous lie from bungling Pete Hegseth - the cosplayer in-chief so called ‘Secretary of War’ - regarding US victory in the Middle East has been exposed. Lawmakers repeatedly asked him recently if his statement that Iran’s military had been destroyed was still true, given its ability to dominate the region and attack US bases.

‌



He was flustered as he argued Iran was now unable to attack the US with a nuclear weapon. Perhaps he has not yet noticed that his morally bankrupt boss Trump is cosying up to Vladimir Putin, whose intelligence leaks to Iran is risking the lives of US soldiers, who are under his charge.

View 6 Images Trump has been cosying up to Vladimir Putin (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

It is widely believed that Moscow has been sharing location intelligence of US bases with Iran and this has led to a number of bloody targetings of US military installations in places such as Jordan and Saudi Arabia. In March, Iranian missiles slammed into Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia, wounding twelve American troops and damaging an E-3 AWACS radar plane.

‌



Two days before the attack fourteen Russian spy satellites passed over the base. U.S. officials later concluded that Moscow’s information made the precision attack possible.

View 6 Images Russian President Vladimir Putin (Image: Mikhail Metzel/Pool Sputnik Krem)

Putin is barely even dealing behind Trump’s back - he is making it so obvious that he’s almost doing it right in front of his face as if to mock him. Trump is stretching the patience of the west with his crash and burn diplomacy that is daily stretching the geopolitical piano wire almost to breaking point.

It is difficult to know exactly where this is going. But everything Trump touches gets broken. So the tension across the Middle East and beyond is going to increase and whatever does happen, it is likely to involve Britain.

News.title: Pride of Britain boy 'learned to walk' thanks to Stephen Hendry
News.content:
Pride of Britain boy 'learned to walk' thanks to Stephen Hendry

Born with a rare neurological condition, Gregor was struggling to get back on his feet at the age of three and a half after he was laid low with a tummy bug. His mum Iona came up with the idea of watching his idol Stephen Hendry giving tips on how to play snooker.

Wee Scot who raised £75K steals the show at Pride of Britain

Pride of Britain winner Gregor Corse was inspired to walk again by his snooker idol Stephen Hendry....then took giant steps to raise £75,000 for charity.

‌



‌



Born with a rare neurological condition, the five-year-old marvel was struggling to get back on his feet at the age of three and a half, after he was laid low with a tummy bug. His mum Iona came up with the idea of encouraging her determined 'wee man' to put his best foot forward.

‌



And she found an unlikely path to recovery - Hendry's YouTube channel giving tips on how to play his favourite game. Little Gregor had only one thing on his mind when he collected his Child of Courage trophy. He wanted a game of snooker with the seven times world champion.

‌



View 3 Images Little Gregor Corse with the Prime Minister in Downing Street (Image: Jonathan Buckmasterr)

Strictly Come Dancing's Kai Widdrington shares Delta Goodrem update ahead of return READ MORE :

Gregor's proud mum Iona, 32, a florist on the Scottish island of Orkney, watched as her son first took on the house on foot. It convinced Gregor, who suffers from a rare neurological condition, that he could walk again - first inside their house from one room to another, and then outside.

Gregor decided he would do walks 'aroon the hoose' to help other children and started wearing uniforms - including a policeman's and a fireman's - before local businesses sponsored him to wear their logos. Hendry promised he would give him a game on Good Morning Britain as he presented their Young Fundraiser award.

‌



View 3 Images GMB Young Fundraiser winner Gregor Corse in the winners room with his mum Iona (Image: David Dyson / Daily Mirror)

He presented him not only with the coveted trophy, but with a new cue and said: "You do what you do, and you have no idea of the people watching it and the impact it might have. Gregor is an amazing little boy, what he has done is just totally incredible.

‌



"To have that mindset, it is great to see."

Speaking at the Daily Mirror Pride of Britain Awards in partnership with P&O Cruises Iona recalled her son dressing as a fireman and police officer and receiving a visit from the Lord Lieutenant as his charity walks captured the hearts of thousands of donors.

‌



View 3 Images GMB Young Fundraiser winner Gregor Corse in the winners room with Sam Thompson and Pete Wicks at the Daily Mirror Pride of Britain Awards (Image: David Dyson / Daily Mirror)

He has now raised more than £75,000 for good causes. She said: "I am so proud of him. His motto is: "I can do this'. One day he was sitting watching Stephen Hendry's snooker programme online. He said to me that he would love to walk like Stephen Hendry on Cue Tips. And then he let himself go and started to walk again. Every time he did a loop around the house, I would put a little ball on the snooker table for him. Right in the very beginning of the fundraising, he was wearing a kilt.

‌



"The second day he had a logo on his top, and then second day, there was a garage. So we got about 28 businesses that he liked, they were all garages and building companies. The police and fire brigades came and each building firm came along too, so in the end it just took off - we knew that we were really onto something."

Former ' I'm a Celebrity ' winner Sam Thompson donned a kilt, blazer and hat to match Gregor's outfit.....and Gregor loved it.

Article continues below

*Don’t miss The Daily Mirror Pride of Britain Awards on Thursday 22 October at 8pm on ITV1 and ITVX.

News.title: Two re-arrested on suspicion of assisting Iran intelligence after RAF Fairford incident
News.content:
Two men have been re-arrested after an incident near RAF Fairford last month, counter-terrorism police have said.

A 24-year-old UK national, and a 25-year-old dual UK-Iranian national, are being held on suspicion of assisting a foreign intelligence service under Section 3 of the National Security Act 2023, with police saying the investigation relates to Iran.

Police had been alerted to three suspicious vehicles near the US airbase in Gloucestershire in the early hours of 27 September - a major incident was subsequently declared and dozens of homes evacuated.

Seven men in total have been arrested as part of the counter-terror police investigation.

Gloucestershire Police said it had received a call about "three suspicious vehicles" travelling towards RAF Fairford at 00:45 BST on 27 September.

A bomb disposal team was deployed to the village to examine a number of vehicles.

Petrol was found in three vans near the airbase and five men were arrested.

They had been initially arrested on suspicion of committing offences under the Explosives Act and then further arrested on suspicion of preparation of a terrorist act.

Police later said they did not find "improvised explosive devices".

The re-arrests announced on Tuesday relate to a 24-year-old man who was initially arrested on 27 September near the base and a 25-year-old who was arrested on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts days later on 1 October in the borough of Westminster.

The other five men - who also include a 22-year-old British national arrested in Westminster on 6 October - remain on police bail.

The head of National Counter Terrorism Policing, Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor said: "This is very much a live investigation, and our evidence gathering continues, but at this time our position remains the same; we consider it highly likely that there is Iranian state involvement.

"Our investigators are continuing to examine what that level of involvement was and the ambition behind it."

The officer added that national security investigations can take time to progress due to their sensitive nature.

"Our specialist teams have been working tirelessly to interrogate the many lines of enquiry involved in this hugely complex investigation," he said.

Days after the incident, Prime Minister Andy Burnham told the BBC there were "strong indications" Iran had played a part in the incident.

He did not provide further details at the time.

Iran has previously denied any involvement.

RAF Fairford has been used as a forward operating location by the US Air Force (USAF) for decades.

In recent months, the US has flown B-1 and B-52 bombers from the base to the Middle East, after the UK approved a request for Fairford to be used for defensive strikes against Iran.

In the week after the incident, it emerged that the US had pulled its bombers out of the base and returned them to America.

US President Donald Trump said the aircraft were removed due to "some threats" to the base without giving specific details.

Vice-President JD Vance said it was done out of an "abundance of caution".

News.title: Government failings allowed Covid 'to spread like wildfire' in care homes, inquiry finds
News.content:
Government failures in care settings created an environment that allowed Covid to spread like wildfire, an official inquiry has said.

The sixth report from the Covid inquiry said the care sector appeared to be "something of an afterthought" in the early stages of the pandemic and there was no "protective ring" put around homes as claimed by ministers at the time.

There were more than 43,000 recorded deaths involving Covid in care homes between March 2020 and July 2022.

The 287-page report also highlighted shortages of PPE for carers and criticised the way hospital patients were discharged into care homes.

It said limits on visits caused enormous harm to residents and their loved ones, though it blamed this on care homes themselves.

Around 1.5 million adults were either living in care homes or receiving support in their own homes when Covid hit.

Action to protect them came too late, causing devastating consequences, the inquiry said.

Chair Baroness Hallet said a lack of testing, PPE and pre-pandemic planning combined with policy decisions early on "created an environment in which the virus could spread like wildfire".

"At the critical early stages of the pandemic, not enough was done to protect those living and working in care homes," she said.

"The overriding focus of the UK government and devolved administrations was on protecting hospitals."

News.title: Google resolves cloud outage affecting UK banks and websites
News.content:
Google Cloud says it has resolved disruption at its UK cloud site which caused an outage affecting UK banks, businesses and the courts.

The company, one of a few large cloud computing firms whose infrastructure and services underpin many online platforms, reported an "issue with multiple services" at its London data centre complex "europe-west2" early on Tuesday.

Revolut, Lloyds Bank and HSBC were among popular UK services that confirmed disruption on Tuesday morning, after thousands of reports of problems were raised by users online.

The tech giant apologised to those affected and thanked customers for their patience.

"We have resolved a disruption to Google Cloud services at a third-party facility in our europe-west2 cloud region due to a power event," a Google Cloud spokesperson said in a statement on Tuesday evening.

"Services have been restored."

They added that the company would publish an analysis of the incident on its service health dashboard, external, where it provides customers with updates about the status of its cloud services globally.

Cloud computing giants like Amazon Web Services (AWS), Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud make their services available to clients in local or regional sites around the world, which they call "regions", containing their data centres.

In updates to its service dashboard on Tuesday morning, Google Cloud had said a number of its cloud services were "experiencing elevated errors and intermittent network failures in europe-west2 region" - its UK cloud facility in London.

It later said that the issues had stemmed from a "power event" within one of its smaller data centre zones, europe-west2-b.

These seemingly affected a host of popular UK platforms and services, with customers flagging issues with sites including Royal Mail, DPD and e-bike service Forest.

The HM Courts and Tribunals Service also said it was aware of an issue affecting the video platform used for remote hearings.

News.title: BBC Three, BBC Scotland and Radio 4 Extra broadcast channels to close
News.content:
BBC Three, which is aimed at young audiences and launched hits such as Fleabag, Normal People and Gavin & Stacey, previously moved online in 2016, but was reinstated as a TV channel in 2022.

BBC Scotland launched as a channel in 2019, broadcasting a variety of Scottish programming including news, sport, documentaries and entertainment.

However, some of the shows that air on the two networks, such as Two Doors Down on BBC Scotland and Sort Your Life Out on BBC Three, are repeats of episodes originally broadcast on other more mainstream BBC channels.

Both networks currently only broadcast TV programming in the evenings, although BBC Scotland simulcasts BBC Radio Scotland during the rest of the day.

The BBC said that the network's nightly programme Reporting Scotland: News at Seven will not move to BBC iPlayer and will cease when the linear channel closes.

Audiences will continue to be served by BBC Scotland's wider news offering, including Reporting Scotland, The Sunday Show, Radio Scotland Breakfast, Debate Night and Scotcast, the corporation said.

While Radio 4 Extra does air some original programming, its schedule is predominantly made up of archive content, much of which is available on BBC Sounds.

Sir Peter Bazalgette, former chairman of ITV and production company Endemol, told BBC News: "This is a modest and pretty well-judged package.

"The essence of it is it protects the spending on content, it really cuts money in the distribution of programmes, and it really had to happen because the BBC has lost 30% of its revenue in 10 years."

But entertainment trade union Equity said Tuesday's announcement "does not signal a thriving BBC, and we are concerned about the UK's preeminent public service broadcaster's ability to meet its duties to the fullest".

Affected staff were told about the changes on Tuesday, although the proposed closure of BBC Scotland and BBC Three had been reported by some media outlets in recent weeks.

The BBC is aiming to cut between 1,800 and 2,000 jobs - almost one in 10 - in an attempt to save Â£500m over two years as it faces "significant financial pressures".

Around 550 job closures have already been announced in news, while more than 30 job cuts have so far been announced for BBC Sport.

The newly appointed director of BBC News, Rachel Jupp, announced on Tuesday that a further Â£5.5m of savings were being proposed, which would represent the closure of around 100 roles.

Meanwhile, several high-profile BBC TV series have been cancelled altogether in recent weeks.

RuPaul's Drag Race UK, Blankety Blank, Celebrity Mastermind, Live at the Apollo, Football Focus, Ski Sunday and Radio 4âs The World Tonight and You & Yours are among the programmes the BBC has dropped so far.

News.title: Harry says he wants to 'reconcile' with his family
News.content:
The Duke of Sussex has said he wants to repair his complicated relationships with his father and brother, in a magazine interview.

"Some people don't want it to work out. I want it to work out. With everything else that's going on in the world, the most important thing is to reconcile - that's the key point," Prince Harry told GQ in New York.

"Scars stick around forever. But what your perception is, and what your mindset is to those things that have happened, letting go of the past, that's something that I would encourage everybody to do," said Prince Harry.

Last week Prince Harry and Meghan carried out their first public engagement together since their return to the UK in the summer.

The GQ interview with Prince Harry was conducted last month and released as the Royal Family were on duty in Windsor welcoming the Sultan of Oman at the start of a state visit.

But a spokesman for the Sussexes said the interview was recorded in late September and it was the entirely the publishers' decision when to run it - and that nothing should be read into the timing.

The spokesman also said that the reference to "some people don't want it to work out" was not a swipe at his brother Prince William or any other member of his family.

Prince Harry and Meghan moved from the UK to the United States in 2020, stepping down as working royals in what was an acrimonious departure.

Harry's memoir, Spare, showed the depth of the family fall out and the damaged relationship with his brother William.

Despite Prince Harry now being physically nearer to his family in the UK, there hasn't seemed to be any more emotional closeness with his brother Prince William, and in this interview Harry seems to be open to reconciliation.

It was a message of wanting to build bridges that he had previously sent in a BBC interview in May 2025, when he had been living in the US.

Prince Harry recognised that this royal story of family disagreements fascinated the public, saying it was "massively relatable".

"Sibling disagreements, broken relationships between kids and their parents, kids and one parent - that continues to come up with me the whole time with people that I speak to," he said.

Asked by GQ about the reason for his move back to the UK, Prince Harry said: "Opportunities for the family. Being able to put the kids in a British school has meant a lot to me. I didn't know how important it was to me."

"They [Archie and Lilibet] are loving it, and it's just giving them a whole different experience."

He told the magazine: "To be back, closer to my family, and to be back on UK soil for longer than a few days or a week here or there".

News.title: Student who stabbed housemate 30 times admits murder
News.content:
A student who stabbed his housemate more than 30 times in a masked ambush has changed his murder plea to guilty.

Zack Coughlan, 23, attacked Jamie Collins, 21, in an alleyway near the garden of their home on 8 April and then left his body outside for eight hours before calling police.

A murder trial had been under way at Bristol Crown Court because Coughlan initially denied the charge, although he did admit killing Collins. He told jurors he stabbed Collins because he feared his housemate would kill him.

However, Coughlan, of Cleve Road, Filton, has now changed his plea to guilty and will be sentenced for murder on Wednesday.

Describing him as "a sensitive and caring young man", Collins' family said he had been "looking forward to finishing his journey" at the University of the West of England (UWE) and returning home to Swansea "in a matter of weeks".

"His passion for equality stood out to everyone who knew him. His unapologetic inclusivity will be his legacy for all of us. We know he was heading for a hugely successful future following his engineering and robotics degree," they added.

News.title: Huge setback for Alberta's separatist movement after decisive defeat
News.content:
It was a decisive result in a referendum that could have strained the bonds of national unity.

But preliminary results show that more than two-thirds of Alberta voters sent a clear message that they want to remain in Canada.

It's possible that once the final tally is counted, the rejection by a comfortable majority of voters to pursue separation through a binding referendum could halt Alberta's separatist sentiment in its tracks.

This would push the idea that had been discussed quietly for decades back into the political fringes.

For leaders of the Alberta separatist movement, while the result was expected given the polling, it was still disappointing after more than a year of campaigning and pushing for a vote on separation.

Asked by the BBC how he felt in one sentence after the results, separatist leader Mitch Sylvestre simply said: "Not happy".

News.title: Woman says she 'couldn't speak or breathe' during alleged rape by Russell Brand
News.content:
Warning - this report contains graphic content

A woman who says Russell Brand raped her at his home in London told police she "couldn't speak or breathe" during the alleged attack, a jury has heard.

The 51-year-old entertainer is accused of raping the woman in 2009 after meeting her at London's Hammersmith Apollo, where he had been performing as a stand-up comedian.

Brand faces seven charges in the trial in total - three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one of indecent assault.

The allegations, made by six female complainants, span a 10-year period between 1999 and 2009. He denies all the charges.

In video evidence of her speaking to a police officer, the woman said she performed a sex act on Brand at the London theatre after being invited for drinks following the show.

She said she gave him her phone number, explaining she was "a massive Russell Brand fan" and a "massive comedy fan" at the time.

After that night, she said Brand messaged her and she went to his house in Hampstead knowing they would have sex.

But she said a consensual encounter became rape when Brand started having anal sex with her and ignored her pleas for him to stop.

She said when she arrived at his home, Brand told her she needed to have a shower "because my hair smelled funny". He then asked her to brush her teeth.

"I was trying to make a joke of what he was making me do", she said. "All of those things made me feel, 'I don't like this'."

The woman said a short while after getting on his bed, she was turned over. It was then she said she was allegedly raped.

She told police: "From the very moment it happened, I felt I had willingly gone there and from what his reputation was, what did I expect?"

She said Brand "hurt me and harmed me, and when I asked him to stop, he didn't". She added: "The horror in anyone that I told was not enough to make me believe I didn't deserve it."

The woman said she told friends and family afterwards, and went through sexual health tests - believing that she had contracted a disease from Brand.

Earlier on Tuesday, another woman who claims Brand sexually assaulted her described the alleged attack as "frenzied" and "violent".

That complainant alleges Brand assaulted her at the Choice FM radio studios in central London in the mid-2000s.

She said she came out of a small room in the building to find Brand outside.

"He said 'aye aye'," she told the jury. "He grabbed me by my face, started to kiss me, and when he was kissing me he started pushing me - his body against me."

The woman continued: "He was kissing me, it was very frenzied. There was no time for me to even understand what was going on.

"He was running his hands over my body and I had my back against the wall at that point."

From behind a blue screen, the woman described the kiss as "sloppy" and "very, very rough", when asked by the prosecution barrister about the alleged attack.

"His hands at the same time were all over me," she said. "He touched my bum, my breasts, his body was pressed up against me."

The woman said she pushed him off and swore at him.

She said there were several people with him who she claims didn't say anything about what happened after the alleged assault.

The woman - now in her 50s - said she had never met Brand before and that she believed he'd been in the building because he was on Channel 4 show Big Brother's Big Mouth.

She told the jury: "His whole body was pressed against me - the kisses were hard and sloppy and going down my neck.

"His hands were moving so much - the reason I used the word frenzied was because it was violent. He just wasn't stopping."

She said she felt "dirty" after the encounter and "never told anybody", adding: "I felt shocked and stunned, shaken."

News.title: UK to deploy jets to defend Saudi Arabia from Houthi attacks
News.content:
The UK will deploy RAF Typhoon jets to defend Saudi Arabia in response to escalating Houthi missile and drone attacks, the government has said.

The defensive mission will help defend Saudi cities and infrastructure - a move authorised by Prime Minister Andy Burnham - against aerial attacks by the Iran-backed group.

It follows Houthi attacks on the Saudi capital Riyadh, as well as on energy sites on the country's coast.

"These aircraft will operate in a defensive role and will not conduct offensive strikes against the Houthis," Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said in a written statement on Tuesday.

News.title: Paddy Power cuts 1,400 jobs and blames betting tax rises
News.content:
Paddy Power-owner Flutter has announced plans to cut up to 1,400 jobs as its boss claimed the company "cannot fully absorb" tax rises imposed on the gambling industry.

Staff based in Leeds and Dublin, as well as workers for its UK and Ireland business at Flutter's Portugal and Romania sites, will be most affected, but what roles are at risk has not been disclosed.

The government announced taxes rises on online casino and sports betting, with an exemption for horse racing, in the Budget last year.

Flutter boss Kevin Harrington said the tax hikes had "fundamentally changed" the economic model of the UK betting and gaming industry, arguing it had helped "fuel the unlicensed, unregulated market".

"We continue to expect these tax increases to have a very significant impact on the overall market," Flutter Entertainment said on Tuesday.

Flutter, which also owns Sky Bet and Betfair, employs 28,500 people across the world, including 9,000 in the UK and Ireland.

As well as its Leeds and Dublin offices, the BBC understands the cuts could also affect staff based in London and Sunderland, as well as Malta and Gibraltar.

Harrington, who is chief executive of the betting giant's UK and Ireland business, said: "As we warned a year ago, we cannot fully absorb a rise of this magnitude without reducing our fixed cost base and therefore must restructure our business so that we can best position ourselves for the future."

A government spokesperson said the job cuts were a "commercial decision for Flutter, not the UK government".

"However, we understand this will be a difficult time for the workers," they added.

Flutter delisted from the London Stock Exchange in August in a blow to the UK, with its shares now solely traded in New York.

In its most recent results, the company reported a $299m (Â£224m) pre-tax loss for the three months to June for its entire business worldwide, compared to a $205m profit in the same period last year. Sales rose 3% to $4.3bn.

However, revenues in the UK and Ireland rose by 4% over the period, due to strong growth in online gambling games.

Some online gambling tax rises announced in last year's Budget took effect in April. This included remote gaming duty, which is paid on online casino betting, rising from 21% to 40%.

General betting duty, paid on the profits made from various forms of sports betting, was kept at 15% in betting shops, but is set to rise from 15% to 25% online in April next year.

Betting firms had warned that cost increases would lead to job losses and betting shop closures, but MPs dismissed the warnings as "scaremongering".

During the summer, Ladbrokes owner Entain announced job cuts, with news agency Reuters reporting 500 roles were being removed.

Punters' winnings from gambling are not taxed in the UK, nor is VAT charged on bets.

Flutter said its restructuring plan would cost between $80m and $90m.

The company has claimed in previous financial results that the impact of UK tax rises would hit its underlying profit by $320m this year and $540m in 2027, before any savings or restructure to mitigate the impact.

News.title: Jane Dodds standing down as Welsh Liberal Democrats leader
News.content:
Jane Dodds has announced she will stand down as leader of the Welsh Liberal Democrats.

Dodds said she would remain the party's only Member of the Senedd (MS), but that work to increase its presence in Wales' parliament "should be led by a new generation".

"Leading the Welsh Liberal Democrats has been the honour of my life," she said in a statement on Tuesday, adding "now is the right time" to hand over the role.

Only Welsh Lib Dem MP David Chadwick is eligible to seek nomination to replace Dodds at this stage, the party said.

The Liberal Democrats have been represented by just one member in Cardiff Bay since 2016, initially by former Welsh Lib Dem leader Kirsty Williams and later by Dodds since 2021.

Dodds, who represents Brycheiniog Tawe Nedd in the Senedd, is a former social worker who was made her party's Welsh leader in November 2017.

She made headlines last year by getting the previous Welsh Labour government to agree to a greyhound racing ban and Â£1 bus fares for under-21s in return for helping it pass its budget.

Relations between Dodds and the UK Liberal Democrat leader became strained after Sir Ed Davey called her leadership into question.

Sir Ed asked Dodds to reflect on her position in 2024 over her handling of a sexual abuse case when she worked for the Church in England.

A 2021 report found Dodds made a "grave error of judgement" by not organising a meeting to discuss a particular case of abuse by a late former bishop who sexually abused at least 18 victims over a 15-year period.

Dodds accepted there were "shortcomings", but said she would continue as leader.

After nearly two years of cool relations over the matter, Davey backed Dodds before May's Welsh Parliament election, describing her as an "excellent member of the Senedd" who deserved to be re-elected.

Nominations to replace Dodds will open on 23 October and close on 16 November.

"After May's election, I've thought hard about what our party needs," she said.

"Wales needs more than one liberal voice in the Senedd.

"Building that team will take years of hard work in communities across the country, and I believe that work should be led by a new generation.

"Now is the right time to hand it over."

Chadwick said Dodds had "given an enormous amount to the Welsh Liberal Democrats and to public life in Wales, and she deserves our sincere thanks for her service as leader".

"There will understandably be questions about what comes next.

"Today should be about Jane and her contribution to our party.

"I will make a statement about my own political future in the coming days."

Welsh Liberal Democrat president Tim Sly said Dodds had "led our party with warmth, determination and integrity through some of the most turbulent years in Welsh and UK politics".

"She leaves the Welsh Liberal Democrats stronger in our communities and ready to build," he said.

Chadwick requires the support of 50 party members to be the only candidate to replace Dodds and take over as leader.

Should that not happen, all members on the party's approved parliamentary candidates list could then throw their hats into the ring.

News.title: Royals roll out red carpet for visiting Sultan
News.content:
Tuesday evening will see Burnham's first state banquet since becoming prime minister. He will take one of the places of honour in St George's Hall, on a lavishly decorated table that can seat about 160 guests.

Burnham previously spoke to the Sultan in July, when they discussed efforts to open the Strait of Hormuz to shipping, and the prime minister said he was grateful for Oman's attempts at mediation.

The guest list does not include non-working royals, like the Duke and Duchess of Sussex.

An interview with Prince Harry with GQ was released as the state visit was getting under way.

He talked about his complicated relationship with his father and brother - recognising that it was something that was "massively relatable" for the public.

"Some people don't want it to work out," he said. "I want it to work out.

"With everything else that's going on in the world, the most important thing is to reconcile - that's the key point... scars stick around forever."

In the interview, which took place in New York, he said he would "encourage everybody" to let go of the past.

"If there's certain things from the past that are still affecting you every day, that's harder to let go of," he told GQ.

"But, for me, there's enough drama in the world and enough drama in people's lives to continue with issues with family."

News.title: Chancellor rejects calls to raise Capital Gains Tax in Budget
News.content:
Chancellor John Healey has dismissed calls from some Labour MPs to increase Capital Gains Tax (CGT).

Cabinet ministers Wes Streeting and Louise Haigh both previously voiced support for raising CGT before Andy Burnham became prime minister in July.

Ahead of next week's Budget, as first reported by the Times, external, Healey is minded not to increase CGT - which is imposed on the profit people make when they sell an asset that has increased in value, such as shares in a company or properties which are not primary residences.

The move followed warnings that it could end up costing the government money if wealthy people leave the country or defer selling off assets.

If you pay income tax at the basic rate then CGT is charged at 18%. For higher and additional rate income tax payers, the CGT rate is 24%.

Last year, HMRC estimated, external that lifting the lower rate of CGT by 1% could raise Â£5m by 2028-9 but increasing the higher rate of CGT by 10% would reduce the Treasury's receipts by Â£3.6bn in 2028-9.

The amount raised could be reduced if people adapt their behaviour to the tax rise, for example by moving abroad or deciding not to sell a property.

The chancellor gave an indication of his approach last month in a speech when he spoke about the importance of businesses and self-employed people making profits.

"I want to see this country as a country of wealth creation. I want our government decisions and policies to raise the levels of confidence, and investment, and profit in British business," Healey said.

Burnham has faced warnings against lifting CGT. His former adviser and Goldman Sachs Chief Economist Lord Jim O'Neill suggested it would send "the wrong message to business".

But influential Labour figures had pushed for equalising CGT and income tax, with the former generally attracting a lower tax rate.

News.title: Three children injured after school bus roof ripped off in crash
News.content:
Three children have been injured when a school bus crashed into a railway bridge, police have said.

Gwent Police said it received a report of a crash in Tregare Street, Newport, at about 07:45 BST on Tuesday.

The bus was travelling with pupils from St Julian's School, Heather Road, and Ysgol Gyfun Gwent Is Coed, a Welshâmedium secondary school on Duffryn Way.

Worried mum Jo Townsend's 13-year-old son, Gruff, was one of the pupils taken to hospital. She said: "I was worried, frantic. I went under the tape, I was getting to my son."

Newport Transport said it takes matters of safety "extremely seriously" and that it was establishing the full circumstances of the incident.

News.title: Watch: Pigs on the loose bring A-road to a standstill
News.content:
Motorists filmed the moment 20 pigs brought cars to a halt on an A-road.

The animals caused mayhem on the A127 at Dunton, near Basildon, as they darted in between cars on Sunday afternoon, leading to the road's closure.

Firearms officers from Essex Police decided to fatally shoot five of the pigs due to the perceived danger to road users, while the rest were safely captured.

A spokesman for the force said the decision "was not taken lightly" and that it was unknown where the animals came from.
