News.title: Care home residents were sacrificed to save NHS during Covid pandemic, damning inquiry report finds
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Care home residents were sacrificed at the expense of “protecting the NHS” and were treated as “something of an afterthought”, a damning inquiry report has found.

Baroness Heather Hallett, the retired Court of Appeal judge who chairs the Covid-19 inquiry, highlighted how government failures resulted in delays in protecting the care sector, allowing the virus to “spread like wildfire”.

The UK Covid-19 Inquiry heard there were more than 43,000 deaths involving the virus in care homes across the UK between March 2020 and July 2022, as ministers – including the then health secretary Matt Hancock – prioritised hospitals.

Baroness Hallett said that the high number of deaths in care homes in April 2020 brought the situation in care homes into “sharp focus”, but the shift in focus “came too late”.

open image in gallery People were prevented from visiting their loved ones in care homes in the pandemic ( Alamy/PA )

“It caused the UK government and devolved administrations to turn their attention to the adult social care sector, as their focus until then had very much been on the response of the healthcare system and ‘protecting the NHS’,” she wrote.

“Given that it was well known that people receiving care were particularly vulnerable to any respiratory disease, let alone a deadly respiratory virus like Covid-19, that shift in focus came too late. Protective measures should have been put in place at the start of a pandemic, not once it had already taken hold.”

During hearings in 2025, a civil servant described the toll as a “generational slaughter within care homes”.

The inquiry found: “The adult social care sector as a whole also appeared to be something of an afterthought, where the mantra of ‘protecting the NHS’ sometimes came at the expense of the users and providers of care.”

The major report also found that former health secretary Matt Hancock’s claim he had tried to throw a “protective ring” around care homes was unfounded, with Lady Hallett adding: “Quite the opposite was true.”

At a Downing Street press conference on 15 May 2020, Mr Hancock, who resigned from government in 2021 after admitting to breaking social distancing guidance by having an affair with a colleague, said: “Right from the start, we’ve tried to throw a protective ring around our care homes.”

open image in gallery The inquiry’s chairwoman Baroness Heather Hallett, said that the high number of deaths in care homes in April 2020 brought the situation in care homes into “sharp focus”, but the shift in focus “came too late” ( PA )

In the latest Covid-19 Inquiry report, published on Tuesday, it was found that his statement “does not accurately reflect the lack of action taken” to protect care homes at the outset of the pandemic.

Key findings from today’s report:

Preventing visits to care homes “caused incalculable harm to residents and their loved ones and often resulted in a significant decline in the health and wellbeing of residents”.

Matt Hancock’s claim that he had tried to throw a “protective ring” around care homes was unfounded and branded a “cruel lie” by bereaved families.

Shortages of personal protective equipment (PPE) for care workers led to some resorting to using festival waterproof ponchos, painters’ overalls, and gloves bought online, as well as homemade PPE from fabric, bin bags, bed linen and other household items.

Vulnerable care home residents were left with “insufficient protection” as patients were discharged from hospitals without knowing if they had the virus.

Do not attempt cardiopulmonary resuscitation (DNACPR) decisions “made during the pandemic based on a person’s age, disability or health conditions, or without a personalised assessment to consider the person’s wishes and feelings, caused considerable distress and confusion for the individual, their loved ones and staff”.

Support for the approximately 5.8 million unpaid carers across the UK “came too late” and the impact of the pandemic on them “was pronounced” as they faced having to give more complex care for longer hours “with less – if any – respite care”.

The inquiry found: “The UK government and devolved administrations knew, prior to the Covid-19 pandemic, of the extreme vulnerability of care home residents to respiratory viruses. Despite this, care homes received insufficient protection at the time they most needed it.”

open image in gallery The major report also found that former health secretary Matt Hancock’s claim he had tried to throw a ‘protective ring’ around care homes was unfounded ( Getty )

Mr Hancock told the inquiry that the phrase was “clearly a piece of rhetoric” and a “form of words rather than the substance”.

But the report said that while his statement “may well have been a piece of rhetoric”, his choice of words “did not reflect what was happening in care homes in the first weeks and months of the pandemic”.

“Much of the action to which Mr Hancock referred did not take place from the start,” it found. “For example, testing all people discharged from hospital into care homes only began in mid-April 2020 and the Infection Control Fund was introduced in mid-May 2020. The delivery of infection prevention and control training by the NHS also took place in May 2020.

“By the time Mr Hancock made this statement, thousands of people had died in care homes in England.”

Covid-19 Bereaved Families for Justice UK said that Mr Hancock’s claim was a “cruel lie”.

Speaking on behalf of the group, Jean Adamson said: “Today’s report is a devastating account of one of the darkest episodes in our country’s history.

“It shows that the government knew the care sector was extremely vulnerable to a pandemic and yet did nothing. Failing to act until it was too late.

“And it shows that Matt Hancock’s claim to have thrown a protective ring around care homes was a cruel lie.”

The inquiry found that vulnerable care home residents were left with “insufficient protection” as patients were discharged from hospitals without knowing if they had the virus.

open image in gallery The inquiry found that vulnerable care home residents were left with “insufficient protection” as patients were discharged from hospitals without knowing if they had the virus ( PA )

Lady Hallett said the pandemic had “a devastating impact” on carers and those they cared for, and efforts to protect these groups “came too late”, with failures as a direct consequence of “an absence of proper pandemic planning for the adult social care sector”.

The report said there was a “severe shortage” of PPE supplies for the adult social care sector, leaving workers in a “wholly unacceptable position” where they had to work in either poor-quality PPE or with no PPE at all.

The report said: “Some care workers reported using ‘festival waterproof ponchos’, painters’ overalls, and gloves purchased from Amazon, DIY shops and other retailers. Others fashioned home-made PPE from fabric, bin bags, bed linen and other household items.

“Some used laminated plastic to make face masks and elastic from leggings to tie them around their heads.”

Care homes were also described as “becoming prisons” for some amid visiting bans and many residents feeling “abandoned”.

Though visiting guidance during the pandemic did allow exceptions to be made for end-of-life visiting, many families were not permitted to be with their loved ones.

The latest Covid Inquiry report found that this resulted in a “significant decline” in the health and wellbeing of residents, causing “profound and enduring effects”.

“Preventing visits caused incalculable harm to residents and their loved ones and often resulted in a significant decline in the health and wellbeing of residents, especially those with complex cognitive conditions such as dementia,” it found.

open image in gallery Prime minister Andy Burnham said the government is “committed to learning the lessons” from the report and pledged to use the findings to develop an “action plan” in case of a future pandemic ( PA Wire )

“As some told the Inquiry’s listening exercise, Every Story Matters, the restrictions left residents feeling “isolated”, “abandoned” and “alone”.”

Prime minister Andy Burnham said the government is “committed to learning the lessons” from the report and pledged to use the findings to develop an “action plan” in case of a future pandemic.

News.title: Jackdaw gas field expected to be approved by ministers following months of speculation
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Ministers are expected to announce their long-awaited decision regarding a new gas drilling project off the Aberdeen coast on Wednesday.

Approval for the Jackdaw gas field is widely anticipated following months of speculation over its future.

It is one of two North Sea sites, alongside the Rosebank oil field, facing a ruling by the Labour Government after consent by the previous Conservative administration was halted by a legal challenge last year.

Donald Trump previously claimed the UK is "sitting on top of gold", urging Prime Minister Andy Burnham to permit more drilling in the basin, as he did to former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer.

Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said deciding on Rosebank, the largest untapped oil field in the North Sea, will take "a bit longer", suggesting a separate decision from Jackdaw.

open image in gallery Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh ( Maja Smiejkowska/PA )

This follows statements from Mr Burnham, who said the government will not back away from the issue.

Scottish Secretary Douglas Alexander said last week ministers are being "cautious" over public announcements to avoid the "mistakes" of the previous government.

Speaking on the BBC’s Radio Scotland Breakfast programme on Friday, Mr Alexander said: “Our predecessors, the Conservatives, made such a mess of the process of approval, both for Jackdaw and Rosebank, that they ended up in court.

“And that’s why we are cautious, careful, and often quite circumspect in what we say publicly about these decisions, because we don’t want to see further delay as a result of more court action.

“I’m careful in what I say publicly because we don’t want to make the same mistakes as our Conservative predecessors, which led to the whole programme being delayed as a consequence of judicial challenge.”

open image in gallery (PA Graphics) ( PA Graphics )

Mr Burnham said he would “take a pragmatic approach when it comes to the North Sea” since coming to power in the summer.

The outcome will be seen by environmentalists as a key test of Mr Burnham’s credibility on climate change.

He has faced pressure from environmental groups to “stick to the spirit of Labour’s manifesto commitment” and refuse consent for either of the schemes.

The 2024 manifesto committed to issuing no new oil and gas licences for the North Sea.

However, proponents of Jackdaw and Rosebank within the party have argued that neither are new fossil fuel fields, given the wheels were in motion to tap them ahead of Labour winning power.

News.title: Russell Brand jury shown photos of comedian’s home where woman claims he raped her
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Read our Privacy notice

One of Russell Brand’s accusers said a “culture of fear” prevented her from reporting the TV star for kissing and groping her in a radio station corridor, a court has heard.

Brand, now 51, is on trial accused of three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault, and one count of indecent assault. He denies all the charges.

The court heard that Brand allegedly attacked the woman at Choice FM in central London in the mid-2000s, when he was shooting to fame as a Big Brother presenter and TV star.

The woman, who worked at the radio station, broke down in tears on Tuesday as she insisted to Southwark Crown Court that she had no ulterior motive to lie about the incident.

“There was a culture of fear,” she said, recalling the atmosphere at the time as “people-pleasing”.

“Russell Brand was an A-lister star, it was Big Brother, people were watching it, we all watched it.”

open image in gallery Brand denies three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault, and one count of indecent assault ( Reuters )

Questioned by Brand’s barrister Ian Winter KC why she had not reported the incident and suggesting she had a professional “obligation”, the woman hit out at workplace “banter” at the time.

She said: “Women were rated by colleagues on what we were wearing, how we looked.

“It wasn’t an environment where management were coming to talk to us about workplace behaviour, that didn’t exist.”

Talking about what may have happened had she raised the alleged assault with her line manager, she told jurors: “I think they probably would have said something along the lines of: ‘Oh, you’re lucky.’”

The woman said she had been “triggered” to come forward to police after seeing a 2023 Dispatches documentary on sexual misconduct allegations about Brand.

open image in gallery Russell Brand appearing in the dock at Southwark Crown Court ( PA )

“I had buried it so deep for so long,” she told the court.

The woman has told jurors she was pinned against a wall by Brand in a corridor, before being groped and kissed “hard” while three men and a woman looked on without intervening.

She broke down in tears in witness box as she insisted: “I don’t gain a single thing” by reporting the incident and giving evidence.

“This was a situation that I don’t need to be in, I don’t gain a single thing by saying Russell Brand did that to me,” she said.

She told the court part of her motive for coming forward was seeing a video of Brand addressing the allegations against him from Dispatches and saying that his past sexual encounters were all consensual.

The woman said: “I was shocked, I was disgusted that he said it was consensual, that really upset me, it triggered in me that anger.”

She also told the court that she struggled to understand why the men and woman who witnessed the incident “didn’t do anything to stop him”.

open image in gallery Brand, now 51, is accused of a ‘violent’ attack on the woman at Choice FM in central London in the mid-2000s, when he was shooting to fame as a Big Brother presenter and TV star ( PA )

The woman added: “I wonder if I was alone with him what would have happened.

“There is a man who is mauling me in front of people.”

She told jurors that she “locked eyes” with the other woman and was “pleading with her” to stop it.

At the end of his cross-examination, Mr Winter suggested that the woman had not known it was Brand at the time, but her allegation “became Brand after Dispatches”.

The woman replied: “No, it didn’t. Definitely not.”

The trial continues.

News.title: Woman who accused Cornell students of rape says president's response made her feel 'disbelieved'
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The woman who has accused seven students of raping her at a Cornell University fraternity house has weighed in on a looming faculty vote of no confidence in the school’s leadership, saying the university’s president questioned why she waited to report being assaulted — an alleged remark she said left her feeling “unsupported and disbelieved.”

Her case has prompted student protests, renewed scrutiny of the university’s disciplinary system and a state investigation into the alleged assault.

In an Oct. 14 letter to faculty leaders obtained by The Associated Press on Tuesday, the woman, identified in court documents as Jane Doe, described a conversation she said took place shortly after she reported the alleged assault in November 2024. According to her secondhand account, the president of her sorority told her that Cornell President Michael Kotlikoff had questioned Jane Doe's delay in reporting the alleged assault, which the sorority leader interpreted as casting doubt on her story.

“President Kotlikoff’s initial response was along the lines of, ‘Why did she wait so long to report it?’” Jane Doe wrote in the letter. She said that conversation made her less confident that the administration could handle her experience with the sensitivity and fairness she had expected.

Kotlikoff did not immediately respond Tuesday to an email inquiry about Jane Doe's letter.

The letter, transmitted through her attorney, comes as Cornell faculty consider a resolution declaring no confidence in the university administration’s ability to address what faculty members have described as an “ongoing crisis” of sexual assault on campus.

The resolution was introduced after revelations about Cornell’s handling of Jane Doe’s allegations that she was raped at the Chi Phi fraternity house in October 2024.

Faculty members began debating the resolution at a meeting last Wednesday, where Kotlikoff faced pointed questions about the university’s response to sexual assault allegations and its oversight of fraternities. The faculty's Senate is expected to resume debate on Oct. 28 before holding an electronic vote.

In her letter, Jane Doe said she wanted faculty members to have information that might be relevant to their deliberations. She emphasized that she was not trying to tell them how to vote.

“My intention is not to prescribe how the Senate should interpret this account, but rather to provide information that its members may wish to consider or investigate further,” she wrote.

Messages seeking comment were left for Jane Doe’s lawyers, Thomas Giuffra and W. Whitney Seals.

News.title: NYC student dies after being drugged and raped in her dorm room, feds say
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The latest headlines from our reporters across the US sent straight to your inbox each weekday Your briefing on the latest headlines from across the US Your briefing on the latest headlines from across the US Email * SIGN UP I would like to be emailed about offers, events and updates from The Independent. Read our Privacy notice

A college student in New York City died after being drugged and raped in her dorm room by two alleged drug dealers accused of lying to her about which drug she was ingesting — and then committing sex assault while she was unconscious, federal authorities said Tuesday.

On the heels of newly revealed gang rape allegations against fraternity brothers that have plagued Cornell University in Ithaca, New York, federal prosecutors downstate announced a new indictment against Moises Freire, a 19-year-old from the Bronx, and Brian Peralta Cabrera, an 18-year-old from Queens, for allegedly conspiring to distribute fentanyl that ultimately led to the fatal poisoning of a student at the Fashion Institute of Technology and the near-death of her friend in March.

Freire has also been accused of raping the woman who died while she was unconscious from the fentanyl. Neither Freire nor Peralta Cabrera were FIT students, according to the school.

“Two young college students, with their entire futures ahead of them, were allegedly deceived into taking fentanyl disguised as cocaine, leaving one dead and the other fighting for her life,” DEA New York Task Force Division Special Agent in Charge Christopher Roberts said in a statement.

“Even more horrifying is the allegation that one of these young women was sexually assaulted while unconscious and defenseless. College should be a place where young people can learn, grow, and pursue their dreams, not a place where predators exploit their vulnerability.”

open image in gallery A college student in New York City died after being drugged and raped in her dorm room. Now, two men face federal charges and could get life in prison if convicted. ( Getty )

Freire allegedly told Peralta Cabrera that he wanted to give drugs to the two college girls that would “last the entire night,” and that if Peralta Cabrera could provide drugs that were strong enough to make the woman addicted, according to federal prosecutors. He allegedly described the scenario as a “win-win situation.”

Peralta Cabrera allegedly provided fentanyl to Freire, and then, on March 18, Freire brought the drugs to the residence hall in Manhattan where the women were living, prosecutors said.

Despite previously calling the fentanyl “fake” and “poison,” Freire allegedly told the women that the drug was “pure cocaine” and did not contain fentanyl, according to prosecutors.

Freire allegedly encouraged the women to take the drug, and when they did, they lost consciousness almost immediately. While the women were passed out, Freire raped one of them and then waited about 45 minutes to get help, prosecutors said.

During those 45 minutes, Freire allegedly sent photos of the women to others. When he eventually went to campus security, he initially lied, saying that the women had too much alcohol, according to prosecutors.

Both women were taken to the hospital, but only one made it home. The woman who was allegedly raped remained in critical condition, while her friend regained consciousness. Prosecutors said the first woman died from complications of acute fentanyl intoxication.

Freire’s lawyer, Mitchell Schwartz, said in an April hearing that his client and the woman who died had a “sexual relationship” for more than a year and that Freire wasn’t trying to deceive the college girls, The New York Times reported. Freire “was repeatedly asked by the decedent to acquire drugs for her” over social media and text messages, Schwartz said.

The Independent has reached out to Schwartz for comment.

open image in gallery Moises Freire and Brian Peralta Cabrera have been accused of conspiring to distribute fentanyl that ultimately led to the fatal poisoning of a student at the Fashion Institute of Technology and the near-death of her friend in March. Freire also allegedly raped the woman who died while she was unconscious from the fentanyl. ( AFP/Getty )

Freire and Peralta Cabrera were first arrested in March and later pleaded not guilty to initial charges that did not include the rape allegation, according to the Associated Press. There was also a third defendant, Harry Rosales Pino, who pleaded guilty in September to conspiracy to distribute narcotics resulting in death and serious bodily injury, per the AP. Rosales Pino will be sentenced in December.

In the superseding indictment, Freire and Peralta Cabrera were charged with one count of conspiracy to distribute a controlled substance resulting in death and serious bodily injury. If convicted, they face a minimum sentence of 20 years in prison and a maximum sentence of life in prison.

Freire is also charged with distribution of a controlled substance resulting in death and serious bodily injury and distribution of a controlled substance with the intent to commit rape. The first distribution charge carries the same potential sentencing as the conspiracy charge. The rape-related charge carries a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison.

After prosecutors announced the new charges Thursday, FIT President Jason Schupbach said in a statement, “Tragically, one of our students lost their life...in what was determined to be a fentanyl overdose. The following week, our community held a celebration of life that was a beautiful tribute to the student and their family and friends. I am grateful for how our community came together to support them.”

“We are also grateful for the swift action of our residential life team and campus public safety, whose actions led to immediate medical response for the victims and the detention of the suspect.”

For those affected by rape and sexual abuse, if you are in the United States, you can call Rainn on 800-656-HOPE (4673).

Rape Crisis also offers support. You can call them on 0808 802 9999 in England and Wales, 0808 801 0302 in Scotland, and 0800 0246 991 in Northern Ireland, or visit their website at www.rapecrisis.org.uk.

News.title: Draft law dealing with legacy of Northern Ireland Troubles passed by House of Commons
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Draft legislation addressing the legacy of the Northern Ireland Troubles has cleared the House of Commons.

Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Chris Bryant insisted that veterans and bereaved families "deserve answers".

MPs backed the Northern Ireland Troubles Bill at its third reading on Tuesday by 330 votes to 178, a majority of 152. It will now go to the House of Lords for further scrutiny.

First brought to Parliament last year, the measure will overhaul the previous Conservative government’s Legacy Act via a reformed Legacy Commission.

An emotional Sir Chris told the Commons on Tuesday evening: "This Bill isn’t about one group or another. It’s not about special favours for one group or another.

"It’s about honesty, candour, the pursuit of justice, and most importantly, truth. Because in the end, it’s only truth that can really set us free."

More to follow...

News.title: Illegal fishermen face new threat from above as satellites are used to intercept trawlers
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

A patrol boat off the coast of Gabon intercepted three trawlers in July 2026, inside the Grand Sud Reserve. This is one of west and central Africa’s largest marine reserves, where industrial trawling is banned.

None of the trawlers held a valid licence. The patrol found them because analysts at the non-profit Global Fishing Watch had studied satellite data and worked out where to look.

Most illegal fishing is not caught at all. In 2024, researchers at Global Fishing Watch found that between 72% and 76% of the world’s industrial fishing vessels never appear in public tracking. Most of that activity is concentrated around south and south-east Asia and Africa.

Africa has about 30,500km of coastline shared among 38 coastal states, and illegal fishing costs African economies an estimated US$11 billion to US$13 billion a year.

The reason illegal fishing continues is not complicated. Public tracking depends on vessels reporting their own positions through the automatic identification system, a transponder designed to stop ships colliding. A crew that does not want to be seen switches it off.

open image in gallery A vessel that has been seen, identified and reported still has to be intercepted, boarded, charged and tried ( AFP via Getty Images )

But African governments are still leaning on the system of self-reporting. In June 2026, at the Our Ocean Conference in Mombasa, 15 governments signed a declaration promising to open up information about who owns fishing vessels and where they operate. Seven were African, Somalia among them.

There is another way to track illegal fishing, however: from satellites that look for vessels directly.

I am a PhD candidate in aerospace engineering at the University of Florida, where I design spacecraft systems and the software that coordinates them. My supervisor, Norman Fitz-Coy, and I designed a tracking system for the Somali Basin, the stretch of the western Indian Ocean off the Horn of Africa between Somalia and Kenya. It is one of the richest tuna grounds in the world and among the least patrolled.

We concluded that the watching is the easy part. A system that could keep these waters under near-constant observation is affordable and can be built with technology that exists today. But it has to be designed for the Equator instead of borrowed from designs built for other latitudes. Also, even a perfect version runs into a limit that has nothing to do with satellites.

That limit is enforcement. A satellite can show you a vessel. It cannot board one, and it cannot bring a case to court. Overcoming that takes the things no spacecraft supplies: neighbouring states willing to share the cost and the patrols, and the political will to act on what they are shown.

Key design elements

Orbit

Almost every Earth observation satellite flies an orbit that passes close to the poles and crosses the Equator at the same local time each day. It spends much of each circuit above the Arctic, the Antarctic, and the near-empty latitudes between. For a country sitting on the Equator, such as Kenya, Somalia or Gabon, most of those laps are wasted.

We modelled a shell of 24 satellites tilted at just 20 degrees to the Equator. Over the Somali Basin it returns roughly every 1.1 hours, against 3.4 hours for the same 24 satellites flown over the poles. Put plainly, satellites hugging the Equator see the basin about three times more often. Commercial radar operators have begun flying tilted orbits at 40 and 45 degrees for this reason, but none fly low enough to concentrate on these waters.

Sensors

Finding a boat and identifying it are two different jobs. Radar picks out a vessel as a bright dot across a wide strip of ocean. Telling whether that dot is a licensed trawler or a 7 metre skiff needs an image sharp enough to resolve detail well under a metre, and no single sensor does both. A wide sensor finds candidates and a sharp one is pointed at them afterwards, so the system must decide in orbit, within seconds, which dots deserve a second look.

Power and data

Radar is power hungry. A 100kg radar satellite carries enough stored energy to image for about 4.5 minutes per orbit and spends the remaining 90 or so minutes charging. Those few minutes still generate roughly 690GB a day, while the ground stations serving the region can pull down between 120GB and 360GB. There are not many of them. The main ones are the Italian-run Broglio Space Centre at Malindi on the Kenyan coast, and the South African National Space Agency’s antennas at Hartebeesthoek, some 4,000km to the south.

So, the satellite must sort its own pictures before sending them, keeping what might be a vessel and discarding the rest. That changes what it has to be. Not a camera shipping pictures home for people to examine, but something that recognises a boat by itself, in orbit, with nobody watching.

Cost

The system we costed has all of those constraints designed into it, the tilted orbit, the two kinds of sensor, the onboard sorting and the thin downlink. It comes to about US$347 million over five years, or roughly US$25 for every confirmed detection. Against US$11 billion in annual losses from illegal fishing, cost is not the obstacle.

The harder part is getting it used

A constellation is only worth building if governments act on what it shows, and some countries have already shown what that commitment looks like using the self-reporting data they have now. Indonesia, Peru, Chile, and Costa Rica publish their national vessel tracking data, turning an enforcement feed that was private into something anyone can check. East Africa has its own version.

About the author Wanjiku Chebet Kanjumba is a Ph.D. Candidate in Aerospace Engineering at the University of Florida. This article was first published by The Conversation and is republished under a Creative Commons licence. Read the original article .

FISH-i Africa, a task force of eight western Indian Ocean states including Somalia and Kenya, has since 2012 pooled intelligence on suspect vessels across borders. It has worked over 35 investigations, caught vessels sailing under forged licences and false identities, and had illegal operators fined and brought to court, largely by sharing information its members already held.

So, what would it take for African governments to buy into a constellation? Mostly, not paying for it alone. The US$347 million works out at about US$69 million a year. Split eight ways across the FISH-i Africa states, that is roughly US$9 million a country per year for continuous coverage of waters they already share. The expensive way to buy this capability is one nation at a time.

What needs to happen next

Our study set out six strategies for using space and airborne systems to support African maritime security. Five are ordinary engineering, covering the constellation itself, fusing radar with other sensors, the ground computing to handle what comes down, smaller and better sensors, and aircraft or drones to fill the gaps between satellite passes.

We rejected the sixth ourselves. It was a concept for microsatellites carrying high-powered lasers to disable a pirate vessel’s engine or communications from orbit, and it failed on the physics before anyone reached the legal objections.

The finding that surprised us most was where the system finally breaks. It is not the cameras. It is the courts. A vessel that has been seen, identified and reported still has to be intercepted, boarded, charged and tried. Where that does not happen, the detection produces a cost and no security.

In Gabon, the patrol was only half the story. The trawlers’ owner later settled with the authorities, and getting there took inspectors, prosecutors, courts and the legal authority to board a foreign vessel. Those are people, institutions, and laws.

Africa can build the eyes. The orbit is understood, the sensors exist and the price is modest next to the losses. The Mombasa declaration is a reasonable place to begin, but it rests on a system three quarters of the fleet has already stepped outside. Seeing the outsiders is an engineering problem with an answer. What happens next is the harder one.

News.title: Boeing 737 Max 10 to finally be approved for US flights after years of safety concerns
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Following years of regulatory delays, the U.S. government is expected to declare on Tuesday that Boeing’s 737 Max 10 airliner has received approval for commercial passenger flights, according to a Transportation Department official.

The official, speaking on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly ahead of the announcement, stated that Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy is scheduled to share the decision Tuesday afternoon during a visit to Boeing's plant in Everett, Washington.

First unveiled at the Paris air show in 2017 to challenge competitor Airbus, the 737 Max 10 can accommodate up to 230 passengers.

However, a series of technical and safety-related issues repeatedly stalled certification for this largest variant of Boeing's bestselling single-aisle family.

The manufacturer has stated it anticipates delivering its initial aircraft in 2027.

Securing approval for the Max 10 completes Boeing’s four-aircraft 737 Max lineup, marking a crucial step in the manufacturer's effort to stabilize its financial position and restore public confidence following years of quality, safety, and production challenges.

Regulatory clearance for the smaller Max 7 variant was granted by the FAA in August.

Boeing 737 Max 10 ( Copyright 2023 The Associated Press. All rights reserved. )

Boeing’s operational crisis has been particularly severe since two fatal crashes involving the smaller Max 8 killed 346 people in 2018 and 2019 off the coast of Indonesia and in Ethiopia.

Concerns over safety and manufacturing protocols were renewed in 2024 when a door panel blew off an Alaska Airlines Max 9 in midair.

Designed as a direct competitor to Airbus's A321neo model family, which entered commercial service in 2017, the Max 10 faces stiff competition; the largest A321neo variants carry more passengers and fly farther without refueling than Boeing's offering.

Still, Boeing designed the single-aisle jet to carry increased passenger loads while consuming less fuel than older models — an advantageous combination for commercial airlines navigating soaring jet fuel costs amid the U.S. war with Iran.

Those rising expenses have placed added pressure on carriers to control operating costs.

In the wake of the fatal Max 8 crashes, the Federal Aviation Administration overhauled how it oversees Boeing.

Over the past 18 months, the agency has gradually eased some restrictions, raising production limits and allowing Boeing in July to resume certifying all of its 737 Max and 787 planes.

In a more recent incident, a FlyDubai 737 Max 8 survived a severe dive that subjected the airframe to forces far beyond its original design limits.

Officials indicated the copilot attempted to hijack and crash the jet, though the plane ultimately landed safely in Saudi Arabia.

Speaking at an investor conference last month, Boeing CEO Kelly Ortberg stated that the Max 10 represents roughly 30% of the company's total 737 backlog.

Boeing's website currently lists its overall 737 backlog at approximately 4,500 aircraft.

The Everett plant offers Boeing added flexibility because the Max 10 is longer than other 737 Max variants.

Ortberg noted the aircraft could not fit nose-to-tail on the Renton, Washington line where Boeing builds the 737, but can be accommodated in Everett, enabling a greater mix of longer planes as output increases.

Major customers for the Max 10 include United Airlines, Delta Air Lines, American Airlines, and Ryanair.

Alaska Airlines joined that group in January, placing an order for 105 Max 10s alongside options for 35 additional aircraft.

News.title: England give lesson on how not to approach a run chase
News.content:
Brendon McCullum wants his team to learn how to adapt as they prepare for the World Cup and this was a lesson in how not to master a run chase.

Failing to overhaul 302 is not an embarrassment, but the way England threw away a good start with some brittle batting gives McCullum plenty to ponder.

Spin exposed familiar failings as left-armer Arafat Minhas added six for 40 to his 59 from 58 with the bat, but it was also short balls from the seamers that hurt England. A two-paced pitch made the back-of-a-length delivery tricky, as it had in the match between Sri Lanka and Pakistan on the same ground at the weekend, but England failed to find a way to adjust their tempo.

Ben Duckett, Joe Root and Sam Curran were all dismissed by seamers hitting the pitch hard and forcing them to play square while Arafat exposed limitations against spin. He bowled Harry Brook for five with a beauty that dipped and straightened as he mixed up his arm ball with consistent accuracy to deadly effect.

News.title: Fried chicken and sugary drinks: Tanzania battles a growing obesity problem
News.content:
In early 2025, Said Shukuru, 31, was experiencing life-threatening health concerns. He weighed 150 kg (over 20 stone); his body mass index (BMI) was over 40 and he had a blood pressure of 190/100.

“It was very serious,” says Shukuru. In April last year, he underwent a successful mini gastric bypass operation at the Aga Khan Specialised Polyclinic in Masaki, Dar Es Salaam. His weight has since halved.

Shukuru’s case may be extreme, but his story serves as a warning. Overweight and obesity levels are increasing fast across East Africa, and particularly in Tanzania. Unless the government responds properly, the country faces a looming public health crisis.

Overweight and obesity in Tanzania have grown over the past 40 years because of economic development and liberalisation, urbanisation and increasingly sedentary lifestyles. Traditional diets, based on whole foods, are being replaced by refined and processed products. To make matters worse, chicken and chips, known as kuku chips, and sugary drinks are everywhere.

“When you live in an urban area like Dar (Es Salaam),” says Shukuru, “junk food is cheaper than groceries.”

The origins of these developments lie in Tanzania’s economic history. During the colonial period, fruits and legumes were exported while high-energy, starchy foods like maize were produced for domestic consumption, says Joyce Kinabo, professor of nutrition at Sokoine University.

“Food security was considered as having a lot of maize,” says Kinabo.

News.title: US warns over travel in Kenya as Ebola cases mount
News.content:
The United States has urged citizens to reconsider travel to Kenya, raising its travel alert level after the country reported an eighth case of Ebola.

The East African nation has recorded a rash of cases linked to a Kenyan businessman who died after travelling from Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC).

DRC is currently enduring the second worst Ebola outbreak on record with more than 4,000 deaths since May, though the true toll is thought to be far higher.

“The level was changed from Level 2 to Level 3 due to health risks,” the US embassy in Kenya said, a day after the State Department issued renewed travel advice for its citizens.

“Reconsider travel in Kenya due to risk of health, crime, kidnapping, terrorism, unrest and traffic safety. Some areas have increased risk,” it said.

The alert came as Kenyan doctors leaders demanded better protective equipment against the highly infectious virus.

Three of the confirmed Ebola cases are reported to be health staff who cared for the businessman and the others are thought to be relatives who visited him.

News.title: US records first human case of H5N1 this year
News.content:
A man in Washington has tested positive for H5N1, marking the first human case of bird flu in the US this year.

The patient, who works on a dairy farm, was reportedly infected after being exposed to two infected cows.

H5N1 has become endemic on US dairy farms after ‘spilling over’ from birds in 2024, and has since infected more than 1,000 herds across dozens of states.

The person is not seriously ill and is isolating at home, according to the Washington State Department of Health.

Scientists have long warned that if H5N1 mutates and gains the ability to spread person-to-person, it could trigger the next global pandemic – and each new infection gives the virus more opportunities to replicate and change.

Last week, a 50-year-old man in Taiwan was infected with a different strain of bird flu, H7N7, genetic analysis of which showed the virus had undergone adaptations to spread more effectively between mammals.

Of the more than 1,000 people who have contracted H5N1 since it was first detected in the late 1990s, almost half have died.

Its “extraordinarily high” mortality rate means that, were it to gain the ability to spread between people, it would be of “enormous concern”, the World Health Organization (WHO) previously warned.

However, the strain circulating among US dairy cattle, clade 2.3.4.4b, has proven less lethal to humans.

News.title: French bond sell-off spreads across Europe
News.content:
Thanks for joining me. The cost of French government borrowing has risen at the fastest pace among G7 nations after a second night of riots.

The yield on 10-year French bonds, known as OATs, climbed from 4.80pc to 4.85pc on Monday, the steepest increase among major world economies.

Bond yields are effectively the interest rate paid by governments when they borrow money by issuing bonds to financial markets.

Emmanuel Macron is facing a crisis after shops were looted and vandalised across the country.

More than 2,300 people were arrested on Saturday after protests against the cost of living and poor school conditions.

Jim Reid, an analyst at Deutsche Bank, said: “This won’t make it easy for the international community to be totally comfortable buying OATs, so the modest recovery in French spreads over the last week or so will be tested today.

“With France already facing a difficult fiscal backdrop and the 2027 election approaching, the weekend adds another layer of political risk for markets.” Here is what you need to know.

5 things to start your day

1) Burnham seeks EU embrace over AI | UK presses for access to a scheme that will prioritise investment in sovereign technology

2) Larry Ellison’s TikTok bans ad account for Musk documentary | Social media company blocks promotion for the film because of its political content

3) Profit warnings rise ahead of Budget | Most companies blame government policy and geopolitical uncertainty for worsening outlook

4) Istanbul airport stockpiles jet fuel over shortage fears | Turkish hub can sustain flights for three weeks without topping up tanks

5) GB News to launch ‘all-British’ radio station | New broadcast venture will attempt to win market share from BBC

What happened overnight

Oil prices fell more than 1pc after Donald Trump’s decision to waive sweeping sanctions on Russia.

On Friday, the President signed an executive order that delayed a wave of fresh sanctions and tariffs as they were set to take effect.

Brent crude edged down by nearly 1pc to just under $109 a barrel, with West Texas Intermediate hovered at around $101 a barrel.

Asian shares were mixed as volatility in technology stocks persisted.

South Korea’s benchmark Kospi index was up 1.1pc to 5,729.58 on Monday, after falling sharply last week. The Kospi is down more than 18pc over the past month, and still well below the 9,000 mark it crossed in June at its peak on the global AI frenzy.

Japan’s Nikkei 225 lost 0.8pc to 64,799.03. Japanese chip equipment maker Tokyo Electron lost 2.1pc, and OpenAI investor SoftBank Group dropped 3.6pc.

Hong Kong’s stock market was closed because of a holiday. The Shanghai Composite index edged 0.2pc higher to 3,722.20, after China reported better-than-expected growth of 4.5pc for its economy in the third quarter.

CXMT, China’s leading memory chipmaker, fell more than 7pc despite the company forecasting a strong profit for the first nine months.

China’s official growth data is set to be issued on Monday, giving the markets a glimpse into how the world’s second-biggest economy is faring.

The data is expected to show that China’s economy expanded by 4.4pc in the third quarter, improving on a multi-year low in Q2 but still falling just short of its annual target.

Beijing is aiming for growth of around 4.5pc to 5pc this year, which is its lowest goal in decades.

However, experts think China is on course to miss its annual economic target, weighed down by the Iran war energy shock.

China’s economy has been under pressure from mounting energy costs and faltering domestic demand. Researchers polled by AFP suggested exports were its sole outperformer.

Taiwan’s Taiex fell 1pc. Shares of Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., or TSMC, the world’s biggest contract chipmaker, were down 0.6pc. Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 was 0.3pc higher at 8,832.20. India’s Sensex edged down 0.1pc.

Indonesia’s benchmark stock index fell another 5pc to its lowest level since 2020, after it plunged over 11pc on Friday following a warning from index provider MSCI that it would downgrade the country from its “emerging market” status.

News.title: Europe records highest ever number of West Nile Virus cases
News.content:
Mainland Europe has seen the largest number of cases of a debilitating mosquito-borne illness, with Italy hardest hit by the disease.

According to the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control there have been 1,715 locally acquired cases of West Nile Virus so far this year, compared to 989 cases at the same point last year. Italy has been hardest hit, with 748 cases, followed by Greece with 445 cases, France with 144 and Spain with 139.

There have been 130 deaths, with the greatest number occurring in Italy, which saw 56 deaths.

The number of cases is likely to tail off over the next few weeks as the weather across Europe becomes cooler and less favourable for the Culex mosquito which spreads the disease.

West Nile Virus is in the same family of viruses as dengue, yellow fever and Japanese encephalitis. It causes flu-like symptoms and sometimes vomiting and diarrhoea but in around one in 150 cases it can develop into a disease that affects the brain and nervous system and can be fatal. There is no vaccine or treatment.

The disease is widespread in birds, but humans can only acquire it if they are bitten by an infected mosquito. The disease does not spread from human to human. Most cases of severe disease occur in older people and those with weakened immune systems.

Sports.title: Real Madrid tell Premier League 'Big Six' to pay for European Super League costs
Sports.content:
Real Madrid tell Premier League 'Big Six' to pay for European Super League costs

Arsenal, Chelsea, Liverpool, Manchester City, Manchester United and Tottenham were among the 12 clubs that agreed to be part of the European Super League in April 2021 before they quickly pulled out

View 2 Images All six Premier League clubs withdrew from the project amid intense backlash (Image: Visionhaus/Getty Images)

Real Madrid are reportedly demanding that the six English clubs that signed up to the European Super League (ESL) pay a share of the project's initial costs, despite its premature collapse. Arsenal, Chelsea, Liverpool, Manchester City, Manchester United and Tottenham were among the 12 clubs involved in the ESL before it was abandoned following widespread condemnation.

‌



‌



In April 2021, the so-called Big Six of the Premier League initially signed up to a shareholders' agreement for the Spain-based European Super League Company. After five other clubs - Atletico Madrid, AC Milan, Inter Milan, Juventus and Barcelona - pulled out in the years since, Real remain the only side who are still committed to the much-maligned project.

‌



The Athletic report that chiefs at the Bernabeu believe Arsenal, Chelsea, Liverpool, City, United and Spurs should be liable for the setup costs of the plan. Those costs could be as high as €80million (£67.3m) in total.

‌



At the time of the project's demise, Real president Florentino Perez commented: "I'm not going to take my time to explain what a binding contract is here. But the fact is, the clubs can't leave."

News of Real's demand comes as the La Liga giants close in on appointing Bernd Reichart as their new head of business operations. Reichart, a German businessman, was formerly the CEO of A22, the management company based in Madrid working on behalf of the ESL.

In December 2023, when only Barcelona and Real were left in the project after Juventus had decided to withdraw earlier that year, A22 announced a change to how the competition would work. It was explained that 64 clubs would compete across three divisions, with relegation and promotion possible and the potential for new clubs to qualify for the league, rather than a closed shop.

‌



There was another change of plan 12 months later. This time, the ESL would be comprised of 96 teams and four divisions, and was branded the 'Unify League'.

"We have two rights: to be compensated for our losses, and to arrange a competition in the future, and we will tirelessly pursue both."

Sports.title: Frenkie de Jong's 'dream' transfer remark, wife dropping hint and Man Utd U-turn
Sports.content:
Frenkie de Jong's 'dream' transfer remark, wife dropping hint and Man Utd U-turn

How Erik ten Hag's hopes of bringing Frenkie de Jong to Manchester United failed to materialise

View 2 Images Erik ten Hag was desperate to sign Frenkie de Jong for Manchester United (Image: Getty Images)

The early months of Erik ten Hag's Manchester United reign were littered with talk of Frenkie de Jong joining the club. Having worked together at Ajax between 2017 and 2019 - and given United's need for midfield reinforcement - it was easy to see why Ten Hag wanted to sign the Barcelona and Netherlands star.

‌



‌



With Barca eager to get him off the wage bill amid a round of cost-cutting at the Nou Camp, it seemed a case of when, not if, he would arrive at Old Trafford. But despite extensive talks, arranged by Ten Hag himself, United couldn't get a deal for De Jong over the line.

‌



Having rebuilt his relationship with Barca, he has gone on to become a lynchpin for the Catalans, with almost 300 appearances to his name. Meanwhile, Ten Hag has been left wondering what might have been had he joined United in 2022.

‌



Here's a look back on United's pursuit of De Jong and why it never became a reality…

Erik ten Hag blasts Cristiano Ronaldo and reveals real reason for Man Utd bust-up READ MORE :

Erik ten Hag slams Man Utd for breaking promises and 'embarrassing' Scott McTominay transfer READ MORE :

Dream transfer

Thanks to Johan Cruyff - the Barca great as a player and manager - the Nou Camp club carries a mystique for Dutch footballers. That certainly applied to De Jong, who called his 2019 move from Ajax a dream come true.

Upon his arrival, he said: "I'm very excited about signing for Barca. I was very happy when I took the decision. I celebrated with my family, but not too much because we're still halfway through the season with Ajax.

‌



"But I'm very happy. I've always dreamed about playing for Barca since I was little. I like the players and the club. It's the team of my dreams. I want to be an important player for Barcelona and win many trophies."

View 2 Images De Jong's determination to stay at Barcelona has paid off (Image: Getty Images)

‌



Make sure you don't miss the best Man Utd coverage by making the Daily Mirror one of your Google preferred sources.

Wife's hint

Three years into his spell in Spain, that dream threatened to turn into a nightmare as the club looked to cut costs by getting their highest earner off the wage bill. There was even talk of Barca taking legal action against De Jong after he declined to take a pay cut.

‌



With United and Chelsea interested in signing him, many players would have happily headed for the exit door but De Jong was determined to stay and live out his dream. That feeling was shared by his then-girlfriend, now wife, Mikky Kiemeney, who made it clear where she saw their future.

With speculation peaking, she posted a video on Instagram of the couple in their car and wakesurfing and wrote: "Meanwhile... living our best life." She captioned another clip: "Found another gem in Catalunya." More than four years on from the saga, she continues to share pictures of her and her family enjoying life in the city.

‌



Content cannot be displayed without consent

United U-turn

Despite that, it seems De Jong did at least consider joining United, holding talks with Ten Hag, chief executive Richard Arnold and football director John Murtough before opting to stay put.

‌



In his recent interview with The Athletic, Ten Hag insisted he did everything he could to make it happen, saying: "Everyone's thinking the manager is doing the negotiations, that I'm involved in financial issues, but I was never.

"Of course, I did my best. I set up meetings with him, where it was Richard and John involved as well, to pursue him to come over. He could have been very important building the team, not only that year but for the future. But we didn't make it."

Roy Keane finally breaks golden rule as Gary Neville mocks 'fawning' Man Utd legend

Manchester United icon Roy Keane showed a different side to himself during a podcast conversation with Hollywood legend Sylvester Stallone

View Image The Man United legend broke his own rule when he met Sylvester Stallone

Roy Keane made an exception to his usual stance on autographs when he asked Sylvester Stallone to sign one during a special episode of The Overlap. The former Manchester United captain travelled with Gary Neville, Jill Scott and Ian Wright to meet the iconic Rocky and Rambo star.

‌



‌



The American actor joined them on the podcast to reflect on his celebrated career. Ahead of the episode's release, a short teaser clip gave fans a glimpse of a different side to Keane. Wearing a Rambo shirt featuring Stallone's face, Keane appeared delighted to meet the Hollywood star.

‌



He was seen adjusting his shirt, prompting fans to comment on the rare sight of him looking starstruck. Stallone also noticed his outfit, telling him: "Nice shirt."

‌



Neville could not resist teasing his former team-mate, saying he would turn into a 'fawning schoolboy' in Stallone’s company. Keane replied: "No, Gary, don't be silly, I'm a professional."

Sports.title: Andoni Iraola must overcome Liverpool weakness to unlock Florian Wirtz and Bradley Barcola
Sports.content:
Under normal circumstances a manager would relish the opportunity to play four successive matches at home - especially after winning two on the road.

Due to the quirks of the fixture list Liverpool have four matches, across three competitions, at Anfield over the next 12 days. They play Villarreal in the Champions League on Tuesday night followed by high-flying Brighton in the Premier League, Chelsea in the Carabao Cup and Arsenal in the league.

That is undoubtedly a clutch of tough tasks for Andoni Iraola to overcome, but especially so given their record this season.

The Reds are yet to win at Anfield in the Premier League this season, having drawn against Nottingham Forest and Fulham and been thrashed by Manchester City. By contrast, they have three wins and one draw on the road in the league following their comeback at previously-unbeaten Brentford on Saturday.

‌



It is a blindingly obvious issue to identify and a much tougher one to resolve. That is partly down to the players at Iraola's disposal.

FOLLOW OUR LIVERPOOL FB PAGE! Latest Reds news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

Liverpool have three players who cost them over £100million. And two of them are much more comfortable playing away from home on the counter-attack.

‌



Florian Wirtz and Bradley Barcola both made an impact at Brentford, with the two stars providing the assists for Victor Munoz and Alexander Isak's goals. Their performances came after Barcola bagged a hat-trick in the 6-3 mauling of LASK in Austria in midweek.

Now they have to prove they can break Liverpool's hoodoo at home - and that is the most pressing task for Iraola.

Wirtz's performance in west London suggests he can do so. The German playmaker created nine chances against Brentford, the most of any player in a Premier League game this season. He has now created 20 chances this season - more than any other Premier League player, one ahead of Brighton's in-form star Pascal Gross on 19.

Make sure you don't miss the best Liverpool coverage by making the Daily Mirror one of your Google preferred sources.

‌



View 4 Images Florian Wirtz had a creative game for Liverpool at Brentford (Image: Marc Atkins/Getty Images)

Those statistics may come as a surprise, given the amount of debate around Wirtz this season, and the fact he has actually registered just two assists from 0.8 expected assists. Nevertheless, Wirtz is leagues ahead of his teammates for creativity, with Cody Gakpo and Dominik Szoboszlai on 11 chances created each.

Liverpool legend Steven Gerrard has backed Wirtz - who has seven goals and 13 assists in 58 games for the club - to come good. “I would be thinking, if you’re on the Liverpool staff or you’re a Liverpool senior player, this kid is a talent,” he said on the Overlap Daily.

“Don’t give up on him. This is not just Florian Wirtz. I’m talking about any young kid who has a dip in form or who is finding it hard to cope with a price tag. Let’s work with him. Let’s try and help him, let’s support him. Let’s get him in a better place, and that’s when I think you will see the consistency.”

‌



View 4 Images Andoni Iraola has to find a way to play against the low block (Image: AFP/Getty Images)

He added: “The easy thing is to try and kill him and try to move him on and just wish him well. Oh, ‘How are we going to sell him or who’s going to buy him?’ When you just need to stop and think: ‘How can you fix it’?

“If you’re the manager of Liverpool, you need Wirtz to be shining. You need him playing well consistently, contributing goals and assists. That’s what the fans want.”

That sounds like a direct message for Iraola, who is still trying to move the jigsaw pieces around to find the right combination. While Isak has been solid, scoring five goals in six league games this season, Barcola has taken time to find his feet.

‌



View 4 Images Bradley Barcola's pace is best used on the break (Image: Shaun Brooks/Getty Images)

Jamie Carragher hinted at the reason why in an analysis segment on Sky Sports' Monday Night Football programme. "Barcola is a transition monster, that's when he's going to be at his best, when he's got space in front of him. He's arguably the quickest player in the Premier League," he said.

"Maybe at Anfield he's going to find it a bit tougher when teams play a low block and there's not much space. He's going to have to improve his finishing if he is to justify his fee."

Liverpool won't often be handed the luxury of transitions against away sides at Anfield. Barcola's lightning pace and Wirtz's eye for a pass were both useful weapons against Brentford, who ended the match with nine men, but they will have to show other strings to their bow in the next 12 days.

‌



It is up to Iraola to build a system which gets the best out of his expensive chess pieces.

Sports.title: Ex-Man Utd star makes Michael Carrick U-turn and names ideal Old Trafford replacement
Sports.content:
Ex-Man Utd star makes Michael Carrick U-turn and names ideal Old Trafford replacement

Manchester United boss Michael Carrick is a man under the cosh and Dwight Yorke, who had backed the ex-player, believes giving him the Old Trafford job may have been the wrong call

View 2 Images Michael Carrick is a man under pressure with one win in seven games to start the Premier League season (Image: Ash Donelon/Manchester United via Getty Images)

Former Manchester United star Dwight Yorke admits he will "hold his hands up" and concede that appointing Michael Carrick perhaps wasn't the right call - despite backing him initially.

‌



‌



The ex-Middlesbrough boss came in to steady the ship in January and enjoyed a stunning interim period, which saw United rise up to third place in the Premier League and return to the Champions League. Those exploits landed him the job on a permanent basis.

‌



However, he's found things much tougher this season and Carrick has now presided over the worst start in 40 years with United winning one of their seven league games thus far and being dumped out of the Carabao Cup.

‌



The pressure is very much on the United boss, who had the backing of several former players last season. United's desire to stick by a manager is clear following several poor calls by the hierarchy, but Yorke is no longer convinced he's the man for the job.

Make sure you don't miss sport's biggest stories and breaking news by making the Daily Mirror one of your Google preferred sources.

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

‌



He told Keys & Gray Unleashed: "That (sacking managers) is the current trend, isn’t it? It’s been the trend for the last five years: you get the manager, you say you’re going to back them and then at some point you end up getting rid of them,’ the former Trinidad and Tobago international went on. Obviously that is something that’s been in the DNA certainly for the past five years.

"Putting my hands up, I was one that said give Carrick the chance, but then I look back at it now, see what we’re doing, and I’m not sure if that was the right decision."

‌



"These guys are brilliant guys when you meet them and you know them like I have done. They’re brilliant. I’m not sure they’re made for managerial jobs when the pressure is on. Like anything else, when the going is good then it’s fantastic. When it’s not so good, I’m not so sure. I’ve seen it with Ole [Gunnar Solskjaer] and I’ve seen it with Carrick."

View 2 Images Dwight Yorke is no longer convinced by Michael Carrick (Image: Matthew Peters/Manchester United via Getty Images)

‌



United have tried several different types of managers over the past decade. They've gone after proven big names, up and coming talents and ex-players - none of whom have worked out.

Antonio Conte is being linked with the job but Yorke admits he's consider going after Eddie Howe, who left Newcastle in the summer after several successful years.

Article continues below

He said: "Who is out there? Howe would be one of those guys who stand out out there at the moment. He’s not in a job, looking for a job. But if you expand it out there even more, who else is out there? There is nobody else and that’s why Carrick will survive for a little bit longer. There are no top managerial candidates out there who can come in and really excite the people and the fans at Manchester United."

Sports.title: Marcus Rashford and Lisandro Martinez absent as EIGHT players miss Man Utd training
Sports.content:
Marcus Rashford and Lisandro Martinez absent as EIGHT players miss Man Utd training

Manchester United are back in Champions League action against Como on Wednesday, but their preparations have been disrupted by injuries

View 2 Images Lisandro Martinez and Marcus Rashford were the notable absentees from Manchester United training

Manchester United are facing a major injury headache ahead of Wednesday's Champions League showdown with Como, with Marcus Rashford and Lisandro Martinez among eight players missing from training on Tuesday. Michael Carrick's side will be desperate to return to winning ways in Europe after suffering a 2-0 defeat against Atletico Madrid last week.

‌



‌



However, their preparations have been disrupted by several injury concerns, particularly in defence. Harry Maguire was the only senior centre-back involved in the session at Carrington, with Martinez absent after suffering a thigh problem during United's recent clash with Leeds United.

‌



The Argentine defender was substituted at half-time and remains a doubt for the trip to Italy. Leny Yoro was another notable absentee, although he is already ruled out of Wednesday's encounter following his red card against Atletico.

‌



The French defender is understood to be working on an individual training programme instead. Rashford's availability is also in serious doubt as he continues to struggle with a hip injury that prevented him from taking part in Tuesday's session.

‌



Ayden Heaven, Kobbie Mainoo and Luke Shaw were also missing as United stepped up their preparations. Shaw has not featured since playing the entire 90 minutes of United's 1-1 draw with Tottenham a fortnight ago.

He subsequently picked up an injury and has remained sidelined. Club sources have indicated that late decisions will be made on the aforementioned players before the squad travels to Italy.

‌



While there is still a possibility that some of the absentees could be included, Carrick faces the prospect of heading into the fixture with severely limited defensive options. Diogo Dalot and Noussair Mazraoui are the only established options at full-back.

Harry Amass and Jaydan Kamason trained with the first team but are unlikely to feature, while it remains unclear who will partner Maguire at centre-back.

‌



View 2 Images Mainoo picked up an injury against Spurs a fortnight ago (Image: Getty Images)

Meanwhile, Benjamin Sesko and Patrick Dorgu remain unavailable as they continue their recoveries from separate injuries. Sesko is currently dealing with a shin problem and there is no clear timeframe for the striker's return.

‌



Dorgu, meanwhile, has been sidelined by a suspected hamstring injury sustained against Wales, which also forced him to withdraw from Denmark's international squad in September.

With several key players struggling for fitness, Carrick faces a difficult selection dilemma as United attempt to bounce back from their European setback.

Article continues below

The Red Devils' only win in the competition so far came in their opening match, when they beat Azerbaijani side Sabah 4-0. Cesc Fabregas' Como have also recorded one victory and one defeat, leaving both teams on three points.

Sports.title: Former world boxing champion cleared of petrol station assault
Sports.content:
Two-time IBF super-featherweight champion Joe Cordina has been cleared of assaulting a man he punched outside a petrol station; a district judge found Cordina, 34, not guilty of assault

Joe Cordina: Former boxing world champion cleared of assaulting man he punched outside petrol station

Joe Cordina has been cleared of assaulting a man he punched outside a petrol station

Former boxing world champion Joe Cordina has been cleared of assaulting a man he punched outside a petrol station.

A district judge found Cordina, 34, not guilty of assault by beating against Jamie O'Brien, 33, following a trial at Cardiff Magistrates' Court.

The court heard Cordina had been filling up his Land Rover at Pentwyn service station in Cardiff in February when he noticed O'Brien staring at him.

Cordina, a two-time IBF super-featherweight champion, approached O'Brien - who was sitting on the pavement near the station exit - believing he was a fan.

Judge Charlotte Murphy described how O'Brien then "shoulder barged him to the chest and chin", in what she found was a "deliberate assault" on Cordina.

She highlighted that the attack had taken place just two weeks after Cordina had been told by police that there was a threat to his life.

In her ruling, the judge said: "I am satisfied that the defendant believed it was necessary to use force to defend himself.

"I am further satisfied that a single, measured, controlled punch was proportionate in the circumstances.

"It is very easy to consider the defendant's response by considering the CCTV in slow motion, however the defendant had a split second to consider his response to the shoulder barge."

The judge said she accepted Cordina's evidence that he had repeatedly pushed O'Brien "while on the floor to keep him away from him".

"In my view, it was necessary and the force used was proportionate in the circumstances," she added.

"I reject any suggestion that the defendant was retaliating in any way.

"This is a person who has lived in the public eye for many years and has interacted with the public on a daily basis.

"For all of those reasons, the crown has not proved to the criminal standard. I therefore find the defendant not guilty and dismiss the charge."

The judge had previously ruled there was no case to answer in relation to the second charge of assault.

CCTV footage played to the court showed O'Brien pushing Cordina with his shoulder, before Cordina punched him.

O'Brien, from Pentwyn, previously pleaded guilty to a charge of assault by beating.

Police began to investigate the incident after footage was circulated online. The judge ruled on Tuesday there was no evidence that O'Brien knew the person who was filming.

She added that Cordina had approached O'Brien "in good faith", believing he was a fan.

During the trial, Cordina said he initially thought O'Brien wanted a photograph and described how he was accustomed to being recognised four or five times a day.

He told the court he had acted in self-defence because he felt threatened after O'Brien assaulted him.

"He had his hands in his pockets, I don't know what people carry on them these days," Cordina said.

After the case, Cordina's lawyer Nadeem Majid issued a statement to the media.

He said: "Today's verdict is a huge relief for Joe and everybody who is close to him.

"He has always maintained he is innocent throughout this.

"On behalf of Joe, I'd like to thank his family, his friends, his loyal fans, his legal team for their unwavering support through what's clearly been a very difficult time.

"Joe would now like to concentrate on his family and in particular his boxing. We'd all like to see him on the bill in December. Thank you all very much."

Sports.title: England crumble to defeat versus Pakistan in ODI tri-series opener
Sports.content:
England crumbled to an 87-run defeat in their ODI tri-series opener against Pakistan in Rawalpindi as the batting severely malfunctioned after an excellent start.

England, who have won their last three bilateral ODI series, were cruising on 91-0 inside 15 overs in a chase of 303, only to end up being bowled out for 215 in 38.4, losing their final seven wickets for just 50 runs, as home spinner Arafat Minhas backed up his maiden ODI half-century with figures of 6-40 in a stunning performance.

Visiting captain Harry Brook (5) was bowled by a beauty from Arafat after Ben Duckett (45) and Tom Banton (57) failed to build on a rollicking opening stand against a Pakistan side who had rallied from 81-4 to 302-9 earlier in the day having being put in to bat.

Score summary - Pakistan vs England, ODI tri-series, Rawalpindi Pakistan 302-9 in 50 overs (put in to bat): Hasan Nawaz (79 off 74 balls), Arafat Minhas (59 off 58), Faheem Ashraf (39 off 26); Sonny Baker (3-65), Gus Atkinson (2-35) England 215 all out in 38.4 overs (target 303): Tom Banton (57 off 53), Ben Duckett (45 off 46), Joe Root (33 off 35), Sam Curran (27 off 39); Arafat Minhas (6-40), Haris Rauf (2-32) Player of the Match: Arafat Minhas Watch England take on Sri Lanka in Rawalpindi on Thursday live on Sky Sports Cricket and Sky Sports Main Event from 8.30am (9am first ball)

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Ben Duckett and Tom Banton smashed 91 for England's first wicket in Rawalpindi before falling for 45 and 57 respectively

The tourists wilted once the hosts snapped a partnership of 31 from 57 balls between Joe Root (33) and Sam Curran (27) from 128-3, with Arafat on a hat-trick after removing Will Jacks (19) and Adil Rashid (1) from successive deliveries in the 39th over before he ran out Gus Atkinson (7) two balls later to clinch victory.

Arafat was involved in each of the final five wickets, including those of Jamie Overton (1), who holed out at long-on in what commentator Stuart Broad described as "an appalling dismissal", and Jordan Cox (18), who fell lbw.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports' Stuart Broad called out Jamie Overton for his 'appalling batting' after he holed out in the deep

England are back in action against Sri Lanka at the same venue on Thursday (9am UK, live on Sky Sports) in a tournament which sees the three sides play each other twice before the top two in the table meet in a final in Lahore on October 31.

Pakistan beat Sri Lanka by 37 runs in the first game of the tri-series on Sunday.

England strike from first ball of the match

Brook's men - whose feast of white-ball cricket continues in Australia in November with three ODIs and five T20s - were on top at various points on Tuesday, starting from the very first ball when Atkinson (2-35) had Fakhar Zaman (0) caught at midwicket.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Atkinson struck from the first ball of the match as Fakhar Zaman chipped low to Joe Root at short midwicket

Fakhar, pouched low by Root, was one of four batters to fall inside 19 overs, with opening partner Saim Ayub (8) bounced out by seamer Sonny Baker (3-65) after being starved of the strike and Babar Azam (34) bowled playing back to off-spinner Jacks.

When leg-spinner Rashid, back from a hand injury that saw him miss the 2-1 win at home to Sri Lanka in September, had Salman Ali Agha - a centurion against Sri Lanka on Sunday - caught sweeping a full toss, you wondered if Pakistan would bat out the overs.

But Shaheen Shah Afridi's side managed that thanks to a middle and lower-order counterattack led by Hasan Nawaz (79 off 74), who pumped his first ball, bowled by Rashid, for six amid nine boundaries all told during his second ODI fifty.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Jamie Overton's brilliant yorker cleaned up Pakistan's Hasan Nawaz for 79 from 74 deliveries on Tuesday

The 24-year-old shared fifty stands with Arafat (59) and Saad Baig (35), while there was then an alliance of 72 from just 49 deliveries between Arafat and Faheem Ashraf (39 off 26).

England sloppy in the field before fluffing lines with the bat

England, who conceded 80 runs from the final eight overs, dropped three catches - Atkinson with one of them and Cox, deputising as wicketkeeper for the injured Jos Buttler (hamstring), guilty of two - while Curran (1-40 off five overs) looked rusty with the ball having not played since The Hundred in August owing to a groin problem.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Atkinson atoned for a mis-field and a dropped catch by having Saad Baig caught for 35, by Surrey team-mate Curran

Pakistan's total was looking ever so lean as Banton and Duckett fired early on - Banton notching his third successive fifty-plus score and third in four knocks since replacing Jacob Bethell (knee) at the top of the order.

However, when Duckett was bounced out by Haris Rauf (2-32) and Arafat had Banton cloth to midwicket and castled Brook with a peach that straightened after gripping, the wobble was on.

Root and Curran stemmed Pakistan's fightback initially, only for Root to be poleaxed by a Naseem Shah ball that kept low and Curran to heave Rauf to deep backward square.

Then it got grisly.

Sports.title: Dubois: Fight with Fury would be 'ground-breaking'

Daniel Dubois is gunning for a "ground-breaking" 2027 showdown with Tyson Fury.

Dubois swept through Fabio Wardley in two rounds of their rematch on Saturday to defend the WBO heavyweight championship.

Fury has his all-British super-fight with Anthony Joshua in December. If he beats Joshua he'd win the WBA 'super' title and Dubois would relish a unification clash with Fury.
