World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - October 20, 2026
World.content:
Rwandan Govt Critic Found Beheaded in Uganda

Robert Kabera, a 50-year-old former Rwandan army sergeant major and outspoken critic of President Paul Kagame, has been found beheaded on the outskirts of Kampala, Uganda. Kabera had fled Rwanda and sought asylum in Uganda, citing political persecution. He later gained a following through his YouTube channel, which featured criticism of Kagame's government. Ugandan police said his head had not been recovered. His widow expressed fears for her family's safety. The opposition Rwanda National Congress has called for a thorough investigation, as his killing renews concerns about the safety of Rwandan dissidents living in exile. Other critics of Kagame have been killed abroad, including former intelligence chief Patrick Karegeya, who was found dead in Johannesburg in 2014.



UN Condemns Deadly Drone Strikes Across Sudan

Drone strikes across Sudan have killed and injured civilians, including children, as fighting between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces continues to intensify. The attacks injured at least 19 people at a market in Abyei and targeted locations in Khartoum, including an area near the airport. The strikes reportedly killed at least 19 people, including 10 children, across several states. The United Nations condemned the attacks and raised concerns over the targeting of humanitarian workers, with 25 Sudanese Red Crescent volunteers reportedly killed since the conflict began in April 2023. An estimated 20 million people face acute hunger, with famine risks rising in parts of Darfur and Greater Kordofan. Despite the insecurity, aid agencies continue delivering assistance, including restoring water supplies to thousands of people in Central Darfur. Sudan's humanitarian response plan remains just over 43% funded.

Zimbabwe's Ruling Party to Discipline MPs Who Missed Constitutional Amendment Vote

Zimbabwe's ruling Zanu-PF party plans to discipline Members of Parliament who failed to attend crucial parliamentary sittings during consideration of Constitutional Amendment No. 3 Bill. Party legal secretary Ziyambi Ziyambi announced the sanctions at the party's annual conference in Chinhoyi, naming several senior officials and deputy ministers among those who did not vote, although their reasons remain unclear. The disciplinary move comes as Zanu-PF advances resolutions to postpone its next elective congress from 2027 to 2029, potentially keeping President Emmerson Mnangagwa at the helm until 2030. Provincial leaders defended resolutions supporting his continued leadership and called for constitutional alignment and greater national self-sufficiency in areas such as medicine, technology and industrial production.

Thabo Mbeki Denies Blocking Apartheid-Era Prosecutions at Inquiry Commission

Former South African president Thabo Mbeki has denied allegations that he held secret meetings with former apartheid-era military and police generals to prevent prosecutions for human rights abuses. Testifying before the Khampepe Commission of Inquiry into delayed Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC) prosecutions, Mbeki said the generals approached him in 1996 seeking a meeting with the ANC over amnesty applications. He argued that former president FW de Klerk and his cabinet should also apply. Mbeki said the ANC subsequently pursued collective amnesty for some of its leaders to encourage the apartheid leadership to do the same, but the courts later overturned the decision. He maintained that his administration never directed the National Prosecuting Authority to halt or suppress investigations, arguing that prosecutions were the NPA's responsibility. He also defended his 2003 parliamentary speech and later arrangements involving pardon requests, saying these aimed to encourage truth-telling rather than grant blanket immunity to those responsible for apartheid-era crimes.

Close 

Nigeria and Rwanda Seek to Strengthen Defence Cooperation

Nigeria's Chief of Army Staff, Lieutenant General Waidi Shaibu, has arrived in Rwanda for a five-day official visit aimed at strengthening defence and security cooperation between the two countries. Shaibu held talks in Kigali with Rwanda Defence Force Chief of Defence Staff General Mubarakh Muganga and Army Chief of Staff Major General Vincent Nyakarundi. The discussions focused on implementing existing agreements covering military training, exchanges of instructional and logistics personnel, and other shared security concerns. Shaibu and his delegation also visited the Kigali Genocide Memorial to pay tribute to victims of the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi and toured the Campaign Against Genocide Museum to learn about the genocide and Rwanda's post-conflict recovery. The visit is scheduled to conclude on October 23.

World.title: South Africa: From First Jab to the Next - The Data System Tracking South Africa's LEN Roll-Out
World.content:
South Africa's LEN roll-out isn't just about getting six-monthly HIV prevention jabs into people's arms. We also need to know whether people return for their next dose, whether clinics have enough stock and who is being left behind. A digital system linking LEN clinics will help us find out.

South Africa's LEN roll-out isn't just about getting six-monthly HIV prevention jabs into people's arms. We also need to know whether people return for their next dose, whether clinics have enough stock and who is being left behind. A digital system linking LEN clinics will help us find out.

Giving someone their first LEN jab is easy to count. Knowing whether they return six months later is what tells us whether the programme is really working.

A digital system called SyNCH connects LEN clinics in all provinces outside the Western Cape, which uses a different system, allowing health workers to see information about a person's previous LEN doses when they visit another participating clinic.

The information feeds into a dashboard that helps health officials see who is using LEN, where uptake is low and where clinics may need more support.

South Africa still doesn't have a comprehensive national electronic patient record. The LEN system shows what becomes possible when health information can follow a patient between clinics.

Giving someone an HIV prevention injection is one thing. Knowing whether they come back six months later for their next one is another.

That difference matters.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

South Africa started rolling out lenacapavir, or LEN, a twice-yearly injection that prevents HIV, in June . But the success of the programme cannot be measured simply by counting how many people receive their first injections.

The health department also needs to know whether people return for their second and third doses. By 15 October just under 79 000 people had received their first LEN dose, and the first group of people who will receive their second dose, will have to do so in early December .

The department needs to see which clinics have high or low uptake, which groups of people are being reached — and which are being missed. And it needs to know whether clinics have enough stock to give people their next injections when they are due.

Without good data, health officials are effectively trying to manage a national programme without being able to see clearly what is happening on the ground.

That is why one of the less visible parts of South Africa's LEN roll-out could turn out to be one of its most important: the digital system behind it.

SA's HIV prevention medicine dashboard (screen grab)

Following a LEN user from one clinic to another

LEN is currently available at 360 public clinics in South Africa. Most of these clinics are connected through an electronic system called SyNCH, short for the Synchronised National Communication in Health system .

SyNCH was developed by the public health intelligence organisation, Health Systems Trust (HST) and ASG Technologies in partnership with the national health department. It was originally built to help manage medicines for stable patients with chronic conditions who collect their treatment from pick-up points outside clinics. It has since been expanded to include HIV prevention medicines — both the daily HIV prevention pill and LEN.

For LEN users, this means something remarkably practical.

When someone receives LEN, their visit is recorded electronically. If they later go to another LEN clinic connected to SyNCH, a healthcare worker can see information about their previous LEN visit, including when they received their last dose.

So a person does not necessarily have to return to the same clinic every six months to continue using LEN.

That matters in a country where people move between towns and provinces for work, study or family reasons.

The exception is the Western Cape, which uses a different electronic patient-record system. LEN users there can move between participating clinics within the province, but their records are not connected to SyNCH clinics elsewhere in the country.

South Africa has spent years trying to build a comprehensive national electronic patient record. We are not there yet. SyNCH is not such a record either. But what is happening with LEN shows what becomes possible when clinics can share important information about an individual patient's care.

A first dose doesn't tell you whether a programme works

The system does more than help individual LEN users.

The information entered at clinics feeds into a LEN dashboard that allows health officials to see what is happening with the roll-out without waiting months for reports to work their way up through the health system.

Officials can see how many people are choosing LEN or the daily HIV prevention pill and break the figures down by age, gender and area — from province all the way down to individual clinics.

That can answer important questions.

Are young people taking up LEN? Are some districts doing much better than others? Are particular groups not being reached? Is a clinic attracting many LEN users while another nearby is seeing very few?

Those differences matter because a national total can hide local problems.

A headline figure might show that thousands of people have received LEN. But it won't necessarily tell officials that uptake is low in one district, that a particular age group is being missed or that a clinic needs extra support.

More detailed data can.

And as the roll-out continues, another number will become increasingly important: how many people come back for their next injection?

LEN protects someone for six months at a time . If large numbers of people receive their first dose but don't return for later injections, the programme will not have the impact we hope for.

Because SyNCH keeps a person-level record of LEN use, the health department can track whether people return for subsequent doses rather than simply counting injections given.

That turns data from a record of what has already happened into a tool for improving what happens next.

Data can also help prevent stock problems

There is another crucial part of the picture: medicine stock.

A successful campaign can create its own problem if demand grows faster than the supply of medicine to clinics.

Digital information can help health officials see how LEN is being used and where stock is running low. That gives managers an opportunity to respond — for example, by moving stock or replenishing a clinic — before shortages interrupt people's prevention.

This is especially important for a medicine that must be given on a schedule.

Someone who has made the effort to return for their next injection should not discover that the clinic has run out.

The dashboard isn't the achievement on its own

It is tempting to think of a dashboard as the innovation. But a dashboard is only as useful as the information underneath it.

Close 

The bigger achievement is connecting what happens to an individual LEN user at a clinic with information that nurses, doctors and programme managers can use.

HST has worked with the national health department and other partners for years to build and support some of the digital systems on which this work depends. LEN shows how that infrastructure can be adapted for a new public health programme rather than building a separate system from scratch each time.

There is a broader lesson here.

South Africa has many ambitious health policies and programmes. But launching an intervention is only the beginning. We need to know whether people are actually getting it, whether they continue using it, whether clinics have enough stock and whether the people who could benefit most are being reached.

That requires good data.

The same principle applies far beyond LEN. A health system needs to be able to follow people through care, whether they are using HIV prevention, collecting HIV or TB treatment, or receiving long-term care for conditions such as diabetes or high blood pressure.

Technology on its own won't fix South Africa's health system. Nor will another dashboard.

But when health workers can see the information they need to care for someone, and managers can see problems early enough to do something about them, data becomes more than numbers on a screen.

It becomes part of healthcare itself.

Ntombi Sigwebela is the chief executive officer of Health Systems Trust.

This story was produced by the Bhekisisa Centre for Health Journalism.

World.title: Mozambique: Chapo Calls for Answers Regarding Crash of Machel's Aircraft
World.content:
Maputo — Mozambican President Daniel Chapo has called for continued efforts to establish the circumstances surrounding the death of the country's first president, Samora Moisés Machel, who died in a plane crash in Mbuzini, South Africa, 40 years ago.

Speaking on Monday at a ceremony marking 40 years of the disaster, Chapo said that investigations conducted over the decades had failed to dispel all doubts about the circumstances of the crash.

"Forty years later, questions remain about the circumstances of the Mbuzini tragedy. The investigations and explanations produced over these decades have not eliminated all doubts," Chapo said.

He stressed that the families of the victims and the Mozambican and South African peoples have the right to know the truth about the events of that night.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

He also reaffirmed the Mozambican State's commitment to preserving the memory and dignity of all those who lost their lives.

The crash occurred on 19 October 1986, when the aircraft carrying Machel, who was returning from a diplomatic mission, went down in South African territory, killing 35 people, including Machel, members of his delegation, journalists, diplomats and crew members.

Chapo also highlighted Michel's legacy in the national liberation struggle, the building of the Mozambican state and solidarity with peoples fighting colonialism and apartheid, particularly in Southern Africa.

He said Machel's ideals continued to inspire efforts to consolidate peace, national unity and inclusive dialogue, as well as Mozambique's pursuit of economic independence.

Chapo identified increasing domestic production, processing the country's natural resources and creating jobs, particularly for young people and women, as priorities for national development.

For his part, Ronald Lamola, South Africa's Minister of International Affairs, representing South African President Cyril Ramaphosa, praised the historic ties of friendship and solidarity between the two countries.

"The tragedy remains one of the most painful chapters in the history of our liberation struggle in Southern Africa. It also symbolizes our shared sacrifices and the ties that unite the peoples of South Africa and Mozambique," Lamola said.

Lamola also highlighted economic cooperation between the two countries, saying that more than 2,500 commercial trucks cross the Maputo Corridor daily in both directions and that around 300 South African companies operate in Mozambique, supporting more than 40,000 jobs.

World.title: Nigeria: Only Three Women Out of 76 Were Invited to Key APC Presidential Campaign Meeting
World.content:
A review of the list of invitees to the inaugural All Progressives Congress (APC) presidential campaign meeting shows a significant gender imbalance, with only three women included among 76 persons listed.

Only three women were included among the 76 persons listed to attend the inaugural All Progressives Congress (APC) presidential campaign council meeting scheduled for Tuesday in Abuja.

The meeting, according to an internal memorandum dated 18 October and signed by the council's Secretary, Governor Hope Uzodimma of Imo State, is scheduled for 2 p.m. at the Presidential Campaign Council headquarters on Herbert Macaulay Way, Central Business District, Abuja.

Gender imbalance



Of the 76 names reviewed, 73 are men, and three are women, representing approximately 3.9 per cent female representation.

Only women playing the role of a secretary were invited to the top-level political mobilisation meeting.

The three women are Zainab Marwa, Secretary of the Directorate of Infrastructure Mobilisation and Sensitisation, Hadiza Usman, Assistant Secretary in the Secretariat, and Stella Okotete, listed as Secretary I in the Directorate of Election Planning, Coordination, Monitoring/Mobilisation.

The memo contains the breakdown of vice chairpersons, state coordinators, director general and deputy director generals, and various directorates listed to be in attendance.

"Kindly note that the meeting is strictly by invitation to the list of attendees as attached herewith," the post reads.

The meeting will be attended by several prominent members of the campaign council, including Minister of the Federal Capital Territory, Nyesom Wike; Osun State Governor Ademola Adeleke; Anambra State Governor Chukwuma Soludo; and Mr Uzodimma.

Also expected at the meeting are Senate President Godswill Akpabio, Speaker of the House of Representatives Tajudeen Abbas and Kwara State Governor AbdulRahman AbdulRazaq, who are listed as deputy vice "Chairmen I, II and III," respectively.

Other senior members of the council include Yobe State Governor Mala Buni, appointed deputy director-General I for the North, and Deputy Senate President Barau Jibrin, who is deputy director-general II for the region.

The reporter could not reach Oguwike Nwachuku, the chief press secretary to Imo State Governor Hope Uzodimma, for comments due to poor network connectivity.

Close 

An SMS seeking his response was sent, but no response had been received at the time of publication.

World.title: Nigeria: Nigeria Daily - Why Does Farmer-Herder Violence Keep Returning?
World.content:
Farmer-herder clashes remain a major security and agricultural challenge in Nigeria, threatening lives, destroying livelihoods and raising concerns about food production. Despite years of government interventions, including the National Livestock Transformation Plan, RUGA settlements and renewed efforts to promote ranching, violence continues to recur in affected communities.

The latest violence in Paikon-Kore, Gwagwalada Area Council of the Federal Capital Territory, has renewed questions about why these clashes persist, the effectiveness of government interventions, and the challenges of finding a lasting solution to disputes over farmland, grazing routes and access to water.

Today on Nigeria Daily, we examine why farmer-herder clashes keep recurring despite government efforts, what has prevented ranching from becoming a widely adopted solution, and what needs to change to restore peace and prevent further violence.

World.title: When will Tiger Woods return to golf following latest DUI arrest? Current signs point to two possibilities
World.content:
The golf world has been posed with the question of when Tiger Woods might make his return to the sport countless times at this point in the 15-time major champion's career.

That question has lingered since Woods' latest DUI-related arrest in March, but we've now reached the point in the proceedings where we're starting to collect legitimate clues about what the answer may be this time around.

The most recent meaningful golf shot Woods hit took place in March 2026 when he competed in a TGL event alongside his Jupiter Links teammates. That same month, he was arrested on charges of driving under the influence and charged with two misdemeanors in Florida. He ultimately completed a months-long inpatient rehab program overseas before entering a plea deal in September in which charges were reduced.

TIGER WOODS MAKES FIRST PUBLIC APPEARANCE SINCE DUI, REHAB STINT AS PGA TOUR ANNOUNCES SWEEPING CHANGES

In early October, Woods was seen hitting golf balls at one of his TGR Live events, and while the video showed him hitting just one shot, it ramped up the speculation that he was in the process of working his way back to competing.

With Woods now eligible to compete on the PGA Tour Champions circuit as a 50-year-old, a competitive return coming in the form of a debut start on the senior circuit would, and still could be, a possibility. However, Woods has never committed to competing on the PGA Tour Champions circuit.

This leads us to the more likely scenarios in which we could see Woods make a return to golf, with evidence supporting each.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

A Tiger return in the Bahamas

Woods has long played tournament host of the Hero World Challenge in the Bahamas, and with the 2026 event set for the first week of December, making a competitive return in a very limited-field event could make for a perfect scenario.

The initial 20-player tournament field was announced on Monday, but only 17 names were listed. The three final spots, all tournament exemptions, are set to be announced at a later date.

Woods could use one of the final three spots in the tournament for himself, but it is worth noting that he has not teed it up in the Hero World Challenge since 2023.

A Woods comeback in the TGL

The 2027 TGL schedule has not been released, but Woods was officially announced as a returning player on next season's Jupiter Links team alongside Tom Kim, Max Homa, Akshay Bhatia and Keith Mitchell.

Woods being listed on the initial roster announced on Tuesday indicates he has plans to compete in some capacity, at the very least.

Woods making his return to the golf spotlight in the TGL, the simulated indoor league he co-founded back in 2022, would certainly make sense.

If the league follows the pattern of the 2026 schedule, the first event of the new season would take place at the end of December and run through late March.

Woods' last tournament start took place at The Open in July 2024.

Rules for thee, not for me.

Monday night in San Francisco, for the second consecutive game of the WNBA Finals, the Atlanta Dream and Golden State Valkyries stepped off the court before the national anthem and then immediately returned to the court after Canadian-born Alanis Morissette finished her performance.

The spineless league hasn't said a word despite the women continuing to break an anthem rulebook provision that requires them to attend the performance. Now that we've reported, it's time for you guys to react and share your feelings on this drama that isn't going away.

WNBA SILENT AFTER FINALS TEAMS SKIP NATIONAL ANTHEM DESPITE RULE REQUIRING PLAYERS TO STAND AND LINE UP

World.title: Sunny Hostin re-visits 'problematic' Kamala Harris answer on 'The View' as hosts question her 2028 potential
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

"The View" co-host Sunny Hostin revisited her widely-discussed 2024 question to former Vice President Kamala Harris during an event on Monday, calling the former Democratic presidential nominee's answer and refusal to distance herself from former President Joe Biden at the time "problematic."

Brian Teta, the talk show's executive producer and host of its "Behind the Table" podcast, selected the moment as Hostin's most memorable on the show. He said it was a "seminal moment" in the 2024 election cycle.

Hostin described the question as a "gift" and said she thought Harris would have to distance herself from Biden because of his approval ratings at the time. She also said "The View" was the perfect venue to ask the question, calling the liberal show's audience "her people."

"I actually thought the answer was going to be, you know, ‘We had a lot of wins in this administration. I was there for those wins, but I, as a woman of color, as a child of immigrants, as I have a different lived experience, and I intend to bring that lived experience with me into the White House. I will do this. I will do that. I will do this. I will do that. I will do that.’ That was what I was expecting. I was not expecting, 'Not a single thing comes to mind.' And I knew honestly when she said it that it was really problematic," Hostin said.

KAMALA HARRIS CALLS TO EXPAND SUPREME COURT, ADD STATES IF DEMS TAKE CONGRESS

The co-hosts noted that the moment was discussed in books published after the 2024 election, including Harris' memoir, "107 Days," and was also featured in a political ad for President Donald Trump.

In "107 Days," Harris wrote that she had no idea she had just "pulled the pin on a hand grenade," with her answer to Hostin's question. She wrote that her staff was beside themselves.

"Stationed at various places around the set, my staff were beside themselves. Political operatives have an eye to see a moment, and I could kick myself for giving the other side that moment. During the commercial break, while I was having a bit of fun with some young students I’d noticed in the audience who were obviously playing hooky, offering to write notes to their teachers after the show, Opal [Vadhan] passed me a note from our team, telling me to return to that question and mention that a big difference would be that I would put a Republican in my cabinet," she wrote in her book.

'THE VIEW' CO-HOSTS CAST DOUBT ON KAMALA HARRIS VIABILITY AS 2028 CANDIDATE

Teta and the co-hosts said they all knew her response was going to be a problem.

Co-host Ana Navarro said Harris' staff "ran" because staff members knew immediately that Harris needed to return to the question and address her answer.

KAMALA HARRIS FACES DEMOCRATIC DOUBTS OVER 2028 AS ALLIES PUSH BACK ON CLAIMS SHE’S SQUANDERED HER CHANCE

During the show on Friday, both Navarro and Haines said they wouldn't tell Harris not to run, but questioned if she would be the best option for the Democratic Party.

"If the Democrats want to win, I don't think she's the right candidate because I think the Democrats have been screaming for new energy. They've been saying we need something new to combat this. This would be her third time on this ballot. From the first time when she didn't ... she was out really early when she ran, and then the time with Biden, this would be the third time. People are clamoring for fresh energy, and there's a lot of candidates," Haines said.

Hostin questioned whether president would be the right position for Harris during an April episode of "The View" and said she wished Harris had pursued a run for California governor.

World.title: Christina Applegate says she was misdiagnosed with multiple sclerosis
World.content:
Emmy-nominated actor Christina Applegate announced Tuesday that she had been misdiagnosed with multiple sclerosis, a condition she believed she had for more than five years, leaving her “back at square one” as she continues to experience debilitating medical issues.

Applegate, who revealed the misdiagnosis on the latest episode of her podcast “MeSsy,” broke down in tears as she recalled a doctor recently telling her: “Congratulations. You don’t have MS.” She said that she was “not happy at all” about the news.

“You don’t get misdiagnosed and then all of a sudden I’m better,” Applegate told her podcast co-host, “The Sopranos” actor Jamie-Lynn Sigler. “I haven’t gotten better, Jamie. If anything, I’ve gotten worse in some ways.

“I’m back at square one, that I don’t know what’s going on with me,” said Applegate, who spent months in the hospital earlier this year and recently took a break from co-hosting “MeSsy” with Sigler, who was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis roughly 25 years ago.

00:20 Christina Applegate says she was misdiagnosed with MS 00:00 00:00

Applegate disclosed that she had been diagnosed with multiple sclerosis in 2021, calling her medical ordeal “a tough road.” She received a standing ovation at the 2024 Emmy Awards, appearing on stage with a cane. In an interview that year, she said she lived “kind of in hell.”

Multiple sclerosis is a progressive disease of the central nervous system that disrupts the flow of information between the brain and body. The immune system attacks the body’s nerve linings, producing unpredictable symptoms such as pain, fatigue or paralysis.

In the two-part podcast episode released Tuesday, Applegate said the lack of clarity about her medical condition was “unnerving” and “confusing.”

“It’s weird because I feel like I let everybody down,” Applegate told Sigler. “It’s this weird feeling because I became this — you and I — the poster children for MS. ... I had a f---ing reason as to why my day sucked every day.”

She said her medical team will work to determine the underlying cause of her symptoms.

“Why did this happen? I had every symptom of someone with MS. Every single one,” Applegate said.

Applegate is best known for her television roles on Fox’s “Married with Children” and Netflix’s “Dead to Me.” She also appeared in both “Anchorman” movies as TV news anchor Veronica Corningstone. She has received eight Emmy nominations, winning in 2003 for her guest appearance on NBC’s “Friends.”

World.title: Pennsylvania warns of rise in congenital measles and infection during pregnancy
World.content:
The Pennsylvania Department of Health issued an alert Monday to doctors about an increase in measles infections in pregnant women, as well as a concerning rise in congenital measles — a disease that’s rarely, if ever, seen in the U.S.

The department said that 66 pregnant women in Pennsylvania had been diagnosed with measles since the state’s outbreak began in April. “Getting measles while pregnant increases the risk of miscarriage, early labor, and low birth weight,” a department spokesperson said in an email.

It’s unclear how many women have miscarried or delivered babies with congenital measles. The department said that state law prohibits it from releasing details of the outcomes of those pregnancies, and there is no national database that tracks cases. True numbers may also be obscured as the outbreak has largely been limited to Amish families who don’t always seek conventional medical assistance.

As of Thursday, there have been 4,410 measles cases in the U.S. this year. In Pennsylvania, there have been 1,286 cases as of Monday.

Even before widespread measles vaccination, congenital measles was rare. That’s because most women had already been infected as children. It’s only now emerging as a threat as measles outbreaks are increasing as vaccination rates fall.

Last month, the American Academy of Pediatrics added a “frequently asked questions” page about congenital measles to its website in response to ongoing and increasing measles outbreaks. According to the AAP, congenital measles occurs in newborns whose mothers have been infected during the two weeks before birth and who test positive or develop measles symptoms within 10 days of delivery.

Anecdotally, doctors have said that at least six babies were born in Pennsylvania with congenital measles. Babies can have a range of symptoms, from a rash and fever to pneumonia, neurological problems and low blood platelets. At least two developed pneumonia and were admitted to an intensive care unit, doctors said.

Congenital measles can be deadly. One father in Lancaster County previously told NBC News that his wife was sick with measles in August and went into labor a month early. Their baby died shortly after birth.

Congenital measles can also lead to severe brain and immune system issues later in life, the Pennsylvania Department of Health said. Those long-term complications can include a very rare and severe inflammatory brain condition called subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, or SSPE. It can occur seven to 10 years after a measles infection and is almost always fatal. There is evidence that SSPE may occur earlier in children born with congenital measles.

There’s no specific treatment for congenital measles other than supportive care, such as fluids, hydration and supplemental oxygen.

The best way to prevent the newborn condition is for women to get vaccinated before getting pregnant, the health department said. Pregnant women who get measles are unable to get the vaccine because the shot contains a weakened but live version of the virus.

Unvaccinated pregnant women who are exposed to measles can get a dose of immunoglobulin within six days of that exposure, the health department said, to “provide protection against measles infection or reduce the risk of serious illness among susceptible people.”

The vaccine can be given to women after they deliver their babies and is safe for breastfeeding mothers, according to state health officials.

World.content: During his rally in Alaska, President Trump pardoned Zachary Czuback and Patrick Fleming, co-owners of a vehicle repair shop in Anchorage. World.title: Jane Doe says Cornell president appeared to question her allegations in letter to faculty senate
World.content:
Jane Doe, the woman who accused several Cornell University fraternity members of sexually assaulting her in 2024, sent a letter to the school’s faculty senate sharing a second-hand account of President Michael Kotlikoff’s response to her allegations ahead of a potential vote of no confidence in his administration.

In a Wednesday letter obtained by NBC News, Doe described a meeting between Kotlikoff and the then-president of her sorority, Tri Delta, months after she reported the alleged assault to the university. Doe wrote that the sorority president subsequently told her that Kotlikoff had allegedly questioned why she waited to report the incident.

“After the conversation she shared with me, with concern, that President Kotlikoff’s initial response was along the lines of, ‘Why did she wait so long to report it?’” Doe said in the letter. “She interpreted his question as an expression of doubt in the veracity of my story.”

Cornell disputed that characterization Tuesday, saying in a statement that Kotlikoff’s question during a January 2025 meeting was focused on bystanders who had not reported the allegations, rather than Doe herself.

The shuttered Chi Phi fraternity in Ithaca, N.Y., Oct. 2, 2026. The university is facing renewed scrutiny following a civil lawsuit filed by a former student alleging sexual assault by members of the Chi Phi fraternity in 2024. Heather Ainsworth / NBC News

The letter comes amid mounting scrutiny of Cornell’s handling of Doe’s allegations and growing debate among school faculty members over whether to hold a no-confidence vote in the university’s administration. Earlier this month, Cornell hired former acting U.S. Attorney General Sally Yates to lead an independent review, which will examine the school’s response to Doe’s allegations and broader policies governing sexual misconduct.

In a civil lawsuit filed last month, Doe accused seven members of the now-dismantled Chi Phi fraternity of plying her with drugs and sexually assaulting her at a party in October 2024 and into the early hours of the next morning.

Orazio Petito, who was named as the former president of the fraternity, was dropped from the lawsuit after his lawyer said he was “mistakenly” identified as the Chi Phi chapter president at the time of the alleged 2024 assault, according to court documents. Petito was not accused of assault in the lawsuit.

Attorneys for several of the men have denied wrongdoing or disputed her account. Doe’s lawyer did not immediately respond to NBC News’ request for comment.

Cornell subsequently investigated the allegations through its Title IX disciplinary process, expelling two students and imposing suspensions or lesser sanctions on others. The university also launched a Presidential Task Force on Campus Sexual Assault in early 2025 and has said in a statement Tuesday that it is implementing recommendations to improve its response to sexual misconduct.

“The second-hand account of the question asked by President Kotlikoff in a January 2025 meeting in the letter is incorrect, based on a documented first-hand account,” the statement added. “The question ‘why did it take so long for the assault to be reported’ was directed at bystanders who did not use Cornell’s anonymous tip line, despite ongoing social media activity about the incident in October 2024. He was not questioning Jane Doe’s reporting.”

In her letter, Doe wrote that the sorority president told her that at least one other faculty member who attended the meeting “appeared distressed” after hearing Kotlikoff’s question. Doe said that the faculty member thought “the President’s response was inappropriate.”

“I felt unsupported and disbelieved by President Kotlikoff,” Doe wrote in the letter. “It diminished my confidence in the administration’s ability to approach my experience with the understanding, sensitivity, and fairness I had hoped for and expected from what had been my dream school.”

Doe added that she is now sharing this account because she does not know how many people know about the meeting or the president’s response.

“My intention is not to prescribe how the Senate should interpret this account, but rather to provide information that its members may wish to consider or investigate further,” she wrote. “I would not want to withhold something potentially pertinent, only for Senate members to later discover that information relevant to their deliberations had not been made available to them.”

The letter has prompted questions from at least one faculty member about how it was handled by Cornell’s dean of faculty, Chris Schaffer. A professor on the faculty senate, who requested anonymity to speak freely about the situation, told NBC News that Schaffer told members Tuesday that he had received Doe’s letter last week, the same day the senate met to discuss whether to hold a vote of no-confidence.

“If he received it on the 14th, he should have said so,” the professor said.

Cornell said Schaffer received the letter as “legal correspondence claiming to be from a law firm representing Jane Doe” and that he “subsequently turned it over to the General Counsel to verify and to share with the Independent Review.”

“Shortly before the start of the Senate meeting on October 14, I received a communication from a lawyer representing Jane Doe, which relayed a second-hand account of President Kotlikoff asking about the timing of reports about the Jane Doe assault in 2024,” he wrote. “I later received a contemporaneous account of the meeting from a university official who was present that indicated President Kotlikoff asked bystanders ‘why did it take so long for the assault to be reported’ through Cornell’s anonymous tip line, given the level of social media discussion of the events. The question was not about Jane Doe or her decision to report.”

Schaffer added that his office “does not have the investigatory capacity to properly follow up on private communications of this kind, nor is this the role of the office.”

“In the interests of transparency, I am writing now to inform the Senate that I received this communication, that I passed it on to the Office of the General Counsel, and that they have sent it to the investigatory team led by Former Deputy Attorney General Sally Yates,” he added. “Any individual who has information they believe is relevant to the deliberation of the Cornell Senate may make such information public or communicate it directly.”

World.title: Democrats jump into Mississippi Senate race
World.content:
Senate Democrats’ top super PAC announced Tuesday it is launching a new ad campaign in the Mississippi Senate race, as Democrats seek inroads in Republican-leaning states to try to flip the Senate majority.

Senate Majority PAC announced a $1.2 million ad campaign in the state through Election Day, beginning with a 30-second spot that boosts prosecutor Scott Colom as a Democrat who will “fight corruption in both parties” and casts GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith as a “do-nothing” incumbent.

“Senate Majority PAC has been watching this race closely, and it is clear Colom is running a competitive race that has put Hyde-Smith on her heels,” Lauren French, the super PAC’s spokesperson, said in a statement, also noting that the group will be advertising on TV and digital platforms.

Senate Majority PAC, which is aligned with Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., has been shifting its focus to deep-red states amid President Donald Trump’s sinking approval ratings. Democrats need a net gain of four seats to win control of the Senate, which means flipping multiple states Trump won handily in 2024.

Mississippi is the reddest state the group has jumped into so far — Trump won it by 23 points two years ago. A Democrat has not won a Senate race in Mississippi since 1982.

Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith. Bill Clark / CQ-Roll Call via Getty

Senate Majority PAC is also spending in Kansas, which Trump won by 16 points, and other states Trump won by double digits in 2024, including Alaska, Texas and Iowa.

Schumer and Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, the chair of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, have long touted Colom as a strong candidate. A district attorney, Colom told NBC News when he launched his campaign last year that Hyde-Smith’s vote to support Trump’s “big, beautiful” tax and spending law, which cut Medicaid funds, spurred him to run.

Colom and Hyde-Smith have history from before this year’s Senate race. Hyde-Smith blocked Colom’s nomination for a federal judgeship during the Biden administration. Colom said when he launched his campaign that he had forgiven her.

Hyde-Smith, who has Trump’s endorsement, is running for her second full term after she was appointed to the Senate in 2018. She won a full term in 2020 by 10 points.

World.title: Top baby names heading into 2027 inspired by ‘The Odyssey,’ ‘Yellowstone’ and ‘Heated Rivalry’
World.content:
Somewhere in a delivery room, a new parent is weighing a name that sounds like a Greek hero, a Montana ranch hand or a brooding hockey player from a streaming series. According to BabyCenter’s latest data, they’re far from alone.

BabyCenter, a digital parenting resource that’s been reporting on baby names and trends for more than 20 years, just released its annual lists of the most popular baby names of 2026 and the trends it expects to shape 2027. The findings, shared with NBC News, draw on more than 350,000 babies born this year to parents registered on the BabyCenter app. Because parents submit names in real time, the company can predict trends before the Social Security Administration releases its official list.

At the very top, little has changed from last year. Noah and Olivia both keep their No. 1 spots.

Just beneath them, though, one name is making a lot of noise. Eliana has shot up to No. 2 for girls, a remarkable climb from No. 14 in 2024 and No. 7 last year. BabyCenter’s baby name advisor, Steph Coffield, calls it the year’s most surprising trend and predicts that if the momentum holds, Eliana could take the top girls’ spot next year.

If there’s a theme running through this year’s data, it’s with that first letter E. E is the most popular starting initial for girls, making up 15% of the top 100 girls’ names. For boys, J leads, with 14% of the top 100.

The E-names are having a moment well beyond the top 10. Elsie rose 23 spots, Evangeline 50, Elodie 87, Elaine 143 and Esme a whopping 222. Among the boys, Josiah surged 33 spots to No. 21 and Jeremiah climbed 28 spots to reach No. 60, while Jaxon, Jaxson and Jasper all hold spots in the top 100.

Scroll further down the list and you’ll find some fresh faces. Magnolia is the only brand-new girls’ name. But on the boys’ side, Stetson, Archer and Milo all debuted, joined by Dean, which is making its first top 100 appearance this century after a heyday in the ’50s and ’60s.

Length is trending upward, too. Nearly three in 10 of the top girls’ names and 31% of the top boys’ names have seven or more letters. The longest name in the mix is Christopher, at 11.

Many of those longer, bolder picks are coming straight from the screen, and nowhere is that clearer than on the ice. In the same year ESPN logged its most-watched NHL playoff season, ice-rink TV dramas, including “Off Campus” and “Heated Rivalry,” sent names like Garrett, Allie, Beau and Jules climbing. The breakout star is Ilya, which rocketed up more than 6,000 spots to No. 2,197 for boys.

Trade the rink for the open range, and another small-screen hit is leaving its mark. The lingering pull of “Yellowstone,” with its cowboy hats, boots and line dancing, is carrying into the nursery. As mentioned earlier, Stetson rose 46 spots to No. 95, the first time it has ever cracked BabyCenter’s top 100. Walker (up 19), Callahan (up 88), Wilder (up 107) and Gunner (up 151) are riding the same wave.

But the cowboys have some competition from across the sea. Names from Greek mythology are washing ashore, boosted by the blockbuster movie “The Odyssey.” Boys’ names on the rise include Atlas (up 5), Orion and Troy (both up 9), Ares (up 32), Evander (up 128) and Perseus (up 249). For girls, Iris (up 18), Lydia (up 38) and Daphne (up 42) are climbing.

“The trends this year show parents are ready to dig into the archives with some modern appreciation for the ancient, the vintage, the classic,” Coffield said.

In some cases, that archive is a cozy Connecticut town. With a “Gilmore Girls” documentary newly announced, fall rewatches are sending Stars Hollow names soaring. Lorelai is up 12 spots and Rory up 31. Among the boys, Christopher is up 4, Luke up 7, Richard up 29 and Dean up 31, which helps explain that name’s return to the top 100.

Not every name is riding the pop culture wave, though, and one has had a rough year. Between Taylor Swift’s wedding, Taylor Farms’ lettuce recalls and a two famous Taylors welcoming a baby with Taylor as the middle name, BabyCenter says parents are over it. For girls, Taylor dropped 24 spots to No. 399. For boys, it plummeted 262 spots to No. 1,093, falling out of the top 1,000 for the first time ever.

So back to that delivery room. Whatever name new parents are landing on, whether it’s a mythic hero, a rugged cowboy or a Stars Hollow favorite, chances are it’s already climbing the charts.

World.title: Elderly couple pleads not guilty to murdering son-in-law, a NYT executive, at local park
World.content:
The couple accused of killing their son-in-law, New York Times executive Jonathan McKinsey, pleaded not guilty to first-degree murder, a defense attorney said Monday.

Defense attorney Curtis Briggs argued that his client, Shili Chen, who is married to Shouyong Zhang, did not premeditate the shooting, NBC Bay Area reported. Instead, Briggs told NBC Bay Area that the couple, both 77, acted out of concern after seeing something disturbing while their son-in-law had a supervised visit with his children.

“My client was absolutely concerned for her own life and also concerned for her grandchildren,” Briggs told NBC Bay Area. Zhang is being represented by a public defender.

Alameda County prosecutors say Chen and Zhang watched and waited in a parking lot in Dublin, California, to attack McKinsey, who was embroiled in a bitter divorce and custody battle with their daughter.

Briggs said that McKinsey, 40, had previously threatened Chen’s life three times through a hit man. The couple purchased firearms in March to defend themselves, Briggs said, and were moved to act last month in the parking lot of a popular park.

“They are not cold-blooded killers. They didn’t premeditate anything,” Briggs told NBC Bay Area.

Briggs did not elaborate on what the elderly couple witnessed that drove them to kill their son-in-law.

If convicted, they could both face life in prison without the possibility of parole.

According to local police, 911 calls started coming in around 3 p.m. on Sept. 26 from terrified witnesses, many of whom were with their young children.

Several witnesses told police they saw a black Honda speeding out of the parking lot and later identified Chen and Zhang as the shooters, police said in a statement. Officers chased down the car and arrested the couple, according to the police report.

Nearly a decade’s worth of court documents revealed a deeply troubled marriage between McKinsey and his wife, Candice Jang, who has not been charged in connection with his death.

Jonathan McKinsey. via Facebook

McKinsey’s death followed years of violent struggle between Jang and McKinsey, who started dating in 2008 and were married in 2011, according to Jang’s petition for a domestic abuse restraining order. They had three children.

McKinsey had recently filed for divorce and was scheduled to appear in court the same week he died, according to court records.

In separate petitions for restraining orders, McKinsey and Jang each argued that the other was physically and mentally abusive during their marriage. McKinsey and Jang both said they wanted full custody of their children, but McKinsey had an ongoing child abuse case that granted him only supervised visits.

The children were living with Jang and her parents when McKinsey was shot.

He had been previously charged with two misdemeanors — cruelty to a child by endangering health and corporal injury to a child. McKinsey was freed on $50,000 bail and had been trying to enter a mental health diversion program, according to court records. Had he successfully completed the program, the charges would have been dismissed.

According to police reports, Zhang admitted to shooting McKinsey with his firearm during interviews with investigators. The husband and wife were each carrying weapons at the time of their arrests.

“Chen and the passenger carried out this shooting in a crowded park parking lot with blatant disregard for public safety where several children were present,” the arresting officer said.

McKinsey allegedly threatened to kill Chen at least three times, NBC Bay Area reported. A bail hearing was set for Nov. 4, followed by a pretrial hearing on Nov. 23.

World.title: 3 more Democrats slated to join summit on political future
World.content:
Nine days after next month's midterm elections, three prominent Democrats who are widely believed to have presidential ambitions will join other potential 2028 party contenders in Denver to discuss the future of the party.

Sens. Cory Booker of New Jersey and Chris Van Hollen of Maryland, as well as Rep. Ro Khanna of California, are among the latest additions who plan to join the "What's Next" summit, according to an updated list of attendees first shared with CBS News.

All three lawmakers identify as progressives, and all three have drawn national attention over their political ambitions in recent years. Booker ran for president in 2020 but dropped out before the first primary contests. Khanna has described himself as a "long-shot presidential candidate," and Van Hollen has acknowledged that he is "kicking the tires" on a possible 2028 run.

The three have also introduced tax plans that could be precursors to 2028 platforms.

The meeting will take place from Nov. 12 to 14, and is being hosted by Majority Democrats, a group formed last year by largely moderate elected officials and other high-profile Democrats who say they are "committed to reshaping and growing the Democratic Party."

Chaired by Rep. Jake Auchincloss of Massachusetts, the organization says it aims to take lessons from the 2026 races into the upcoming presidential election, in part by bringing together leading voices from across different factions within the party.

"Democrats have talked a big game about building a 'big tent' that can hold onto a majority. The sad reality is, we were all hat, no cattle when it came time to live up to those ideals," said Matt Corridoni, a spokesperson for Majority Democrats. "What's Next is an opportunity for Democrats from every wing of the party to have the open and often difficult conversations we need to win in 2028."

The three latest entrants join an initial lineup of other possible presidential candidates including former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg and Sens. Raphael Warnock of Georgia, Ruben Gallego of Arizona and Chris Murphy of Connecticut.

Govs. Abigail Spanberger of Virginia and Mikie Sherrill of New Jersey plan to attend, as well as other members of Congress and political strategists.

Democrats hope to win control of the House in November's midterm elections and carry the momentum into the 2028 presidential race.

Many feel the party has not settled on a political identity after losing the White House in 2024, and moderate and progressive Democrats disagree on the party's direction.That split has not helped the party win over voters: In a February CBS News poll, most voters described the Democratic Party as "weak."

Presidential contenders could begin launching their campaigns in the coming months, and some possible 2028 candidates have sought to raise their profile on the midterm trail, appearing alongside Democrats in key states. New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio Cortez and former Vice President Kamala Harris have both visited Michigan this fall to campaign with Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed. California Gov. Gavin Newsom campaigned in New Hampshire last weekend with Rep. Chris Pappas, who is in a tight race for Senate.

Organizers chose to hold the inaugural What's Next summit in Denver as it is one of the cities under consideration to host the 2028 Democratic National Convention. Over 2,000 people are expected to attend, according to a person familiar with the planning.

"Winning in 2028 will require us coming together to take the best ideas from every corner of the Democratic Party and forging them into an agenda that can build a durable majority and deliver for the American people," said executive director of Majority Democrats Rohan Patel.

World.title: Gun used in Bend school shooting was birthday gift from shooter's mom
World.content:
The gun used by a 16-year-old who shot and killed three children and a teacher at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon, last week was a birthday gift from the shooter's mom, sources told CBS News.

The Maverick 88 pump-action 12-gauge shotgun was purchased legally in August 2026 by Shauntai Nickerson, the mother of Griffin J. John II, and given to him for recreational use, the sources said.

In 2020, Nickerson told a local television station that her son, who was 10 years old at the time, had special needs and was struggling with remote learning during the pandemic. She told KTVZ, "It'll be great for my son to get back in there and get the help that he needs with the skilled teachers that he needs to get it from."

The shooter initially fired at a passing pickup truck, whose driver made the initial 911 call, before forcing his way into the school by shooting through the glass panes of a set of double doors, police said last week. He then went into the first classroom to the left of those doors, where he killed all four victims and wounded two others.

The children killed in the shooting were ages 5, 8 and 11, police said. The teacher who was killed was identified as 25-year-old Megan Lambert. The 5-year-old victim was identified by police and his family as Rhoam Summer. The families of the two other children have not made their names public, Bend police said.

Two wounded victims are a 7-year-old girl and a 54-year-old teacher.

Flowers and candles are placed at a makeshift memorial at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Ore., on Friday, Oct. 16, 2026, a day after a deadly shooting. (AP Photo/Haven Daley)

Police said Monday there were a total of nine people — four adults and five children — in the classroom at the time.

The shooter was shot and killed by a bystander, 36-year-old Kaylub Giamanco, who saw the first shooting with the pickup truck and followed the shooter into the school. Giamanco is a Bend resident with two daughters who attend Silver Rail Elementary School.

The suspect was a former student of Silver Rail Elementary, police said. No motive for the attack has been provided.

The Bend Police Department said Monday it expected to finish collecting evidence at the school by the end of the day, and would then turn the building back over to the school district.

Law enforcement sources previously told CBS News that investigators are combing through the computer, phone, social media, search history and other online activity of the attacker.

World.title: Trump announces $8 billion in diesel relief for U.S. farmers
World.content:
President Trump said his administration will provide $8 billion in aid to farmers hurt by record diesel prices.

"Tonight I'm also pleased to announce that the Department of Agriculture will be launching a new Harvest Fuel Relief program, providing our farmers with $8 billion in support to offset diesel costs during this harvest season," Mr. Trump said at a rally in Kansas Monday night.

"When Republicans win, we will pass even more funding for our farmers. We love our farmers," he added.

Earlier this month, Mr. Trump also signed an executive order to ease limits on the tax-free use of red-dyed diesel, a move aimed at lowering costs for farmers and truckers. That came after a $12 billion aid package for farmers announced by the Trump administration in December.

Farmers have faced financial pressures from soaring diesel prices, which are used to run agricultural machinery. Diesel reached a record of $6.53 a gallon on Sept. 22, although it's eased slightly since then, with average U.S. prices now at $6.32 a gallon, up from $3.62 a year ago, according to AAA data.

"This $8 billion investment will help bring certainty to our farmers during this harvest so they can continue to feed our nation," U.S. Department of Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins said in a statement.

Farmers would benefit more from a resolution in the U.S. war with Iran, which would likely result in lower energy prices, Gbenga Ajilore, chief economist at the nonpartisan Center on Budget and Policy Priorities and formerly a senior adviser in the Office of the Undersecretary for Rural Development at the Department of Agriculture, said in an email. Ending the Trump administration's tariffs would also help ease prices for farmers, he added.

"The president's economic aid to farmers ahead of the midterm elections follows a pattern dating back to his first term: He imposes policies that harm farmers, then spends taxpayer money to offset the damage his policies create," Ajilore said.

The USDA said the plan, called the Harvest Fuel Relief program, will pay farmers to cover part of their estimated losses for the 2026 crop year, using a standard formula. The calculation will use planted acreage reported to the Farm Service Agency, estimated production costs and crop yields and prices from the USDA's World Agricultural Supply and Demand Estimates report.

The agency said it will announce payment rates for major commodity crops in November, with details for other eligible products to follow. Farmers won't need crop insurance to qualify and can prepare to apply by creating a Login.gov account linked to USDA.

The USDA estimates that net farm income will drop 2.6% this year as production costs rise 4.5%. Fuel and oil expenses alone are expected to jump nearly 30%, according to a September forecast by the agency.

World.title: 2 men rearrested for alleged spying for Iran in U.K. air base incident
World.content:
British police said Tuesday they have rearrested two men on suspicion of assisting Iran's intelligence service over the suspected plot at a U.S.-run air base in England last month.

Counter Terrorism Policing said the men, a 24-year-old British national and a 25-year-old dual U.K.-Iranian national, were arrested under the National Security Act.

The men were earlier arrested but had been bailed pending more investigation.

Police are investigating a suspected terror plot on Sept. 27 against the U.S.-run base at RAF Fairford in western England, which has been used to bomb Iran during this year's war.

Scores of residents were evacuated from their homes near the base as armed police officers and army bomb-disposal experts swarmed the rural area. Police later said they had found a quantity of an accelerant - gasoline - in three vans at the site, but no explosives.

British authorities have linked Tehran to the incident, which led the U.S. to pull its bombers from RAF Fairford.

Five other men who were also arrested earlier remain on bail. No one has yet been charged.

Laurence Taylor, head of National Counter Terrorism Policing in the U.K., said detectives are looking at "many lines of enquiry involved in this hugely complex investigation."

"This is very much a live investigation, and our evidence gathering continues, but at this time our position remains the same; we consider it highly likely that there is Iranian state involvement," he said in a statement.

"Our investigators are continuing to examine what that level of involvement was and the ambition behind it," he added.

Iranian officials have said several times since the beginning of the war that any bases used to attack the country would be considered legitimate targets. But the Iranian Embassy in London said in a previous statement that the regime "categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations published by some British individuals and media outlets attempting to link Iran" to the incident.

Earlier this month, the U.S. Air Force removed all of its bombers from the air base following the security incident.

World.title: Egypt weighs sending troops to Saudi Arabia in war with Iran-backed rebels
World.content:
Cairo - Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi has asked the country's Parliament to authorize the military to help defend Saudi Arabia after Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels intensified their attacks on the kingdom, targeting airports and oil infrastructure.

Al-Sisi stressed that it would be a defensive mission and only if the kingdom requests assistance.

"Egypt will take any measures requested by Saudi Arabia to protect and defend it," al-Sisi said Saturday during a military graduation ceremony.

Under Egypt's Constitution, the president must consult the National Defense Council and obtain approval from two-thirds of Parliament before deploying the armed forces on a combat mission abroad.

On Sunday, al-Sisi chaired a meeting of the National Defense Council, which reviewed what the Egyptian presidency described as the "grave escalations unfolding in the region" and the "unacceptable attacks" against Saudi Arabia.

The council pledged to provide "all necessary and possible forms of support to the sisterly Kingdom of Saudi Arabia to defend its security and stability, and to safeguard its resources, territorial integrity, and Islamic holy sites."

Egypt has managed, so far, to stay out of all the recent military conflicts in the region and has tried to de-escalate and find political solutions. For some, this is one of al-Sisi's greatest achievements.

Egypt's President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi attends the Africa Forward Summit in Nairobi, Kenya, May 12, 2026. Ludovic Marin/AFP via Getty Images

But Samir Ragheb, a retired army brigadier and political and strategic analyst, told CBS News that it was time for Egypt to make good on commitments it had made to helping secure the region.

"Egypt has repeatedly pledged to support the security of the Gulf states and has issued numerous statements reaffirming this commitment," Ragheb said. "However, this is a time of war, not politics and statements. If Egypt fails to deliver on these promises, they will lose their meaning and amount to nothing more than empty threats."

"The Gulf states have invested billions of dollars in Egypt. Morally, it's Egypt's turn to return the favor," he said.

Parliament convened an emergency session on Sunday and was expected to approve the resolution on Tuesday, but the vote was postponed until next Monday.

The Egyptian Social Democratic Party instructed its parliamentary bloc to abstain from voting on the resolution, saying in a statement it had not received sufficient information about "the mission's scope, costs, and risks, as well as the arrangements in place to protect Egyptian forces."

Ragheb is certain the region is heading toward a more severe escalation.

"Egypt is not going to defend the kingdom against the Houthis," he said. "The threat is much bigger than the Houthis. This includes Iran, Iraqi militias and sleeper cells within the kingdom itself."

However, he also believes Egypt will lose much of its influence in the region if it doesn't intervene.

"If you want to be a regional player, you must play a role," he said. "Otherwise, you will lose your seat at the table."

Ragheb argued that the United States' refusal to attack the Houthis in support of Saudi Arabia created a vacuum that must be filled by others. He said Egypt should take on the Arab share of that role.

Other regional powers are also trying to fill the vacuum. In August, Saudi Arabia signed a joint defense agreement with Turkey and Pakistan known as the Mecca Accords.

"Even before Saudi Arabia asked for Egyptian support, the Mecca Accords was a death certificate for the idea of relying on America for any form of defense," Ragheb said.

World.title: Vanessa Kerry is the new WHO envoy for health resilience. What's on her to-do list?
World.content:
Vanessa Kerry is the new WHO envoy for health resilience. What's on her to-do list?

toggle caption i Joel Saget/AFP via Getty Images

Resilience is one of those buzzy buzzwords. But what does it mean, exactly? Bouncing back from tragedy? Conquering obstacles? Having the inner strength to follow a dream when the odds are against you?

For Dr. Vanessa Kerry, the definition is pretty straightforward. It boils down to being prepared. In the world of global health, she says, that means "strong systems, primary care and the ability to respond."

Those are the ideas that will guide her in her new job as special envoy for health resilience at the World Health Organization.

Sponsor Message

It's the latest addition to an impressive resume. Kerry was WHO's first special envoy for climate change and health, is director of global health and climate policy at Harvard School of Public Health and is the founder and CEO of Seed Global Health. That nonprofit group has been building resilience in lower-resource countries for over a decade, dispatching coaches and mentors to educate and train local healthcare students and practitioners as well as building financial and material resources.

Kerry's activism reflects seminal moments from her younger years. In grade school, she decided she wanted to become a doctor. At age 14, she traveled to Vietnam with her father, former Senator and Secretary of State John Kerry, and was deeply struck by the poverty she saw.

A high-risk delivery

Then came the crisis in Rwanda.

Between her third and fourth years in medical school, she spent time in a hospital in Rwanda. One day she was asked to "be a helping hand" with a woman's labor and delivery, working with a nurse.

Kerry said, "I'm a student." So that was the team — this medical student from the U.S. and a Rwandan nurse.

"The mother was pushing, but the baby was not advancing," Kerry remembers. "The shoulder had gotten stuck, and so we needed to do the maneuvers to help to deliver." She tried to remember everything she could from time spent in a "labor rotation a while back." There was no imaging, no specific training either she or the nurse had had for this type of situation.

Sponsor Message

"We were lucky," she says, "Because what we remembered worked." Mother and child survived.

Kerry, now 49, recalls: "I remember walking out of that room thinking, that was extremely distressing — more than that, extremely shocking and terrifying.

She could only conclude "this whole system doesn't work."

That harrowing delivery was the germ for Seed Global Health. She knew that many of her colleagues wanted to work to improve global health. But many of the opportunities involved flying in to perform certain procedures, then returning home.

"They made a contribution in that moment, but what then?"

When she returned to Boston from Rwanda to finish her residency at Massachusetts General, she began hatching the idea of working with the Peace Corps to send doctors and nurses to sub-Saharan Africa as medical educators to train health care workers who could then train others — building a country's internal health care system. Seed's collaboration with the Peace Corps lasted from 2012-2018, focusing on the development of country-led efforts at HIV/AIDS epidemic control.

Today, Seed is active in several sub-Saharan African countries for its training efforts. In Uganda, for example, Kerry says that her group has partnered with the Ministry of Health to build up emergency medicine by training 30 emergency medicine physicians. When an Ebola outbreak occurred there earlier this year, she says that these emergency physicians and other specialists were able to train over 3,000 health workers around the country in Ebola case management and infection prevention and control.

Seed, she says, has taught her that building resilience "is not a daunting task. If you train health workers, they can monitor and provide healthcare, they can provide surveillance, they can provide prevention."

Building responsive healthcare systems is what her new job is all about, she says. "We've been funding disease by disease and crisis by crisis. We can be thinking about this differently."

Sponsor Message

Her goal is not merely to jump in when a new outbreak occurs. "If a nation does not have a health system infrastructure in place, they will probably not be prepared to respond to the emergency. Resilience means building a system that will already be in place."

And it also means listening to local voices. "Countries know what their priorities are to care for their population," she says. As the resilience envoy, she wants to make sure there is ample funding so "we more effectively address the biggest burdens of disease."

Diane Cole writes for many publications, including The Wall Street Journal and The Washington Post. She is the author of the memoir After Great Pain: A New Life Emerges. Her website is DianeJoyceCole.com

For stories about life in our changing world, subscribe to NPR's Global Health newsletter.

World.title: DOJ charges 28 with voting crimes. And, TikTok ignored staff's child safety concerns
World.content:
DOJ charges 28 with voting crimes. And, TikTok ignored staff's child safety concerns

Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Today's top stories

The Justice Department has charged 28 green card holders in California with election crimes for allegedly illegally registering to vote or voting in U.S. elections. This marks a significant escalation in the Trump administration's feud with the state over its voting system as the midterm elections approach. The DOJ also filed an emergency request to prevent California from processing ballots returned by people on the voter rolls that the federal government says are "likely noncitizens." California has sought clarification on the federal government's conclusions but has not received any. Last week, the DOJ sued California and Los Angeles County after local officials refused to investigate allegations made by the administration about noncitizen voting.

toggle caption i Frederic J. Brown/AFP via Getty Images

🎧 The DOJ wants California to segregate ballots of those on its list and to delay counting them until investigations are complete. Election law experts doubt the DOJ will succeed, given its past attempts to change state voting processes, Miles Parks tells Up First. He adds that it would be surprising to see a shift just two weeks before the election with ballots already distributed. Research shows that in many cases, when legal permanent residents register to vote, it is due to a misunderstanding of the rules. Experts tell Parks they are concerned that federal law enforcement might use accusations to confiscate ballots during counting, but many local voting officials are preparing by keeping county attorneys on speed dial.

Sponsor Message

Democrats and Republicans are deciding which races to prioritize with Election Day just two weeks away. President Trump is campaigning in key perennial purple states like Georgia, North Carolina, Kansas, Iowa and Florida this week.



🎧 Trump's rally in Kansas and trip to North Carolina aren't where the leader of the Republican Party's attention should be, NPR's Stephen Fowler says. Kansas hasn't elected a Democratic senator in nearly a century, and many Republican groups have ceased ad spending in North Carolina, viewing the Senate race as a lost cause. Republicans are prioritizing efforts to save their Senate majority over saving the House majority, while Democrats are capitalizing on opportunities in conservative areas, Fowler says. In Georgia, with a million voters already casting ballots, Fowler says he sees an increase in Black voter turnout in the state and across the South.

Staff alerted management about minors engaging with sexual content, which the company profited from. They also identified loopholes that allowed users under 18 to bypass age restrictions and block parental oversight of their app activity. The records show that TikTok avoided conducting age surveys, fearing it would have to share results with the Federal Trade Commission.

Life advice

Andee Tagle/NPR

Cold and flu season in the U.S. starts this month and lasts through May, according ot the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Cooler temperatures and drier air can increase our vulnerability to illnesses like the common cold, flu, RSV and COVID-19. Get ahead of the game now by putting together a cold-and-flu prep kit. Here's what experts say you should have in your home.

🤒 Over-the-counter medications are good options, but always follow the recommended dosage to avoid risks or side effects. Some good medications to have include ibuprofen or naproxen, which can relieve headaches, body aches and sore throats by reducing inflammation and Acetaminophen, which can lower body temperature.

🤒 Honey acts as an anti-inflammatory and soothes the throat, making it useful for young children who can't take cough medicine. But don't give it to children under 12 months due to the risk of botulism.

🤒 A thermometer is a must-have for checking your temperature. For children 3 and under, a rectal option is preferred.

🤒 A saline spray or rinse for your nose can help keep the mucous membranes moist and help relieve symptoms by loosening thick mucus during a cold.

For more advice on how to stock your medicine cabinet for cold and flu season, listen to this episode of NPR's Life Kit. Subscribe to the Life Kit newsletter for expert advice on love, money, relationships and more.

Picture show

toggle caption i Lanna Apisukh for NPR

Pleasant Rowland launched Pleasant Company in 1986 with three dolls — Samantha, Molly and Kirsten — creating an empire known as American Girl. To celebrate its 40th anniversary, author Fiona Davis was asked to write a historical fiction book for adults titled Samantha: The Next Chapter, featuring Samantha Parkington, who has turned 25. The story picks up after Samantha's last book, in which she attended a suffragist rally with her aunt Cornelia. The book is set 15 years later, in 1920, just after the ratification of the 19th Amendment. Samantha learns that her grandmother's inheritance has been stolen, forcing her to transition from socialite to shopgirl overnight. NPR's Samantha Balaban visited the American Girl store in New York with her own Samantha doll to explore the character's evolution over the years, drawing on insights from its staff and Davis. Check out photos from the visit and read more about the history of American Girl dolls.

3 things to know before you go

toggle caption i BSIP/Universal Images Group/Getty Images

The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists has updated its menopause treatment guidelines for the first time since 2014. The group now recommends using hormone replacement therapy along with some other treatments to alleviate symptoms. A wedding day can be one of the costliest days in a couple's life. Some are opting to save money by choosing grocery-store cakes over specialty bakers' cakes. Vegemite is such an iconic breakfast spread in Australia that a convicted killer is suing the state of Victoria for the right to eat it in prison. The state has banned Vegemite because it could potentially be used to brew alcohol and throw off dogs.
