World.title: Fi Wi Land: Beyond the duppy stories, discover the value of Jamaica’s bats
World.content:
Often misunderstood and surrounded by folklore, bats are among nature’s hardest-working environmental protectors, helping to control insect populations, pollinate plants and disperse seeds. Discover more about these fascinating creatures as the Jamaica Observer in association with the National Environment and Planning Agency (NEPA) premieres ‘Fi Wi Land’ on Monday.

In the debut episode, host Carlysia Ramdeen is joined by NEPA Environmental Officer Damany Calder who shares insights about bats, their importance to Jamaica’s ecosystems and why they deserve greater appreciation.

The new 12-week environmental series by the Jamaica Observer and NEPA explores Jamaica’s unique wildlife, ecosystems and natural resources while highlighting efforts to protect the island’s environment for future generations.

Catch the premiere on the Jamaica Observer’s YouTube channel and other digital platforms.

World.title: Proud moment for Barnswells as husband and wife conferred with national award
World.content:
Councillor Scean Barnswell and wife Danielle pose for a photograph after receiving their Badge of Honour for Gallantry at the 2026 Ceremony of Investiture and Presentation of National Honours and Awards at King’s House on Monday, October 19. 2026. (Photo: Llewellyn Wynter)

It was a historic and proud moment for the Barnswell family from Clarendon, when the husband and wife team of Councillor Scean Barnswell and Danielle Anna-Marie Barnswell stood on the dais at King’s House Monday morning to accept their national award – the Badge of Honour for Gallantry, from Governor General Sir Patrick Allen.

The occasion was the 2026 Ceremony of Investiture and Presentation of National Honours and Awards.

The Barnswells were among 149 Jamaicans who were honoured for outstanding contributions in various fields.

The two were recognised for their “quick and courageous” actions that led to the rescue of a six-year-old girl who was reportedly abducted from the St Thomas More Preparatory School in May Pen Clarendon on December 9 last year.

“In growing up you’re told to mind your business but in Jamaica, the children are all our business so in this case I’m happy we did that and I wouldn’t change anything,” said Mrs Barnswell during rehearsals for Monday’s ceremony.

Scean Barnswell is the councillor for the Hayes division in the Clarendon Municipal Corporation and a former Mayor of May Pen. He is looking to return to that position as the balance of power in the corporation recently swung from the Jamaica Labour Party (JLP) to the Opposition People’s National Party (PNP).

This came after the JLP-elected councillor for the May Pen North division, Tanya-Lee Williams, resigned from the JLP, giving the PNP a clear 12-10 majority in the corporation. The PNP has stated that this gives it the right to appoint the mayor and deputy mayor but a court injunction granted last Friday has stalled those plans. The PNP has said it will be going back to court.

According to reports from December 2025, Barnswell and his wife spotted a man walking with a small child along Bustamante Highway and, sensing something was wrong, immediately intervened. Their actions resulted in the safe recovery of the child and the capture of the suspect, who was arrested by the police.

In a statement at the time, the PNP described the incident as an act of humanity, noting that Councillor Barnswell showed decisive, selfless leadership in a moment of crisis. The party said his response reflected the values of community vigilance and public service and urged others to do likewise.

WATCH: Barnswell honoured for rescuing abducted six-year-old

The PNP also expressed gratitude to members of the public who raised the alarm and commended the Jamaica Constabulary Force for its swift response.

“It emphasised the importance of strong community–police partnerships in protecting children and preventing crimes of this nature,” the party said.

-Lynford Simpson

World.title: US to offer Putin face-to-face talks with Zelenskyy and Trump
World.content:
Steve Witkoff will fly to Russia for discussions about peace proposals on Wednesday.

U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff will offer Vladimir Putin direct talks with President Donald Trump and Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy in an effort to secure a ceasefire.

The proposal for three-way leaders’ negotiations on a peace proposal, which would be the first such summit since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in 2022, was announced at a press conference following talks in Norway between Zelenskyy and Witkoff on Tuesday.

Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, who hosted the talks, said Witkoff will travel to Russia Wednesday and set out proposals for peace terms, including the idea of a three-way summit between the leaders. The meeting in Oslo came after days of high tensions between Ukraine and the U.S. president.

World.title: China threatens retaliation if UK follows the EU on tariffs
World.content:
A worker inspects an electric car at a Zeekr factory in Meishan Island in Ningbo, in China's eastern Zhejiang Province on April 18, 2025. | Hector Retamal/AFP via Getty Images

China urged Britain to follow World Trade Organization rules and warned it against copying Brussels’ approach, arguing that tariffs on Chinese EVs would be discriminatory.

LONDON — Beijing has threatened to retaliate if the U.K. raises tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles, aligning with the European Union.

Responding to POLITICO’s story that Britain was looking to act in “lockstep” with the bloc to counter China’s market dominance in electric cars, a spokesperson from the Chinese Ministry of Commerce said: “If the U.K. insists on imposing restrictions on Chinese electric vehicles, China will resolutely retaliate and safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese industries.”

The U.K. is currently working with its European partners to avoid a 10% electric vehicle tariff from the beginning of next year, when stricter rules of origin under the Brexit trade deal kick in.

World.title: French presidential race largely unaffected by unrest, first post-riot poll shows
World.content:
The poll was conducted online from 8 p.m. Saturday — after rioting and looting had begun — until Monday.

Le Pen remains well ahead of the pack with 34% to 38% of the vote in the various scenarios tested. Given France’s presidential election moves to a two-person runoff if no candidate obtains a majority of votes on the first round, the battle for second place is shaping to be the most crucial story of the election.

That fight looks like it will be a tight one.

Mélenchon’s position remains similar to what it was before Saturday, despite the attempt by the government and his opponents to tie him to the unrest. The Ifop Fiducial survey has him either in sole possession of second place or tied for it in the various scenarios tested, though his lead on his nearest competitors — center-right former Prime Minister Edouard Philippe and center-left MEP Raphaël Glucksmann — is in some cases within the margin of error.

“The first feedback we’ve had from the ground — including from areas where we’re not held in high regard — is that the tactic of blaming us for everything isn’t working,” said a high-level Mélenchon campaign operative, granted anonymity to discuss internal campaign analysis.

Paris prosecutor Laure Beccuau told broadcaster TF1 on Monday that she “absolutely [could] not confirm” the government’s analysis based on the profiles of those arrested and placed under investigation in the French capital so far.

World.title: 5 things the EU wants to change about its Arctic policy
World.content:
The EU plans to set up a pilot research project using satellite and maritime observation in 2027 and share ship-tracking data to help identify Russian shadow fleet vessels.

In the longer term, it wants EU countries to lead on a maritime security hub to pool intelligence on threats ranging from undersea cable sabotage to illegal fishing. It also calls for setting up an Arctic Cable Hub alongside NATO to monitor and protect subsea cables in the North Atlantic and the Arctic. The strategy lacks any information on funding for these projects, however.

Finnish MEP Mika Aaltola of the European People’s Party said the new focus on the Arctic is long overdue.

“Europe hasn’t been thinking about [the Arctic] enough,” Aaltola said. “Because of the ice melting and climate change, it’s becoming kind of the next great game. And if that happens, then what are the European positions when it comes to Russia, China and also the United States?”

2. Access to energy resources

The new policy sticks with EU promises not to drill for fossil fuels in the Arctic.

“The EU remains committed to ensuring that oil, coal and gas stay in the ground, including in Arctic regions,” it reads. Instead, Brussels promises to develop renewable energy projects in the region but drops an old commitment to convince the rest of the world to follow its lead.

World.title: Kallas buys time on EU response to US sanctions against the ICC
World.content:
Multiple lawmakers continued to push for a faster response in a plenary session in Strasbourg. But while Kallas acknowledged their calls, she said the EU executive would take time "to analyze the full legal implications, to open dialogue and look for solutions." The sanctions are expected to be implemented after a 180-day delay starting from Oct. 9.

U.S. President Donald Trump's administration had already targeted nine judges and the chief prosecutor of the Court, cutting them off from all U.S. service providers, including banking services.

Irish European Affairs Minister Thomas Byrne, who represents Dublin's presidency of the Council of the EU, told lawmakers that the sanctions delay provides "an opportunity for dialogue, which we should take advantage of while remaining ready to take all necessary measures," as laid out by EU leaders in a statement issued after their gathering last week.

Washington is openly campaigning to dismantle the ICC “brick by brick,” and urging countries to quit the court’s founding charter. Kallas said that "decisions by Niger, Mali, Burkina Faso, Chad and Venezuela to reject or even withdraw from the ICC risk eroding the foundations of global justice."

"The ICC is under attack at precisely the moment when we need it the most," Kallas said, citing the Court's investigations of Russian war crimes in Ukraine. The EU will continue to engage with partners to strengthen the court, she said, warning countries under pressure from the U.S. to leave the body: “This also has clear consequences for their relationship with the European Union.”

"The European Union has practical means to do more," Kallas said, adding that she would be in the Hague this week.

World.title: Government expected to approve Jackdaw gas field on Wednesday
World.content:
An oil rig is seen off the coast of Scotland on April 24, 2026. | Andy Buchanan/AFP via Getty Images

Developers have been waiting for a fresh decision on the controversial gas field since January 2025.

LONDON — The government is set to approve Jackdaw, a major proposed gas field off the coast of Scotland, on Wednesday.

One senior government official and two people briefed on the plans told POLITICO they believed an announcement was planned for Wednesday. The official and one of the two people said it was expected in the early morning.

Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh is scheduled to sign off the environmental statement, overseen by the Offshore Petroleum Regulator for Environment & Decommissioning. The North Sea Transition Authority is also expected to rubber stamp the project's field development plan.

World.title: Rubio insists the US isn’t trying to hurt Ukraine
World.content:
Rubio's comments come as Russia escalates its attacks and Washington moves toward positions more favorable to Moscow, raising European concerns that the U.S. is not a dependable source of support for Ukraine.

Rubio was speaking shortly after the EU’s top diplomat Kaja Kallas accused Washington of trying to force Ukraine to surrender to Russia. "American negotiators have been trying to push Ukraine into surrender for already almost two years," she told the European Parliament on Tuesday morning.

On military equipment, Rubio said Ukraine's urgent appeals for more interceptors for Patriot air defense systems had to be balanced against U.S. needs — which are trying to restock thanks to the war against Iran— as well as the demands of other allies.

"I know one of the things that President Zelenskyy has been talking about is that he's been trying to buy interceptors. And I understand. So does every other country in the world," Rubio said. "I also talked to Saudi Arabia today. They'd like interceptors. Israel would like interceptors. We would like interceptors. Every country in the world would like interceptors."

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Monday accused the U.S. of holding back on sending air-defense missiles paid for by allies under the NATO-led Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List program.

“Unfortunately, the Pentagon is delaying the delivery of missiles that our partners have already paid for through the program PURL,” Zelenskyy said during a video briefing to U.S. lawmakers.

World.title: Romania’s political crisis gets 6-month truce as new government formed
World.content:
The new deal keeping the government afloat expires in six months, and parties will need to renegotiate the pact with no agreement yet on what comes next.

During this period, the Social Democrats will try to pass an investment-focused 2027 budget by the end of November, steering Bucharest away from austerity, party leader Sorin Grindeanu told POLITICO Playbook Capitals in an interview.

“Romania needs an economic recovery plan, not austerity,” he said. “Our priorities are protecting purchasing power and supporting business, restarting public investment, and improving essential public services.” Grindeanu added that he aims to revise the 2026 budget by the end of October and to fast-track implementation of EU projects to unblock funds.

The Social Democrats in May teamed up with AUR to topple the coalition government led by centrists and centre-right liberals, as unpopular debt-cutting reforms drove Social Democrat voters toward the populist right. PNL and USR have refused to govern with the Social Democrats again.

The formation of the new government makes snap elections harder to trigger once the six-month deal expires, as Romania’s constitution requires two failed attempts to install a government before Parliament can be dissolved.

Grindeanu hopes to persuade his former coalition partners to reunite in six months, but with a different economic program. Fearing an uptick in support for the far right, he wants to avoid further cuts.

World.title: Investment summit: German government strikes AI deal with Nvidia
World.content:
Shortly before the investment summit in Berlin, Nvidia boss Jensen Huang delivered a slap in the face to Germany. It pained him, he said, to see how far this economically advanced country had fallen behind. And the 63-year-old CEO of the world’s most valuable company offered what he sees as sidelined Germany one piece of advice: "Just get to work!" (in German: "Macht euch einfach an die Arbeit!")

 

Yet Jensen Huang apparently still believes in Germany. During a fireside chat with Chancellor Friedrich Merz, an important AI deal was agreed, according to media reports. As first reported by Handelsblatt, the federal government plans to contribute a nine-figure sum to the partnership.

The combination of German engineering expertise and state-of-the-art AI technology is intended to give Germany’s business location lasting strength, Merz and Huang stressed.

Amazon to invest 16 billion euros in Germany

Another US conglomerate, internet giant Amazon, is planning to invest around 16 billion euros in Germany in 2027, as was also announced at the investment summit in Berlin. One third of the money is to be channelled into expanding data centres for Amazon’s cloud provider AWS.

According to Amazon, around 3,000 employees already work for its cloud services subsidiary AWS in Germany. The planned 4.8 billion euros for AWS in Germany will be invested mainly in the Frankfurt am Main region.

Companies urged to make their data available to AI

Nvidia says it invested almost one billion dollars in Germany in 2025. The US company, headquartered in California, holds stakes in numerous German start-ups and established firms. Huang repeatedly emphasises that data must be treated as a national resource that should not be exported but used to develop a "national intelligence".

Around a dozen German companies are expected to join the government-backed project with Nvidia – including Siemens, Audi and AI start-up Black Forest Labs from Freiburg im Breisgau.

Chancellor Merz called on companies in Germany to open up their industrial data for artificial intelligence, in order to safeguard the competitiveness of sectors such as the car industry. Preserving Germany’s industrial base is a crucial advantage over other economies, the CDU leader argued.

Did Friedrich Merz manage to win over leather-jacket fan Jensen Huang with his praise of traditional German virtues?

In Berlin the chancellor actually said: "Germans are considered hard-working, they go to bed early and get up before sunrise. (...) On holiday we are the first on the beach and spread out our towels before breakfast. And when we agree delivery dates, we keep to them."

On the beach in Travemünde – how is Germany’s economy doing? Michael Probst/Copyright 2026 The AP. All rights reserved

Most recently, the outlook for the German economy had brightened slightly. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) now expects growth of 1.3 percent in Germany in 2026, after previously forecasting only 0.7 percent. Whether the further upswing will materialise thanks to investment by US tech giants remains to be seen.

World.title: EU Parliament approves standard form for claiming refunds on disrupted travel
World.content:
The European Parliament has approved, by an almost unanimous vote, new rules to protect passengers when their travel is disrupted.

 

Travellers across the EU will be able to claim a refund using a standard form, which will be made available on the European Commission’s website in all EU languages and will cover all modes of transport.

Passengers are entitled to a full refund within 14 days and intermediaries such as travel agents or online booking platforms are included in the reimbursement obligations, which was not clear in the previous legislation.

If an intermediary does not provide the reimbursement in the time due, the airline is obliged to step in and make the payment to the passenger concerned.

"We are prioritising the rights of our citizens over the profits of airlines,” said Italian Socialist Matteo Ricci, the MEP in charge of the regulation.

The rules also strengthen the rights of people with disabilities: where necessary, a companion will be able to travel with them on a flight free of charge, as is already the case on buses, trains and ships.

The regulation passed with 652 votes in favour, two against and eight abstentions. It builds on a major overhaul of air passenger rights adopted in July, which made refunds easier to obtain and requires airlines to include one free item of hand luggage in the fares displayed online.

World.title: France's Macron begins state visit to Qatar as part of wider Gulf tour
World.content:
Qatar’s Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani welcomed French President Emmanuel Macron with full state honours, including cannon salvos and a cavalry procession, as he began his two-day state visit to the Gulf nation on Tuesday.

 

After the official welcome ceremony, the two leaders held talks at Lusail Palace on strengthening the strategic ties between France and Qatar, which include energy security, defence and regional stability as well as investments and cooperation in multiple fields.

Macron was received at Hamad International Airport by Qatar’s Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of State for Defence Affairs, Sheikh Saoud bin Abdulrahman bin Hassan Al Thani, after fighter jets escorted his plane on arrival as part of the state visit honours, followed by a state motorcade procession through Doha towards Lusail Palace.

Macron's state visit to Qatar concludes his regional Gulf tour to develop the strategic partnerships also with the United Arab Emirates, Kuwait and Bahrain, where the French leader secured pledges of additional energy supplies from Gulf partners.

The tour has already produced commitments for additional diesel. The French presidency said France had secured pledges for an extra 200,000 tonnes a month from the UAE and Bahrain, around 100,000 tonnes from each.

Including supplies from Saudi Arabia, the commitments totalled 295,000 tonnes a month, equivalent to just over 10% of French consumption, the Élysée said.

In a speech to the French nation on Sunday after a weekend of violent protests that engulfed France, Macron said he would travel to the Gulf countries to secure France’s energy supplies and to address the grievances over fuel prices and the cost of living, while his government worked with fuel distributors to ensure those efforts translated into lower prices for consumers.

Energy security and regional ties

French business leaders are part of the French delegation to the state visit in Qatar, including TotalEnergies chief executive Patrick Pouyanné. The French energy company already has substantial interests in Qatar, including a partnership with QatarEnergy in the North Field East gas expansion project.

Qatar’s foreign ministry said Tuesday’s talks would be followed by a strategic dialogue on Wednesday to discuss "many regional matters of mutual concern,” covering energy, the economy, investment and defence.

Speaking at a briefing in Doha, the ministry’s director of media and communication, Ibrahim bin Sultan Al Hashmi, described France as a friend and ally and underlined its position during the ongoing regional crisis.

France was among Qatar's main defenders during the Iran war, securing the Gulf country's air defence with fighter jets and other capabilities.

The visit also builds on wider investment ties. During the Emir’s 2024 state visit to France, Qatar pledged €10 billion in investment across sectors including energy transition, artificial intelligence, aerospace, and healthcare.

World.title: IRGC mines set tankers ablaze as Tehran threatens expanded attacks
World.content:
Iran's IRGC said two oil tankers struck mines the elite paramilitary had laid in the Strait of Hormuz, setting both vessels ablaze, as Tehran threatened further attacks on shipping and cutting undersea cables while promising to unveil new weapons in its arsenal.

 

The IRGC said in a statement that the tankers tried to use what Iran unilaterally designates an unauthorised route through the strait's southern section, near the Omani coast.

"With the explosion of mines laid by the IRGC Navy in the illegal passage south of the Strait of Hormuz, two offending tankers were set on fire and brought to a standstill," the IRGC statement said. Neither vessel was named nor was the precise location disclosed.

Tehran has no recognised authority under international maritime law to restrict or authorise passage through the Strait of Hormuz, which is subject to the right of transit passage under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea.

The UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) reported on Tuesday that it had received an account of "an incident between an oil tanker and military forces" on Monday, some 121 nautical miles east of the Omani city of Duqm. UKMTO reported no damage or casualties and did not identify the vessel.

The IRGC also claimed that their air defence system had shot down a US MQ-9 drone over the strait on Monday night. A US official, speaking to US media outlets, dismissed the claim as untrue.

Some Iranian domestic outlets, including the state-affiliated Fars agency, reported that a US airstrike hit a naval base in Konarak in Sistan and Baluchistan province on Monday, wounding two military personnel and targeting an air defence installation. Washington has not commented on the report.

IRGC spokesperson Hossein Mojabi threatened on Monday to target undersea internet cables in the Gulf and the strait, saying "new weapons will be unveiled" with the aim of, in his words, removing US military presence from the region.

'We do not leave any blow unanswered'

Iran's foreign ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei said Tehran would retaliate against any US attack.

"In practice we have shown that we absolutely do not leave any blow unanswered," he said in response to reports that Washington had urged Iran to hold back in the event of a strike on Kuh Kalang.

"A US attack on Kuh Kalang and Iran not responding is fantasy and empty talk," Baghaei said.

The IRGC-affiliated Tasnim news agency quoted an unnamed Iranian security source as saying uncertainty over decision-making authority in Washington was complicating negotiations, naming Vice President JD Vance, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Trump administration negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner as figures whose respective roles remained unclear to Iranian officials.

Arsenio Dominguez, secretary-general of the International Maritime Organisation, said about 6,000 seafarers have been stranded in the strait since the war began. He criticised shipowners for continuing to send crews into the area.

US media have previously reported that the Pentagon was deploying the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group and the 13th Marine Expeditionary Unit to the Middle East, adding approximately 10,000 sailors and Marines to the region by the end of November. Washington has not confirmed the deployment.

Roughly one-fifth of the world's oil passed through the Strait of Hormuz before the war that began with US-Israeli strikes on Iran in late February. Both Tehran and Washington have implemented blockades in the strait, while Iran has repeatedly targeted cargo vessels using the southern section of the waterway.

World.title: Latest news bulletin | October 20th, 2026 – Evening
World.content: Catch up with the most important stories from around Europe and beyond in this Euronews news bulletin. In just a few minutes, our newsroom brings you the latest news and breaking news across world affairs, business, politics, culture, entertainment and travel, with the context you need to make sense of a fast-moving day. Reported with the independence and the European perspective that define Euronews, this regular round-up gives you a clear and reliable overview of the stories shaping our world right now, wherever you are watching from.

World.title: France vows 'massive' security operation involving military forces for expected weekend protests
World.content:
French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said on Tuesday that a "massive" security operation would be in place during further expected protests on Saturday after cost-of-living demonstrations turned violent across France over the weekend.

 

Speaking to parliament on Tuesday, Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez also announced plans to deploy military forces from Operation Sentinelle to free up police and gendarmes for the expected demonstrations.

Nuñez said their mission would be "to replace internal security forces mainly on static guarding duties" in order to "free up police officers and gendarmes to carry out public-order missions."

Operation Sentinelle, launched in January 2015, has 10,000 soldiers deployed across France to defend against potential terrorist attacks.

Troops are usually stationed outside sites deemed sensitive, such as places of worship, schools, tourist locations, railway stations and airports. Sentinelle soldiers have previously deployed at events such as the Paris 2024 Olympics and the Paralympic Games.

Nuñez added that the aim on Saturday would be for security forces to operate with increased "responsiveness and mobility" in order to deal with "scattered" and "extremely mobile" groups.

A soldier from Operation (Photo AP/Christophe Ena)

The interior minister said he was also "considering the possibility of banning demonstrations that have not been declared and that could lead to public disorder."

Demonstrations declared to the prefecture, as is required, could also be affected, but only where "the organiser or the security team do not give us reason to believe that the demonstration will not get out of hand."

With regard to demonstrations that do not pose a risk to public order, Nuñez said it was "essential to prioritise routes away from public buildings and high streets," as well as to "step up intelligence-gathering efforts in order to identify as accurately as possible the number of participants, particularly the most radical ones, so that security measures can be adapted accordingly."

The minister also promised to show "resolve," adding: "We will be there."

World.title: Qatar revamped its entire defence system in six hours, intelligence chief reveals
World.content:
In a rare public appearance, Qatar’s head of the Intelligence and Security Authority Brigadier General Khalid Mohammed Al-Nuaimi revealed how Qatar took the dramatic decision to redeploy its entire defensive systems in just six hours to counter Iran's war threats.

 

Addressing the Global Security Forum in Doha on Tuesday, Al-Nuaimi said the redeployment was “unprecedented and successful”, based on eight months of adapting Qatar’s forces, defence capabilities, and military doctrine, which had been built for a totally different threat landscape.⁠ ⁠

When asked about Qatar’s response to countering drones during the war, Qatar’s head of Intelligence replied that the six-hour overhaul was based on fast-moving changes to Qatar’s defence systems, both at concept level, but also in the allocation of defence assets.

“We adapted. we redeployed and we did it within six hours,” Al-Nuaimi revealed, adding that “we were caught off guard, yet we adapted rapidly, out of sheer necessity.”

Also during the Global Security Forum, Qatar’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson Dr Majed al-Ansari said the Qatar-mediated US-Iran negotiations “are ongoing and we are seeing engagement from both parties.”

“The fact that we are not hearing about it is a good sign that we are doing our job properly,” the Qatari diplomat added amid the rising tensions and concerns that the Iran war may restart.

Washington's fundamental shift in the Middle East

In addressing those worrying concerns, US ambassador to Turkey and Special Presidential Envoy for Syria and Iraq Tom Barrack told the forum that "America wants a peace deal” which would be based on “ceasefire in the straits” as well as a focus on “easing the pain on the Iranian people”.

"Prosperity is the only answer," Barrack underlined as a way out of the current standoff, adding that "we don’t need a reboot" of the previous US-Iran peace memorandum.

He identified the obstacle to a deal as a “lack of trust.”

“What has happened from the beginning of these discussions and negotiations is a lack of trust," Barrack explained, which comes down to the fact that the "IRGC does not trust the US. And the US does not trust IRGC."

The US envoy said he did not know if the Iran war was a mistake but admitted that it had “unintended consequences” and that US President Donald Trump is a "no forever wars president."

Barrack told the forum in Qatar that the US will not leave the Middle East, even if in the region “what everybody is saying: OK, I cannot rely on America to solve all my problems,” explaining that “the bargain is not to control, but to not leave. We are not leaving.”

"America is the guarantor to the world for the last 80 years and it is no longer there," the US diplomat said, explaining that "what is happening in this administration is not an abandonment, it is a message for realignment."

The US envoy appeared to contradict one of the US administration’s declared goals in launching the Iran war, which was regime change in Tehran.

Barrack spoke broadly about how the US pursued 23 regime changes across the Middle East and concluded that "every time we try and intervene, change the person or the regime, it seems to have been a mistake."

Instead, he said, the US’ goal is to "bring everybody, put them in a tent, give them coffee, put the guns and daggers on the table, and let’s figure something else out," through “patience, presence, dialogue."

In this context, the top US diplomat also commented on the escalating tensions between Israel and Turkey, saying that "my belief is Israel is way too smart to actually pick a real fight with Turkey. I don’t think Israel wants that, I know Turkey does not want that."

'Houthis are here to stay,' former MI6 chief says

Meanwhile at the forum, Qatar’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson Dr al-Ansari also reiterated his country’s position on Yemen that alongside the other Gulf nations “Qatar is supporting our brothers in Saudi Arabia in defending their sovereignty against this attack.”

Also commenting on the Yemen war, the former head of the UK’s foreign intelligence agency MI6 Sir John Sawers told the Doha Global Security Forum that “the Houthis are here to stay.

"They are not going to be defeated, and they are going to remain in control of a large part of Yemen for the foreseeable future," Sawers said.

"The Houthis have got their own national Yemen agenda," he explained, adding that the group "exposed the limited options that Saudi Arabia has in terms of dealing with" them over the last 10 years, as their efforts "to sustain an alternative government (in Yemen) have not been successful over the last 10 years."

World.title: Tourist attractions shut and cattle starving: How El Niño is wreaking havoc around the world
World.content:
From starving cattle in parched El Salvador to a "terrifying" threat to the world's coral reefs, this year's exceptionally strong El Niño is being felt across the globe.

 

The natural weather phenomenon occurs when sea temperatures in the Eastern Pacific Ocean become unusually warm, which happens roughly every two to seven years.

Previous El Niño events have contributed towards record-breaking heat, fuelling long-standing droughts, flash floods and deadly wildfires across the globe.

While most El Niño events increase global average temperatures by around 0.2°C – enough to trigger extreme weather across the Global South – it is a fraction of the additional human-caused warming from climate change.

Here is how this year's so-called 'Super El Niño' is playing out around the world.

FILE - A fish swims through a coral reef in the Dutch Cays of Guna Yala on Panama's Caribbean coast, Aug. 25, 2026. AP Photo/Matias Delacroix, File

El Niño threatens coral reefs and forests

This year's El Niño adds "a terrifying level of additional risk" for the world's coral reefs, according to David Obura, chair of the UN's expert nature panel.

Corals are highly sensitive to heat, and climate change is already making bleaching events more frequent and intense.

The fourth global bleaching event and this year's El Niño have put corals in even greater jeopardy.

Obura led a major reassessment of coral health, published in the science journal Nature, that found reef-building species had deteriorated sharply since the last global census in 2008, with 44 per cent threatened with extinction.

Forests are also at risk. Global deforestation slowed last year, according to the independent Forest Declaration Assessment, but the gains are unlikely to last as conditions worsen in Central Africa and El Niño raises fire risks across the tropics.

Livestock suffer as drought strikes El Salvador

Drought fuelled by El Niño is wreaking havoc across Central America's Dry Corridor, which stretches from Mexico to Panama.

In El Salvador, where August temperatures were 4.3°C above normal, livestock are suffering the impacts.

"Imagine how thin this little animal is! Why? Because of a lack of grass," says Antonio Aguilar, a 54-year-old rancher, pointing to a cow reduced to skin and bones at a livestock market in Sensuntepeque.

The El Niño, expected to peak by year's end, is unfolding amid accelerating human-caused warming, which amplifies its effects. A warmer atmosphere dries out soil, deepening drought, and holds more moisture, making rains more extreme.

A tourist stands on a walkway overlooking Iguazu Falls in Foz do Iguacu, Brazil, Friday, Oct. 16, 2026. AP Photo/Jorge Saenz

Heavy rain closes Iguazu Falls

Extreme downpours fuelled by El Niño caused the Iguazu River to flow at six times the normal rate last week. Park authorities in Argentina responded by closing tourist trails, including the walkway to the Devil’s Throat, the largest and most dramatic of the Iguazu Falls' cascades.

South America, the southern US, East Africa and Central Asia have all experienced heightened flood risks during previous El Niño events.

In Argentina's northeast, tthe Paraná River rose to a dangerous 4.7 metres on 15 October, prompting evacuations in nearby towns. Flooding has also forced thousands from their homes in Paraguay and Uruguay.

Vidanaarachchige Wimalasuriya sits under a tree in his paddy field, where his crops failed weeks ago due to drought in Medirigiriya, Sri Lanka, Sunday, Sept. 13, 2026. AP Photo/Eranga Jayawardena

Global poverty risks stoked by extreme weather

UN development chief Alexander De Croo warns that El Niño, combined with surging energy costs and higher interest rates, could push millions into poverty as the vulnerable are hit by crisis after crisis.

In particular, severe drought linked to El Niño is affecting more than half of Sudan – where conflict is already fuelling famine – causing localised crop failures and depriving households of food and income.

Many staple imports, such as maize and beans, could also put Europe's food security at risk, according to the IHE Delft Institute for Water Education in the Netherlands.

While El Niño is out of our control, human-caused warming can be minimised by cutting emissions. De Croo urges private investors to recognise both the "economic cost" of climate change and the "business case" for tackling it.

Sri Lanka's central bank warns that El Niño could undermine the island's fragile recovery from its worst economic crisis in decades, with torrential rains forecast through December and prolonged drought early next year.

Will this year's El Niño be record-breaking?

How this El Niño ranks depends on how it is measured, and agencies' differing methods make direct comparisons difficult.

Britain's Met Office calls it "unprecedented" and Japan's weather agency calls it the strongest ever observed, but US forecasters have not declared a record – yet.

The strongest El Niño year in NOAA's dataset is 1982. The agency says the current event will likely surpass it.

"By any measure, we are looking at a very strong El Niño," says climate scientist Emily Becker of the University of Miami. She adds that only once it is over will scientists know "where it fits in the context of history".

Because climate change is warming oceans everywhere, the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) now measures how warm or cool the east-central Pacific is compared with the rest of the tropical ocean. That difference is what drives global weather impacts.

How do a few degrees of warming in the Pacific exert so much influence?

Under NOAA's updated index, a 2.5°C anomaly in a key Pacific region relative to the rest of the tropical ocean, sustained over three months, would make for the most intense El Niño on record.

That might not sound like much, but the El Niño-Southern Oscillation is the leading natural driver of year-to-year climate variability.

Shifts in where the ocean releases heat into the atmosphere ripple across global weather, leaving some regions cooler and wetter and others hotter and drier. These effects are known as "teleconnections".

But while El Niños, and their opposite number La Niñas, when the equatorial Pacific is colder than normal, load the dice toward certain outcomes, they do not guarantee them.

World.title: Lebanon faces uncertainty as UNIFIL mandate nears end
World.content:
As UN peacekeeping forces prepare to withdraw from Lebanon, Israel remains present and Hezbollah is still armed. A new EU support mission aims to strengthen Lebanon's army, but will not replace UN peacekeepers.

As the mandate of the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon, or UNIFIL, nears its end, uncertainty over the future of southern Lebanon is growing. Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam has warned of the need to "avert the vacuum that UNIFIL's withdrawal could create, were it to take place without agreement on a new international force to replace it."

The Lebanese government has also been pushing for a last-minute extension of UNIFIL's mandate, but so far without success. It is most likely that the 7,565 peacekeepers from 46 countries will begin withdrawing from the UN-patrolled so-called Blue Line zone on December 31, 2026.

The Blue Line, which stretches for 120 kilometers (75 miles), is a UN-identified line of withdrawal between Israel and Lebanon, not an internationally agreed border. It was established in 2000. However, as early as in 1978, multinational UNIFIL troops were deployed to this region to monitor the area after Israel invaded Lebanon in response to attacks by Palestinian armed groups.

After the 2006 Israel-Hezbollah war, the mandate was expanded to support the Lebanese army in implementing UN Security Council Resolution 1701. The resolution calls for an area between the Blue Line and the Litani River to be free of armed personnel, assets and weapons other than those belonging to the Lebanese government and UNIFIL. It also calls for the withdrawal of Israeli forces from southern Lebanon.

However, following cross-border attacks by Hezbollah in October 2023 and the ensuing war in 2024, Israel has been occupying large swaths of Lebanese territory in a self-declared security zone called the Yellow Line, which is located north of the Blue Line.

Of the more than 1.2 million people displaced in Lebanon during the renewed conflict in 2026, around 329,000 remained internally displaced as of September 29, according to the International Organization for Migration. Israel has also caused extensive destruction to homes and key infrastructure in southern Lebanon, saying it needs to protect its citizens in northern Israel from attacks launched from the area.

Hezbollah — which is designated as a terrorist organization by several countries, including the United States and Germany, while the European Union designates its armed wing as a terrorist organization — continues to reject disarmament, citing the need to defend itself for as long as Israeli forces remain in Lebanon.

Hezbollah is also closely linked to Iran, and in case of renewed conflict between Iran and Israel, it's likely that Hezbollah would open a second front in Israel's north in support of Iran.

Around 1.2 million people were displaced in Lebanon this year. However, the majority have since returned to their homes in the south Image: Mohammed Zaatari/AP Photo/picture alliance

"The situation in southern Lebanon remains tense," Kandice Ardiel, UNIFIL's spokesperson, told DW. "We are seeing continued Israeli military operations, including overflights of Lebanese airspace by jets, helicopters and drones, airstrikes, artillery strikes and mortar fire."

"Until our mandate ends on December 31, we continue to monitor and report what is happening, and we are liaising between the parties on a daily basis to ensure safe movements of civilians, humanitarian aid, and peacekeeping patrols," she said, adding that the drawdown and withdrawal would then take place in stages.

The end of the mandate also means the end of the mission for thousands of UNIFIL troops in southern Lebanon. "People have built careers, friendships, skills and a sense of purpose together," Ardiel said. "Endings are never easy, especially when there is a sense that the work we do is still needed."

Beirut's lack of authority, money compounds disarmament dilemma

The upcoming withdrawal of UNIFIL also highlights two major dilemmas for Lebanon's government.

"Beirut is concerned that violations of any agreements, whether on the Israeli or the Hezbollah side, can't be tracked in the absence of an international military force," Paul Shaya, a Washington-based Middle East researcher and adjunct professor at George Washington University, told DW.

Furthermore, after years of political deadlock, the COVID-19 pandemic, soaring inflation and economic crises, the Beirut port blast in 2020 and the destruction caused by the 2024 war between Israel and Hezbollah, Lebanon's economic lifeline depends on international funding. However, a large share of the much-needed investment from the United States and Gulf states is tied to Hezbollah's disarmament.

"Ultimately, it is going to be dependent on President Joseph Aoun and Prime Minister Nawaf Salam to secure sufficient funding and resources to support the Lebanese military," said Shaya.

Can Lebanon's peace experiment work? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Until that happens, Aoun and Salam have very limited options for disarming Hezbollah, said David Wood, Lebanon researcher at the International Crisis Group. "They have opened direct talks with Israel to bring about an end to the disastrous conflict, but that process includes neither Hezbollah nor its backer Iran — both of which oppose the group's disarmament," he said.

In Wood's view, Beirut has few bargaining chips in negotiations with Israel because it has been unable to secure Hezbollah's compliance. He is also worried that Lebanon's leaders have little leverage to force Hezbollah to surrender its weapons, as this could trigger a deadly domestic conflict in the country. In the past, Hezbollah has openly warned that trying to seize its weapons by force would lead to war.

Despite Israel's destruction of many Hezbollah tunnels and weapons-storage facilities in Hezbollah-dominated areas in southern Lebanon and parts of Beirut, the limitation or disruption of supply routes due to the wider Iran war, as well as the fall of their ally, Syrian President Bashar Assad, observers say Hezbollah remains better equipped than the Lebanese armed forces.

Could the new EU mission replace UNIFIL in Lebanon?

On October 12, European Union foreign ministers agreed to establish a European Union Support Mission in Lebanon, or EUSM Lebanon, with an initial three-year mandate.

"It has a civilian and military pillar," EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said, adding that "this is highly welcomed by the local authorities."

The Iran-backed Hezbollah group maintains a political arm as well as a military arm in Lebanon Image: Hussein Malla/AP Photo/picture alliance

According to the European Council, the mission is to contribute to peace and security in Lebanon by strengthening the capabilities of the Lebanese armed forces and internal security forces, including in border security in accordance with the UN Security Council Resolution 1701.

However, the mission is not intended to replace UNIFIL. Rather than deploying peacekeepers to patrol southern Lebanon, it is set to initially operate north of the Litani River.

Several existing UNIFIL contributors, including Italy, France, Spain, Ireland, Germany, Austria, Finland and Poland, already expressed interest in contributing personnel and resources to the new EUSM Lebanon mission.

For the government in Beirut, this is a positive signal, noted Shaya. He added that Lebanese society also strongly supports the Lebanese military, "which many see as the only institution in the country that can uphold Lebanon's sovereignty and represent the entire country."

World.title: Sudan drone strike kills around 150 in Abyei market
World.content:
A drone strike hit a market in the Abyei border region disputed by Sudan and South Sudan and killed dozens. The drone caused a large fire when it hit a fuel depot. South Sudanese officials blamed Sudan's military.

A drone strike in a busy market in the disputed region of Abyei has killed more than 150 people, according to local officials.

South Sudanese officials blamed Sudan's military for the attack, without providing evidence, amid the long-running civil war between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) militia, which is reportedly active in the Abyei area.

The special UN mission in Abyei warned in May that the RSF's presence in the resource-rich region had put residents in additional danger, and risked intensifying the older territorial dispute between Sudan and the world's newest sovereign state, South Sudan.

Satellite images gave a sense of the scale of the damage after the large fire triggered by the drone strikes Image: Planet Labs PBC/REUTERS

What do we know about the drone strike?

According to local authorities, the attack hit the busy Amiet Market at around midday on Monday.

Yohana Akol Ngor, the caretaker information minister in Abyei, told Reuters news agency on Tuesday that the death toll had more than doubled, reaching at least 153 compared to a stated figure of 73 the previous day.

He said that Sudan's military was responsible for the attack but did not provide evidence. Akol Ngor said around 8,000 people had been displaced by the bombing.

South Sudan's Foreign Ministry also blamed the Sudanese army and said the drone struck multiple locations around the busy market.

One of these, judging by witness accounts, was a fuel depot — and this led to a large fire that proved difficult to bring under control overnight and was still ablaze on Tuesday.

South Sudan said it had summoned Sudan's ambassador to protest and urged Sudan to "refrain from any actions that endanger civilian lives and property."

Medical charity Medecins Sans Frontieres (MSF), or Doctors Without Borders, said that its staff was treating some 20 wounded people at the nearby Ameth Bek hospital.

"So far we received over 20 patients, including several critical cases. Patients with burns were also admitted," said Dr. Christian Lindauer, MSF's medical activities manager at the hospital.

Many of the wounded were taken to Ameth Bek hospital for treatment Image: Medecins Sans Frontieres/REUTERS

What's the backstory of Sudan, South Sudan and Abyei?

The oil-rich Abyei region's status was not resolved by the 2005 peace agreement that broadly ended decades of civil war in Sudan.

It was also not settled in 2011 when South Sudan became an independent country.

A referendum was planned but never materialized, stalling over disputes on who should be allowed to vote. This left Abyei in a state of limbo, jointly administered and with an interim UN security force on site for 15 years.

The region's majority Ngok Dinka population favors joining South Sudan, while Misseriya nomads who use its pastures favor Sudan.

Amiet Market, the site of the attack, is an important trading hub for both communities.

The unstable region has also experienced intercommunal violence in recent years between Ngok Dinka and neighboring Twic Dinka communities and is home to other armed militias.

Medecins Sans Frontieres said its staff were providing surgical services, wound dressing and other emergency care to more than 20 wounded Image: Medecins Sans Frontieres/REUTERS

How does this fit into Sudan's army's war with the RSF?

The April 2023 outbreak of fighting between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the Rapid Support Forces paramilitary — which has turned into a conflict with fairly entrenched battle lines, putting Sudan into a de facto state of partition — is increasing tension in the already-strained region.

Abyei borders South Kordofan state in Sudan, which has become a major center of fighting in the war.

Sudan's military alleges that the RSF is also operating out of Abyei. The United Nations Interim Security Force for Abyei (UNISFA) issued a similar statement in May.

Officials in Abyei and South Sudan dispute this, however.

Sudan's military and the RSF have both been using drones extensively in the conflict.

"We remain alarmed by the relentless drone attacks across Sudan, as well as the damage they are causing to critical infrastructure — these attacks are taking a devastating toll on communities already struggling with the consequences of more than three years of conflict," UN spokesperson Stephane Dujarric told reporters in New York on Tuesday when asked about the attack.

Sudan's civil war — the limits of humanitarian aid To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

World.title: North Korean workers treated as 'slaves' at Russian drone factory, says new report
World.content:
A new report reveals the plight of North Korean workers at a drone factory in Russia. It also raised concerns that Pyongyang could gain hands-on knowledge of advanced weapons systems through the workers it sends there.

As many as 12,000 North Koreans working at a Russian drone factory are victims of "gross human rights abuses and human trafficking," according to a new report.

The figures were part of a joint report published on October 14 by the Washington-based Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) and the Dallas-based George W. Bush Institute. It analyzes how Russia, North Korea, China and Iran are involved in expanding unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) production at the Yelabuga plant in Tatarstan, and what each country stands to gain.

While Moscow gets access to more than 5,500 drones a month for its war against Ukraine, China benefits from being the main supplier of dual-use components, including batteries, internal electronics, engines and navigation systems.

Iran has supplied Russia with Shahed drones, which has helped Moscow produce upgraded domestic variants, known as Geran.

Meanwhile, North Korea is earning money by retaining as much as 90% of the wages of the laborers, the report stated.

"The geographical locations of these four countries… means that any kind of international interdiction is impossible," Dan Pinkston, a professor of international relations at the Seoul campus of Troy University, told DW.

North Korea gains critical intel by aiding Russia in Ukraine To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Russia and North Korea defy UN resolutions

The joint report says Russia and North Korea are defying United Nations Security Council Resolution 2397, of December 2017 , which requires any UN member state to send North Korean workers home within two years.

"The North Korean regime… is selling the labor of its citizens under a state-to-state arrangement, controlling whether they may leave and collecting most of their wages," it said. This, according to the report, "is the definition of forced labor."

Song Young-Chae, a Seoul-based academic and human rights activist with the Worldwide Coalition to Stop Genocide in North Korea, says Pyongyang is "effectively conducting slavery of its own people and for its own profit."

"This is just a terrible situation, and we know that it is not happening only at Yelabuga," he told DW. "We know there are construction workers in the occupied Ukrainian territories, North Koreans in lumber camps and, of course, tens of thousands of soldiers have been sent to fight — and die — on the front lines in Ukraine," Song added.

"Life in North Korea is not easy, but these people are being sent to Russia as slaves, with no freedom, and they are only allowed to keep a fraction of the money they earn," he said.

The challenge, he admits, is to find a way to halt this "trade in humanity."

North Korea expands role in Russia's war with Ukraine To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

How much can realistically be done?

"These countries share a border, so it is easy to transport workers, and no other agency can intervene," Song said. "Russia and China are both permanent members of the UN Security Council but are ignoring its resolutions on this issue. There is very little that can be done."

Song's rights organization is attempting to highlight the plight of North Korean workers and to create a "coalition of like-minded nations and agencies" to protect laborers — although he admits to being "pessimistic."

Pinkston shares those concerns, as well as fears over the emergence of a powerful bloc that appears to be "ripping up the post-World War II order on the rule of law and human rights" and is intent on taking a confrontational approach to other nations.

The weapons being manufactured at Yelabuga will assist in achieving those aims, he said.

"UN Security Council resolutions on North Korean workers, on weapons proliferation, on the sale of dual-use technologies are all being ignored, so I think we can say that the UN's sanctions regime is pretty much dead," Pinkston added.

North Korea developing its drone capabilities

It is clear that both Russia and Ukraine have gained important insights into the modern battlefield through their ongoing conflict, Pinkston said, with the emergence of drone technology arguably one of the most critical advances.

"And like everyone else, North Korea has been watching closely, 'learning-by-doing' and innovating its own drone capabilities," Pinkston said, adding that there are "serious implications" for the South Korean military as it also attempts to keep up its defensive capabilities against a new generation of drones in the North.

Why Russia and North Korea can't quit each other (for now) To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

To curb the deployment of North Korean laborers to Russia and the proliferation of weapons, the joint report calls on the US State Department to work with other countries to disrupt human trafficking networks and sanction those responsible.

It also urges the UN to work multilaterally to investigate the Yelabuga complex and to catalogue the abuses that have taken place. Moreover, it demands accountability for those who have carried out abuses and for victims to be protected.

The report adds that foreign companies that are operating as part of the Yelabuga special economic zone — there are "several" European companies and at least one US firm with a presence at the site — should be pressured to leave.

Edited by: Emmy Sasipornkarn

World.title: New EU plan for Arctic warily eyes influence of Russia, US
World.content:
The EU unveiled its priorities in the Arctic as it vies with Russia, China and the US for influence. EU foreign affairs chief Kaja Kallas said drone incursions, GPS jamming and cable sabotage undermine Arctic security.

The EU on Tuesday presented a new Arctic Strategy that outlines the bloc's priorities in the key region amid challenges such as security threats, climate change and mining.

Russia is building up its military power in the Arctic, and US President Donald Trump has threatened Greenland, saying the Danish territory is needed for American security interests but later signed a deal with Denmark over US military access to the territory. China is also investing in the region and has shipping ambitions there.

The northern parts of Finland and Sweden, along with Greenland are located within the Arctic, meaning part of the region is in the European neighborhood. Iceland and Norway, two other Arctic states, are also involved in the European single market.

'Tectonic plates of geopolitics' colliding in Arctic

"The Arctic is one place where the tectonic plates of geopolitics are colliding," European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said.

"When we see that sovereignty, territorial integrity and the rules that have underpinned security in the region can no longer be taken for granted, we have to act and change our strategic posture," she added.

EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Kaja Kallas said Russia "has reopened Soviet-era bases and is testing new weapons" in the Arctic.

"Drone incursions, GPS jamming and the sabotage of undersea cables undermine Arctic security," Kallas continued. Russia's shadow fleet, which is an attempt to circumvent Western sanctions, is active in the Arctic.

On Arctic security, the EU plans to develop a maritime security hub in the region "to facilitate information sharing form seabed to space." The bloc also intends to expand European icebreaker capacity and extend its satellite surveillance program in the region.

Russia's Arctic buildup is Iceland's security headache To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

However, the EU does not intend to compete with NATO in the region, EU Commissioner for International Partnerships Jozef Sikela told DW. Twenty-three EU countries are members of NATO.

"NATO will remain basically the center of defense and the center of deterrence, but NATO doesn't have a budget, the member state has," Sikela said. "This is first about the proper focus and the proper use of resources of the NATO member states and about better coordination."

EU Arctic strategy highlights security and raw materials To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

EU to boost climate research as Arctic faces ice melting crisis

In regard to the climate, the Arctic is warming about four times faster than the global average. The melting of ice and glaciers in the Arctic pose risks to Europe such as prolonged heatwaves, drought and flooding.

Sikela said, "Collaboration among the Arctic is very difficult," adding, "We're not getting information about the permafrost from the biggest part of the Arctic territory."

Sikela accused Russia of "unprecedented" actions in the Arctic and said the "catastrophic level of drilling and opening new mines" in the region is contributing to its rapid warming. The Arctic is rich in critical minerals and rare earth elements such as nickel.

As part of the EU Arctic Strategy, the bloc intends "to strengthen climate research, observation and monitoring" and launch flagship projects utilizing AI to "anticipate extreme weather and cascading disasters such as coastal flooding."

Norway, which is not an EU member state, is home to Western Europe's largest LNG plant near the city of Hammerfest [FILE: March 14, 2024] Image: Lisi Niesner/REUTERS

Although Russia and other non-EU countries such as Norway drill in the Arctic, the EU does not want to expand new drilling in the region. European Commissioner for Energy and Housing Dan Jorgensen said the EU's view "on drilling in the Arctic remains the same and it's very clear: oil, coal and gas must stay in the ground."

Greenland submarine cable route project bypasses US

Regarding economic interests in the Arctic, the bloc may take further steps to bypass the US. The strategy calls for "resilient submarine cable connectivity linking Greenland directly to Europe, with potential future extensions towards Canada and Japan."

The EU also outlined new plans regarding the residents of the Arctic region. The bloc wants to strengthen dialogue with Indigenous people along with expanding Erasmus+ opportunities for Arctic youth.

Denmark apologizes for abuse of Greenlandic Indigenous women To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

World.title: France plans 'massive' weekend police surge amid protests
World.content:
Skip next section What restrictions on gatherings are in place in major cities besides Paris?

Lyon's tourism office on the Place Bellecour was set ablaze over the weekend [FILE: October 17, 2026] Image: Jeff Pachoud/AFP

At least four other cities — Lyon, Bordeaux, Nice and Marseille — have announced continued localized restrictions that will take effect on Tuesday night.

In Lyon, the prefect of the Rhone region, ordered another curfew from 9 p.m. to 6 a.m. in what's known colloquially as the hypercentre of the old city — an area spanning the first and second Arondissements and other key historic zones like the city hall, the Place Bellecour pedestrian square and the commercial and historic neighborhood Les Cordeliers.

Prefect Etienne Guyot also said a ban on what French authorities term attroupements — gatherings of people deemed to have the potential to threaten public order — from 4 p.m. until 9 p.m. would also apply.

In Bordeaux, unaccompanied minors will not be allowed on the streets from 10 p.m. until 7 a.m. "in the sectors particularly affected by the pillages of October 17," Gironde prefect Sophie Brocas said.

She said this was aimed to "prevent all new attacks on businesses" in a series of key central streets and squares. The restrictions were set to apply until next Monday, October 26.

And to the south in Nice, the city center sector, the old city and the Trachel-Gare du Sud sectors will be restricted from 9 p.m. until 6 a.m. until Sunday, October 25.

Authorities in Marseille, France's second-largest city, announced a nightly curfew for unaccompanied minors from 10 p.m. to 5 a.m. through Friday in central shopping streets and sensitive areas.

World.title: Germany news: Hackers release AfD party emails
World.content:
Skip next section Young workers need to develop skills away from AI — Siemens

German industrial giant Siemens has warned against eliminating entry-level jobs that are now increasingly left to artificial intelligence (AI), saying young workers could be left without essential skills, including those needed to monitor AI-generated work.

Judith Wiese, the company's chief people and sustainability officer, said that handing certain routine tasks to AI meant that young employees would not gain hands-on experience that could benefit them later in their careers.

Wiese said it was necessary, for example, for software developers to be able to write their own code so they could critically examine the code produced by AI.

"The crucial question is always: What do I need to have done, checked and seen myself to avoid being misled by AI?" she said.

However, Wiese said AI could also help employees acquire skills more quickly, while older colleagues could learn from younger ones who had grown up using AI.

Wiese said it was still too early to say how AI would impact employment.

Noting that Siemens has some 30,000 software engineers, she said: "You can use the additional productivity either to do the same work with fewer people or to do more with the same number of employees."

Wiese also pointed out that AI was speeding up work processes, enabling the exploration of new ideas and creating projects that would not have been possible without it.

World.title: Brazil's Lula, Flavio Bolsonaro tied ahead of runoff vote
World.content:
With just under a week to go before the decisive presidential runoff election, polls show left-wing incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and his right-wing challenger Flavio Bolsonaro are virtually tied.

There are only a few days left until Brazil's runoff election on October 25, with neither left-wing incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva nor right-wing populist Flavio Bolsonaro a clear favorite.

While three polls from last week showed a razor-thin lead for Bolsonaro, the PoderData polling institute has now projected 50% voter backing for each candidate.

Brazil election: Lula faces Flavio Bolsonaro in runoff To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

This election could end up as close as the one held in 2022, when Lula narrowly beat Flavio Bolsonaro's father, Jair Messias Bolsonaro, with just 50.9% of the vote. Jair Bolsonaro, incidentally, was later jailed for attempting a coup to hold onto power.

His son, Flavio, surprisingly won the first round of voting on October 4 by securing 47% of the vote. Bolsonaro's right-wing bloc also won many additional seats in Congress, primarily at the expense of Brazil's centrist parties. And in the week following the first round of voting, polls showed Bolsonaro commanding a lead of up to six percentage points.

Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's large rallies have helped mobilize his supporters Image: Silvia Izquierdo/AP Photo/picture alliance

Yet last week, Lula managed to gain momentum through nationwide mass rallies and his dynamic social media presence. Bolsonaro, in contrast, had scaled back street campaigning in light of his strong poll numbers.

That turned out to be a mistake. Now he, too, is once more mobilizing supporters to stage major rallies across Brazil as the country readies for the runoff.

A polarized nation

The rivalry between Lula's left-wing camp and Bolsonaro's far-right bloc has shaped Brazilian politics for the past decade.

Jair Bolsonaro gained nationwide recognition during the 2016 impeachment proceedings against Lula's political protegee, then-President Dilma Rousseff. He went on to win the 2018 presidential election while Lula was serving a prison sentence on corruption charges.

But when Lula's conviction was overturned, the former trade union leader staged a political comeback in 2022.

Brazilian politics has become deeply polarized Image: Cris Faga/Sipa USA/picture alliance

This polarization is responsible for the disappearance of centrist parties and a political alternative, or "third way," said political scientist Marco Aurelio Nogueira.

"The divide between Lula and Bolsonarism has paralyzed Brazilian politics, and anything that didn't belong to one pole or the other has disappeared," Nogueira told DW. This polarization is fueled by social media, the expert added, saying that "platforms' algorithms thrive on conflict and reward excitement."

Flavio Bolsonaro a toned-down version of his father

Nogueira said Flavio Bolsonaro's calm demeanor could explain why he has a realistic chance of defeating Lula, unlike his father in 2022.

"Jair Messias Bolsonaro was a crude, rhetorically aggressive figure," said Nogueira. "Flavio Bolsonaro, on the other hand, casts himself as more moderate and gives Bolsonarism a more youthful image. He communicates skillfully, posts well-produced videos, and addresses workers' issues, such as the introduction of the five-day workweek."

Lula's recent promise to shorten workweek hours has lent momentum to his campaign. Alarmed by Lula's rising poll numbers, Bolsonaro gave up his opposition to the move and voted in favor of the five-day workweek.

Flavio Bolsonaro's backers also support his father, Jair Bolsonaro Image: Alexandre Meneghini/REUTERS

Bolsonaro is now taking a less radical stance on fiscal policy, too. Although he had announced drastic budget cuts before the first round of voting, modeled on the policies of his libertarian Argentine ally Javier Milei, he now intends to continue Lula's social programs. That said, Bolsonaro has not presented a plan for how he intends to reduce Brazil's high public debt.

Banco Master corruption scandal shapes race

The election campaign has been overshadowed by a massive corruption scandal surrounding the insolvent financial institution Banco Master. Daniel Vorcaro, the bank's former owner, is under investigation for fraud, money laundering and corruption.

Vorcaro is accused of having bribed decision-makers in the world of politics, finance and the judiciary. Several Supreme Court justices are said to be involved in the scandal, which involved dubious sex parties and millions in reported payouts. Judges from both the Lula camp and some appointed by Jair Bolsonaro are said to be tied up in the scandal.

Flavio Bolsonaro is alleged to have accepted goods and services from Vorcaro, including a €10 million donation for a film about his father's life. Yet Lula has not been able to capitalize on his rival's alleged failings. After all, his very own son is implicated in another corruption scandal. Moreover, Bolsonaro has repeatedly drawn attention to Lula's 2017 conviction for corruption, even though it was later overturned by the Supreme Court.

Friday's debate key to reaching voters

Political scientist Nogueira believes the mudslinging between both candidates over who is more corrupt has left voters jaded.

"There are constant reports about scandals and mutual accusations from all sides," said Nogueira. "As a result, the effect is essentially canceled out in the election campaign. The average voter tunes out and no longer attaches much importance to these accusations when making a voting decision."

The upcoming debate will have a major impact on the election, experts say Image: Amanda Perobelli/REUTERS

Both candidates held their first live television debate on Sunday. On Friday, two days before the runoff election, they will face off once more on Brazil's largest broadcaster, Globo. The debate will likely have a significant influence on the October 25 vote.

Experts believe the key for both candidates will be to not be rattled by provocations from the other side. Concrete policies, in turn, will only play a minor role in the debate.
