It was not the first time that media got hurt by police during a protest coverage. During the September 21, 2025 riots that followed an anti-corruption protest, police grabbed and hit photojournalist Zedrich Xylak Madrid while he was taking photos in Mendiola.

The Alyansa ng Kabataang Mamamahayag of the PUP where Cruz was a campus journalist also joined in condemning the incident.

QC Mayor Belmonte orders probe

On Tuesday, October 20, Quezon City Mayor Joy Belmonte ordered an investigation into the confrontation.

“Pinaiimbestigahan na ni Mayor Joy Belmonte ang pangyayari. Gaya ng lagi, ang paniniwala ng Lungsod: Dapat panagutin ang sinuman na mapatutunayang gumamit ng kapangyarihan para manakit, manakot, o humadlang sa mapayapang pagpapahayag. Binigyang-diin ng alkalde ang atas na maximum tolerance dapat ang ipinapatupad ng QCPD,” the city government said in a statement.

(Mayor Joy Belmonte has ordered an investigation into the incident. As a matter of practice, the City believes: Those who are proven to have used their power to hurt, intimidate, or obstruct the peaceful assembly should be held accountable. The mayor also stressed the order of maximum tolerance that should be implemented by the QCPD.)

The city government also said that it has allowed the farmers to continue their “peaceful and orderly” mobilization until noon of Wednesday, October 21.

“ Ang kanilang mga hinaing ay dapat pakinggan at tugunan sa pamamagitan ng dayalogo (Their grievances should be heard and addressed through dialogue),” the city government added.

The city government also met with DAR, the police, and representatives from the farmers’ groups on Tuesday on how to maintain order and ensure safety and cleanliness in the area during protests. – Rappler.com

World.title: Super Typhoon Rosal slightly strengthens over Philippine Sea
World.content:
The trough or extension of Super Typhoon Rosal (Champi) may cause scattered rain and thunderstorms in Bicol and Eastern Visayas on Tuesday evening, October 20

MANILA, Philippines – Super Typhoon Rosal (Champi) slightly intensified over the Philippine Sea on Tuesday afternoon, October 20, with its maximum sustained winds again reaching 195 kilometers per hour from the previous 185 km/h.

The super typhoon’s gustiness also increased from 230 km/h to 240 km/h, said the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical, and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) in its 5 pm bulletin on Tuesday.

Rosal was last spotted 1,270 kilometers east of Central Luzon at 4 pm, still moving west northwest at 25 km/h. It had entered the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR) at 10:40 am.

The super typhoon is not expected to make landfall in the Philippines, but it will still affect parts of the country due to its size and intensity. It will be closest to extreme Northern Luzon from Thursday, October 22, to Friday, October 23.

On Tuesday evening, Rosal’s trough or extension may cause scattered rain and thunderstorms in more areas, with the latest forecast now covering the entire regions of Bicol and Eastern Visayas.

From Thursday afternoon to Friday afternoon, or a 24-hour period, these two provinces in Northern Luzon are seen to have significant rain due to Rosal:

Heavy to intense rain (100-200 millimeters): Batanes

Moderate to heavy rain (50-100 mm): Cagayan

For now, Batanes, along with Ilocos Norte and Babuyan Islands, will just have isolated light rain due to the northeasterly windflow.

Meanwhile, more areas were placed under Signal No. 1 as of 5 pm on Tuesday, which means they should prepare for strong winds from the super typhoon:

Batanes

Babuyan Islands

northern part of Ilocos Norte (Pagudpud)

northern and eastern parts of mainland Cagayan (Santa Ana, Gonzaga, Lal-lo, Santa Teresita, Camalaniugan, Aparri, Buguey, Gattaran, Baggao, Peñablanca, Santa Praxedes, Claveria, Sanchez-Mira, Pamplona, Ballesteros, Abulug, Allacapan)

northeastern part of Isabela (Maconacon, Divilacan, Palanan)

northeastern part of Catanduanes (Pandan, Bagamanoc, Panganiban, Viga, Gigmoto)

The highest possible tropical cyclone wind signal due to Rosal is Signal No. 2 or 3.

The northeasterly windflow and the periphery or outer bands of the super typhoon will also bring strong to gale-force gusts to the following areas:

Tuesday, October 20

Batanes, Ilocos Norte, Cagayan, Isabela, Polillo Islands, Camarines Norte, Camarines Sur, Catanduanes, Northern Samar, Eastern Samar, most of Caraga, Camiguin, Misamis Oriental, Sarangani, Davao del Sur, Davao Occidental

Wednesday, October 21

Ilocos Region, Cordillera Administrative Region, Cagayan Valley, Polillo Islands, Bicol, Romblon, Eastern Visayas, Iloilo, Guimaras, Negros Occidental, Siquijor, Bohol, Northern Mindanao, Caraga, Davao Region, Sarangani, Zamboanga del Norte

Thursday, October 22

most of the country

Seaboards affected by Rosal will gradually see worsening conditions. Here is PAGASA’s updated forecast for the next 24 hours:

Up to very rough seas (travel is risky for all vessels)

Northern and eastern seaboards of Catanduanes; seaboard of Isabela; northeastern seaboard of mainland Cagayan; southeastern seaboard of Batanes; northeastern seaboard of Babuyan Islands – waves up to 4.5 meters high

Up to rough seas (small vessels should not venture out to sea)

Northern and eastern seaboards of Batanes; remaining eastern seaboards of Babuyan Islands and mainland Cagayan; northern seaboards of Camarines Norte and Camarines Sur; northern and eastern seaboards of Northern Samar and Eastern Samar; eastern seaboards of Albay and Sorsogon – waves up to 4 meters high

Northern and eastern seaboards of Polillo Islands; northern seaboard of Aurora; remaining seaboard of Batanes – waves up to 3.5 meters high

Seaboards of northern Quezon; eastern seaboards of Dinagat Islands and Siargao-Bucas Grande Island Group; remaining seaboards of Cagayan, Aurora, and Camarines Norte – waves up to 3 meters high

Up to moderate to rough seas (small vessels should take precautionary measures or avoid sailing, if possible)

Seaboards of Surigao del Sur, Surigao del Norte, and Davao Occidental; eastern seaboard of Davao Oriental; northern and eastern seaboards of Quezon; remaining seaboard of Catanduanes – waves up to 2.5 meters high

Seaboards of Ilocos Norte and Ilocos Sur; southern seaboard of Davao Oriental; remaining northern and eastern seaboards of Camarines Sur; remaining seaboards of Polillo Islands, Dinagat Islands, and Siargao-Bucas Grande Island Group – waves up to 2 meters high

ALSO ON RAPPLER

PAGASA said Rosal will move generally west northwest until Wednesday, October 21, before heading generally northwest until Friday morning. Afterwards, it may turn north northwest to north starting Friday afternoon, until it leaves PAR by Friday evening or early Saturday morning, October 24.

The weather bureau also sees possible intensification in the coming hours as Rosal moves over the Philippine Sea, but it could weaken into a typhoon on Thursday evening or early Friday morning.

Rosal is the Philippines’ 18th tropical cyclone for 2026, and the first for October. PAGASA earlier estimated the country may have one or two tropical cyclones during the month.

The Philippines is currently in a transition period to the northeast monsoon or amihan, following the end of the southwest monsoon or habagat, which was announced last October 5.

The northeast monsoon typically brings surges of cold temperatures, but the upcoming amihan period could be warmer as the existing strong El Niño in the tropical Pacific Ocean is predicted to become very strong in the fourth quarter of 2026. – Rappler.com

World.title: Big IPO, big bonus: GCash employees get their own payday
World.content:
From first-time investors to the country's business elite and the President himself, everyone turned out for GCash. Now, can its record-breaking IPO wake up the sleepy PSE?

When no less than the President shows up to ring the bell at your stock market debut, you know it’s a big deal. For GCash employees who have been through the wringer to get the IPO done, there was an even sweeter reason to celebrate.

Sources told Rappler that employees of GCash parent Mynt are getting a prorated P100,000 bonus delivered straight to, you guessed it, their GCash wallets. And it wasn’t just the top brass getting a little something extra, with sources confirming that the payout reached employees across ranks.

Not everyone in Mynt’s nearly 2,600-strong workforce – which helped turn a once-obscure SMS payment service into the homegrown giant it is today – could cram onto the trading floor of the Philippine Stock Exchange (PSE) Tower. But word has it they held a watch party at their office a few blocks away in BGC, with plenty to cheer about.

Talk about an IPO payday!

On Tuesday, October 20, Mynt pulled off the biggest IPO in Philippine history, raising P60.9 billion and knocking Lucky Me! maker Monde Nissin’s offering in 2021 off the top spot.

And what a crowd it drew.

Among the familiar faces were the Zobel brothers Jaime Augusto and Fernando, Monetary Board member Romeo Bernardo, BPI chief TG Limcaoco, and former transportation secretary turned San Miguel director Jaime Bautista.

The stock market elite was there, too, including PSE chairman Jose Pardo, president Ramon Monzon, and the “dragon lady” Vivian Yuchengco, alongside government bigwigs Securities and Exchange Commission chairman Francis Lim and Finance Secretary Frederick Go.

LISTED. President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. (center) leads the bell-ringing for GCash parent Mynt’s IPO. (Left to right) Ayala director Fernando Zobel de Ayala, Mynt CFO Evelyn Ng, Ayala CEO Bong Consing, Ayala chairman Jaime Augusto Zobel de Ayala, Mynt chairman Ernest Cu, Mynt CEO Martha Sazon, Marcos, PSE chairman Jose Pardo, PSE director Vivian Yuchengco, PSE CEO Ramon Monzon, BSP Monetary Board Member Romeo Bernardo, Finance Secretary Frederick Go, SEC Chairman Francis Lim, PSE COO Roel Refran, and PSE issuer regulation division head Marigel Baniqued-Garcia. Photo from Mynt.

And, of course, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. himself, who hoped the record IPO might finally stir the sleepy beast that is the Philippine stock market.

“We recognize that investors have become more cautious and that attracting fresh capital remains a challenge,” he said. “But Mynt’s initial public offering gives us reason for optimism. The strong interest it has attracted from local and international investors is proof of the continued confidence in Filipino enterprise.”

Play Video

Even on the day of its biggest IPO, the benchmark PSE index ended at around the 5,800 level, practically where it stood at the end of 2012. (READ: PSE enters new territory with GCash’s IPO. But to thrive, it must go further.)

It’s been a rough stretch for the local bourse. Had you put P100 into a fund tracking the Philippine index back then, you’d still have roughly P100 nearly 14 years later, excluding dividends and fees. The same P100 invested in a fund tracking Wall Street’s S&P 500 would now be worth around P830, thanks to US market gains and the weakening peso.

An eightfold gap. That’s how far Philippine stocks have fallen behind.

No wonder GCash’s dealmakers had to work hard to drum up interest. At a post-listing briefing, Mynt investor relations head Jep Tang said the company spent three months courting investors, meeting 137 after filing its registration statement, followed by 213 investor follow-ups and another 110 in the final round.

Any dividends for investors?

On its first day, GCASH climbed as high as P6.76 in the early trading hours before ending its first trading day at P6.60, back where it started. Not the spectacular first-day rally some might have hoped for, but it avoided the dreaded listing day slump, never falling below its offer price.

For now, anyone hoping to collect dividends might have to wait.

“We don’t have instituted a dividend policy yet,” Tang said, pointing instead to the many opportunities where the company intends to put its money to work. (READ: After the IPO party, GCash comes for 5-6 lending next)

Speaking of waiting, what about GCash’s rival Maya?

Maya chairman Manny Pangilinan had earlier floated a 2026 IPO, but the timetable has since slipped to 2027. When Maya cheekily congratulated GCash with a “Congrats, GCash. Welcome to Maya” post featuring the newly listed stock, even the PSE couldn’t resist joining in.

“So, Maya IPO when?”– Rappler.com

World.title: Supreme Court declares 2024, 2025 budgets unconstitutional
World.content:
(1st UPDATE) The SC rules that in so far as the 2024 and 2025 budgets are concerned, the doctrine of operative fact applies. This recognizes the validity of an assailed act prior to the determination of its unconstitutionality.

MANILA, Philippines – The Supreme Court (SC), on Tuesday, October 20, declared the 2024 and 2025 General Appropriations Acts (GAA), or budget laws, unconstitutional.

“The Supreme Court (SC) declared as unconstitutional, first, the 2024 General Appropriations Act (GAA) because of Congress’ increase of the unprogrammed appropriations by P449.5 billion, which resulted in an increase in the President’s total recommended appropriations; second, Special Provisions 1(a) and (b), Chapter XLIII of the 2026 GAA; and third, the 2025 GAA because of Congress’ increase of the Special Road Fund by P17.99 billion, which also resulted in an increase in the President’s total recommended appropriation,” said the ruling penned by Senior Associate Justice Marvic Leonen.

The SC en banc granted the petition of former lawmaker Edcel Lagman and partly granted the legal action of former senator Koko Pimentel challenging the increase in unprogrammed appropriations made by Congress in the 2024 budget.

“It declared unconstitutional Republic Act No. (RA) 11975 or the 2024 GAA because the total appropriations were effectively increased by P449.5 billion,” said the SC.

Unprogrammed funds are standby appropriations that may only be used once specific conditions are met, such as when government revenues exceed targets or when foreign grants and loans are on the table.

In its ruling, the High Court also granted the petition filed by Filipinos for Peace, Justice and Progress Movement, Inc. et al., and declared RA No. 12116, or the 2025 budget law, unconstitutional because of the P17.99-billion increase to the Department of Public Works and Highways’ Special Road Fund. The SC said this “resultantly increased” the budget’s total recommended appropriations.

“As regards the P12.75-billion increase to certain agencies’ Special Accounts in the General Fund, these were found to have violated Book VI, Chapter 4, Section 25 of the Administrative Code, which prohibits increasing amounts in special provisions beyond those proposed by the President,” said the SC.

As to the petition questioning the constitutionality or legality of unprogrammed funds itself, the SC only partially granted the challenge filed by Caloocan City 2nd District Representative Edgar Erice and Mamamayang Liberal Representative Leila de Lima.

The High Court explained that unprogrammed appropriations are not unconstitutional per se, but they need clear limits and safeguards to ensure fiscal discipline, transparency, and accountability.

“They (unprogrammed appropriations) become constitutionally infirm when they lack sufficient standards, effectively granting the executive unchecked spending authority that weakens fiscal discipline and undermines funding for programmed projects when estimated government revenues are not realized,” said the ruling.

But will the funds be returned? The SC ruled that in so far as the 2024 and 2025 budgets are concerned, the doctrine of operative fact applies to these funds. This legal principle recognizes the validity of an assailed act prior to the determination of its unconstitutionality.

“However, the doctrine covers only irreversible programs whose beneficiaries acted in good faith. It does not shield authors, proponents, or implementors from criminal, civil, or administrative liability unless the proper tribunals explicitly find that they acted in good faith,” the SC explained.

Apart from this, the SC also declared Special Provisions 1(a) and (b) of Chapter XLII under the 2026 budget law unconstitutional.

According to the SC, to ensure that unprogrammed appropriations are constitutional, they must comply with the following rules:

There should be no lump sums in unprogrammed appropriations.

The conditions for using new income and additional earnings from the government’s non-tax revenue incomes should be differentiated from programmed and unprogrammed expenditures.

Congress should have sufficient standards in terms of prioritization for spending if there is more than one purpose under unprogrammed appropriations.

The provision for the unprogrammed appropriations should be within the national fiscal program plan found in the budget and “consistent with its nature as a narrow contingent appropriation.”

– Rappler.com

World.title: 2 Serbian opposition figures targeted with spyware, research group says
World.content:
CYBERSECURITY. Figurines with computers and smartphones are seen in front of the words 'Cyber Security' in this illustration taken, February 19, 2024.

The incident is the latest of several in which researchers say surveillance technology was used against students, opposition politicians and others in Serbia, which will hold a parliamentary election on October 25

Two Serbian opposition figures were recently targeted with powerful cyberespionage tools, according to one of the men and a report issued on Monday, October 19, by the Canadian cyber watchdog group Citizen Lab.

The incident was the latest of several in which researchers say surveillance technology was used against students, opposition politicians, and others in Serbia, which will hold a parliamentary election on Sunday.

Citizen Lab said on Monday that a joint investigation with the Share Foundation, a digital rights group, determined that Serbian academic Vladan Djokic’s iPhone had been hacked using the Pegasus spyware tool made by Israeli group NSO.

At the same time, former prosecutor Rade Bajic told Reuters he received a warning from Apple on August 13 that his phone had been targeted using “mercenary spyware,” although he and Citizen Lab both said they had been unable to establish with certainty whether he was hacked or how a hack might have happened.

Serbia’s Interior Ministry did not return messages seeking comment. Officials there have previously dismissed allegations of cyberespionage. NSO, which was blacklisted by the US government in 2021 following years of reports of alleged human rights abuses, did not return emails. NSO, which says it only sells to governments, has previously said it would terminate commercial relationships that result in serious wrongdoing.

Apple confirmed having sent a batch of warnings to users on August 13 but did not directly address questions about Bajic’s or Djokic’s cases.

Both men have crossed Serbia’s ruling party, which has been buffeted by two years of student-led anti-corruption protests.

Djokic, the rector of the University of Belgrade, has been under pressure from authorities following his expressions of solidarity with the students. About 20 minutes before this story was published, a pro-government tabloid published an article describing Djokic as a “vulture” and purporting to carry audio of him talking about his political ambitions.

The source of the audio was not explained. Djokic said in a statement that the hacking of his phone “points to a serious attack on my privacy, security, and the integrity of the office of Rector” and called for those behind it to be punished. The statement did not address the article and he did not immediately return an email seeking comment about it.

Bajic said he was involved in prosecuting senior government officials over allegations that they improperly removed cultural protections on a historic Belgrade army compound that an investment company founded by US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner, had planned to redevelop. Kushner’s company pulled out of the plan late last year, saying it was doing so out of respect for the people of Serbia and the city of Belgrade.

“In my opinion, my involvement in this case was the sole reason for this unlawful spyware attack,” Bajic said.

Last month, the Share Foundation said that at least 14 people, including students, activists and opposition party members, had been targeted with advanced spyware ahead of local ​elections in March. At least one of the devices was compromised using Pegasus, it said. – Rappler.com

World.title: ‘Disappointed’ Ateneo coach Alas demands maturity from Blue Eagles
World.content:
REGROUP. Kieffer Alas (center) and the Blue Eagles huddle on court during UAAP action.

‘I’m super disappointed, but I will not give up on these guys,’ says Ateneo coach Louie Alas after the Blue Eagles’ dismal first-round run

MANILA, Philippines – Ateneo showed flashes of a contender early in the UAAP Season 89 men’s basketball tournament. Now, head coach Louie Alas wants his Blue Eagles to grow up before their season slips further away.

Ateneo opened the first round with a promising 3-1 record, putting itself among the league’s top teams.

Given the difficult months the program endured following the deaths of student-athletes Divine Adili and Rene Baterbonia, that start was already a significant achievement.

But the Blue Eagles have since lost three straight games, falling to La Salle, FEU and UST, with two of those defeats coming by double-digit margins.

At 3-4 and seventh in the standings, Ateneo finished the first round well below its coach’s expectations.

“I’m disappointed, super disappointed,” Alas said after the Blue Eagles’ 80-68 loss to UST. “My expectations about our record were higher than this.”

Alas pointed to the team’s immaturity, particularly in the second half, when Ateneo has struggled to keep games competitive late in the round.

“Immaturity. It’s immaturity. That’s it,” Alas said. “That’s one thing I really have to improve. We have to become more mature because we are not kids. We have veterans. We are all adults.”

The numbers back up his frustration as Ateneo surrendered at least 80 points in each of its final three games of the first round, while holding opponents below that mark in all three of its wins.

The Blue Eagles allowed the second-most points per game in the league at 81.14, trailing only the winless UE Red Warriors, who gave up 91.71 per contest.

Kieffer Alas, Louie’s 19-year-old son, has led the Blue Eagles with averages of 14.43 points, 4.57 rebounds, 2.43 assists, and 1.57 steals per game. However, he has shot just 34.55% from the field and 20.57% from three-point range.

Jared Bahay has also had difficulty finding his rhythm, averaging 13.0 points, 3.0 rebounds and 4.29 assists while shooting below 40% from the field in the opening round.

His 1-of-13 shooting performance against UST was his worst outing of the first seven games.

Shawn Tuano, Andrew Bongo, Travis Roberts, and Ian Espinosa have likewise struggled to find consistent form, leaving Ateneo searching for more reliable contributions across the roster.

Alas plans to intensify the Blue Eagles’ preparations and practice on top of making the adjustments needed to get them back on track.

“I’m super disappointed, but I will not give up on these guys,” Alas said. “I know they can do a lot better. Maybe we just have to adjust a bit to our practices.”

“I know they can get it right.”

Despite their three-game skid, Ateneo remains within reach of the teams ahead of it in the standings, as a couple of wins to start the second round could quickly change the Blue Eagles’ position.

The Blue Eagles will have home-court advantage to begin the second round when they host the FEU Tamaraws on Saturday, October 24, at the Blue Eagle Gym. – Rappler.com

World.title: Thousands Flee as Regime Troops Push Into Myanmar’s Oil Hub
World.content:
Regime troops backed by airstrikes are pouring into Magwe Region’s Myaing Township as the battle for Myanmar’s oilfields escalates, forcing thousands of residents to flee.

Reinforcements from the Light Infantry Division in Pakokku, an hour to the south, are bolstering the offensive to seize territory — nicknamed “Anyar Dubai” for its oil wealth — from resistance groups.

Resistance forces have controlled the area since 2022, repelling repeated efforts to choke off their crucial revenue stream. However, a regime offensive backed by 1,000 troops gained a foothold on May 24, seizing the Well-2 oil field in Tae Gyi village.

The latest push began on October 18, when regime reinforcements arrived in Kamma town, Pakokku Township while gyrocopters bombed the nearby village of Ohntaw, killing five people, including children, and injuring four others.

On Monday, the troops arrived in Myaing’s Twinma village, controlled by regime-aligned militia, and set up camp there. According to Sayar Htwe from the Anyar Myay Civil Society Organization, up to 5,000 residents fled neighboring villages as airstrikes and troops advanced.

“We have no information on where the troops are heading, but we can assume they are reinforcements for Tae Gyi village,” Sayar Htwe told The Irrawaddy.

Regime troops suffered heavy losses in the three-month battle for Tae Gyi, where they are now encircled and entirely reliant on airdrops for ammunition and supplies.

On September 28, the regime reported that troops had seized 131 small-scale oil rigs in the area, torching some to prevent them from falling back into resistance hands.

On Monday, the Magwe resistance’s Anyar Myay Coalition urged the public to remain on high alert for airstrikes and attacks, as regime troops were mobilizing in Pakokku, Myaing and Pauk townships. It warned that regime troops camped in Tae Gyi had killed around 50 civilians and torched 600 houses since May.

World.title: Regional Body Expels Myanmar Regime’s Human Rights Fig Leaf
World.content:
The South East Asia National Human Rights Institutions Forum (SEANF), a regional umbrella group, has expelled a fig-leaf human rights body controlled by Myanmar’s military regime after it refused to cooperate with a compliance review.

SEANF on Monday said it has terminated the membership of the Myanmar National Human Rights Commission (MNHRC) because it is not an independent institution promoting and protecting human rights.

Established in 2007, SEANF now consist of just five national human rights commissions aiming to strengthen regional cooperation, from Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand, the Philippines and Timor-Leste.

The decision, made on Oct. 1 and put into effect immediately, came at the 11th hour before Myanmar was to assume the umbrella group’s rotating chairmanship in 2027.

It follows a review of whether the MNHRC still met the Paris Principles standards for independence, effectiveness, and integrity, which SEANF uses to define a national human rights institution.

SEANF told the MNHRC in early September to respond, but the MNHRC refused, saying the review “did not comply with” the network’s procedural rules—a frequent fallback by the putschist regime in dealing with regional organizations of which it has fallen foul.

SEANF then decided unilaterally that the MNHRC “no longer satisfies the definition of a national human rights institution under amended Article 1 of the SEANF Rules of Procedure,” namely being independent to promote and protect human rights, it said in Monday’s statement. The decision was made in “a fair, transparent and evidence-based manner,” it added.”

The MNHRC was also kicked out of the Global Alliance of National Human Rights Institutions (GANHRI) and the Asia-Pacific Forum (AFP) in 2025.

SEANF added the MNHRC can reapply for membership if it can demonstrate efforts to comply with the Paris Principles.

Established under the quasi-civilian Thein Sein administration in 2011 and once recognized as a “partially independent” body, the MNHRC went rapidly downhill when its leadership was replaced with regime loyalists after the 2021 coup.

It has since remained conspicuously silent about the regime’s glaring human rights violations while offering it a veneer of respectability and protection from scrutiny. Anecdotal evidence suggests that anyone coming to the MNHRC with a complaint could expect a knock on the door from the regime’s enforcers soon after.

Rights groups in Myanmar and beyond have long called its removal from global networks.

Prominent activist Khin Ohmar of Progressive Voice told the Irrawaddy that SEANF’s decision was “a long-awaited principled action” and “strips the criminal military junta-controlled MNHRC of regional legitimacy.”

“This decision sends a clear message that this body can no longer hide behind a SEANF membership card,” she added.

World.title: Myanmar Regime Bombs Civilians While Claiming Military Operations Serve Peace
World.content:
Framing its aerial bombardment of civilians as a peace initiative, the Myanmar regime continued aerial attacks across five regions and states over the weekend, killing over two dozen civilians.

Addressing humanitarian concerns raised in the media over the targeting of civilians, newly appointed Defense Minister Lieutenant General Yar Pyae, who is also chair of the National Solidarity and Peacemaking Negotiation Committee (NSPNC), claimed that the current military operations—a reference to the bombing of civilians in resistance-held territories—were conducted in the pursuit of peace.

He made the remark at the closing ceremony of an event marking the 11th anniversary of the Nationwide Ceasefire Agreement (NCA) in Naypyitaw on October 16.

At the event, the regime again called on ethnic armed organizations (EAOs) to join its purported peace talks while encouraging the People’s Defense Force (PDF), the armed wing of the civilian National Unity Government (NUG), to surrender.

Meanwhile, from October 16-18, the regime bombed civilian targets in Magwe, Sagaing and Mandalay regions and Rakhine and Chin states, killing at least 27 people and injuring 11, according to media reports.

On Friday evening, regime aircraft bombed a Starlink-based WiFi shop in Thitgyitaw Village in Yesagyo, Magwe Region. The attack on the shop, which locals rely on to bypass the regime’s restrictions and access the internet, killed at least 12, including two children aged 1 and 10, and injured two, the NUG said on Sunday.

The number of casualties was likely to increase as bomb damage was making it difficult to determine the number and identities of the dead, the NUG’s Human Rights Department said.

“This is a blatant violation of international humanitarian law and a war crime,” it said.

The operation was carried out by two Russian-made Mi-35 attack helicopters, two fighter jets from Magwe and Nyaung Oo, and two drones from the Pakokku-based No. 101 Light Infantry Division, the NUG said.

However, local media reported that at least 15 civilians were killed in the incident.

On the same day, the regime bombed Magyikan Village in Sagaing’s Myaung, injuring one.

The regime’s airstrikes continued on Sunday, as Y-12 utility aircraft bombed Arakan Army (AA)-controlled ethnic Rakhine villages in Rathedaung. Wai Hun Aung, a prominent ethnic Rakhine writer and aid worker, said five people were killed.

The regime also bombed a jetty in AA-controlled Paletwa, Chin State, on the same day, resulting in 20 casualties according to media reports, though there has been no official statement yet.

A regime drone attacked Shwebayet Village in Mandalay’s Singu Township on October 18, killing three people and injuring four women and girls, including a 5-year-old, the Singu People’s Defense Force reported on Monday.

Three regime gyrocopters bombed Ohntaw Village in Magwe’s Pakokku Township on Sunday, killing five including children and senior citizens. Local media reported that four were injured, including a 2-year-old.

At the NCA anniversary event, regime leader Min Aung Hlaing invited 2015 signatories that have been fighting the Myanmar military since the 2021 coup—the Karen National Union, Chin National Front and All Burma Students’ Democratic Front—to join his peace process. The regime demands that the PDFs surrender.

Lt-Gen Yar Pyae insisted the aerial bombing was conducted for peaceful purposes. “Some parts are military actions, while others are steps to achieve peace,” Yar Pyae said.

World.title: Detained Aung San Suu Kyi Receives UK Royal Package: Regime
World.content:
YANGON—Myanmar’s Aung San Suu Kyi received a package from Britain’s King Charles III on Monday, authorities said, releasing the first pictures of the detained Nobel laureate in two months and describing her as a “special female prisoner.”

It is the first time Myanmar authorities have used the term to describe Aung San Suu Kyi, who was deposed in a military coup in 2021, triggering an ongoing civil war that has killed more than 100,000 people, according to monitor ACLED.

The coup leader and former junta chief Min Aung Hlaing was installed as civilian president in April following elections that did not include Aung San Suu Kyi’s party, and she was moved to house arrest soon afterwards.

Home Ministry officials met her on Monday to deliver a package of two books about soil, “one sealed envelope, and a sealed diplomatic communication sent by King Charles III of the United Kingdom to the special female detainee,” Myanmar’s presidential spokeswoman said on her Facebook page.

Britain is Myanmar’s former colonial power and the monarch is known to have a keen interest in gardening and the environment.

Accompanying the statement were two images of Aung San Suu Kyi meeting two men with their backs to the camera.

The pictures appeared to be in a similar room to the last released images of her, when she met a Red Cross representative in August, her first publicized meeting with a foreign official since her ouster.

Fact-checkers from AFP examined the latest photos and found no evidence of manipulation using Meta Generative AI or OpenAI tools.

Aung San Suu Kyi remains detained on charges rights groups say were concocted to return power to the military, which has historically ruled Myanmar since independence.

“I have been extremely lenient toward her,” Min Aung Hlaing said in an interview with Time magazine published last month.

In response to questions from AFP, the Foreign Office in London did not say whether British diplomats had sought to deliver the package in person, or been refused permission to do so.

Britain condemns what it describes as Aung San Suu Kyi’s “arbitrary detention” and calls for her immediate and unconditional release.

World.title: Myanmar Regime’s Sittwe Counteroffensive Hits the Rocks on Nga Pyi Island
World.content:
The Myanmar military’s push to land troops on Nga Pyi Island in Rakhine State’s Pauktaw Township has suffered fresh setbacks as the ethnic Arakan Army (AA) strikes regime vessels and tightens its siege on the state capital Sittwe.

Frontline sources said AA artillery hit another navy vessel off the island on Sunday, the third to be damaged in recent days. “The boat was struck and caught fire,” a local source close to the AA confirmed. Intense clashes are raging both on and around Nga Pyi Island as regime forces continue efforts to secure a beachhead despite mounting casualties.

Sources said commanders are driving conscripts forward in near‑suicidal assaults, but few have managed to reach land.

Since Oct. 7, the military has deployed more than a dozen gunboats and landing craft backed by airstrikes and artillery from encircled Sittwe, in an effort to seize the island. The move aims to break the AA’s blockade of the Kaladan River corridor and shield the navy’s Shwe Mingan base in Sittwe, which sits on a peninsula surrounded by water on three sides.

Nga Pyi Island is a key AA stronghold, blocking regime access upriver to AA-controlled Pauktaw and Ponnagyun townships.

“Junta soldiers keep coming despite heavy casualties, but few have made it to shore,” said a source close to the AA.

Meanwhile, AA columns have seized several regime outposts elsewhere in Sittwe and are pressing toward Shwe Mingan naval base and the Sittwe Regional Operations Command.

The assault on Nga Pyi was launched as advancing AA troops threatened to encircle the military’s Sittwe stronghold. Fighting has also intensified just down the coast in Kyaukphyu Township, where AA forces are attacking outposts near Taung Maw Oo naval base.

The AA controls 14 of Rakhine State’s 17 townships along with Paletwa Township in neighboring Chin State, with the regime maintaining a foothold in Sittwe, Kyaukphyu, and the sparsely populated Manaung island.

A regime counteroffensive launched from neighboring Magwe, Bago, and Ayeyarwady regions is bogged down amid fierce resistance and heavy losses.

World.title: Myanmar Regime Defense Minister Claims Airstrikes Are Aimed at Achieving Peace
World.content:
Despite widespread domestic and international condemnation of the military junta’s airstrikes on civilian targets, newly appointed regime Defense Minister Lieutenant General Yar Pyae said the bombing operations were intended to achieve peace.

“Mainly, they [questions raised in the media] are based on human rights and humanitarian concerns regarding the bombings. From our perspective, the current military operations are actually steps taken to obtain peace,” Lt-Gen Yar Pyae, who also serves as chairman of the National Solidarity and Peacemaking Negotiation Committee (NSPNC), said during his closing address to a workshop marking the 11th Anniversary of the Nationwide Ceasefire Agreement (NCA) on October 16.

The military regime routinely bombs civilian targets in resistance-held territories in an effort to undermine anti-regime groups’ administration and to coerce them into joining its purported peace talks. The tactic worked well in northern Shan State and Mandalay Region, where it managed to force the Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army (MNDAA) and its ally, the Ta’ang National Liberation Army (TNLA), to stop fighting, agree to China-brokered ceasefires and hand over some seized towns.

The regime continues to use the tactic in other regions and states including Rakhine State, which is almost entirely controlled by the Arakan Army (AA), an ally of MNDAA and TNLA.

On September 28, the regime conducted an airstrike targeting the busy Indian Market in the AA-controlled town of Kyauktaw, killing at least 50 people. The attack drew fierce condemnation from the UN, the UK, ASEAN Parliamentarians for Human Rights and various human rights organizations.

Since the 2021 military coup, the Myanmar military has consistently launched airstrikes across revolutionary strongholds, including the Anyar region (also known as the Dry Zone) and ethnic minority regions—targeting not only military sites, but also schools, hospitals, religious buildings and civilian homes.

Even as it makes peace overtures, the regime continues to engage in heavy fighting with the Kachin Independence Army (KIA) in Bhamo, and clashes are ongoing with the AA in Rakhine State. Airstrikes also continue to target civilians in the Anyar region, where People’s Defense Forces (PDFs) maintain a strong presence.

Amid the ongoing air raids on resistance-held areas, junta leader Min Aung Hlaing made what he called an unconditional peace invitation during the 11th NCA anniversary event in Naypyitaw on October 15. The regime nonetheless continues to pressure the PDFs—the main armed resistance groups across the country—to lay down their arms and surrender.

According to statements made during a press conference at the close of the NCA anniversary workshop, invitations to peace talks were extended to the KIA, but not to the AA.

Furthermore, Min Aung Hlaing stated on October 15 that if ethnic armed organizations (EAOs) wish to engage in politics, they must disarm and form political parties; if they wish to conduct business, they must do so legally; and if they wish to serve in defense, they must join the Border Guard Forces (BGF).

In 2009, the military heavily pressured EAOs to transform into Border Guard Forces. With few exceptions, however, the initiative largely failed.

The KIA, which is currently engaged in intense fighting with the military, was one of the major ethnic armed groups that refused to transform into a BGF at that time. During the Spring Revolution that erupted in response to the coup, the KIA earned the Myanmar military’s ire by providing military training, weapons and combat support to anti-junta PDF forces.

Similarly, following Operation 1027, the AA seized control of most towns in Rakhine State, including a regional military command center. Since then, the regime has launched several offensives to retake lost territory in the state.

While urging PDFs to surrender and asking EAOs to join the BGF, Min Aung Hlaing also told ethnic representatives attending the NCA ceremony that he would cooperate with those willing to work together on peace, while actively finding methods to handle those who refuse to cooperate.

World.title: Solar Mandate Crushes Myanmar Builders as Regime Chief’s Son Profits
World.content:
Contractors warn that a new regime mandate requiring installation of solar power systems in all high-rises and commercial buildings will send construction costs soaring in Myanmar. The directive further squeezes construction companies already pinched by a shortage of materials, import restrictions, and severe currency volatility.

The Yangon City Development Committee’s Engineering Department issued the order on October 1 as part of a nationwide push for solar amid deepening power blackouts.

From November 1, all commercial projects and high-rise buildings must install solar panels sufficient to power elevators and emergency lighting. For commercial buildings, solar systems must be integrated with power supplied by the Yangon Electricity Supply Corporation (YESC).

The order applies to existing projects, buildings under construction, and those awaiting Building Completion Certificates required for habitation.

“We have been handed the order at a time when prices of solar panels and related equipment are rising daily,” complained a Mandalay‑based builder. “Steel and cement prices are already soaring, so this adds yet another burden.”

Meanwhile, industry insiders warn of a scarcity of skilled technicians capable of installing large solar systems, creating technical and financial hurdles. “Household systems won’t power elevators, which require commercial‑grade solar systems,” the manager of a solar dealership explained. “Installation takes at least two months and costs around 100 million kyat.”

Solar imports to feed surging demand created by the new mandate are controlled by Aung Pyae Sone, son of regime chief Min Aung Hlaing.

Aung Pyae Sone swiftly cornered the lucrative market after his father’s regime waived tax on solar imports in April 2023 under the pretext of boosting the energy grid. His Venus Essential company also holds licenses to supply solar equipment for projects in Naypyitaw and planned 40-megawatt solar power plants in Taungdwingyi, Salin, Pakokku, Pauk, Chauk and Kyunchaung.

The solar mandate comes as regime energy rationing intensifies with more frequent rolling blackouts this year.

“They cut electricity during extreme heat, then order solar systems to be installed,” said a former political prisoner from Mandalay. “But only one company — belonging to the coup leader son — is allowed to import and sell the equipment nationwide. This is not aimed at solving the power crisis, but exploiting authority for personal profit.”

On October 5, the Electricity and Energy Ministry introduced rolling four-hour blackouts under the pretext of surging demand during the El Niño heatwave. Since then, households in Yangon, Mandalay and Naypyitaw have faced daily outages.

The power crisis has driven prices of solar panels and related equipment to record highs. In early August, a 500‑watt panel cost around 650,000 kyat. By mid‑October, the price had surged past one million kyat, putting solar systems beyond the reach of ordinary families.

World.title: An ‘All-for-Arakan’ Approach Is Needed to Address the Rohingya Refugee Crisis
World.content:
As resistance against long-term Rohingya presence in host countries grows, the refugees’ fate is back in the headlines. Malaysia is a recent example. Its government has yielded to growing hate speech against Myanmar refugees, and Rohingya in particular. In September, Malaysia and Myanmar negotiated a controversial repatriation agreement for 5,000 refugees that is not supported by the UN or its refugee agency. Resentment in India and Indonesia has also grown.

Following large-scale Rohingya returns from Bangladesh to Myanmar in the 1970s and 1990s, repatriation efforts started again in 2017, after the enforced flight of 750,000 Rohingya from Myanmar to Bangladesh. Initially, they were based on a Chinese offer to mediate between the two countries. Even though these and later efforts failed, Bangladesh’s pursuit of repatriation continues, and Malaysia has now joined in.

There are many reasons why the repatriation initiatives of the past 10 years have not been successful. A largely unmentioned one is that many initiators wrongly assume that traditional diplomatic relations between states can lead to meaningful dialogue and conflict resolution. This state-centric approach overlooks the key question at the heart of Myanmar’s decades-old volatility: how power and political authority are shared between Myanmar’s center and its highly diverse regions and ethnic nationalities. Moreover, since the country’s 2021 military coup, the regime in Naypyitaw has lost control over much of the country. In Arakan (Rakhine State), the birthplace of most Rohingya refugees—and where some 500,000 of them still live—the current regime has control over only three of the state’s 17 townships.

Today’s Myanmar is in transition. It is a country with multiple centers of authority. In some, local territorial control has been in place for decades; in others, it has been established since the military coup of 2021. These ethnic and regional authorities are not against a federal state as such. They are against the current federal union that is based on a constitution that concentrates significant power at the center, and particularly with the armed forces.

Right now, the key question is whether a new form of federalism can emerge, one that leaves a highly centralized system behind and, instead, focuses on existing and newly emerging centers of political authority. A long road lies ahead but in many parts of the country progress is clearly visible.

Arakan is a prime example. As the territorial dominance of the United League of Arakan/Arakan Army (ULA/AA) grows, particularly since 2023, it has been transforming into a central administrative authority with local administrative, security and judicial mechanisms. The Institute for Strategy and Policy in Chiang Mai recently reviewed the progress that has been made and concluded that “despite persistent challenges, a solid institutional framework is emerging”. But it also cautions that following rapid territorial expansion, a performance gap has emerged between public expectations and the administration’s delivery capacity.

A key reason for the delivery gap is that right now Arakan is a war zone with almost daily ground clashes between the AA and Myanmar’s armed forces, as well as attacks by Bangladesh-based Rohingya militias. Moreover, Arakan is now a prime target for attacks by Myanmar’s air force, which deliberately targets civilian structures with bombs of up to 500 pounds. The devastation on the ground is massive, with hundreds of civilians killed and maimed, while schools, markets, clinics and prayer houses have been destroyed. Physical infrastructure is also heavily affected, including by recent massive floods, leading to large-scale disruption of livelihoods and food security.

According to a recent report by the UN Development Programme, 68.4 percent of Arakan’s population (all ethnicities) experience multi-dimensional poverty, while a further 20 percent is at risk of falling into that category. Arakan’s current population is thought to stand at just over 2.4 million, while a Doctors Without Borders report in 2024 estimated that only 636,000 Rohingya remained in Arakan. Today that number will have fallen significantly, as approximately 150,000 more Rohingya have fled to Bangladesh since then.

To be clear, Rohingya repatriation from Bangladesh and other countries will take time. Refugees cannot return if armed conflict continues and before the underlying reasons for their flight have been addressed. To achieve this, a central role for both ULA/AA and the people of Arakan, including the Rohingya, is critical. But at the same time, various factions on the Rohingya side stand in the way of a united approach, particularly those supporting armed militias. Moreover, some of them have been used as a divide-and-rule tool by Myanmar’s military-backed regime.

Arakan’s problems are manifold and a broader vision of identity is critically important, one that acknowledges inclusion and equality as basic building blocks for a stable, secure and prosperous Arakan.

This understanding led the Rakhine Advisory Commission of 2016-17, chaired by former UN Secretary-General Kofi Annan, to focus on solutions to address the legitimate grievances and suffering of all Arakan’s diverse people. Its report and recommendations to Myanmar’s leaders remain highly relevant, based as they are on the central objective of developing conditions in Arakan that will lead to a peaceful, fair, harmonious and prosperous future for all communities. In 2018, the commission published a lessons-learned report focusing on how it operated in Myanmar’s highly politicized and complex context.

Obviously, much has changed since the report was released but it remains relevant, even after the National League for Democracy’s violent removal in 2021. It analyzes Arakan’s situation around three major crises: a security crisis, an economic and development crisis, and a human rights crisis. These crises persist and could form the basis for an all-of-Arakan approach.

Since 2017, the Annan report has been re-acknowledged annually by an overwhelming majority of the UN General Assembly and the UN Human Rights Council. Yet, no efforts have been made to establish how it might serve Arakan’s people under their current circumstances, and particularly since 2024, when most of Arakan came under the control of the ULA/AA.

Any process leading to a comprehensive plan for Arakan will be complex, not least because of the wide range of actors, functioning at diverse levels. In “The Dilemma of Hard Choices”, published in August, the Center for Arakan studies identifies the heterogeneity of agents as a key issue and adds that it is compounded by the problem of ownership, where most states, armed groups, civil society and international bodies each deflect overall responsibility while pursuing their own narrow strategic interests.

Precisely these diverging interests would make the Annan report a helpful starting point for dialogue. For good reasons, the commission’s recommendations are not highly prescriptive. Its general understanding was that, while basic principles of governance and human rights should guide the implementation process, details could be developed as part of dialogue processes. The report contains 88 recommendations on a comprehensive set of issues, ranging from economic and social development to freedom of movement, citizenship, health, access to justice, intercommunal cohesion, humanitarian access and internally displaced persons.

Obviously, dialogue cannot be based on the Annan report alone, but it could be a starting point. Additional questions must be raised to take account of developments since 2017. The first is the clarification of victimhood. Who are the victims of decades of oppression, persecution and violent conflict? A second is the “fog of war” that distorts a clear view of what is happening on the ground.

Obviously, it is not necessary to argue that the Rohingya are victims; that is accepted around the world. But what about the other communities in Arakan—the Rakhine, the Maramagyi, the Mro, the Chin, the Hindus and others?

They too are victims, yet their plight has been getting far less attention. They too have had their villages bombed and burned, their clinics, schools and livelihoods destroyed, while thousands are displaced in areas where relief goods cannot reach them. But their plight is not as widely documented. Acknowledgment that all Arakan’s people are victims could be a first step in reconciliation. And clearly, there are different degrees of victimhood and these too must be acknowledged.

The second point concerns the current “fog of war” and the urgent need to establish independent investigations. As in other places around the world, violent conflict, displacement and hunger obscure a clear view of developments on the ground. In such situations, deliberate disinformation thrives. We should not pretend that we have a clear view of what is happening in Arakan and in the refugee camps in Bangladesh. Lack of independent access and blocked internet facilities compound the problems.

Independent investigations will be needed to establish what has happened in Arakan and Bangladesh since 2017. While a significant body of research about the Rohingya exists, research on Arakan’s other communities remains scant. Moreover, research should also focus on disturbing allegations about what has been happening in Bangladesh. How did Rohingya militias manage to get a firm grip on the population in the refugee camps? Where did funding for their arms and operations come from? And how can large numbers of refugees and militia fighters continue to cross the Bangladesh-Myanmar border seemingly unnoticed?

Since 2018, the Independent Investigating Mechanism for Myanmar (IIMM) has been collecting and preserving evidence to facilitate criminal prosecutions of those most responsible for atrocity crimes. But it only shares its findings with investigative, prosecutorial and judicial authorities in national and international courts. As a result, a vast body of information remains inaccessible to the public. Moreover, IIMM’s mandate does not cover other truth-seeking needs, such as documenting and public acknowledgment of crimes through truth and reconciliation bodies and publicly accessible archives. These limitations underline the importance of establishing additional mechanisms to ensure that accountability is pursued as an integral part of transitional justice and reconciliation. This should be part of a comprehensive approach: an all-for-Arakan approach.

Using the Annan report as a credible starting point for dialogue could be a first step towards creating a better understanding of the needs of all Arakan’s people. Moreover, its repeated recognition by the UN General Assembly might help to rally much needed support for such an exercise at a time when resources are scarce.

Laetitia van den Assum is a former Dutch diplomat. She was also a member of the Rakhine Advisory Commission (2016-2017), chaired by Kofi Annan, former UN Secretary-General.

World.title: Kazakhstan Begins $1.8 Billion Copper Smelter Project in Abai Region
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan has launched construction of a $1.8 billion copper smelter in Aktogai, the Abai Region, with an annual production capacity of 300,000 tons of cathode copper, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev announced on Oct. 20.

Speaking at the launch ceremony via video link, Tokayev described the project as a major industrial initiative expected to strengthen Kazakhstan’s metallurgical sector, increase domestic processing and create more than 1,000 jobs.

The plant is being developed by KAZ Minerals Group, with Chinese company NFC serving as its engineering partner. The first copper cathode is scheduled to be produced in 2030.

“The capacity of the new enterprise will reach 300,000 tons of cathode copper per year. This will fully meet the needs of the domestic market. After the plant begins operations, Kazakhstan will enter the world’s top 10 producers of high-quality refined copper,” Tokayev said.

The facility will also produce metallic gold, silver and sulfuric acid. It is designed to cover the full production cycle, from ore extraction and processing to finished metal production, using its own copper concentrate as a raw material.

Tokayev said the project reflects Kazakhstan’s broader efforts to develop its mining and metallurgical industry and make more effective use of the country’s natural resources.

“Natural resources located beneath the ground belong to the people,” he said, adding that industrial projects should primarily serve the interests of Kazakhstan and its citizens.

Kazakhstan has more than 9,500 mineral deposits, extracts nearly 160 million tons of ore annually and produces around 3.5 million tons of copper concentrate, according to the figures cited by Tokayev. He also highlighted growth in the country’s manufacturing sector, whose output reached $60 billion last year. Over the past three years, 540 industrial projects have been implemented across Kazakhstan, creating approximately 50,000 permanent jobs, he said.

The new smelter is expected to increase the value added within Kazakhstan by processing domestically produced copper concentrate into refined metal rather than relying solely on the extraction and sale of raw materials.

Focus on technology and workplace safety

Tokayev called on the project’s shareholders and contractors to prioritize workplace safety, digitalization and the use of artificial intelligence in industrial operations.

“Applying advanced solutions contributes to higher productivity, improved workplace safety and effective prevention of industrial injuries,” he said.

He also stressed the importance of maintaining construction quality and meeting established deadlines, while thanking Kazakh specialists and Chinese partners involved in the project. Tokayev called on the government and local authorities to maintain close communication with workers and address their legitimate social needs.

The Aktogai copper smelter is expected to strengthen Kazakhstan’s domestic metallurgical capacity and support the country’s ambitions to expand industrial production and move toward higher-value processing.

World.title: Kazakhstan Eyes Greater ICAO Role Amid Global Aviation Challenges
World.content:
ASTANA — International Civil Aviation Organization Security Week 2026 kicked off in Astana on Oct. 20, bringing Kazakhstan’s bid for a seat on the ICAO Council, growing cybersecurity threats, aviation risks in conflict zones and prospects for direct flights between Kazakhstan and the United States into focus.

The three-day event has brought together more than 1,000 participants from 62 countries, including government officials, aviation regulators, airline executives and security experts.

“In 2027, ICAO will convene the third high-level conference on aviation security. The ideas that emerged from Astana will reach the global conversation as we prepare for it,” ICAO Secretary General Juan Carlos Salazar said during the opening ceremony.

Beyond the conference’s contribution to global aviation security discussions, Salazar also addressed Kazakhstan’s bid to join the ICAO Council during a press briefing. The candidacy comes ahead of an extraordinary ICAO Assembly in Montreal on Nov. 19-20, when four additional members will be elected to the organization’s governing body, expanding it from 36 to 40 seats.

“The success of ICAO is always informed from the voices that every region of the world has in the ICAO Council. And in that regard, the aspiration of the candidature of Kazakhstan is very welcome and is very well rooted in the representation of the voices of the region,” he said.

Kazakhstan has been an ICAO member since 1992 and became the first Central Asian country to establish a permanent mission to the organization in 2024. According to Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Transport, the country has achieved a 95.7% effective implementation score under ICAO’s aviation security audit framework, placing it among the world’s top 20 countries by this measure.

Salazar said Kazakhstan was among the countries with the highest levels of compliance with international aviation security standards, supporting its potential as a regional hub for passenger and cargo transportation. He identified workforce development as a key priority for maintaining those standards, noting that Kazakhstan already has regulations and technology in place but needs to continue investing in training and attracting qualified personnel.

From cyberattacks to conflict zones: aviation’s changing threats

Opening the event, Salazar called for a fundamental shift in global aviation security, warning that emerging threats are evolving faster than traditional regulations can respond.

“Threat actors are adaptive. They learn, they innovate, and they exploit new technologies faster than regulation has traditionally moved. (…) Digitalization connects every part of our operations, and with it every vulnerability. Supply chains grow more complex every day. Airspace that was routine yesterday can become dangerous overnight,” he said.

Salazar emphasized that aviation authorities must increasingly anticipate threats rather than respond only after incidents occur, relying on intelligence-led risk assessments, faster information sharing and closer coordination between governments and the industry.

“So the ambition for this week and for the year ahead of us is to move from reacting to anticipating,” he said.

He also warned that even attempted attacks can trigger far-reaching economic consequences, forcing flight diversions, causing delays and disrupting travel and business operations.

“That means foresight. It means risk-based decisions informed by intelligence, where we understand not only the threat but also the vulnerabilities and consequences that together determine the risk. And it means working together earlier and sharing information faster between states, within states, and with the industry,” said Salazar.

The conference agenda includes discussions on cybersecurity across airports, airlines and air navigation systems, artificial intelligence in security screening, risks to flights operating over or near conflict zones, and the protection of international cargo and mail supply chains.

Participants will also examine the effectiveness of aviation security audits, workforce development and the challenges of sustaining security modernization with limited resources.

Direct U.S. flights, aviation expansion

Speaking to reporters, Kazakh Vice Minister of Transport Talgat Lastayev said direct flights between Kazakhstan and the U.S. could begin in 2027, subject to regulatory approval and operational preparations.

“A few weeks ago, Kazakhstan was visited by a team of auditors from the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration [FAA]. There were approximately seven or eight inspectors who worked here for a week, and at the final briefing, they gave a fairly positive assessment of our civil aviation system and its compliance with international standards,” he said.

The FAA conducted its International Aviation Safety Assessment in Kazakhstan on Sept. 21-25, examining the country’s aviation safety oversight system and compliance with applicable ICAO standards. Lastayev said the official report is expected in November, with Kazakhstan aiming to secure authorization for flights to the U.S. by the end of 2026.

“We expect to receive a Dreamliner in December, a long-haul aircraft capable of operating such flights. Before it can enter service, flight crews and technical personnel need to accumulate a certain number of operating hours. I think that over the course of next year, provided all these conditions are met, we expect to launch a direct flight,” he said.

According to Lastayev, New York is being considered as the destination in the U.S, while Astana is the priority departure point in Kazakhstan. When asked whether the route would be commercially viable, he expressed confidence in its long-term profitability, citing growing economic and investment ties between the two countries. Ticket prices have yet to be determined.

World.title: Japan Eyes Middle Corridor to Expand Trade With Central Asia and Caucasus
World.content:
ASTANA – Japan is exploring opportunities to strengthen transport and trade links with Central Asia and the Caucasus through Kazakhstan’s Middle Corridor, with planned direct flights between Tokyo and Almaty and a proposed 719 million yen (US$4.7 million) project to modernize customs inspections at the Port of Aktau, reported the Ministry of Foreign Affairs’ press service.

The initiatives were discussed at a conference in Tokyo on Oct. 19, attended by nearly 100 representatives of Japanese government agencies, the Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA), the ROTOBO association and logistics companies.

The event focused on attracting Japanese investment into the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route (TITR), also known as the Middle Corridor, and improving transport connectivity between Japan, Central Asia and the Caucasus.

Japan’s State Minister of Economy, Trade and Industry Kei Takagi highlighted the route’s strategic importance for diversifying international transport and logistics networks. He said the Middle Corridor offers additional opportunities to strengthen Japan’s trade and economic ties with countries across the two regions.

Kazakhstan’s Ambassador to Japan Yerlan Baudarbek-Kozhatayev and Azerbaijan’s Ambassador Farid Talibov presented their countries’ transport development strategies and discussed ways to improve logistics efficiency and expand international transport cooperation.

Japan plans to support customs modernization in Aktau

Japanese companies have conducted trial shipments along the Middle Corridor to assess delivery times, transportation costs, customs procedures and the quality of logistics services. The findings provided practical insight into the route’s performance and areas where efficiency could be improved.

One initiative focuses on customs infrastructure at the Port of Aktau, a key link in Kazakhstan’s transport network across the Caspian Sea. Japan plans to support the installation of a stationary, large-scale X-ray scanning system. The equipment is expected to reduce cargo inspection times by approximately threefold, helping improve customs processing and the efficiency of freight movement through the port.

The project forms part of broader efforts to make the Middle Corridor a more competitive option for international cargo flows as countries seek to diversify transport routes.

Direct flights to connect Almaty and Tokyo

The conference also addressed the planned launch of regular direct flights between Almaty and Tokyo’s Narita International Airport by Air Astana. The first flight from Almaty is scheduled for Nov. 30, with the return flight from Narita planned for Dec. 1. The airline intends to operate the route twice a week using Airbus A321LR aircraft.

The flight is expected to take seven hours and 30 minutes. The service will establish Kazakhstan’s first regular direct air connection with the Japanese capital, creating another link for business, tourism and broader bilateral exchanges.

Air Astana’s Senior Regional Manager for South Korea and Japan, Adel Dauletbek, presented the prospects for strengthening air connectivity during the conference.

Digital infrastructure adds another dimension

Participants also discussed the development of digital infrastructure along the Middle Corridor.

Baudarbek-Kozhatayev highlighted the Trans-Caspian fiber-optic communication line, which was officially commissioned in Baku on Oct. 15 with the participation of Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev and Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev.

The project is intended to expand international data exchange and strengthen the resilience of digital communications between countries in the region. Together, the transport, customs and digital infrastructure initiatives reflect efforts to strengthen Kazakhstan’s role as a transit link between Asia and Europe while expanding economic cooperation with Japan.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Rybakina Extends Lead at Top of WTA Rankings
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s Elena Rybakina continues to lead the Women’s Tennis Association (WTA) singles rankings, holding a lead of more than 1,600 points over her closest rival, Aryna Sabalenka of Belarus, while Kazakhstan’s Yulia Putintseva has climbed 13 places to 66th, according to the latest rankings.

Rybakina has 9,196 points, ahead of Sabalenka with 7,550. Russia’s Mirra Andreeva ranks third with 6,306 points. Americans Jessica Pegula and Coco Gauff round out the top five with 6,235 and 5,974 points, respectively.

Putintseva now holds 969 points after improving her position by 13 places. At the recent WTA 1000 tournament in Wuhan, China, she advanced through the first round before losing to Russia’s Diana Shnaider in the second round.

Several other Kazakh players feature in the WTA singles rankings. Sonya Zhiyenbayeva is ranked 381st, followed by Zhibek Kulambayeva at 479th. Aruzhan Sagandykova holds 678th place, while Asylzhan Arystanbekova ranks 692nd and Ekaterina Dmitrichenko is 884th.

Kazakhstan also has a representative in the top 10 of the WTA doubles rankings. Anna Danilina has retained seventh place with 6,135 points. The doubles ranking is led by Czech player Katerina Siniakova with 11,260 points. American Taylor Townsend ranks second with 9,415 points, followed by Brazil’s Luisa Stefani with 9,220.

World.title: CICA’s Moment to Turn Confidence Building into Secure Connectivity
World.content:
The seventh Summit of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence Building Measures in Asia (CICA) in Baku on Oct.15 adopted the Baku Declaration, admitted Laos as the 29th member, extended Azerbaijan’s chairmanship through 2028 and appointed a new Secretary General. The CICA Charter, which would complete the forum’s transformation into a full international organization, was not yet adopted, and leaders called for continued work on it. The next two years are therefore the moment of graduation. How CICA defines its purpose in the charter will decide whether it becomes a working instrument or remains a dialogue club. We argue that the organization should make one link explicit, the link between conflict prevention and secure, efficient connectivity. The disruption of Asia’s transit corridors over the past year shows why this link cannot wait, and it is squarely in Kazakhstan’s interest.

A forum that kept its distance from hard security

Kazakhstan proposed CICA in 1992 because Asia had no common security structure, and it still has none. ASEAN, the SCO, the Arab League and the Gulf Cooperation Council each cover a subregion, while the continent’s most dangerous disputes run between states belonging to different groupings. CICA is the only format where India and Pakistan, Israel and Palestine, China and its maritime neighbours all sit together.

That breadth came at a price. Decisions are taken by consensus, and the forum has generally steered clear of conflict resolution. The notable exception came at the first summit in Almaty in June 2002, at the height of the India-Pakistan standoff after the attack on India’s parliament. Atal Bihari Vajpayee and Pervez Musharraf both attended, and while they did not meet directly, Vladimir Putin relayed messages between them on the margins. In 2004 members adopted a Catalogue of Confidence Building Measures that included military notifications and consultations on border incidents. In 2007, however, they agreed to begin with economic, environmental and human measures and to postpone the military-political ones.

Although military-political confidence-building measures have since been developed and implemented, their practical role in preventing disruptions to regional connectivity remains limited. Given the diversity of the membership, the caution is understandable. It has also left CICA without a role in the crises that now matter most to Asian trade.

A year of broken corridors

The past 12 months have shown how quickly conflict closes trade routes. The war that began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran on Feb.28, 2026 disrupted the International North-South Transport Corridor and the southern branch of the East-West route through Iran, cutting Central Asia’s shortest access to open water. Southern routes became unusable or uninsurable for extended periods, and freight was rerouted at higher cost.

Further east, Pakistan closed its five main trade crossings with Afghanistan after clashes in 2025, and a year later they remain shut. Trade between the two countries had been estimated at about $2.35 billion a year. The closure also halted transit of goods from China, Malaysia and Vietnam. Mediation by Qatar and Turkiye produced a ceasefire in October 2025, but fighting resumed and escalated to Pakistani air strikes on Kabul in February 2026. In May 2025 India and Pakistan had already exchanged strikes for four days.

All of these conflicts involve CICA members, and each struck at routes that Central Asia had been counting on. For landlocked economies, connectivity is a security question. A corridor is only as reliable as the most fragile border it crosses.

The Middle Corridor as the test case

The Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, or Middle Corridor, which runs from China and Kazakhstan across the Caspian to Azerbaijan, Georgia and Turkiye, shows both the promise and the vulnerability. Volumes through Kazakhstan rose from 0.8 million tonnes to 4.5 million tonnes a year, and total corridor traffic reached 4.5 million tonnes in 2024, up 62%. The World Bank estimates that volumes could reach around 11 million tonnes by 2030. The disruption of routes through Iran has shifted more of the burden onto it.

The corridor’s growth has been underwritten by conflict management. The initialling of the Azerbaijan-Armenia peace agreement in Washington in August 2025 opened the prospect of new links across the South Caucasus, and the Kyrgyz-Tajik border treaty of March 2025 reopened crossings in the Fergana Valley. Yet the war in Iran underscored how quickly instability could spill into the South Caucasus segment. Baku, which hosted the summit and has coordinated CICA’s transport track since 2007, sits at the centre of this equation.

At the summit Kassym-Jomart Tokayev proposed two initiatives that point in the right direction. One is a CICA Transport Connectivity Strategy covering major routes, including the Middle Corridor. The other is a Mechanism for Preventive Diplomacy, which he justified with the line that peace is best built before crises emerge. The value lies in treating these 2 proposals as one agenda.

What CICA can do

First, CICA can make corridor security part of its confidence building work. The measures adopted in 2004 already provide for notification of military activity and consultations on dangerous incidents near borders. Applied to transit routes and border crossings, they would give governments and logistics operators earlier warning and a channel to contain incidents before they close a route.

Second, the organization can articulate a norm that trade crossings and third-country transit stay open during bilateral disputes. No member would surrender its position in a dispute, yet all would gain predictability. The Afghanistan-Pakistan border is the obvious first case. Kazakhstan or Uzbekistan, which trade with both sides and have their own plans for routes to Pakistani ports through Afghanistan, could coordinate such an effort. The obstacle is representation. Taliban authorities were not invited to the 2022 summit in Astana, and despite their efforts to take part, they were absent again in Baku, even though Afghanistan formally remains a full member and its seat is held in reserve. The Secretariat has nonetheless kept a channel open, holding its first informal consultative meeting on engagement with Afghanistan in August 2025, and expert-level work on border and transit issues does not require settling recognition.

Third, the Charter should write this linkage into CICA’s mandate. A charter that lists cooperation areas side by side will reproduce the old division between soft and hard issues. A charter that defines secure connectivity as a core purpose, with preventive diplomacy as one of its tools, would give the new organization a reason to exist that its members can measure.

Azerbaijan’s extended mandate

Azerbaijan’s first term strengthened the economic side of CICA. The 2025 implementation plan included 44 events, about 20 of them proposed by Baku, with a focus on transport digitalization, data protection and cybersecurity, and ministers established a Women Council and a Finance Summit. Security received less attention in the public record of the chairmanship, a limit of the consensus model more than of Baku. The extension through 2028 and the appointment of an Azerbaijani Secretary General give Baku the time and the institutional levers to close that gap and to steer the Charter negotiations toward the security-connectivity link. CICA would not replace bilateral negotiations or existing mediation mechanisms. Its contribution would be to facilitate voluntary consultations, improve communication among participating states and support practical arrangements for transit continuity. Such efforts would require the consent of the states concerned and, where relevant, cooperation with countries outside CICA.

Why it matters for Kazakhstan

CICA is a Kazakh initiative, and its Secretariat remains in Astana. Kazakhstan’s transit strategy rests on routes it does not control, from the Caspian crossing to the planned railway to Pakistan through Turkmenistan and Afghanistan. As a land-locked country like its other Central Asian neighbors, an effective transit corridor strategy must be a very high priority. At the summit Tokayev also outlined plans with Azerbaijan to raise volumes of Kazakh oil shipped through the Baku-Tbilisi-Ceyhan pipeline. Every one of these projects depends on predictable borders. An organization that can lower the risk of conflict along these routes would serve Astana’s interests more directly than any additional dialogue platform.

If CICA uses the 2026 to 2028 window to adopt a Charter that ties conflict prevention to secure connectivity, it can become the first Asian institution with a practical answer to the corridor disruptions of the past year. If the Charter instead codifies the existing separation of soft and hard issues, the organization will gain legal status without gaining relevance, and Asian trade will continue to depend on ad hoc mediation by outside powers each time a border closes.

The authors are Eldaniz Gusseinov, a Co-Founder and Head of Research of Nightingale Int., a geopolitical foresight and advisory firm focused on Central Asia and Greater Eurasia, and Andrew Kuchins, a Senior Fellow at the Center for the National Interest in Washington, who also teaches at Johns Hopkins SAIS.

Disclaimer: The views and opinions expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the position of The Astana Times.
