World.title: bp starts offshore work on $2.9B Shah Deniz compressor project (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 20. Construction has begun on the offshore section of the $2.9 billion Shah Deniz Compression (SDC) project at the Shah Deniz gas and condensate field.

This was announced in a statement published by bp Azerbaijan.

The installation of four tubular piles, which will form the foundation of the platform’s support block, has been successfully completed as part of the project. Over the past few weeks, the piles were safely transported offshore and installed using the underwater construction vessel “Khankendi.”

Each pile is approximately 70 meters long, 108 inches in diameter, and weighs 292 metric tons, making it the largest-diameter tubular pile ever installed by bp in the Caspian Sea. A specially designed 188-metric-ton underwater support slab was used to ensure stability and vertical alignment during installation.

In addition, pile plug installation technology was used for the first time in bp’s operations in the region during this project.

The completion of this phase paves the way for the installation of the platform support block, scheduled for the first half of 2028.

The Shah Deniz field is located on the deepwater shelf of the Caspian Sea, 70 kilometers southeast of Baku, and covers an area of more than 140 square kilometers. According to preliminary estimates, the field, discovered in 1999, holds approximately 1 trillion cubic meters of gas and 2 billion barrels of condensate.

Development of the field proceeded in phases. In 2003, a final investment decision was made for the first phase, and commercial production began in 2006. In 2013, the Shah Deniz 2 project was approved, and production began in 2018.

The project is currently in its next phase, the compression facility project. This $2.9 billion project aims to increase production from the field’s low-pressure gas reserves and is expected to yield an additional 50 billion cubic meters of gas.

At the same time, the Shah Deniz project has made a significant contribution to the development of local industrial capacity and a skilled workforce in Azerbaijan. The project has created thousands of jobs, and local construction and service companies have been integrated into international energy projects.

According to bp, the current production capacity of the Shah Deniz field’s operational infrastructure is approximately 76.8 million standard cubic meters of gas per day, or about 28 billion cubic meters of gas per year.

The ownership stakes in the Shah Deniz project are distributed as follows: bp (operator) – 29.99%, LUKOIL – 19.99%, TPAO – 19%, SGC – 16.02%, NICO – 10%, and MVM – 5%.

World.title: Loan of $20m to troubled smelter deemed high risk, govt went ahead anyway
World.content:
The Tasmanian government was advised to approve a $20 million loan to the country's only manganese smelter last year despite knowing the risk of not getting all the money back was high, as inaction was deemed too risky, an internal document shows.

The Liberty Bell Bay manganese smelter, in Tasmania's north, closed in July this year and was subsequently liquidated, resulting in the loss of more than 200 jobs.

More than two years earlier, a tropical cyclone damaged South32's GEMCO manganese ore operation in the Northern Territory, hobbling Liberty Bell Bay's access to its main source of ore and sparking a chain of events that would lead to its liquidation.

In May 2025, the smelter had entered limited operations due to what its then-owner — UK billionaire Sanjeev Gupta's GFG Alliance — said were ore supply issues, international price volatility and US tariffs.

More than 200 workers lost their jobs when Liberty Bell Bay closed. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

A document obtained by the ABC under right-to-information shows in July 2025, the Tasmanian government was told Liberty Bell Bay "may run out of available capital by the end of July" and was given four options.

The paper, from Tasmania's coordinator-general John Perry, recommended the government provide an urgent loan of up to $20 million to Liberty Bell Bay — stating there was a "very high risk" the smelter would not be able to restart without an immediate capital injection.

"LBB's owners GFG Group appear unable and/or unwilling to provide any capital into the business," the paper stated.

Every risk category for loan was rated high

The Tasmanian government ultimately decided to proceed with the $20 million loan to allow Liberty Bell Bay to purchase ore and restart operations at the smelter.

But the document from the coordinator-general shows his office rated every risk category for the loan as "high".

The document stated manganese producers carried "industry and sector risks" including fluctuations in steel demand and pricing — as manganese is used to make steel — exchange rate volatility, supply chain disruptions, geopolitical instability, and environmental regulations.

Liberty Bell Bay's administrators ordered its closure in July. (ABC News: Maren Preuss)

It also stated there was a "high risk that the value of security provided would not be sufficient to cover the outstanding loan amount" — meaning the government may not see the full value of the loan returned.

But ultimately, the document stated the risks of Liberty Bell Bay's closure were greater.

"While there is clearly an elevated risk in relation to this transaction the broader economic and strategic implications of inaction could prove to significantly more severe," it said.

Doing nothing considered riskier than loan

The paper from the coordinator general canvassed three other options, in addition to the $20 million loan.

The options were:

Option 1: do nothing.

Option 2: provide a staged financial support package with an immediate $20 million loan.

Option 3: support a "solvent" sale of Liberty Bell Bay through US-based private equity firm White Oak.

Option 4: provide a smaller loan, conditional on security strong enough to force administration of the smelter.

Liberty Bell Bay was Australia's only manganese smelter. (Supplied)

"Do nothing" was deemed a "significant risk" to the smelter, with the paper estimating its closure could impact the state economy by $500 million a year if it failed to reopen.

Option 3, the sale of the smelter through White Oak, was considered "more than what is required" and "does not represent good value for money for the Tasmanian government".

The paper said option 4 would have enabled the Tasmanian government "to take control of the business" but was "fully expected this is likely to be unpalatable to GFG".

Liberty Bell Bay said it was solvent at time of loan

Minister for Business, Industry and Resources Felix Ellis said the government stood by its decision to loan Liberty Bell Bay $20 million to give "its workers the best possible chance of a future".

"We understood the risks were present, but the released documents show the advice was that the consequences of doing nothing were greater," he said in a statement.

Felix Ellis says the Tasmanian government will recover funds through the sale of the ore. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

The smelter's administrator EY Parthenon said it believed the company had been insolvent from as early as May 1, 2025.

But Liberty Bell Bay's directors signed a declaration to the Tasmanian government in August that year stating it was solvent.

"The loan followed independent financial and legal advice, and Liberty Bell Bay company directors provided a signed declaration of solvency before the loan was executed," Mr Ellis said.

"The loan was secured, and funds were paid directly to the ore supplier.

"State-appointed receivers are pursuing recovery through the secured ore, with the final amount recoverable dependent on the sale outcome."

World.title: What's behind the pile-on for 'Oscar contender' and stinging satire, Digger?
World.content:
Imagine being at the top of your game in Hollywood after a lifetime of hard work and using that privilege to create one of the most daringly original art-house satires since Dr. Strangelove.

Then imagine being in an era of online film criticism in which reviewers can appear eager to take the wind from the sails of a high-stakes project the moment it's launched.

Digger director Alejandro González Iñárritu and the film's star, Tom Cruise, must feel stuck in the doldrums.

With accusations of "auteurist grandstanding", being an "insufferable slog", and an obsession with opening weekend box office takings, words such as "flop" have been bandied about as if Digger was a terrible "misfire".

What it is, however, is a brilliantly executed modern take on the satire that will almost certainly be nominated for several Oscars, and one with a sharp sting that will ache long after you've left the cinema.

Film review: Digger Tom Cruise is almost unrecognisable under piles of prosthetics as Digger Rockwell, but his performance isn't the most shocking aspect of the searing satire.

That's my subjective view, of course, and Digger is not without flaws. But I wonder if some critics unable to objectively credit the craftsmanship at work here — whether they liked the film or not — had something else on the mind.

Indeed, a large divide has already appeared between published reviews and audience feedback. Aggregator sites such as Metacritic and Rotten Tomatoes are giving the film audiences score of 7.2 and 76 per cent, respectively, compared to aggregated critic scores of 46pc and 53pc.

There has also been a surge in passionate defenders of Digger on social media as people encourage others to ignore the commentary and see it themselves — a request Warner Bros (in damage control) has also adopted while urging viewers to "decide for yourself".

"There definitely seems to be a push for the film to fail, with reports immediately surfacing about much the film is losing after a less than stellar opening weekend," Adelaide University's Peter C Pugsley said.

The School of Communication, Media and Journalism associate professor said "attention-seeking headlines throw around figures like a '$250-million loss' without indicating the film's important messages about the excesses of corporate greed, political corruption, and our willingness to stand by as environmental devastation occurs".

"Some critics write at length how 'awful' the film is, but then engage in some serious fence-sitting about how it might be a worthy Oscar contender."

Loading Instagram content

Ben Affleck has likened the phenomenon of the pile-on to "high school bullying" and "cultural schadenfreude" or, in regular speak, tall poppy syndrome and taking pleasure in seeing prominent figures fall.

So what is going on?

A 'sport' in trashing big budget films

Melbourne Cinematheque president and RMIT University Associate Professor Adrian Danks said the film's trailer may have contributed to animosity because it was largely seen as being misleading.

The politics of reviewing Film reviewing is disappearing as a profession and is being replaced by multitudes of "enthusiasts", experts say.

He also said it was becoming increasingly difficult to distinguish between professional reviews and "the much wider ecology of film reviewing and commentary".

"That said, there is a trend to treat some large budget Hollywood films in this fashion," Dr Danks said.

"There is a tendency to be critical of high-budget, seemingly somewhat personal films that might seem something of an overstretch, and in this case starring an actor hardly beyond criticism … in the social media age, once this process starts, it's hard to stop."

He said it was not uncommon for the public to occasionally round on Cruise, usually for his wider public profile rather than his acting.

"This is also something of a sport," Dr Danks said.

"Think of the many films that have suffered this fate, for one reason or another, dating back to at least the 1960s and including films like Paint Your Wagon, Heaven's Gate, which is probably the closest parallel, Waterworld, etc."

John Goodman and Tom Cruise, who was covered in prosthetics for the film, while shooting Digger. (Instagram: @TomCruise)

Dr Pugsley said prosthetics made Cruise mostly unrecognisable in Digger but, because his role was necessarily "over the top", some critics might have seen it as "blatant Oscar-bait appeal for him to finally win Best Actor".

"Or is it a case of rewriting Iñárritu's legacy of films like The Revenant and Birdman, the latter described disparagingly by one critic as a film defined by its 'splashy theatrics'?" he said.

"Quite the accusation. Has that critic seen Barbie, perchance?"

There have been plenty of highly favourable reviews published about Digger, of course, and they continue to emerge. But for now, at least, they remain outnumbered.

Is it group think?

Dr Danks said the early negatively that emerged was unlikely to be a case of group think, but rather a matter of needing to get a review or opinion "out there as fast as possible".

Film reviewing has shifted a long way since the rise of the internet and social media. (891 ABC Adelaide: Malcolm Sutton)

"We are a long way from an era where longer-form criticism — say, the writing of Pauline Kael — could make a significant difference, as a film was released in stages," he said.

"But there is also some glee in playing the game that the major studios play, where a film is made or broken on its first weekend."

Dr Danks also pointed out that there were "far fewer paid reviewers" today, and that the modern mode of criticism was often dependent on "less measured reviews".

"Most reviewers are required to give a star-rating and, I imagine, encouraged to be a bit more polarising, in keeping with the wider culture," he said.

It's worth pointing out that another satire that took aim at political failures and corruption regarding climate change mitigation, 2021's Don't Look up, was also panned by critics on its release.

Don't Look Up Don't Look Up director Adam McKay takes aim at criticisms of his new film, suggesting that if audiences don't like it, it's because they don't get it.

Like Digger, it shares a disparity between critic responses and audiences': 49pc and 6.6 respectively on Metacritic, and 56pc and 78pc on Rotten Tomatoes.

On that occasion, however, there was a sense some media agencies didn't like how the film held a somewhat unflattering mirror to their faces.

Newsrooms are packed with big egos, after all, and having their image bruised by a film like Digger, in which Cruise's character sinks a cowboy boot into society's hypocrisy over its addiction to oil, is unlikely to win it friends — even if it's true.

"The negative reviews all seem to touch on the same 'problems' with the film, including that it is too 'heavy-handed' in its critiques of capitalism," Dr Pugsley said.

" To take a more conspiratorial stance, one could argue that the owners of the mass media are increasingly willing to take the sides of the mega-rich and the fossil fuel industries, adding pressure on critics or editors to downplay such a revolutionary film as Digger. "

As well as Affleck, a growing list of celebrities and artists including Anne Hathaway, Jane Fonda, Neil Young, Tom Waits, Guillermo Toro, Ron Howard and Alfonso Cuarón have come out publicly to defend the film.

They've warned that when daring, big-budget films such as Digger are rejected, it results in less risk-taking by studios and more homogenised films (think Marvel and tired superhero franchises).

"I think a stand is also being made here, by people like Affleck and Young, that we do need to support films like this emerging from the mainstream, films that are outside the norm, ambitious and socially critical," Dr Danks said.

Alejandro G Iñárritu (far left) during the filming of Digger. (Supplied: Warner Bros.)

He said many films suffering the fate of Digger found supporters and were often reassessed at a later date.

"I would say it's generally true that we don't really know the true value of a film until much later," Dr Danks said.

" Many of the films we celebrate now, particularly from Hollywood, were much less successful, financially and critically, when first released. "

This includes classics like Blade Runner, John Carpenter's The Thing, Fight Club, The Shining, Vertigo and Metropolis.

Regardless of your tastes, a cultural phenomenon is underway in our cinemas.

For me, Digger is a level-four — sorry, four-star — film at least, and I'll probably see it again, if I can convince someone to join me.

World.title: Game developers pitch for funding at speed dating-style event in Melbourne
World.content:
A giant countdown timer, a DJ sitting on the side of the room spinning tunes, nerves and anticipation, and a bell that rings when it's time to rotate partners.

The Play Now marketplace feels a lot like a speed dating event, or like the Shark Tank television program.

Held during Melbourne International Games Week, game developers from across the country are matched with prospective publishers and put their best foot forward in an attempt to secure funding for their game.

Tables and screens with laptops and controllers are arranged around the room as pitch decks are presented and developers lay out their plans to make the next big hit.

The converted conference room in a Melbourne hotel was set up with tables and screens. (Supplied: Daniel Mahon, VicScreen)

VicScreen CEO Caroline Pitcher says the event, now in its fourth year, is attracting international and local publishers searching for rare Australian talent.

"We've gone from strength to strength in terms of growing the number of publishers that are coming here, growing the number of game devs that are participating," she says.

"There's a maximum of 10 meetings so someone like Nintendo, their dance card is full."

She says that because publishers choose the teams they are going to meet with, the ice is already broken and game developers can get right into the pitch.

Opportunity for feedback for every pitch

During a pitch, a developer will often deliver a small presentation about their game outlining their previous work, their current team and what sort of funding they are looking for to finish their work.

It's a nerve-wracking experience as last-minute bug fixes in playable demos are patched on the couches surrounding the presentation tables.

Some of the pitches immediately click, with a joy of play evident as publisher scouts disappear into the game.

Others falter, with nerves overwhelming the rehearsed spiel, or a mismatch of game format to prospective publisher.

But these are met with kindness even when they don't go well.

Previously pitched games at Play Now have been successfully funded. (Supplied: Daniel Mahon, VicScreen)

To avoid too many incompatible projects and to maximise the time between developers and publishers, VicScreen acts as matchmakers, pairing up projects and organising meetings.

Rebecca Lautner, chief business officer at Swedish game developer-turned-publisher, Evil Landfall, wants to find "wacky physics-based games" and to give back after their success.

"So we follow this [event] from outside of Melbourne Games Week, we're fascinated by the Australian games industry in general and we already have two projects that we invested in from here," she says.

"Usually, we have to do a lot of research before and find the games that are interesting for us, here it's basically done for you.

"You just arrive and you meet the right people and it's an amazing time."

Kirsten-Lee Naidoo and Rebecca Lautner travel from Sweden to take part in the Play Now marketplace. (Supplied: Daniel Mahon, VicScreen)

Evil Landfall CEO Kirsten-Lee Naidoo says developers in Australia are prepared and it's leading to some success.

"In other parts of the world there's a lot less guidance on how to pitch and how to polish your demo and it's very, very clear that people who are pitching at PlayNow, they know what they're doing," she says.

"They don't include their budget, they don't include their timeline, they're missing some key details, and coming to Australia we never have that problem because they are taught to know how to do things."

'We want video games that make us lots of money'

Bridie Roman and Daniel Lucic from publisher Devolver Digital are at Play Now to find the next big hit.

The publisher has a long history of signing games from Australia, including the hugely successful Cult of the Lamb and upcoming games like comedic fantasy game The Dungeon Experience and pachinko-like Hyper Drop.

Bridie Roman and Daniel Lucic take pitches from at Play Now. (Supplied: Daniel Mahon, VicScreen)

Roman says finding a magic recipe for breakaway success isn't clear cut.

"I think the only answer that we've ever really settled on is games that we would play as gamers ourselves," she says.

"Something that makes us more connected, a fun gameplay twist, a little bit of humour, but none of these things necessarily make it a Devolver game."

Lucic says he remembers when being pitched Hyper Drop at Play Now last year, which was developed in Perth by Aaron Dark, the rest of the world just disappeared.

"When we saw the pitch and I started playing it at one point I just zoned out, I just wanted to play it," he says.

" I was quite open with it. I was like, 'Sorry, I'm just going to focus on this and I'll let the others talk to you', and that's really what made it stand out. "

Cult favourite

Julian Wilton, creative director at Massive Monster, developer of Cult of the Lamb, has also transitioned from developer to publisher, supporting two locally made games.

The studio also launched MASS, a co-working space in Collingwood to further support the local development scene with hot desks and a game-specific fit-out.

Julian Wilton is the Creative Director of Massive Monster, a Melbourne based developer who is funding other studios to make video games and opened a co-working space for developers. (Supplied: Daniel Mahon, VicScreen)

Wilton said it was nice to be on the other side of the pitch and to share his success with others.

"It's the best position to be in. It's better than trying to pitch to people, you can just get them pitched to you, I love it," he says.

"We've got two games we're invested in at the moment, some local games, we just meet with them every couple of weeks, give feedback, give them the best chance of success.

"I love the business side of games and the marketing of it, so I'm kind of trying to impart to them how important saying what your game is and communicating it to someone."

As the final countdown clock ends the bell chimes, laptops are closed, hands are shaken and business cards are exchanged.

Some of these developers will have secured the financial and business support needed to continue making their games and might end up in players hands around the world.

Others will go home without a new prospective partner this time, but will be ready for the next round of pitching next year.

World.title: Seven West Media had 'diabolical' culture, secret review hears
World.content:
A bombshell review of Seven West Media in 2024 has been told of a "diabolical" corporate culture, with allegations that sexism, bullying and harassment were rife and "sacred cow" executives favoured by then-chairman Kerry Stokes were protected amid a ratings obsession.

The ABC has seen a copy of the 65-page review, conducted by independent consultancy Interchange.

It was concluded in July 2024 and has never been made public.

The review was commissioned by the former Seven West board in May that year in the wake of Federal Court claims by former Spotlight producer Taylor Auerbach, that the network had reimbursed ex-Liberal staffer Bruce Lehrmann for drugs and sex workers in order to secure an interview with him.

Former producer Taylor Auerbach's claims to Federal Court were partly why the culture review was commissioned.

Mr Auerbach acknowledged he had never seen an invoice for this and Seven vehemently denied the claims, saying it was "appalled" by them.

Former Seven chief executive James Warburton resigned in April 2024 following those claims as well as the network's on-air misidentification of the Bondi stabber, and was replaced by Jeff Howard.

Mr Warburton had previously announced his intention to step down in June.

Kerry Stokes was chairman of Seven West Media at the time of the review. (ABC News: Andrew O'Connor)

Mr Lehrmann was ultimately found by the Federal Court, on the balance of probabilities, to have raped colleague Brittany Higgins in a federal Parliament House office in 2019.

That finding was made as part of a defamation trial and remains untested in a criminal court. Mr Lehrmann has denied the rape allegation.

The Interchange review into the network's corporate culture interviewed Kerry Stokes and the rest of the board, as well as half a dozen advertising clients and agencies, and did 127 interviews or small focus groups with Seven employees across Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane and Perth.

Interchange also drew on more than 800 responses to a company survey.

The report does not suggest that Mr Stokes, Mr Warburton or other senior management were aware of or involved in the alleged incidents discussed by staff.

Mr Stokes declined to comment for this story.

"Immoral, unethical and illegal behaviour has been prevalent for a very long time," one anonymised NSW Seven West leader told the review.

The Seven West Media board commissioned the review in 2024. (ABC News: Glyn Jones)

Another interviewee said: "There are people in this office every day crying and there is nothing I can do about it."

"The culture here is abhorrent … I know the stuff they have been exposed to. Some of them have been touched up; the less pretty ones get verbally abused. Pick your poison. It's not just the girls either, but they cop it the worst."

"We've had some diabolical situations culturally, but they've been allowed to keep going," another said.

"Certain people in power who have continually abused their position time and time again; nothing happens because they are a protected species."

Interviewees told Interchange that they immediately believed the Lehrmann allegations "because of other misconduct they witnessed."

Other testimonies in the final report include:

"The news guys are ruthless and get away with really bad behaviour because of their legacy and results. People are scared to cross them because they're sacred cows."

A senior leader in NSW said: "I think decisions made in the past indicate that people are protected by the Stokes'."

One executive said: "The way to leave Seven with very heavy pockets is to behave appallingly".

A Queensland leader said: "The ambulance was called due to someone who 'mentally snapped' after an incident of bullying at the office — it included seven senior males piling onto a female".

A Victorian leader said: "We are a man's world in media. It is a big swinging dick culture, unfortunately. It's got better than it used to be, but everyone's having affairs, and people are getting ahead because of those things."

A Victorian team member said a manager once threw a chair at a colleague. "It didn't hit him, but it didn't miss by much either. I noticed him crying a bit later at his desk, but he was embarrassed when I went over, so I left him to it."

A WA team member said their manager was "a chronic gaslighter … I saw a psychologist for a while because I started having panic attacks at work".

A WA leader said: "It's relationship and loyalty to Kerry over all else — and the people that play that game play it very well".

The company-wide survey found 63 per cent of respondents did not know what Seven West Media's organisational purpose was, 59 per cent were not clear on its future strategy, and 48 per cent said "yes" there were psychosocial hazards in the workplace.

Ratings dips had to be justified to Stokes, review told

If you "lose the ratings, you've got Kerry on your doorstep," one staff member told the review. (AAP Image: Richard Wainwright)

The review also painted a picture of an organisation with "low commercial acumen", fixated on Channel Nine and divided into "territorial tribes" with the executive committee "Kings and Queens of the drama cyclone".

"We make drama, but internally, if you want drama, you can set the clock for 8:58 every morning when the ratings come out," one executive said.

The consultants noted the influence of proprietor Kerry Stokes on Seven West Media in contrast to Channel Nine, which is controlled by a board representing institutional investors.

Kerry Stokes to stand down as chair of Seven West Media Media magnate Kerry Stokes will stand down as chair of Seven West Media after the company announces it will merge with Southern Cross Media.

"Numerous interviewees mentioned phone calls or emails from the chairman that required them or their direct reports to justify a dip in ratings," the review wrote.

"If you lose the ratings, you've got Kerry on your doorstep," said one team member in NSW. "That's what we're worried about."

The review found Seven West Media was operating "more like a not-for-profit, in service of society, yet is unwilling to part with the glamorous side of what traditional media offered when the money flowed."

Even board members joined in the criticism, telling Interchange the company "generates a billion dollars of revenue but also a billion of costs," and there were "so many people on old media salaries that just don't add up anymore".

Southern Cross buys up Seven

Ryan Stokes (left) is now chairman of Southern Cross Media, which owns Seven, previously run by his father (right). (AAP: Mick Tsikas)

The review also found Seven "didn't pivot fast enough" after the arrival in Australia of streaming services like Netflix, Disney+ and Amazon, and digital advertising platforms like Google and Meta, resulting in "anxiety, denial and outlets of bad behaviour" in the company.

The Interchange review was conducted as the ABC's Four Corners program was investigating the culture at Channel Seven — an episode which subsequently went to air in August 2024.

Since the review, Seven West Media was bought for $385 million by Southern Cross Media in a deal completed in January.

'Crushing, soul destroying': Current and former staff describe life working at Channel 7 Four Corners has spoken to more than 200 people to investigate allegations of Channel Seven's toxic culture, uncovering allegations of bullying, sexism, and exploitation.

The Stokes family emerged with a 20 per cent stake in the combined company, and through the course of the year crept up to 23 per cent — enough for Kerry Stokes' son Ryan to be appointed as chairman.

Earlier this year a longtime Stokes lieutenant, Bruce McWilliam, acquired an additional 9 per cent of Southern Cross Media — funded by rival mining billionaire Gina Rinehart — however he did not secure a seat on the board.

A Southern Cross Media spokesperson told the ABC everyone in its business "should feel safe, respected and supported".

"Measuring workplace culture and acting on employee feedback are essential responsibilities of any contemporary business," they said.

Mark McGowan set to take up Southern Cross role Former WA premier Mark McGowan will be appointed to the board of Southern Cross Media Group, which owns Channel 7, newspapers, websites and radio services across Australia.

"Seven West Media commissioned Interchange more than two years ago to give employees an anonymous, independent platform to speak up and identify where workplace culture needed to improve.

"As you would expect, the organisation has fundamentally changed over the past two years. There has been a merger and a cultural reset, with a new board, a new CEO and a new executive team.

" That work is supported by ongoing employee feedback and rigorous measures to track progress, and we are immensely proud of the business and culture we are building. "

In its most recent annual report for 2025–26, Southern Cross' accounts showed its audio business, which includes the Triple-M and Hit networks, was the division with the highest profit margin and the only division to report growth in revenues and earnings before interest, tax and depreciation (EBITDA).

The television division, including the Seven network, recorded a 32 per cent drop in EBITDA, while the publishing division, including the West Australian newspaper, recorded a 2 per cent drop.

Former NRMA, Seven West and Foxtel executive Rohan Lund took over as chief executive in May.

Southern Cross will hold its annual meeting in Sydney on November 5, at which all seven non-executive directors will face election, including recently appointed former WA Premier Mark McGowan and former Twitter Australia boss Karen Stocks.

World.title: Calls to beef up security for Victorian election in wake of Haines attack
World.content:
Victorian state politicians have pleaded for increased security, in response to death threats and abuse that have made some MPs reluctant to attend pre-polling centres when they open in four weeks' time.

The ABC understands Premier Ben Carroll will meet with the Victorian electoral commissioner today to discuss security arrangements in the lead-up to the state's November 28 poll.

It is also understood the premier has called a special cabinet meeting to discuss safety concerns with elected members in the wake of Monday's attack on federal MP Helen Haines.

On Tuesday, Premier Ben Carroll said there was a "live conversation" between government, police and the electoral commission about boosting security at voting centres.

Helen Haines live updates: Get the latest about the attack on the Victorian MP in our blog.

The ABC has spoken to more than a dozen state parliamentarians from across the political spectrum who all reported threats to their safety and that of their family, staff and volunteers.

Most wanted security to be ramped up and for state parliament and the Victorian Electoral Commission (VEC) to do more to protect them, warning that the tenor of debate was having a chilling effect on democracy.

There is a consensus among MPs that social media has escalated abuse and harassment, with some retiring from parliament or considering stepping back because of the constant stream of online hate.

Several MPs said threats and abuse directed at them and their staff had accelerated, particularly during the pandemic, when protesters performed a fake execution of an effigy of then premier Daniel Andrews on the steps of parliament.

Protesters brought a noose to Victorian Parliament when they protested pandemic laws in November 2021. (ABC News)

At the time, security arrangements for Mr Andrews moved to around-the-clock protection, the ABC understands.

During her time as premier, Jacinta Allan worried an MP was going to be killed.

"I do not remember a time when our foundations have felt so unsteady,'' Ms Allan said in her last media appearance in August to announce her retirement.

" Social cohesion is under pressure. Public debate is deteriorating. The line between truth and lie is increasingly blurred. "

A billboard targeting former premier Jacinta Allan was condemned after it appeared in Melbourne earlier this year. (Facebook: Sherele Moody)

Campaigning for the Victorian election paused on Tuesday out of respect for Ms Haines, which prompted Mr Carroll to reach out to state leaders including Opposition Leader Jess Wilson.

"Whether it's your volunteer wearing a red t-shirt or a blue t-shirt or a green t-shirt or an orange, let's just make sure that as leaders that respect civility is first and foremost," he told 774 ABC Melbourne on Tuesday morning.

Labor volunteers told not to campaign alone

The Labor Party has advised its volunteers to campaign in pairs, but preferably in larger groups and to remain alert to security risks.

MPs and ministers have repeatedly raised the alarm in cabinet and Labor caucus meetings, several sources said. Opposition MPs have also lobbied for increased security.

Some politicians were hesitant to attend pre-polling booths, which open 10 days before Victoria's November election.

Victorian MP Georgie Purcell says she has had to change her behaviour over safety concerns. (ABC News)

Upper house Animal Justice MP Georgie Purcell said the situation was particularly dire for women with a profile.

"It does change the way you move about the world. I consider my movements everywhere I go for my physical safety and I can't do a lot of things other politicians, particularly men, can do,'' she told the ABC.

Ms Purcell, whose partner is federal Labor MP Josh Burns, said Victorian MPs needed to have the same security arrangements as their federal counterparts.

One parliamentarian felt frustrated that they did not receive protection like the prime minister or premier. "Don't make decisions on behalf of us when you get personal protection," they said.

A VEC spokesperson said maintaining safe elections was its priority, adding: "Political violence has no place in our democracy."

Abuse driving candidates, MPs out of politics

Broadcaster Tracee Hutchison said she endured gendered attacks when she contested the May by-election in Nepean as an independent candidate.

"One of the reasons I decided not to recontest in Nepean in November was because of the relentless sustained attacks on me, verbal abuse, online abuse, defacing of my political materials," Ms Hutchison told 774 ABC Melbourne on Tuesday.

Independent candidate Tracee Hutchison says she suffered online attacks during the Nepean by-election earlier this year. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

Candidates and political parties reported that the mood had shifted at the last state election in 2022, shortly after COVID-19 restrictions were lifted.

"We were exposed to danger. We were not safe," Narre Warren South MP Gary Maas wrote in a submission to the parliament's review of the conduct of the election.

" As people grew tired towards the end of a two-week pre-poll, I was fearing that someone might get hurt. "

Deakin University extremism expert Josh Roose said targeted threats to politicians and their electorate offices began to spike during the pandemic.

"One of the key drivers of that has been distrust in government," Dr Roose said.

He said people were profiting from a polarised environment.

"That might be economic capital, i.e. clicks, and traffic being driven and advertising dollars online, but it's also political capital. Political parties are exploiting quite raw emotion out there, driven by the cost-of-living crisis, affordability, even diesel prices in our regions. People are angry," Dr Roose said.

He said rural and regional communities were particularly vulnerable to radicalisation, and that this seemed to be correlated with poorer services.

Extremists have hijacked events with MPs, and sovereign citizens — who do not believe governments hold legitimate authorities to make laws — are an increasing risk.

Nationals MP Tim McCurdy, the state member for Ovens Valley, told radio station 3AW that the safety of politicians, especially women, needed to be addressed.

"People have said to me, 'Do we need to up the ante with security?' Well, if that means bodyguards walking around with politicians, that's not the answer. I mean, we've got to be able to get out and do what we need to do in our communities," he said.

"We've still got to do our job, and that's what Helen was doing, walking down the street doing her job."

There were 48 security incidents recorded at Victorian Parliament between June 2025 and April 2026, a reduction on the year prior.

Security incidents at state electorate offices over the same period increased to 303.

World.title: Retired judge lashes NSW decision to rewrite laws to support coalmine
World.content:
A former Supreme Court Judge says a NSW government plan to draft special laws for a Hunter Valley coalmine "obliterates" the legal process and should be independently reviewed.

The premier has announced the government will legislate to allow the Mount Pleasant mine to continue operating at expanded production rates, despite a High Court ruling against it this month.

"The idea that a substantial mining venture can approach the government and say look, let's go behind the court processes and sort this out between ourselves is a very dangerous precedent, and that's exactly what appears to have happened here," said Anthony Whealy, who is now on the board of the Centre for Public Integrity.

"They've effectively ignored what I would call respect for the rule of law by overriding it.

"It is, on the face of it, reprehensible".

Anthony Whealy says there is no justificiation for DPS being exempt from FOI laws. (ABC News)

The ABC can reveal the Hunter Valley mine is already being investigated over allegations it breached its coal production limits, as it scaled up construction during the court process.

In 2022, the mine was given approval to double its capacity, from 10.5 to 21 million tonnes of coal per year, until 2048. But that approval was deemed invalid after a NSW Court of Appeal ruling in July 2025 that planning authorities had failed to consider the effect of overseas or Scope 3 emissions caused by the 406 million additional tonnes of coal exports over the life of the mine.

The Court of Appeal ordered a lower court, known as the Land and Environment Court, to revisit the expansion's approval, which was now "invalid", subject to that lower court's review.

But MACH Energy did not want to wait for a decision from the lower court.

In August 2025, weeks after the ruling, the company started earthworks to pave the way for millions more tonnes of coal to be produced, in what it described in company documents as "the next phase of the Mount Pleasant expansion".

The company lodged a swift appeal with the High Court, and by December 2025 the mine had produced 12.78 million tonnes of coal.

The Mount Pleasant coalmine is in the Hunter Valley region of New South Wales. (Supplied: Nearmaps)

Department increases mine output while under investigation

The residents' group that had won the NSW Court of Appeal case, known as the Denman Aberdeen Muswellbrook Scone Healthy Environment Group (DAMSHEG), lodged a complaint with the planning department through its lawyer, Elaine Johnson.

By her reading, the NSW Court of Appeal decision meant the company should not be furiously expanding while the matter was still before the courts.

And the mine should instead be required to rely on its first planning approval from 1999, which only allowed 10.5 million tonnes of coal to be extracted.

A department spokesman told her that it would "consider" her concerns.

As the expansion gained pace, Elaine Johnson wrote another letter, and the planning department finally confirmed it was investigating.

A close-up of the open pit at the MACH Energy coalmine near Muswellbrook in NSW. (Supplied: Nearmaps)

"The Department is committed to timely and appropriate compliance action," its letter from August 14, 2026 stated.

"Thank you for your correspondence."

On the same day, the department announced it would "modify" MACH Energy's first planning approval from 1999, which was not being challenged in court, to increase its 10.5 million tonne coal output to 12.5 million tonnes per year.

It also extended the mine's life for another six years, so there was no threat of it closing in December, when the existing 1999 permit was due to expire.

The "modification" could be done at the stroke of a pen because it met the "substantially the same development" test, according to a department spokesman.

High Court loss puts mine on back foot

When the High Court ruled against MACH Energy this month, it threw its expansion plans into disarray.

For months the company had publicly forecast its 2026 production would reach 16.5 million tonnes, a figure it could only justify if its appeal was successful.

That level of production relied on its second planning approval, the one tied to the expansion, being valid.

Legislation to allow mine's higher production The NSW government will introduce the legislation, that will allow an Upper Hunter mine to increase its output, despite a recent High Court ruling against it.

But the High Court found planning authorities had failed to do what was required of them in that case, which was to "consider imposing conditions to minimise to the greatest extent practicable all greenhouse gas emissions, including Scope 3 emissions".

The approval was invalid, and had to go back to the lower court, which could take months.

The mine's plan to extract 16.5 million tonnes over 2026 was now in jeopardy, because it was unclear if it was allowed to extract the extra 4 million tonnes.

Premier wants to 'sidestep' law to increase output again

Less than a fortnight after the High Court decision, NSW Premier Chris Minns announced new laws would be introduced to allow the mine to extract 16.5 million tonnes per year, the precise amount it had already scaled up to produce.

In his statement, the premier said the laws would "address the unique legal uncertainty arising from the High Court's judgement", and "protect 400 jobs" while the court process continued.

Chris Minns intervened after the High Court decision. (ABC News: Abubakr Sajid)

Retired Supreme Court Judge Anthony Whealy said the move had "obliterated" the legal process and appeared to be a "hollow" claim.

Mr Whealy said there were no clear exceptional circumstances justifying the move, and that there was "no evidence whatsoever to show that 400 jobs are under threat here".

"All this talk about 400 jobs being lost before Christmas is hyperbole, and not at the moment justified by any evidence that the government has produced," he said.

In parliament yesterday, Upper House Greens MP Cate Faehrmann asked the NSW Resources Minister Courtney Houssos what evidence the government had that 400 jobs were under threat before Christmas, so that "standalone legislation was necessary".

Ms Houssos told parliament the government had checked employment data records with both the company and the union.

She acknowledged the company had scaled up its operation over the past 18 months.

"Because they have legal advice that they had approval to operate at the higher rate, and as a result they took on additional workers," Ms Houssos said.

"We're not prepared to stand by in circumstances where we could see 400 workers lose their jobs before Christmas only to have the consent validated … in a matter of months."

High Court ruling on coal and climate An expert says a High Court ruling on coal said "the quiet part out loud".

Cate Faehrmann accused the government of "state capture".

"State capture is the undue influence of powerful individuals or corporations in shaping the formation of laws, policies, and regulations and institutions to their own advantage at the expense of society."

"This is state capture, right here."

Mr Whealy has called for an independent review into the government's decision.

"I remain very concerned that this is a dangerous precedent where governments just override the senior courts in order to get some sort of political advantage for themselves," Mr Whealy said.

Working 'hand-in-glove'

MACH Energy posted a statement on its website welcoming the premier's announcement, which it said would "provide locals with much-needed reassurance that the Mount Pleasant project will continue to deliver critical benefits in the future".

"MACH Energy obtained legal advice that confirmed the 2022 consent remained valid during the High Court proceedings," it said.

Tony Lonergan is part of the community group that appealed against the expansion. (ABC News: Sue Lannin)

Tony Lonergan, a co-founder of the DAMSHEG residents group fighting the mine, said the NSW government was working "hand-in-glove" with its "gung-ho" operators.

"[They're] pretty certain that planning and the government is going to back them," he said.

"And they think that they can just keep doing what they're doing."

A spokeswoman for the NSW Department of Planning, Housing and Infrastructure told the ABC it would not comment on active investigations.

World.title: Prince Harry: ‘I want family reconciliation ... but some people don’t’
World.content:
WorldEuropeRoyal family Prince Harry: ‘I want family reconciliation ... but some people don’t’ India McTaggart October 21, 2026 — 5:28am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. London: Prince Harry has said reconciliation with the royal family is “the most important thing” to him, but has claimed that “some people” do not have the same ambition. In an interview, the Duke of Sussex said mending ties with his family was his main goal, but admitted that “scars stick around forever”. Harry’s sit-down interview with GQ was his first since returning to the UK in August. Internet “I want it to work out,” he told GQ in his first sit-down interview since relocating to the UK in late August. “With everything else that’s going on in the world, the most important thing is to reconcile – that’s the key point. Scars stick around forever,” he said.



The duke said he was often asked how he would resolve his estrangement from the Prince of Wales, his older brother and heir to the throne. Related Article Royal family ‘It’s wonderful to be back’: Harry and Meghan on first outing since UK return It is thought the pair have not spoken for four years after a succession of damaging allegations by the Sussexes against the royal family, including during an interview with Oprah Winfrey, in a Netflix docuseries and in the duke’s memoir, Spare. “Some people don’t want it to work out,” he told GQ. “For me, there’s enough drama in the world and enough drama in people’s lives to continue with issues with family.” The duke has previously called for ties with the royal family to be mended, and told the BBC last year that he “would love a reconciliation”.



He and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, reunited with the King during a July visit to the UK. Father and son are understood to speak regularly on the phone. ‘We’re way past that’ Last Thursday, during the couple’s first joint engagement since returning to Britain, the Duchess of Sussex said it was “wonderful” to be back. The Sussexes greeted crowds of well-wishers in what appeared to be a royal engagement-style event during a day trip to Nottingham. Harry and his wife Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, appear in Nottingham last week. Getty Images



Elsewhere in the interview, the duke insisted he did not “want any sympathy” any more, explaining: “We’re way past that.” “Why? Because I’m a prince. I’ve got a support network around me, I’ve done different forms of therapy, and I put in the work.” He also mused: “I wonder where I would be if I didn’t [do therapy] – it could be a very different situation.” The duke has written extensively in his memoir about how therapy helped him “break the cycle” of generational trauma. He added that family squabbles were a “massively relatable issue for so many people”, emphasising “sibling disagreements” as well as “broken relationships between kids and their parents”.



“That continues to come up with me the whole time with people that I speak to, so I know how relatable it is,” the duke said. Related Article Royal family ‘Gaslighting’: Diana’s brother hits back at palace over his claim about the King He also said that he still found himself seeking advice from his mother, Diana, Princess of Wales, who died in a car accident in Paris when he was 12. “Sometimes there are questions that I ask her, looking for some kind of response. And sometimes, I do get a response,” he said. “Having done the work that I’ve done, there is a connection still with my mum that I do feel her energy at certain times, in certain parts of my life.” Prince Harry is in talks to make a documentary about his mother to mark the 30th anniversary of her death next August.



The Telegraph understands he has approached several friends and relatives of his late mother, including her brother, Earl Spencer, to ask whether they would take part in the project. The Sussexes’ Archewell Productions would produce such a programme, and Netflix would likely buy it, which continues to have a first-look deal with the duke and duchess. A spokesman for the Sussexes said of the duke’s comments to GQ: “It was absolutely not intended as a swipe at his brother or any other member of his family. The comment was made in a general context and was not directed at his family in any way.” The Telegraph, London Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

The US stock market is rising following strong profit reports for Equifax, Hasbro and other companies, while oil prices ease back after nearing their highest levels since the war with Iran began. The S&P 500 added 0.4 per cent. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 539 points, or 1 per cent, as of 1:48 p.m. Eastern time, while more swings for the artificial-intelligence industry had the Nasdaq composite up a more modest 0.2 per cent. Wall Street climbed on the back of strong earnings reports as well as a slide in oil prices. AP The Australian sharemarket is set to advance, with futures at 4.57am AEDT pointing to a rise of 34 points, or 0.4 per cent, at the open., The ASX lost 0.3 per cent on Tuesday. The Australian dollar was trading higher at US70.03¢. Stock prices tend to follow the path of corporate profits over the long term, and several companies delivered results for the latest quarter that were better than analysts expected. Big expectations for growth generally are what have allowed the US stock market to hit records recently despite worries about high inflation, higher interest rates and other challenges weighing on Wall Street.



Equifax rallied 10.6 per cent for one of the market’s biggest gains after reporting a bigger profit for the summer than analysts expected, despite high mortgage rates slowing some parts of its business. Hasbro climbed 9.3 per cent after the toy company said its Magic: The Gathering game made more than $US600 million during a quarter for the first time. 3M rose 5.8 per cent after the company behind Ace bandages and Scotch-Brite sponges likewise reported a stronger-than-expected profit, even as shoppers broadly feel discouraged by high inflation. Related Article Opinion

Trade wars China’s export boom is becoming its Achilles heel Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Stocks also got a lift after the price for a barrel of Brent crude erased an early gain to fall 0.8 per cent to $US108.70. Earlier in the morning, it got near $US112 and approached its highest price since the war with Iran began in late February. The drop in oil prices will relieve some of the pressure on inflation, if it lasts. Brent’s price has been yo-yoing between $US97 and $US112 per barrel this month on uncertainty about when the energy industry will return to normal.



For now, airlines and other companies with big fuel bills enjoyed the benefit of Tuesday’s drop. American Airlines rallied 4.4 per cent, and United Airlines flew 2.8 per cent higher. Another winner was Braze, a customer engagement platform. Its stock soared 51.5 per cent to $US45.51 after Salesforce said it would buy the company for $US47.50 in cash for each share. Salesforce fell 1.4 per cent. Keeping the market in check was General Motors, which sank 8.2 per cent despite reporting a bigger profit than analysts expected. It also announced a program to send up to $US20 billion to investors by buying back its stock. The pressure is on companies to deliver bigger profits not only now, but also in the future. GM gave a forecasted range for profit over the full year of 2026 whose midpoint fell short of analysts’ expectations. AI stocks, meanwhile, continued to swirl. They’ve been at the center of the market’s recent uneasiness, as euphoria around the technology’s boom gives way to worries that high interest rates in the bond market will slow the borrowing that’s allowed companies to buy so many AI chips. Last week was the US stock market’s worst since June because of weakness for AI-related companies.



CoreWeave has been particularly shaky. It initially fell more than 6 per cent at the start of Tuesday’s trading, only to swing to a gain of 5 per cent before pulling back to a rise of 2.3 per cent. Such reversals are nothing new for the company, which has borrowed money to buy AI chips that it rents out to customers over the cloud. A day earlier, it careened between a gain of 7 per cent in the morning and a loss of 3.5 per cent in the afternoon following last week’s tumble of roughly 25 per cent. Tuesday’s struggles for AI stocks began in Asia, where a South Korean AI company, Elice, confronted a rough welcome to the stock market. Its stock dropped 32 per cent in its first day of trading in Seoul. South Korea’s Kospi index fell 3.7 per cent overall. Related Article Australian Council of Trade Unions New ACTU president warns AI is automating entire jobs In other stock markets abroad, indexes in Europe pared bigger losses from earlier in the day. The CAC 40 in Paris slipped 0.4 per cent, and the FTSE 100 in London fell 0.3 per cent.



A day earlier, indexes fell sharply across Europe following violent protests that could ultimately force governments on the continent to increase their spending to ease voters’ anger. That in turn could put more pressure on their bond markets, which are already strained because of worries about heavy debt loads and strained budgets. World.title: Is it better to pay extra on your mortgage, or add it to your super?
World.content:
MoneySuper & retirementRetirement living Is it better to pay extra on your mortgage, or add it to your super? Kaye Fallick October 21, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Fifty-somethings often feel a long way from retirement. Currently, they’re generally too busy working, supporting families and managing cost of living pressures. Yet, they are probably at their ‘peak mortgage’ moment. And the decisions they make today can have a profound impact on their lives in 10 or 20 years. Here’s how. It’s always helpful to have some straightforward sums at hand when you have a financial ‘turning point’ decision to make. Getty Take the example of Gavin – 55, single, and paying off a home in Adelaide. He is typical of his age group, according to Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) data which notes that more than half of the 55-64 demographic is still paying down a home loan. Here’s what he wants to know: “I have about $30 per week I can save. My father says to put money away for retirement, by salary sacrificing, saying the tax saving and compounding of super will be the most effective long-term use of this money.



But with a $600,000 mortgage, and an interest rate of 6.75 per cent I wonder if an extra $30 per week against the principal is a smarter way to go? What are the numbers over a 10-year period? What are the final dollars for each option?” Financial Adviser, Nicole Bell from Retirement Essentials agreed to answer Gavin’s question. To do so, she made the following assumptions: that super compounds at 7.5 per cent over the period,

that Gavin’s marginal tax rate is 30 per cent

he is making minimum mortgage repayments over a loan term of 20 years So which option delivers a higher net gain? Option 1: Additional $30 per week mortgage repayments: An extra $30 repayment means that Gavin will now pay $1082 ($1052 plus $30) weekly, saving $5255 in interest and reducing his principal by $15,600. The total benefit over 10 years is $20,855.



Option 2: Salary sacrifice $42.86 to super per week: This option will reduce Gavin’s net income by $30 per week. His salary sacrifice amount is $42.86, less a contributions tax of 15 per cent or $6.43, thus $36.43. Editor's pick Superannuation There are three types of super fund. Are you in the right one? Using a projected compounding rate of 7.5 per cent, the total extra super Gavin will have after 10 years is $28,185. This means that the net benefit of the second option, salary sacrifice, delivers $7330 more than the first option, paying extra off the mortgage. However, this result is not advice that Gavin should choose salary sacrifice over mortgage repayments. There is more to Gavin’s decision than this net benefit from the super contribution option. His attitude to carrying higher debt is one factor. If he has a mortgage with a redraw facility, he may consider that the extra money in this account provides an accessible financial buffer for unexpected needs – not available if the money is tied up in super, at least until he turns 60.



His planned date of retirement is also relevant. And if he was partnered, his other half’s financial situation would also need to be considered. Nevertheless, it’s always helpful to have some straightforward sums at hand when you have a financial ‘turning point’ decision to make. World.title: Should we give away some super so we qualify for the age pension?
World.content:
MoneySuper & retirementAsk an expert Opinion Should we give away some super so we qualify for the age pension? Noel Whittaker Money columnist October 21, 2026 — 5:01am

October 21, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

We keep hearing about the advantages of qualifying for even a small part-age pension. Apart from the fortnightly payment, what are the benefits, and why is it considered so important? Our combined superannuation balances put us above the assets test limit, and we’re wondering whether we should give some money to our children to bring ourselves below the threshold. Even a small part-age pension can be valuable because it generally comes with a Pensioner Concession Card, which provides access to cheaper PBS medicines, bulk-billed medical appointments where available, and various state government concessions on expenses such as electricity, council rates, water and transport. Be wary of offloading your super too quickly. Simon Letch Depending on where you live, these savings can be substantial. There may also be advantages under the proposed capital gains tax changes from July 2027, which include an exemption from the minimum 30 per cent tax for people receiving the age pension in the year of sale. However, don’t rush into giving money away to qualify. Centrelink’s gifting rules allow a couple to give away $10,000 in a financial year, subject to a maximum of $30,000 over five financial years, without affecting their pension assessment.



Amounts above those limits continue to count as assets for five years and are subject to deeming. You could therefore give away a substantial sum and still find yourselves ineligible for a pension. Editor's pick Opinion

Ask an expert Will inheriting my mum’s CBA shares trigger a big capital gains tax? Paul Benson Money contributor Before making any gifts, check exactly how far you are above the assets test cutoff and whether you might qualify for a Commonwealth Seniors Health Card instead. That card has no assets test and can provide valuable concessions without the need to give away your savings. My wife, 77, and I, 83, have been retired since 2014 and hold Commonwealth Seniors Health Cards under the grandfathering provisions. We operate our own SMSF, and our individual total superannuation balances are below the relevant limits, with our transfer balance accounts also within our allowances. Our investment income is approximately equal to our minimum annual pension withdrawals, so we have not needed to draw down our capital. Our super fund currently pays no tax. Our SMSF also owns all 600 units in a fixed unit trust, which holds a holiday rental property and cash investments in several registered first mortgage loans. At present, the trust distributes its profits to our SMSF as the sole unitholder, and neither the trust nor the fund pays tax on that income.



My concern is the proposed minimum 30 per cent tax on capital gains made by trusts from July 1, 2027. Would this tax apply to gains made within our fixed unit trust before the profits are distributed to our SMSF, even though the fund itself is tax-exempt? There is an important distinction between the proposed minimum 30 per cent tax on capital gains and the separate proposed rules for trust distributions. They should not be confused. The capital gains legislation has been enacted, while the wider trust taxation arrangements are still being developed. The critical issue in your situation is whether a fixed unit trust wholly owned by an SMSF will retain the benefit of the fund’s tax-exempt status when distributing income and capital gains. Given the substantial amounts potentially involved, I would seek specialist advice on the application of the new rules to your particular structure before drawing any firm conclusions. I have a hypothetical question about the proposed capital gains tax changes commencing on July 1, 2027. Suppose a 75-year-old retiree lives in a modest home, has a low income derived entirely from a self-managed superannuation fund and has not needed to lodge a tax return for several years. They purchase some Australian shares and subsequently sell them at a small profit. Would the capital gain automatically attract the proposed minimum 30 per cent tax, regardless of how little other income they receive? And would they have to start lodging tax returns simply because they made a capital gain?



Julia Hartman of Bantacs confirms that you’ve raised an excellent point, and it highlights one of the more extraordinary consequences of the proposed changes. If the minimum 30 per cent tax applies to the gain, even somebody whose income is below the tax-free threshold could face a tax liability. In theory, you could make a taxable capital gain of just $1 and find yourself liable for 30 cents in tax. Fortunately, the low-income tax offset and the seniors and pensioners tax offset can be used to offset the minimum tax, so minuscule gains would not in themselves require an income tax return to be lodged. The rules regarding SMSFs and the trust changes are yet to be clarified. Louie Douvis Nevertheless, it could create a tax return lodgement obligation for somebody who hasn’t lodged one for years. There’s an important exception: under the proposed rules, people receiving the age pension in the year of sale would be exempt from the minimum 30 per cent tax. Even a small part pension could therefore make an enormous difference. Remember, a capital gain itself is generally not treated as income under Centrelink’s age pension income test, although the proceeds and any resulting financial assets may affect your pension entitlement. It’s another example of how complicated these changes could become.



My spouse and I are homeowners receiving a part-age pension, which we understand is assessed under the assets test. Our assets comprise $30,000 in household contents, $250,000 in shares, $150,000 in cash and $50,000 in motor vehicles. I’m finding Centrelink’s deeming rules difficult to understand. Could you explain how deeming works and whether it affects our pension? The age pension is assessed under both an assets test and an income test, with whichever produces the lower pension determining your entitlement. Deeming is Centrelink’s method of calculating a notional income from financial assets such as shares, cash and superannuation, regardless of what they actually earn. In your case, the $250,000 in shares and $150,000 in cash give you $400,000 subject to deeming, producing assessable income of approximately $492 a fortnight. Household contents and motor vehicles are not subject to deeming. Based on the figures you’ve supplied, and assuming you have no other assessable income or assets, my calculations indicate that you would receive a pension of approximately $909 each per fortnight under the income test. Importantly, it is the income test, not the assets test, that would determine your pension entitlement in this situation. Noel Whittaker is the author of Retirement Made Simple and other books on personal finance. Email: noel@noelwhittaker.com.au.
