World.title: How a walk among gum trees planted seed for new airport’s showstopper
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

As the new airport opens in western Sydney, we take a look at how it became a reality. See all stories .

It is one element that will undoubtedly strike passengers when they walk off aircraft into the new airport terminal on Sydney’s western fringe. From the aerobridges to the spacious departure area and baggage claim, the opportunity for natural light to reach into the deepest recesses of Western Sydney International Airport’s multi-level terminal is everywhere. That is no coincidence. One of its distinguishing characteristics reflects design work that began almost a decade ago, led by COX Architecture principal David Holm and Zaha Hadid Architects director Cristiano Ceccato. The genesis for the terminal’s eye-catching ceiling, which scatters light into the building, lies under what was once a eucalypt canopy several kilometres from where the terminal now stands. COX Architecture principal David Holm holds a model that aided work on the terminal’s concept design. Sitthixay Ditthavong After Ceccato flew from London to work with Holm in 2018 on an entry for an international design competition for the terminal, the pair drove to the sprawling airport site at Badgerys Creek to search for inspiration. At the time, it was still farmland dotted with eucalypt forest. “We sort of slightly trespassed onto the site,” Holm quips. “I was telling him about the idea about gum trees. In Australia, they generally don’t lose their leaves in a sort of deciduous pattern. The leaves fall, but it is the bark that is actually changing. He was fascinated by that.”



It led to the idea of light shining through eucalyptus bark becoming the inspiration for the terminal’s wave-like ceiling. “Where the ceiling undulates and the light that dapples through it, the idea of that is walking through an Australian eucalypt forest,” Holm says. A year after their walk through the eucalypt forest, COX Architecture and Zaha Hadid won the international competition for the airport terminal, and over the following two years finalised plans as the concept design architects. Working with Indigenous design consultant Carol Vale from Murawin early on, it was a rare opportunity to design the key part of an airport before a future city was built near it at Bradfield. Loading Later, Woods Bagot realised the concepts as design and delivery architect for the terminal’s builder Multiplex. It involved thousands of decisions, the biggest of which included lifting the roofline and expanding view lines. An early instruction was that it should be regarded as western Sydney’s first airport, instead of the city’s second. That struck a chord as Holm and Ceccato set about ensuring passengers feel the terminal is about what makes up western Sydney and what it can be. As such, passengers will arrive in what is designed to feel like a “very Australian landscape”. And the “idea of walking in a Cumberland Plains forest” as they pass through the terminal is aimed to help subliminally allay the stress people often feel at an airport. “Part of the experience is about a richness of natural light, a richness of colour, a richness of material. You’re getting a true sense of what it’s like to be in an Australian landscape,” Holm says.



Across the globe, airport terminals often comprise departure areas on an upper level and arrivals underneath, which means passengers usually step off planes and walk into grey, dreary corridors. Setting the new $6 billion international airport apart is the fact the terminal’s floor plan has been split, resulting in the “great Australian light” streaming onto each level, including the baggage hall and departures area. The ceiling allows natural light into the terminal. Sitthixay Ditthavong An aerobridge at Western Sydney International Airport, which opens to passengers on Sunday. Sam Mooy The arrivals area for international passengers is on the terminal’s highest level, which is unusual in airport designs. Looking out to the Blue Mountains, western Sydney is etched into the brownish colours of materials such as terrazzo floors. The international arrivals floor also offers views over the departures area, which has a large high-ceiling space with windows that encourage a view westwards out to the runway and the mountains. Related Article Aviation ‘Slick operation’: Flying into Sydney’s new airport beats Mascot congestion The terminal’s signature ceiling will become visible to arriving international passengers when they turn a corner and approach border control. And after a long-haul flight, the prospect of natural light reaching passengers who are picking up their luggage from baggage carousels on the ground floor is intended to buoy their spirits. As a prolific hand-sketcher, Holm drew his first for the terminal of the baggage hall bathed in light.



In his work previously for architecture firm Woodhead, Holm was involved in designing the interior of Changi Airport’s Terminal 3 in Singapore for a decade from 2000 to 2010. Back then, Singapore’s reputation as a garden city was transported into the terminal in the form of a butterfly garden, along with a focus on allowing in light. “Singapore had to make itself interesting as a transit destination. So all the things you necessarily would not think about in a transport hub, Changi Terminal 3 has,” Holm recalls. In the same way, ideas that were used in Singapore about light and place have been adopted in western Sydney. Apart from the underground Victoria Cross metro station at North Sydney, Holm also worked on the design of a large dome – known as the marketplace – at Sydney Airport’s international terminal, as well as other airports around the country and overseas. For Ceccato, the terminal will be a “more human experience” for passengers than larger airports he has played a role in designing. Under the long-term plans for Western Sydney Airport, the terminal that has been built will be the first of four which will eventually be capable of handling more than 80 million passengers a year. A view from the top floor where international passengers will arrive. Sitthixay Ditthavong Escalators and stairs link a bag-drop area to departures on the first level. Sitthixay Ditthavong “Building it with these smaller terminals certainly gives you an opportunity of having a human understandable scale,” Ceccato says. “It’s not one of these mega-airports on day one, which overwhelm you with size and scale and being bludgeoned with retail.” While hesitating at selecting a favourite terminal from those he has designed, Ceccato says Western Sydney Airport’s is the one that resonates in terms of scale and intimacy.

World.title: Can my boss really tell me what I can or can’t do on my lunch break?
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsGot a Minute? Can my boss really tell me what I can or can’t do on my lunch break? Kirstin Ferguson October 21, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Each week Dr Kirstin Ferguson tackles questions about workplace, career and leadership in her advice column Got a Minute? This week: lunch break dos and don’ts, a threatened manager and another missed opportunity. Trust needs to flow both ways in the workplace. Dionne Gain Everyone at my workplace has been told not to schedule personal appointments during lunch breaks. This follows several colleagues booking haircuts or other lengthy appointments, returning late and then taking additional time to eat. It seems unfair to impose a blanket restriction because some people abused the arrangement. Can an employer dictate what employees do during their lunch break, and wouldn’t it be more reasonable to simply manage those who return late? Collective punishments for a few bad apples is never a good idea. And how does management intend to enforce this rule? Follow everyone to see where they go at lunchtime? Whether an employer can dictate what someone does on their lunch break depends on whether the break is paid or unpaid, and what your award, enterprise agreement, contract or workplace policy might say. All that said, dictating how employees use a genuine lunch break is difficult to justify simply on the basis some employees have returned late.



A better approach would be for management to speak with anyone who returns late from lunch. They should have this conversation individually, consistently and on the day in question. It is reasonable for you to expect your employer to trust you to return to work after lunch on time, and it is reasonable for them to speak to you if you do not. The idea of a blanket rule to deal with this issue is only going to impact workplace culture negatively. Trust needs to flow both ways. I am a highly experienced senior employee with an exemplary record. I intend to progress elsewhere, but personal circumstances mean delaying that move for about 18 months. Meanwhile, my boss has become increasingly irrational and unethical, making political decisions that are damaging our team. After I respectfully challenged one decision and set a boundary, my boss said I should be more deferential and has effectively excluded me for six months. I suspect they feel professionally threatened by me. How do I protect my peace, and my career, until I can leave? Related Article Got a Minute? My colleagues exclude me from conversations. Why are people so rude? I think the first thing you can do to help with the next 18 months is to stop trying to diagnose your boss’s motives. They may feel threatened by you, sure, but they may also experience your confidence a little differently than you do. Are you confident the way you challenged a decision was flawless?



To try to make this situation a little better, rather than simply having to endure the next 18 months, try to have an open conversation with your boss. Acknowledge your earlier discussion had been difficult. Let them know you want to work together effectively – ask them to clarify what they meant about being more deferential and ask how they would like you to raise concerns with them in future. At the same time, document your concerns if you observe your boss doing anything unethical. This does not mean just decisions you think are political or examples of where they may exercise poor judgment. If needed, you can report your concerns to someone more senior based on factual evidence only. I applied for a short-term higher-level position in my government organisation and prepared using the position description. At interview, however, the questions seemed unrelated to it. The successful applicant is the same person repeatedly given acting opportunities, despite failing to meet performance targets and struggling to retain staff. I am frustrated by what appears to be a self-perpetuating system: they receive opportunities that give them the experience needed to secure the next one. Am I missing something, and how should I respond? Your preparation was a great idea, but unfortunately a position description is not an advance copy of the interview script. Panels will often use unexpected questions to test judgment, adaptability and how you might apply your experience, not just how well you have rehearsed predictable examples. It is worth asking for detailed feedback on why you were unsuccessful. Something like, “Could you explain what capabilities the questions were designed to assess, where my responses were less competitive and what evidence I need to demonstrate next time?”

World.title: Two zero-stress family recipes from Julie Goodwin to help lighten the load
World.content:
RecipesCookbook extracts Two zero-stress family recipes from Julie Goodwin to help lighten the load The cook, author and presenter shares her recipes for an ultra-simple chilli con carne and speedy fridge-shaker frittata that can be eaten hot for dinner, or cold for lunch or a snack. Julie Goodwin October 21, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

For someone who loves being in the kitchen as much as Julie Goodwin, it might be surprising to learn she doesn’t necessarily consider what ends up on the plate to be the most important part of cooking. “In the grand scheme of things, the food is secondary,” the cook, author and presenter writes in her latest recipe collection. “If you’re overloaded and under-resourced and not organised but you still want to see your kids’ faces light up and share a few minutes with them over dinner, then chuck a few snags on the barbie and call it a sausage sizzle night.” You can always make up on the “green stuff” later on, she says. When you’re juggling the day-to-day demands of family life, cooking is about survival. “Give your housemates the gift of participation”: Julie Goodwin. Steve Brown



As Goodwin explains, this doesn’t necessarily change as children grow. When kids are younger, the question of “what’s for dinner” is a daily inevitability. Now that Goodwin’s own boys are grown, that question has become “who’s home for dinner”. That shift adds an extra layer of logistics to accommodate changing commitments and lifestyles: how many people will be eating, whether friends or partners will be coming over, and if they need to eat early or late. The best recipes from Australia's leading chefs straight to your inbox. Sign up Goodwin’s cookbook is about managing those fluctuating demands. Home for Dinner aims to make meal time as easy as possible by creating space and time for family to connect and check in with each other, and breaking down the “barriers that stand between us and a beautiful, beneficial daily ritual”. The collection includes tips and strategies alongside inexpensive recipes that can be prepped or cooked ahead and easily reheated, served in solo portions or stretched out for many people, and allow anyone in the household to pitch in. Because ultimately, Goodwin says, if you share the food, you should share the load. “Each person can pitch in to their own capabilities,” she writes. “You will see such a reward, not just from the meal but also from the lightening of what truly is, quite often, a serious burden on one member of the household. Give your housemates the gift of participation. You never know what passions, skills, future careers or hobbies you might be unlocking.” – Megan Johnston



Serve with rice or tortillas, and sour cream. Steve Brown Chilli con carne INGREDIENTS 2 tbsp olive oil

500g minced beef

2 brown onions, diced

4 garlic cloves, chopped

3 long green chillies, seeded and finely diced

1 tsp chilli powder

1 tbsp ground cumin

¼ cup (70g) tomato paste

800g can chopped tomatoes

2 x 400g cans red kidney beans, drained and rinsed

½ tsp sea salt flakes

¼ tsp cracked black pepper

1 cup (250ml) beef stock METHOD



Preheat oven to 180C fan-forced (200C conventional). In a non-stick chef’s pan or large frypan over medium-high heat, place 1 tablespoon olive oil and add the mince. Spread mince over the bottom of the pan and leave it for about 1 minute, until a rich golden colour develops. Break up the mince with a wooden spoon and stir it until it is cooked through. Remove to a bowl. Reduce the heat to medium. Add the remaining olive oil, then saute onion, garlic, chilli and spices until the onion is translucent. Return the mince to the pan, add the tomato paste and saute for one minute, then add the tomatoes, kidney beans, salt and pepper. Reduce the heat to low. Add the beef stock and simmer, stirring occasionally, for 20 minutes. Serve with rice or tortillas, and sour cream. Serves 4 Make the most of leftovers. Steve Brown Fridge-shaker frittata INGREDIENTS



1 tbsp olive oil

1 cup vegetables, sliced and diced (onion, capsicum, mushrooms, asparagus, zucchini, corn kernels, spring onions, cooked pumpkin or sweet potato etc)

up to ½ cup protein, sliced or diced, optional (leftover cooked bacon, ham, salami, salmon or smoked salmon, feta, tofu etc)

6 eggs

3 tbsp thickened cream

½ cup (60g) grated tasty cheese

1 tsp salt

½ tsp ground white pepper METHOD In a 26cm non-stick frypan over medium-high heat, place olive oil and add vegetables. Saute, stirring, until beginning to soften. Stir through added protein, if using. In a large bowl, whisk together eggs and cream then stir in the tasty cheese, salt and pepper. Pour the egg mixture into the frypan and reduce the heat to low. Stir for only a moment, to evenly distribute the ingredients around the pan. Cook over low heat until the egg is setting and golden brown on the bottom. This should take around 5 minutes. You can check this by very carefully lifting an edge with a silicone spatula. When the frittata has mostly set, release it from the pan with a spatula and invert it onto a plate. Using a second plate, invert it again, then put the pan over the top and return it to the pan so it is now upside down to finish cooking. Alternatively, once the frittata has set on the bottom you can finish it off by placing the pan under a hot grill to cook on top. Note: “Fridge-shaker” refers to the use of leftovers – shake the refrigerator, and whatever falls out goes in the frittata! This makes it extremely economical as well as being super-quick to cook. It can be eaten hot for dinner, or cold for lunch or a snack.



This is an edited extract from Home for Dinner by Julie Goodwin, published by Penguin, RRP $49.99. Photography by Steve Brown.

The place Te Arikinui Pullman Auckland Airport The hotel is an easy stroll from Auckland Airport. Check-in Auckland’s newest on-airport hotel touts a “one-minute” walk from the international terminal. I start a timer as I stroll briskly. There is some licence with that 60-second claim – it’s 134 seconds, to be precise. Still convenient, nonetheless.



Lobby area at Te Arikinui Pullman Auckland Airport. 



Soundproof windows ensure Auckland Airport noise does not bleed into rooms. The room Soundproof windows are calming, as Auckland Airport runs curfew-free. My Superior King room feels modern, luxurious but tastefully subdued and influenced by local touches. The ocean’s wash onto the shores of Manukau Harbour is reflected in the custom carpets. Dark blue curtains blend with cream-coloured walls of textured fabric with brass accents. Earth tones give the bathroom a sharp look. A Nespresso machine is welcome for the early start, and the open closet ensures nothing is left behind. I appreciate the fast Wi-Fi and that Chromecast works effortlessly. Te Kaahu, on the top floor, has amazing views of distant mountains and the nearby airport.



Food + drink At Te Kaahu, the buffet breakfast begins at 5am, but that’s still not early enough for travellers on the multiple 6am flights to Australia. Food selections are standard, not standout, and barista coffee adds to the $NZ45 ($36.20) bill. The venue’s calling card is its stunning view. Courtesy of its position on the top floor, distant vistas of mountains combine with sights of the nearby airport. I relax with a pleasant coffee as the sunlight helps me transition from sleepy to sane. Later in the day, the venue morphs into a cocktail bar for another chance to take in the views. On the ground floor, Kuriri Cafe & Eatery covers quick brews and bites if you’re on the move. Its coffee is also up to scratch. Out + about A cosy but well-equipped 24-hour gym overlooks the airport forecourt: perfect after a long period of sitting. There’s no pool – standard in airport hotels – as most stays don’t allow time for a swim. Beyond the Pullman’s walls, don’t expect much in the way of offsite activities or exciting walks, unless you venture beyond the airport precinct.



Related Article Air travel Ten terrific airport hotels (almost) worth missing your flight for The verdict I normally despise airport hotels, but this isn’t one of those times. It may not be a 60-second stroll, but a quick walk from baggage claim to bed is hard to beat. I’d love some more variety at breakfast, though – you’re mostly just paying for the view. Essentials From $NZ349 a night ($NZ332 for Accor Live Limitless members, free to join), or from $NZ199 for day use (9am-6pm). There are 15 accessible rooms. 37 Tom Pearce Drive, Auckland Airport, Auckland, New Zealand. See pullmanaucklandairport.com



Our score out of five ★★★★ Highlight Supreme comfort and convenience with local culture at its core – something often overlooked during an on-airport stay. Lowlight



Trying to get the staff’s attention to order coffee during breakfast is like flagging a taxi on New Year’s Eve. Everyone is working hard – there just aren’t enough staff to keep up with demand. The writer stayed at his own expense

World.title: Prince Harry: ‘I want family reconciliation ... but some people don’t’
World.content:
WorldEuropeRoyal family Prince Harry: ‘I want family reconciliation ... but some people don’t’ India McTaggart October 21, 2026 — 5:28am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. London: Prince Harry has said reconciliation with the royal family is “the most important thing” to him, but has claimed that “some people” do not have the same ambition. In an interview, the Duke of Sussex said mending ties with his family was his main goal, but admitted that “scars stick around forever”. Harry’s sit-down interview with GQ was his first since returning to the UK in August. Internet “I want it to work out,” he told GQ in his first sit-down interview since relocating to the UK in late August. “With everything else that’s going on in the world, the most important thing is to reconcile – that’s the key point. Scars stick around forever,” he said.



The duke said he was often asked how he would resolve his estrangement from the Prince of Wales, his older brother and heir to the throne. Related Article Royal family ‘It’s wonderful to be back’: Harry and Meghan on first outing since UK return It is thought the pair have not spoken for four years after a succession of damaging allegations by the Sussexes against the royal family, including during an interview with Oprah Winfrey, in a Netflix docuseries and in the duke’s memoir, Spare. “Some people don’t want it to work out,” he told GQ. “For me, there’s enough drama in the world and enough drama in people’s lives to continue with issues with family.” The duke has previously called for ties with the royal family to be mended, and told the BBC last year that he “would love a reconciliation”.



He and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, reunited with the King during a July visit to the UK. Father and son are understood to speak regularly on the phone. ‘We’re way past that’ Last Thursday, during the couple’s first joint engagement since returning to Britain, the Duchess of Sussex said it was “wonderful” to be back. The Sussexes greeted crowds of well-wishers in what appeared to be a royal engagement-style event during a day trip to Nottingham. Harry and his wife Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, appear in Nottingham last week. Getty Images



Elsewhere in the interview, the duke insisted he did not “want any sympathy” any more, explaining: “We’re way past that.” “Why? Because I’m a prince. I’ve got a support network around me, I’ve done different forms of therapy, and I put in the work.” He also mused: “I wonder where I would be if I didn’t [do therapy] – it could be a very different situation.” The duke has written extensively in his memoir about how therapy helped him “break the cycle” of generational trauma. He added that family squabbles were a “massively relatable issue for so many people”, emphasising “sibling disagreements” as well as “broken relationships between kids and their parents”.



“That continues to come up with me the whole time with people that I speak to, so I know how relatable it is,” the duke said. Related Article Royal family ‘Gaslighting’: Diana’s brother hits back at palace over his claim about the King He also said that he still found himself seeking advice from his mother, Diana, Princess of Wales, who died in a car accident in Paris when he was 12. “Sometimes there are questions that I ask her, looking for some kind of response. And sometimes, I do get a response,” he said. “Having done the work that I’ve done, there is a connection still with my mum that I do feel her energy at certain times, in certain parts of my life.” Prince Harry is in talks to make a documentary about his mother to mark the 30th anniversary of her death next August.



The Telegraph understands he has approached several friends and relatives of his late mother, including her brother, Earl Spencer, to ask whether they would take part in the project. The Sussexes’ Archewell Productions would produce such a programme, and Netflix would likely buy it, which continues to have a first-look deal with the duke and duchess. A spokesman for the Sussexes said of the duke’s comments to GQ: “It was absolutely not intended as a swipe at his brother or any other member of his family. The comment was made in a general context and was not directed at his family in any way.” The Telegraph, London Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to climb as Wall Street rises; $A over US70c Stan Choe October 21, 2026 — 5:17am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. The US stock market is rising following strong profit reports for Equifax, Hasbro and other companies, while oil prices ease back after nearing their highest levels since the war with Iran began. The S&P 500 added 0.4 per cent. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 539 points, or 1 per cent, as of 1:48 p.m. Eastern time, while more swings for the artificial-intelligence industry had the Nasdaq composite up a more modest 0.2 per cent. Wall Street climbed on the back of strong earnings reports as well as a slide in oil prices. AP The Australian sharemarket is set to advance, with futures at 4.57am AEDT pointing to a rise of 34 points, or 0.4 per cent, at the open., The ASX lost 0.3 per cent on Tuesday. The Australian dollar was trading higher at US70.03¢. Stock prices tend to follow the path of corporate profits over the long term, and several companies delivered results for the latest quarter that were better than analysts expected. Big expectations for growth generally are what have allowed the US stock market to hit records recently despite worries about high inflation, higher interest rates and other challenges weighing on Wall Street.



Equifax rallied 10.6 per cent for one of the market’s biggest gains after reporting a bigger profit for the summer than analysts expected, despite high mortgage rates slowing some parts of its business. Hasbro climbed 9.3 per cent after the toy company said its Magic: The Gathering game made more than $US600 million during a quarter for the first time. 3M rose 5.8 per cent after the company behind Ace bandages and Scotch-Brite sponges likewise reported a stronger-than-expected profit, even as shoppers broadly feel discouraged by high inflation. Related Article Opinion

Trade wars China’s export boom is becoming its Achilles heel Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Stocks also got a lift after the price for a barrel of Brent crude erased an early gain to fall 0.8 per cent to $US108.70. Earlier in the morning, it got near $US112 and approached its highest price since the war with Iran began in late February. The drop in oil prices will relieve some of the pressure on inflation, if it lasts. Brent’s price has been yo-yoing between $US97 and $US112 per barrel this month on uncertainty about when the energy industry will return to normal.



For now, airlines and other companies with big fuel bills enjoyed the benefit of Tuesday’s drop. American Airlines rallied 4.4 per cent, and United Airlines flew 2.8 per cent higher. Another winner was Braze, a customer engagement platform. Its stock soared 51.5 per cent to $US45.51 after Salesforce said it would buy the company for $US47.50 in cash for each share. Salesforce fell 1.4 per cent. Keeping the market in check was General Motors, which sank 8.2 per cent despite reporting a bigger profit than analysts expected. It also announced a program to send up to $US20 billion to investors by buying back its stock. The pressure is on companies to deliver bigger profits not only now, but also in the future. GM gave a forecasted range for profit over the full year of 2026 whose midpoint fell short of analysts’ expectations. AI stocks, meanwhile, continued to swirl. They’ve been at the center of the market’s recent uneasiness, as euphoria around the technology’s boom gives way to worries that high interest rates in the bond market will slow the borrowing that’s allowed companies to buy so many AI chips. Last week was the US stock market’s worst since June because of weakness for AI-related companies.



CoreWeave has been particularly shaky. It initially fell more than 6 per cent at the start of Tuesday’s trading, only to swing to a gain of 5 per cent before pulling back to a rise of 2.3 per cent. Such reversals are nothing new for the company, which has borrowed money to buy AI chips that it rents out to customers over the cloud. A day earlier, it careened between a gain of 7 per cent in the morning and a loss of 3.5 per cent in the afternoon following last week’s tumble of roughly 25 per cent. Tuesday’s struggles for AI stocks began in Asia, where a South Korean AI company, Elice, confronted a rough welcome to the stock market. Its stock dropped 32 per cent in its first day of trading in Seoul. South Korea’s Kospi index fell 3.7 per cent overall. Related Article Australian Council of Trade Unions New ACTU president warns AI is automating entire jobs In other stock markets abroad, indexes in Europe pared bigger losses from earlier in the day. The CAC 40 in Paris slipped 0.4 per cent, and the FTSE 100 in London fell 0.3 per cent.



A day earlier, indexes fell sharply across Europe following violent protests that could ultimately force governments on the continent to increase their spending to ease voters’ anger. That in turn could put more pressure on their bond markets, which are already strained because of worries about heavy debt loads and strained budgets. World.title: Is it better to pay extra on your mortgage, or add it to your super?
World.content:
MoneySuper & retirementRetirement living Is it better to pay extra on your mortgage, or add it to your super? Kaye Fallick October 21, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Fifty-somethings often feel a long way from retirement. Currently, they’re generally too busy working, supporting families and managing cost of living pressures. Yet, they are probably at their ‘peak mortgage’ moment. And the decisions they make today can have a profound impact on their lives in 10 or 20 years. Here’s how. It’s always helpful to have some straightforward sums at hand when you have a financial ‘turning point’ decision to make. Getty Take the example of Gavin – 55, single, and paying off a home in Adelaide. He is typical of his age group, according to Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) data which notes that more than half of the 55-64 demographic is still paying down a home loan. Here’s what he wants to know: “I have about $30 per week I can save. My father says to put money away for retirement, by salary sacrificing, saying the tax saving and compounding of super will be the most effective long-term use of this money.



But with a $600,000 mortgage, and an interest rate of 6.75 per cent I wonder if an extra $30 per week against the principal is a smarter way to go? What are the numbers over a 10-year period? What are the final dollars for each option?” Financial Adviser, Nicole Bell from Retirement Essentials agreed to answer Gavin’s question. To do so, she made the following assumptions: that super compounds at 7.5 per cent over the period,

that Gavin’s marginal tax rate is 30 per cent

he is making minimum mortgage repayments over a loan term of 20 years So which option delivers a higher net gain? Option 1: Additional $30 per week mortgage repayments: An extra $30 repayment means that Gavin will now pay $1082 ($1052 plus $30) weekly, saving $5255 in interest and reducing his principal by $15,600. The total benefit over 10 years is $20,855.



Option 2: Salary sacrifice $42.86 to super per week: This option will reduce Gavin’s net income by $30 per week. His salary sacrifice amount is $42.86, less a contributions tax of 15 per cent or $6.43, thus $36.43. Editor's pick Superannuation There are three types of super fund. Are you in the right one? Using a projected compounding rate of 7.5 per cent, the total extra super Gavin will have after 10 years is $28,185. This means that the net benefit of the second option, salary sacrifice, delivers $7330 more than the first option, paying extra off the mortgage. However, this result is not advice that Gavin should choose salary sacrifice over mortgage repayments. There is more to Gavin’s decision than this net benefit from the super contribution option. His attitude to carrying higher debt is one factor. If he has a mortgage with a redraw facility, he may consider that the extra money in this account provides an accessible financial buffer for unexpected needs – not available if the money is tied up in super, at least until he turns 60.



His planned date of retirement is also relevant. And if he was partnered, his other half’s financial situation would also need to be considered. Nevertheless, it’s always helpful to have some straightforward sums at hand when you have a financial ‘turning point’ decision to make. World.title: Should we give away some super so we qualify for the age pension?
World.content:
MoneySuper & retirementAsk an expert Opinion Should we give away some super so we qualify for the age pension? Noel Whittaker Money columnist October 21, 2026 — 5:01am

October 21, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

We keep hearing about the advantages of qualifying for even a small part-age pension. Apart from the fortnightly payment, what are the benefits, and why is it considered so important? Our combined superannuation balances put us above the assets test limit, and we’re wondering whether we should give some money to our children to bring ourselves below the threshold. Even a small part-age pension can be valuable because it generally comes with a Pensioner Concession Card, which provides access to cheaper PBS medicines, bulk-billed medical appointments where available, and various state government concessions on expenses such as electricity, council rates, water and transport. Be wary of offloading your super too quickly. Simon Letch Depending on where you live, these savings can be substantial. There may also be advantages under the proposed capital gains tax changes from July 2027, which include an exemption from the minimum 30 per cent tax for people receiving the age pension in the year of sale. However, don’t rush into giving money away to qualify. Centrelink’s gifting rules allow a couple to give away $10,000 in a financial year, subject to a maximum of $30,000 over five financial years, without affecting their pension assessment.



Amounts above those limits continue to count as assets for five years and are subject to deeming. You could therefore give away a substantial sum and still find yourselves ineligible for a pension. Editor's pick Opinion

Ask an expert Will inheriting my mum’s CBA shares trigger a big capital gains tax? Paul Benson Money contributor Before making any gifts, check exactly how far you are above the assets test cutoff and whether you might qualify for a Commonwealth Seniors Health Card instead. That card has no assets test and can provide valuable concessions without the need to give away your savings. My wife, 77, and I, 83, have been retired since 2014 and hold Commonwealth Seniors Health Cards under the grandfathering provisions. We operate our own SMSF, and our individual total superannuation balances are below the relevant limits, with our transfer balance accounts also within our allowances. Our investment income is approximately equal to our minimum annual pension withdrawals, so we have not needed to draw down our capital. Our super fund currently pays no tax. Our SMSF also owns all 600 units in a fixed unit trust, which holds a holiday rental property and cash investments in several registered first mortgage loans. At present, the trust distributes its profits to our SMSF as the sole unitholder, and neither the trust nor the fund pays tax on that income.



My concern is the proposed minimum 30 per cent tax on capital gains made by trusts from July 1, 2027. Would this tax apply to gains made within our fixed unit trust before the profits are distributed to our SMSF, even though the fund itself is tax-exempt? There is an important distinction between the proposed minimum 30 per cent tax on capital gains and the separate proposed rules for trust distributions. They should not be confused. The capital gains legislation has been enacted, while the wider trust taxation arrangements are still being developed. The critical issue in your situation is whether a fixed unit trust wholly owned by an SMSF will retain the benefit of the fund’s tax-exempt status when distributing income and capital gains. Given the substantial amounts potentially involved, I would seek specialist advice on the application of the new rules to your particular structure before drawing any firm conclusions. I have a hypothetical question about the proposed capital gains tax changes commencing on July 1, 2027. Suppose a 75-year-old retiree lives in a modest home, has a low income derived entirely from a self-managed superannuation fund and has not needed to lodge a tax return for several years. They purchase some Australian shares and subsequently sell them at a small profit. Would the capital gain automatically attract the proposed minimum 30 per cent tax, regardless of how little other income they receive? And would they have to start lodging tax returns simply because they made a capital gain?



Julia Hartman of Bantacs confirms that you’ve raised an excellent point, and it highlights one of the more extraordinary consequences of the proposed changes. If the minimum 30 per cent tax applies to the gain, even somebody whose income is below the tax-free threshold could face a tax liability. In theory, you could make a taxable capital gain of just $1 and find yourself liable for 30 cents in tax. Fortunately, the low-income tax offset and the seniors and pensioners tax offset can be used to offset the minimum tax, so minuscule gains would not in themselves require an income tax return to be lodged. The rules regarding SMSFs and the trust changes are yet to be clarified. Louie Douvis Nevertheless, it could create a tax return lodgement obligation for somebody who hasn’t lodged one for years. There’s an important exception: under the proposed rules, people receiving the age pension in the year of sale would be exempt from the minimum 30 per cent tax. Even a small part pension could therefore make an enormous difference. Remember, a capital gain itself is generally not treated as income under Centrelink’s age pension income test, although the proceeds and any resulting financial assets may affect your pension entitlement. It’s another example of how complicated these changes could become.



My spouse and I are homeowners receiving a part-age pension, which we understand is assessed under the assets test. Our assets comprise $30,000 in household contents, $250,000 in shares, $150,000 in cash and $50,000 in motor vehicles. I’m finding Centrelink’s deeming rules difficult to understand. Could you explain how deeming works and whether it affects our pension? The age pension is assessed under both an assets test and an income test, with whichever produces the lower pension determining your entitlement. Deeming is Centrelink’s method of calculating a notional income from financial assets such as shares, cash and superannuation, regardless of what they actually earn. In your case, the $250,000 in shares and $150,000 in cash give you $400,000 subject to deeming, producing assessable income of approximately $492 a fortnight. Household contents and motor vehicles are not subject to deeming. Based on the figures you’ve supplied, and assuming you have no other assessable income or assets, my calculations indicate that you would receive a pension of approximately $909 each per fortnight under the income test. Importantly, it is the income test, not the assets test, that would determine your pension entitlement in this situation. Noel Whittaker is the author of Retirement Made Simple and other books on personal finance. Email: noel@noelwhittaker.com.au.

World.title: How a walk among gum trees planted seed for new airport’s showstopper
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

As the new airport opens in western Sydney, we take a look at how it became a reality. See all stories .

It is one element that will undoubtedly strike passengers when they walk off aircraft into the new airport terminal on Sydney’s western fringe. From the aerobridges to the spacious departure area and baggage claim, the opportunity for natural light to reach into the deepest recesses of Western Sydney International Airport’s multi-level terminal is everywhere. That is no coincidence. One of its distinguishing characteristics reflects design work that began almost a decade ago, led by COX Architecture principal David Holm and Zaha Hadid Architects director Cristiano Ceccato. The genesis for the terminal’s eye-catching ceiling, which scatters light into the building, lies under what was once a eucalypt canopy several kilometres from where the terminal now stands. COX Architecture principal David Holm holds a model that aided work on the terminal’s concept design. Sitthixay Ditthavong After Ceccato flew from London to work with Holm in 2018 on an entry for an international design competition for the terminal, the pair drove to the sprawling airport site at Badgerys Creek to search for inspiration. At the time, it was still farmland dotted with eucalypt forest. “We sort of slightly trespassed onto the site,” Holm quips. “I was telling him about the idea about gum trees. In Australia, they generally don’t lose their leaves in a sort of deciduous pattern. The leaves fall, but it is the bark that is actually changing. He was fascinated by that.”



It led to the idea of light shining through eucalyptus bark becoming the inspiration for the terminal’s wave-like ceiling. “Where the ceiling undulates and the light that dapples through it, the idea of that is walking through an Australian eucalypt forest,” Holm says. A year after their walk through the eucalypt forest, COX Architecture and Zaha Hadid won the international competition for the airport terminal, and over the following two years finalised plans as the concept design architects. Working with Indigenous design consultant Carol Vale from Murawin early on, it was a rare opportunity to design the key part of an airport before a future city was built near it at Bradfield. Loading Later, Woods Bagot realised the concepts as design and delivery architect for the terminal’s builder Multiplex. It involved thousands of decisions, the biggest of which included lifting the roofline and expanding view lines. An early instruction was that it should be regarded as western Sydney’s first airport, instead of the city’s second. That struck a chord as Holm and Ceccato set about ensuring passengers feel the terminal is about what makes up western Sydney and what it can be. As such, passengers will arrive in what is designed to feel like a “very Australian landscape”. And the “idea of walking in a Cumberland Plains forest” as they pass through the terminal is aimed to help subliminally allay the stress people often feel at an airport. “Part of the experience is about a richness of natural light, a richness of colour, a richness of material. You’re getting a true sense of what it’s like to be in an Australian landscape,” Holm says.



Across the globe, airport terminals often comprise departure areas on an upper level and arrivals underneath, which means passengers usually step off planes and walk into grey, dreary corridors. Setting the new $6 billion international airport apart is the fact the terminal’s floor plan has been split, resulting in the “great Australian light” streaming onto each level, including the baggage hall and departures area. The ceiling allows natural light into the terminal. Sitthixay Ditthavong An aerobridge at Western Sydney International Airport, which opens to passengers on Sunday. Sam Mooy The arrivals area for international passengers is on the terminal’s highest level, which is unusual in airport designs. Looking out to the Blue Mountains, western Sydney is etched into the brownish colours of materials such as terrazzo floors. The international arrivals floor also offers views over the departures area, which has a large high-ceiling space with windows that encourage a view westwards out to the runway and the mountains. Related Article Aviation ‘Slick operation’: Flying into Sydney’s new airport beats Mascot congestion The terminal’s signature ceiling will become visible to arriving international passengers when they turn a corner and approach border control. And after a long-haul flight, the prospect of natural light reaching passengers who are picking up their luggage from baggage carousels on the ground floor is intended to buoy their spirits. As a prolific hand-sketcher, Holm drew his first for the terminal of the baggage hall bathed in light.



In his work previously for architecture firm Woodhead, Holm was involved in designing the interior of Changi Airport’s Terminal 3 in Singapore for a decade from 2000 to 2010. Back then, Singapore’s reputation as a garden city was transported into the terminal in the form of a butterfly garden, along with a focus on allowing in light. “Singapore had to make itself interesting as a transit destination. So all the things you necessarily would not think about in a transport hub, Changi Terminal 3 has,” Holm recalls. In the same way, ideas that were used in Singapore about light and place have been adopted in western Sydney. Apart from the underground Victoria Cross metro station at North Sydney, Holm also worked on the design of a large dome – known as the marketplace – at Sydney Airport’s international terminal, as well as other airports around the country and overseas. For Ceccato, the terminal will be a “more human experience” for passengers than larger airports he has played a role in designing. Under the long-term plans for Western Sydney Airport, the terminal that has been built will be the first of four which will eventually be capable of handling more than 80 million passengers a year. A view from the top floor where international passengers will arrive. Sitthixay Ditthavong Escalators and stairs link a bag-drop area to departures on the first level. Sitthixay Ditthavong “Building it with these smaller terminals certainly gives you an opportunity of having a human understandable scale,” Ceccato says. “It’s not one of these mega-airports on day one, which overwhelm you with size and scale and being bludgeoned with retail.” While hesitating at selecting a favourite terminal from those he has designed, Ceccato says Western Sydney Airport’s is the one that resonates in terms of scale and intimacy.

World.title: Can my boss really tell me what I can or can’t do on my lunch break?
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsGot a Minute? Can my boss really tell me what I can or can’t do on my lunch break? Kirstin Ferguson October 21, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Each week Dr Kirstin Ferguson tackles questions about workplace, career and leadership in her advice column Got a Minute? This week: lunch break dos and don’ts, a threatened manager and another missed opportunity. Trust needs to flow both ways in the workplace. Dionne Gain Everyone at my workplace has been told not to schedule personal appointments during lunch breaks. This follows several colleagues booking haircuts or other lengthy appointments, returning late and then taking additional time to eat. It seems unfair to impose a blanket restriction because some people abused the arrangement. Can an employer dictate what employees do during their lunch break, and wouldn’t it be more reasonable to simply manage those who return late? Collective punishments for a few bad apples is never a good idea. And how does management intend to enforce this rule? Follow everyone to see where they go at lunchtime? Whether an employer can dictate what someone does on their lunch break depends on whether the break is paid or unpaid, and what your award, enterprise agreement, contract or workplace policy might say. All that said, dictating how employees use a genuine lunch break is difficult to justify simply on the basis some employees have returned late.



A better approach would be for management to speak with anyone who returns late from lunch. They should have this conversation individually, consistently and on the day in question. It is reasonable for you to expect your employer to trust you to return to work after lunch on time, and it is reasonable for them to speak to you if you do not. The idea of a blanket rule to deal with this issue is only going to impact workplace culture negatively. Trust needs to flow both ways. I am a highly experienced senior employee with an exemplary record. I intend to progress elsewhere, but personal circumstances mean delaying that move for about 18 months. Meanwhile, my boss has become increasingly irrational and unethical, making political decisions that are damaging our team. After I respectfully challenged one decision and set a boundary, my boss said I should be more deferential and has effectively excluded me for six months. I suspect they feel professionally threatened by me. How do I protect my peace, and my career, until I can leave? Related Article Got a Minute? My colleagues exclude me from conversations. Why are people so rude? I think the first thing you can do to help with the next 18 months is to stop trying to diagnose your boss’s motives. They may feel threatened by you, sure, but they may also experience your confidence a little differently than you do. Are you confident the way you challenged a decision was flawless?



To try to make this situation a little better, rather than simply having to endure the next 18 months, try to have an open conversation with your boss. Acknowledge your earlier discussion had been difficult. Let them know you want to work together effectively – ask them to clarify what they meant about being more deferential and ask how they would like you to raise concerns with them in future. At the same time, document your concerns if you observe your boss doing anything unethical. This does not mean just decisions you think are political or examples of where they may exercise poor judgment. If needed, you can report your concerns to someone more senior based on factual evidence only. I applied for a short-term higher-level position in my government organisation and prepared using the position description. At interview, however, the questions seemed unrelated to it. The successful applicant is the same person repeatedly given acting opportunities, despite failing to meet performance targets and struggling to retain staff. I am frustrated by what appears to be a self-perpetuating system: they receive opportunities that give them the experience needed to secure the next one. Am I missing something, and how should I respond? Your preparation was a great idea, but unfortunately a position description is not an advance copy of the interview script. Panels will often use unexpected questions to test judgment, adaptability and how you might apply your experience, not just how well you have rehearsed predictable examples. It is worth asking for detailed feedback on why you were unsuccessful. Something like, “Could you explain what capabilities the questions were designed to assess, where my responses were less competitive and what evidence I need to demonstrate next time?”

World.title: Two zero-stress family recipes from Julie Goodwin to help lighten the load
World.content:
RecipesCookbook extracts Two zero-stress family recipes from Julie Goodwin to help lighten the load The cook, author and presenter shares her recipes for an ultra-simple chilli con carne and speedy fridge-shaker frittata that can be eaten hot for dinner, or cold for lunch or a snack. Julie Goodwin October 21, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

For someone who loves being in the kitchen as much as Julie Goodwin, it might be surprising to learn she doesn’t necessarily consider what ends up on the plate to be the most important part of cooking. “In the grand scheme of things, the food is secondary,” the cook, author and presenter writes in her latest recipe collection. “If you’re overloaded and under-resourced and not organised but you still want to see your kids’ faces light up and share a few minutes with them over dinner, then chuck a few snags on the barbie and call it a sausage sizzle night.” You can always make up on the “green stuff” later on, she says. When you’re juggling the day-to-day demands of family life, cooking is about survival. “Give your housemates the gift of participation”: Julie Goodwin. Steve Brown



As Goodwin explains, this doesn’t necessarily change as children grow. When kids are younger, the question of “what’s for dinner” is a daily inevitability. Now that Goodwin’s own boys are grown, that question has become “who’s home for dinner”. That shift adds an extra layer of logistics to accommodate changing commitments and lifestyles: how many people will be eating, whether friends or partners will be coming over, and if they need to eat early or late. The best recipes from Australia's leading chefs straight to your inbox. Sign up Goodwin’s cookbook is about managing those fluctuating demands. Home for Dinner aims to make meal time as easy as possible by creating space and time for family to connect and check in with each other, and breaking down the “barriers that stand between us and a beautiful, beneficial daily ritual”. The collection includes tips and strategies alongside inexpensive recipes that can be prepped or cooked ahead and easily reheated, served in solo portions or stretched out for many people, and allow anyone in the household to pitch in. Because ultimately, Goodwin says, if you share the food, you should share the load. “Each person can pitch in to their own capabilities,” she writes. “You will see such a reward, not just from the meal but also from the lightening of what truly is, quite often, a serious burden on one member of the household. Give your housemates the gift of participation. You never know what passions, skills, future careers or hobbies you might be unlocking.” – Megan Johnston



Serve with rice or tortillas, and sour cream. Steve Brown Chilli con carne INGREDIENTS 2 tbsp olive oil

500g minced beef

2 brown onions, diced

4 garlic cloves, chopped

3 long green chillies, seeded and finely diced

1 tsp chilli powder

1 tbsp ground cumin

¼ cup (70g) tomato paste

800g can chopped tomatoes

2 x 400g cans red kidney beans, drained and rinsed

½ tsp sea salt flakes

¼ tsp cracked black pepper

1 cup (250ml) beef stock METHOD



Preheat oven to 180C fan-forced (200C conventional). In a non-stick chef’s pan or large frypan over medium-high heat, place 1 tablespoon olive oil and add the mince. Spread mince over the bottom of the pan and leave it for about 1 minute, until a rich golden colour develops. Break up the mince with a wooden spoon and stir it until it is cooked through. Remove to a bowl. Reduce the heat to medium. Add the remaining olive oil, then saute onion, garlic, chilli and spices until the onion is translucent. Return the mince to the pan, add the tomato paste and saute for one minute, then add the tomatoes, kidney beans, salt and pepper. Reduce the heat to low. Add the beef stock and simmer, stirring occasionally, for 20 minutes. Serve with rice or tortillas, and sour cream. Serves 4 Make the most of leftovers. Steve Brown Fridge-shaker frittata INGREDIENTS



1 tbsp olive oil

1 cup vegetables, sliced and diced (onion, capsicum, mushrooms, asparagus, zucchini, corn kernels, spring onions, cooked pumpkin or sweet potato etc)

up to ½ cup protein, sliced or diced, optional (leftover cooked bacon, ham, salami, salmon or smoked salmon, feta, tofu etc)

6 eggs

3 tbsp thickened cream

½ cup (60g) grated tasty cheese

1 tsp salt

½ tsp ground white pepper METHOD In a 26cm non-stick frypan over medium-high heat, place olive oil and add vegetables. Saute, stirring, until beginning to soften. Stir through added protein, if using. In a large bowl, whisk together eggs and cream then stir in the tasty cheese, salt and pepper. Pour the egg mixture into the frypan and reduce the heat to low. Stir for only a moment, to evenly distribute the ingredients around the pan. Cook over low heat until the egg is setting and golden brown on the bottom. This should take around 5 minutes. You can check this by very carefully lifting an edge with a silicone spatula. When the frittata has mostly set, release it from the pan with a spatula and invert it onto a plate. Using a second plate, invert it again, then put the pan over the top and return it to the pan so it is now upside down to finish cooking. Alternatively, once the frittata has set on the bottom you can finish it off by placing the pan under a hot grill to cook on top. Note: “Fridge-shaker” refers to the use of leftovers – shake the refrigerator, and whatever falls out goes in the frittata! This makes it extremely economical as well as being super-quick to cook. It can be eaten hot for dinner, or cold for lunch or a snack.



This is an edited extract from Home for Dinner by Julie Goodwin, published by Penguin, RRP $49.99. Photography by Steve Brown.

World.title: I normally despise airport hotels. This Kiwi stay gets it right
World.content:
★★★★ Reviews & adviceHotel reviews I normally despise airport hotels. This Kiwi stay gets it right Chris Chamberlin October 21, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. The place Te Arikinui Pullman Auckland Airport The hotel is an easy stroll from Auckland Airport. Check-in Auckland’s newest on-airport hotel touts a “one-minute” walk from the international terminal. I start a timer as I stroll briskly. There is some licence with that 60-second claim – it’s 134 seconds, to be precise. Still convenient, nonetheless.



Lobby area at Te Arikinui Pullman Auckland Airport. 



Soundproof windows ensure Auckland Airport noise does not bleed into rooms. The room Soundproof windows are calming, as Auckland Airport runs curfew-free. My Superior King room feels modern, luxurious but tastefully subdued and influenced by local touches. The ocean’s wash onto the shores of Manukau Harbour is reflected in the custom carpets. Dark blue curtains blend with cream-coloured walls of textured fabric with brass accents. Earth tones give the bathroom a sharp look. A Nespresso machine is welcome for the early start, and the open closet ensures nothing is left behind. I appreciate the fast Wi-Fi and that Chromecast works effortlessly. Te Kaahu, on the top floor, has amazing views of distant mountains and the nearby airport.



Food + drink At Te Kaahu, the buffet breakfast begins at 5am, but that’s still not early enough for travellers on the multiple 6am flights to Australia. Food selections are standard, not standout, and barista coffee adds to the $NZ45 ($36.20) bill. The venue’s calling card is its stunning view. Courtesy of its position on the top floor, distant vistas of mountains combine with sights of the nearby airport. I relax with a pleasant coffee as the sunlight helps me transition from sleepy to sane. Later in the day, the venue morphs into a cocktail bar for another chance to take in the views. On the ground floor, Kuriri Cafe & Eatery covers quick brews and bites if you’re on the move. Its coffee is also up to scratch. Out + about A cosy but well-equipped 24-hour gym overlooks the airport forecourt: perfect after a long period of sitting. There’s no pool – standard in airport hotels – as most stays don’t allow time for a swim. Beyond the Pullman’s walls, don’t expect much in the way of offsite activities or exciting walks, unless you venture beyond the airport precinct.



Related Article Air travel Ten terrific airport hotels (almost) worth missing your flight for The verdict I normally despise airport hotels, but this isn’t one of those times. It may not be a 60-second stroll, but a quick walk from baggage claim to bed is hard to beat. I’d love some more variety at breakfast, though – you’re mostly just paying for the view. Essentials From $NZ349 a night ($NZ332 for Accor Live Limitless members, free to join), or from $NZ199 for day use (9am-6pm). There are 15 accessible rooms. 37 Tom Pearce Drive, Auckland Airport, Auckland, New Zealand. See pullmanaucklandairport.com



Our score out of five ★★★★ Highlight Supreme comfort and convenience with local culture at its core – something often overlooked during an on-airport stay. Lowlight



Trying to get the staff’s attention to order coffee during breakfast is like flagging a taxi on New Year’s Eve. Everyone is working hard – there just aren’t enough staff to keep up with demand. The writer stayed at his own expense

World.title: Costs keep rising: Cafe faces impossible choice
World.content:
Audio player for " Should you buy a house from your mother-in-law? " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/business/2045782%2Fcosts-keep-rising-cafe-faces-impossible-choice

Angela Clements says the decision to close Pure Café in Whangārei is the result of increasing pressure from multiple directions - and economists are warning the situation could get worse.

Pure has been open for six years but will close on 27 November.

She said a lot of things had become a lot more expensive over that time. "We've been in the industry for about 15 years and things like dairy, milk cheese, those things have gone up probably 60 percent.

"I think the hardest thing is that the things we used to buy that were good quality are now out of our price range and the things that we can afford are just rubbish.

"Take cocoa powder, for example. We used to buy good quality cocoa powder for a reasonable price. Now the rubbish cocoa powder is the same price as the good stuff and the good stuff is out of our range.

"We either use a poor quality product or we put our prices up exponentially and then people just can't, they just don't buy, you know. Or the third option is the one that we've been taking lately is that we use a good quality product, but we don't put our prices up and then we just swallow the cost ourselves."

The cost of things like gas and power had also increased a lot, she said.

Stats NZ data showed restaurants and cafés may be trying to pass on some of the increases. The "restaurant and ready to eat" food group was up 3.1 percent over a year in its most recent data, compared to overall food price inflation of 2.4 percent.

Restaurant Association general manager Nicola Waldren said that group included everything from restaurants and cafés to takeaway food and it could involve a lot of different cost structures.

Restaurant Association general manager Nicola Waldren. Supplied

"Looking at the September index where prices in the group rose 3.1 percent, and 0.2 percent for the month, the annual rise is similar to grocery food at 3 percent and meat, poultry and fish at 3.2 percent, although the overall food figure is lower mainly because fruit and vegetable prices have fallen.

"Beyond food costs, hospitality businesses have also been dealing with some large increases in other costs they can't easily avoid. The same release shows household electricity prices up 9.5 percent over the year and gas up 11.4 percent. Commercial rates vary, but energy is a significant cost for businesses running kitchens, refrigeration and hot water throughout the day. Petrol prices also rose sharply in September, and some businesses are seeing higher fuel costs passed on through delivery surcharges.

"Having said that, we know any menu price increase is carefully considered, and our businesses are very aware that many households are under pressure. It's a careful balance between offering value for customers and keeping the business sustainable."

Clements said she was stuck in a position where the business could not afford to support even one full-time person.

"We consider ourselves fairly resilient but that's kind of running out. I don't think there's a great future for the industry for people that actually want a quality product. I'm uncomfortable serving up something that is not good for you and not made with quality ingredients. Look at bacon. We used to buy only New Zealand bacon but now New Zealand bacon is twice the price of imported bacon. So do you buy New Zealand bacon and price yourself out of the market or do you put imported bacon on a plate and feel bad about it?"

Westpac senior economist Satish Ranchhod. Supplied

Westpac senior economist Satish Ranchhod said its internal card spending data indicated there had been a lift in spending on takeaways and at restaurants since the start of this year.

But he said it was clear ingredient prices had increased, especially meat.

"Just as that's adding to households' grocery bills, it's also adding to the cost of producing takeaways and restaurant meals. I haven't heard anything from restaurant operators about fuel prices affecting their production costs. However, I have heard anecdotes from those in the agricultural sector about fuel prices pushing up their operating and transport costs. Over time, that could flow through to higher food prices."

BNZ chief economist Mike Jones said consumer demand in some of the discretionary spending categories was under significant pressure again as higher energy costs were felt.

Clements said she did not think there would be an improvement in the sector until households were feeling less pressure.

"It's not just the cost of stuff for us. It's the cost of people's grocery bills and power bills … we still have a lot of the same customers we used to have they just come less often and spend less money."

Hospitality was responsible for 15 percent of liquidations in the year to August, at a rate of 1.4 percent.

World.title: Gower becalmed as Hipkins and Luxon double down on interruptions in final debate
World.content:
Analysis: "Last one" was heard as the two leaders of the largest political parties came together for a handshake ahead of their third and final head-to-head debate last night. Then, the two Chrises went at it.

The Stuff debate was by far the most pugilistic of the three - moderator Paddy Gower promised a clash and he made room for exactly that with interruptions almost doubled on the prior debates. But there was also the return of what by now are familiar patterns: Luxon talks much more than Hipkins and he says "actually" an awful lot; Hipkins loves a one-word answer and is extremely keen to claim Luxon is not telling the truth.

RNZ's data analysis of what was said shows how this debate broke down in detail.

Who talked the most?

In each of the three debates, Luxon has increased the number of words he's used to argue his corner. In the TVNZ debate he said 6031, at last week's NZ Herald debate it was 6255 and last night he topped 6360, giving him 44% of the total. Hipkins stuck with his 'less is more' approach taking 29% of the words on the night.

What was surprisingly different about the Stuff debate was the role of the moderator. Gower promised at the outset to let viewers see a serious debate with "no silly questions". There were three "face-off" sections where the leaders were allowed to go head-to-head. Gower also shared moderation duties, handing the leaders off for two rounds with The Post's Luke Malpass.

This all added up to a far less prominent role for Gower in this debate. In 2020 and 2023 when he moderated debates for Newshub, Gower topped the leaders both times in speaking 37% of the words. Last night, he spoke 22%. This was lower too than Ryan Bridge (39%) and Jack Tame (34%) in this year's other clashes. Even when accounting for Malpass's 4% contribution, the leaders got the floor for longer in last night's debate.

Luxon also took more speaking turns than Hipkins. There were 156 instances of six or more words spoken by Luxon compared with 114 by Hipkins.

The longest answer of the night was Luxon's on climate change adaptation. At 245 words it was his longest response to any question in all three debates and longer than Hipkins' longest answer of 208 words about education.

Luxon's second longest answer was related to education, a topic he has spoken strongly about in all three debates.

On average, Luxon said 32 words each time he spoke, compared to Hipkins' 26. This average has been consistent across the three debates.

Towards the end of the debate, Gower showed a glimpse of his more animated former self, firing up to introduce the "quickfire" round.

As in the NZ Herald debate, Hipkins embraced the format more than Luxon. He said "yes" to the idea of banning gambling ads next to sport (twice). He said "no" to the need to have a bill to define a man and a woman and "no" when asked if the Dame Julie Christie documentary on Tom Phillips should go ahead. He used the same approach elsewhere in the debate too, agreeing the health system was in crisis, promising to end "corridor care" in hospitals, and agreeing the war on Iran was a mistake.

Luxon gave a single one word answer, saying "yes" to being willing to buy a Chinese-made electric vehicle.

The final debate was the feistiest when it came to interruptions, with 114 instances of interruptions or cross-talk recorded, by far eclipsing the first debate's 59 and 27 in the second.

Our analysis logged an interruption as when one leader cut in and the other stopped to respond. An attempted interruption, or cross-talk was counted when one leader spoke over the other, but the speaker ignored him and carried on.

They talked over each other frequently, Hipkins talked over Luxon 64 times, causing him to pause or respond 10 times.

One of the few audience laughs came from Hipkins' interjection when Luxon criticised school attendance under the Labour government and accused Labour of not tracking the number of students in class: "So if we didn't record attendance at schools, how is it that you're able to say it was so bad?"

Luxon landed seven interruptions where he broke Hipkins' flow, and talked over him a further 43 times. While still less combative than Hipkins, this was a huge leap for Luxon from the 18 times he chimed in over Hipkins at the TVNZ debate and his four attempts at the NZ Herald debate.

What was said

Once again, the leaders have stuck to their habits when it comes to fallback words.

Over all three debates Luxon has participated in this election, the word "actually" has been the one he said the most. The word can be used in a variety of ways, including as a way to push back on what somebody has said or correct the record, or it can be used to emphasise a point, or pivot to a different point. Often it can be a filler word, to give the speaker a moment to think mid sentence.

Luxon used "actually" 77 times in last night's debate, up from 68 times in the first debate and 64 in the second.

Hipkins' top word for the third debate in a row was "going".

For the third debate in a row Luxon used variations of "challenging".

Hipkins used "not true" six times. Four times in relation to the number of nurses Luxon said were employed under the National government's time, and twice in relation to Luxon saying Labour's fiscal plans were unfunded.

The leaders addressed each other by their first names with Luxon doing it far more than Hipkins.

Dodging the hard questions

A common tactic to avoid answering a question is to use what's referred to as a 'block and bridge'. The politician acknowledges the question using a 'block' and then uses a 'bridge' phrase to move the topic to something they are more comfortable with. Common bridging terms are "I would say", "what I can tell you", "the reality is". The bridge allows them to transition the conversation to their own talking points.

Luxon used variations of the term "as I said" five times during the debate. Hipkins did not use any common bridging terms.

What was the vibe?

According to a language sentiment data dictionary, which rates words as either positive, neutral or negative, the leaders used the same percentage of positive words with Hipkins using a slightly higher percentage of negative words than Luxon.

World.title: Environmental groups, chiefs file lawsuit as US pushes on with American Samoa deep sea mining plans
World.content:
Audio player for " Fresh lawsuit challenges Trump’s American Samoa mining plans " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/pacific/2046468%2Fenvironmental-groups-chiefs-file-lawsuit-as-us-pushes-on-with-american-samoa-deep-sea-mining-plans

Fresh lawsuit challenges Trump’s American Samoa mining plans Pacific Waves Download MP3 5m

An environmental group is challenging the United States' legal authority to sell seabed mining leases covering waters off the coast of American Samoa, as the Trump administration pushes ahead with plans for a deep sea mining auction around the Pacific territory.

The US is proposing to lease more than 31 million acres of seabed, with the sale scheduled for 19 November. The decision marks the first time the US has offered such leases and comes despite widespread opposition from locals and environmental groups.

Fa'asao Amerika Samoa co-founder Seumalu Elora Raymond told Pacific Waves that the group is pursuing legal action to stop the sale, warning it would become much harder to challenge the plans once the leases are secured.

"I think every hour we spend on this before that event is worth weeks and months of effort," she said.

"It gets so much harder to fight this when there are so many fewer options once a mining company has purchased parts of the seabed floor."

The US is proposing to lease more than 31 million acres of seabed, with the sale scheduled for 19 November. Marine Minerals Administration

In April 2025, President Donald Trump issued an executive order declaring activities in deep-sea science and technology as "a core national security and economic interest".

A concurrent request was made by American firm Impossible Metals to open leasing off American Samoa territory, amid growing interest in the polymetallic nodules on the seabed, including nickel, copper and cobalt.

On Monday, Fa'asao Amerika Samoa, the Conservation Council for Hawai'i and the Faleula o le Manu'atele council of matai filed a new lawsuit - represented by Earthjustice - to block the lease sale.

The groups argue the Marine Minerals Administration (formerly known as the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management), the agency overseeing the proposed sale, does not have the legal authority to issue the leases under treaty requirements that must be met before mineral leasing can take place in American Samoa.

The new case follows a separate lawsuit filed in August by Fa'asao Amerika Samoa and the Conservation Council for Hawai'i.

Seumalu said a hearing in that case is scheduled for 30 October, with the judge agreeing to an expedited process because of the November 19 deadline.

She said a decision in the first case could affect the government's ability to proceed with the lease sale.

However, it is not yet clear whether the new lawsuit will be heard before the auction.

Questions over US authority in American Samoa

Seumalu rejected the idea that American Samoa had little say over what happened in its surrounding waters because the US controls the territory.

She said the relationship between American Samoa and the US does not give the federal government unlimited authority.

Seumalu points to historical instruments of cession signed by Samoan matai, saying the agreements established protections for the territory's lands and ocean.

"Anybody who just assumes that the US can do whatever they want here is not really thinking carefully about the relationship between American Samoa and the United States and about the agreement that was signed by the matai generations ago."

She argued that those agreements remained relevant under US federal law and must be considered when determining whether the government can issue the proposed leases.

In 2024, American Samoa banned deep sea mining in its territorial waters, but the auction relates to areas beyond that limit, in the federally controlled Outer Continental Shelf.

However, the groups launching legal action argue that the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act does not authorise mineral leasing in any of the US territories, including American Samoa, and that the agency is violating its own leasing regulations
