World.title: EDS doctor Chris Holdaway restricted from seeing patients by Medical Council
World.content:
Hundreds of patients seeking treatment for a controversial group of vascular conditions have been left in limbo after the Medical Council imposed restrictions on one of the few doctors helping them.

Hamilton vascular surgeon Chris Holdaway is no longer able to consult patients with the connective tissue disorder Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome (EDS) who are also suspected of having abdominal vascular compression syndromes.

The 71-year-old has become one of the country's most prominent advocates for patients with EDS and suspected vascular compression syndromes. He has seen around 200 EDS patients with the condition, which can cause chronic pain, gastrointestinal symptoms and often an inability to tolerate food.

Holdway, who was interviewed for the RNZ podcast All In Her Head - which examines the debate around EDS and vascular compressions - believes many patients have been misdiagnosed or dismissed before reaching him. His advocacy has attracted strong support from some patients who say they have struggled to obtain diagnoses, but criticism from some medical colleagues.

While individual abdominal vascular compression syndromes are recognised conditions, there is no medical consensus about whether it is possible to have more than one at a time. Yet EDS patients are being diagnosed with multiple abdominal compression syndromes - sometimes up to four - at once.

Medical Council's intervention

The Medical Council said it could not comment on the circumstances of any individual doctor but it could impose conditions on a doctor's scope of practice where necessary to protect public safety.

"The Medical Council's role is to protect the health and safety of the public by ensuring doctors are competent and fit to practise," council chair Dr Kenneth Clark said in a statement to RNZ.

Dr Holdaway declined to comment on the decision or its impact but a note circulated to patients from advocates Rachel McKenna and Zalie Doyle said the restrictions preventing him from consulting EDS patients with abdominal vascular compression syndromes were temporary.

He could still see EDS patients for other conditions, including thoracic outlet syndrome and Eagle Syndrome. Patients already undergoing investigations may be eligible for a follow up appointment to review scan results, the letter said.

RNZ understands the council is set to review Holdaway's case on Thursday, with a decision expected next week.

'Desperate' patients

Holdaway was an advocate for patients seeking surgical treatment overseas, despite Health New Zealand warning these operations were experimental and risked death. Despite the warnings, dozens of New Zealand patients had undergone surgical treatment for multiple compressions in Germany, and more recently in Australia.

Whakatāne woman Rachel Weatherly, a former patient of Dr Holdaway, believed the current restrictions on his practice would leave patients without anywhere else to go.

"I think it will eventually cost lives. My inbox is already full of parents reaching out desperate to know if there's someone else that they can take their child to see, and I just don't have the answer for them," she said.

Weatherly had surgery in Australia with vascular surgeon Gert Frahm-Jensen in September 2025 which resolved many of her symptoms.

Holdaway diagnosed her vascular compressions, which had been dismissed by Health New Zealand specialists, and gave her hope she could find someone to help her.

"I think that hope's now been stripped away for others, which is not going to be really good for families."

In their note to patients, McKenna and Doyle said it was understandable people would feel frightened, angry or disappointed by the situation.

"But how we respond to this situation matters. How we conduct ourselves as a patient community is particularly important right now."

World.title: Wellington residents call for action six months on from flooding
World.content:
Audio player for " Months after floods, Wellington residents face costly repairs " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/regions_wellington/2031085%2Fwellington-residents-call-for-action-six-months-on-from-flooding

Months after floods, Wellington residents face costly repairs Morning Report Download MP3 6m

Residents in affected parts Wellington's southern suburbs are calling out for action as they continue to struggle with the aftermath of flooding in April.

One person died and hundreds fled from their homes when severe thunderstorms overwhelmed storm water systems and flood water, mud and silt swept into homes.

Six months on and some residents say their neighbourhoods have been reduced to ghost towns while others are suffering the stress of an uncertain and costly future.

'They just walked'

Lena Walton and her partner had lived in four different locations since the floods hit their Berhampore home of over 30 years.

Wellington residents are calling out for action as they continue to struggle with the aftermath of flooding in April. Supplied

She said repair work stalled as a collective of residents considered offers to buy out the homes on her street from developers.

But the deal fell through and now the neighbourhood felt like "a ghost town".

Audio player for " Wellington residents still struggling six months after floods " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/regions_wellington/2031085%2Fwellington-residents-call-for-action-six-months-on-from-flooding

Wellington residents still struggling six months after floods Morning Report Download MP3 3m

"There are homes that are just sitting there, just empty.

"In Berhampore there was one house and the washing [that] was left there, on the line, on the day of the 19th is still there. Tenants that were in there, they just walked," Walton said.

If the council offered 'I would go'

Naomi Bowen said her family was still unable to use the lower level of its South Wellington home after water damage and slips left parts of the building's foundations "hanging like teeth".

Naomi Bowen's family is still unable to use the lower level of its South Wellington home. Supplied

She said she couldn't sleep when it rained and stress of the situation was impacting her physical health.

"I love my street [but] right now, if the council offered to buy us out and it was enough to buy elsewhere, I would go.

"If anyone had been downstairs during that flood, when 1.2 metres [of water and mud] smashed down and through walls, [they] could have been seriously hurt or died.

"My niece was down there over Christmas and God knows what would have happened if they'd still been sleeping down there," Bowen said.

Bowen said external work to protect her property from inundation was unlikely to be approved as she'd been told it could increase the risk to others.

She said she and her husband were caught between the massive cost of raising the building and the need to keep her family safe.

"We know that the stormwater infrastructure isn't set up to work, and we also know, from their flood mapping, our property is the overflow path for our street and surrounding streets.

"How can we make our home resilient when there's all these barriers against us?" Bowen said.

Naomi Bowen. Supplied

Storm water systems still 'clogged up'

Repairs at Sonja Steinmetz's Emerson street home were nearing completion.

But she worried that, for all the effort and money the family had poured into the rebuild, the whole scenario could repeat again.

She said the community needed assurance from the council that the infrastructure could cope with future events.

"Something as simple as making sure the stormwater drains are not clogged up. It happens now still," she said. "When we are having just regular rainfall the stormwater drains are getting clogged up."

Resident calls for council and central government to 'step up'

Catherine Leech's family had been renting since it fled its Owhiro Bay home through chest deep water in the middle of the night.

Leech said central government needed to do more to support the people impacted by the floods and to work alongside councils to find long term strategies to cope with future severe weather events.

"The response to Auckland and Cyclone Gabrielle compared [with] floods recently has been significantly different.

"We need them to step up and start listening to people that are saying 'help us'. They can't put their head in the sand and hope that the rain's going to go away, it's not going to happen," Leech said.

In June, Emergency Management and Recovery Minister Mark Mitchell told RNZ he was open to proposals to assist the city's recovery but the matter would need to instigated by local council.

"As with past flooding events, these matters sit with the relevant local council in the first instance," Mitchell told RNZ.

Government confirmed no buyouts, council says

A spokesperson for Wellington City Council they had revisited the government's decision not to provide buyout assistance for affected residents.

Naomi Bowen says slips left parts of her home's foundations "hanging like teeth". Supplied

"The Minister confirmed this again over the weekend, saying that he would consider extra funding in future if another disaster strikes," they said.

The spokesperson said a catchment study of the Ōwhiro Stream would be under way before the end of the year and a stormwater assessment for the wider Paekawakawa catchment was expected to be presented to council by April next year.

Councillors had also requested officers review what had happened in response to recommendations following a previous flooding event in Island Bay in 1995.

"Ultimately, decisions about repairs, rebuilding, and insurance requirements are primarily matters for property owners and their insurers," the spokesperson said.

They said, in the months following the floods, crews had worked to clear blocked culverts, slips and debris and conducted emergency stream-bank works.

"The 20 April storm was an extreme, localised flash-flood event, with more than 75mm of rain falling in an hour in some places. That volume of rainfall would overwhelm most urban stormwater systems in New Zealand, but it is still important we do what we can to strengthen Wellington's resilience and reduce the risks from future severe weather," the spokesperson said.

They said the government's Disaster Relief Fund contribution of $100,000, the maximum amount available, had been matched by the Mayoral Relief Fund.

Nearly $380,000 had been raised through the fund and council had instigated welfare support, provided building consent advice and prioritised consents for affected homeowners.

The spokesperson said Council would advocate that stormwater resilience work would be included in Tiaki Wai's "statement of expectations" to fulfil their responsibilities in managing the city's pipe and stormwater network.

In a statement Minister for Emergency Management and Recovery, Mark Mitchell said, following Cyclone Gabrielle, the government had stepped in to reconnect communities and sure up regional economies.

"Cyclone Gabrielle was one of New Zealand’s most significant weather events ever experienced which caused devastating damage across several regions that no single council could possibly fund alone."

He said, in Wellington, the National Emergency Management Agency had provided $46,000, on top of the government's contribution to the Mayoral Relief Fund, for accommodation to support people displaced by the floods.

"As is standard practice for local emergencies, recovery is locally led, with local authorities responsible for making decisions about how they resource their emergency management responsibilities to keep their communities safe.

World.title: Rollout of new radio system for all emergency services continues
World.content:
"World best", "game changer": Some of what's being said about the new communications system being built for police, ambulance and fire frontliners.

So what does it take to build a $1.6 billion system required to do much better both day in and out, as well as in the next Cyclone Gabrielle-type mass disaster?

It takes installers like Rob Hardgrave with Novacomm, who has been in the garage among the vans at Wellington Free Ambulance in Thorndon.

"We are tasked with fitting the new PSN [Public Safety Network] radios to them," Hardgrave said.

They had 104 Wellington Free vehicles to do, removing all the interior panels - "lower panel, B pillar, top and bottom, C pillar, top and bottom, all the visors, all the grab handles, the interior light ... so we can put the antennas up top".

The job, repeated over and over nationwide, is to wire all four emergency services into 19,000 terminals of the same digital radio technology for the first time, wherever they are.

Hardgrave uses a new ambulance handset to beep across the zones.

"So all these zones that are in the radio... Wellington and Wellington New Zealand Police Network, South Island, South Island Mass Incident, North Island Mass Incident ...

"So if you have an incident where you're attending outside of the zone, outside of your district, then you should be able to get onto the same channels as everyone. ... You jump on the Taranaki zone and you go into Taranaki and you're on their channels."

Ambulance general manager of operations Eric Tibbott has juggled keeping the fleet on the road, as well as off it for each vehicle's day-long fitout.

He has just four to go.

It's all about timing. "Every call, it saves lives you know, so time is of the essence. So in order to ensure we've got a reliable, resilient communications network, it's just this game changer," Tibbott said.

"I feel really confident now that we've got the best system, probably one of the best systems in the world."

High site: A Land Mobile Radio relay tower on Mt Trovatore, part of the Opera Range, within the Lewis Pass Scenic Reserve. Supplied/ SafetyNet

The network would have far fewer blackspots than the existing fragmented comms, plus it would be fully encrypted outside the main centres for the first time.

"We don't want people rushing in," Tibbott said.

But the timing is off in some ways: The system was meant to be running about now - alongside a network of hardened cellphones that 30,000 frontliners are already using - instead, construction is yet to start on over half the 500 relay sites.

Steve Mellsop is with main contractor Tait Systems.

Steve Mellsop of Tait Systems. Phil Pennington

"That was on the back of everybody assuming that the sites would be a bit of a cookie cutter, so once you've done 10, then you can replant," said Mellsop.

"[But] every single site is different and every single site is hard."

A Treasury report in March said the project had spent less than a third of its budget but used up over 80 percent of its time.

At this point, Tait has acquired 351 of 500 transmission sites; 187 have been built for testing, with 40 under construction.

The Christchurch company, which will operate the network for a decade, had more than doubled its design engineers, from seven to 15 or 16.

"They're just churning out site designs."

The relay on Mt Trovatore Supplied/ SafetyNet

Once they were ready, they would be tough.

"In [Cyclone] Gabrielle the radio networks held up a lot better than the cell towers. Even the existing networks have a lot more resilience," Mellsop said.

They use microwave for connecting rather than the fibreoptic cables that got taken out when the 2023 cyclone snapped bridges. And the batteries on key remote sites are designed to be longer lasting.

Canterbury is expected to go live with the radios first, and all regions by 2028.

Meantime, responders will keep using their existing radios - and Rob Hardgrave will keep on getting all the new gear onto the same frequency.

World.title: Bavuma's brilliant knock flips the script and puts Australia on the ropes
World.content:
South Africa has surged into ascendancy in the second Test against Australia after captain Temba Bavuma led a spectacular batting rearguard on day three.

Beginning the day at 5-97 and on the ropes, Bavuma's 179 helped guide South Africa to 9-425 declared.

Bavuma was aided by the lower order runs of Simon Harmer (82) and Marco Jansen (85) while the Australian bowlers toiled through a difficult a fruitless day.

Bavuma's fifth Test century is the best of the skipper's career, full of fight and resilience and plenty of class.

Marco Jansen hit back with some stunning strokes on the third morning. (Getty Images: Richard Huggard)

It was the arrival of Jansen at the crease that kickstarted South Africa. Coming in at 6-110, Jansen immediately took the attack back to Australia and from there the hosts never looked back.

Jansen was on track for a maiden Test ton, but was caught at midwicket off the bowling of Scott Boland in his first over with the second new ball.

It was Boland's (5-81) fifth wicket of the innings, and it came only a few deliveries after Jansen had been struck in the box and brought to his knees.

Harmer too stared down the prospect of a first Test ton, but his stellar knock was ended by Marnus Labuschagne, clean bowled in the pursuit of quick late runs.

Bavuma was caught behind from the bowling of Mitchell Starc with half an hour left in the day, and his subsequent declaration set the Australians up for a difficult stint with the bat.

Australia's day only got worse when Nic Maddinson fell in the first over of that mini-session, edging Kagiso Rabada to the slips for another duck.

Bad light meant South Africa had to turn to spin for the final overs of the day, and Travis Head and nightwatchman Boland reached the close at 1-3.

Look back at how the action unfolded in our live blog.

World.title: Tedesco parachutes in as Kangaroos captain in first Test since 2023
World.content:
James Tedesco will be elevated straight to the captaincy when he runs out for his first game for the Kangaroos in three years.

Tedesco has been named at fullback for Australia's men's Rugby League World Cup clash with Fiji in Brisbane on Sunday.

It marks the 33-year-old's first cap in green and gold since the 2023 Pacific Championship final, when he led the Kangaroos to a shock 30-0 loss to New Zealand.

Since his last Test appearance, Tedesco has won back his NSW jersey, claimed last year's Dally M Medal and was the Clive Churchill medallist as Roosters captain earlier this month.

On Sunday night at Lang Park, Tedesco will return to the team after coach Kevin Walters made the decision to rotate through his squad to try to find his best line-up.

Rugby League World Cup quick hits From Kalyn Ponga's magnificent Test debut to a mighty Tongan victory years in the making here are the quick hits from week one of the Rugby League World Cup.

Walters named four debutants in the 23-strong squad, with halfback Sam Walker, centre Bradman Best, hooker Blayke Brailey and back rower David Fifita all set to start.

Walker's debut will double as a play-off with halves partner Tom Dearden as both bye to replace the injured Mitchell Moses in the seven jersey for the rest of the campaign.

The bench and extended squad are filled out by starters from the Kangaroos' 24-22 win over the Kiwis in their tournament opener, including regular captain Isaah Yeo and fullback Reece Walsh, who staked his claim in a barnstorming return from injury with a long-range solo try and a try-saver on opposite number Kalyn Ponga.

If Tedesco aims up, it could leave Walters with a major selection call to make at the pointy end of the tournament.

"Those big moments; he hadn't played in six, seven weeks but he turned up in big moments and nailed them," Tedesco, the oldest member of the squad at 33, said of Walsh.

"He was great all week, asking for advice, but it's not a competition. I've got an opportunity and all I can do is make the most of it and do my role.

"Walshy does things on the field so it's about knowing my game and being an experienced leader.

"Walshy, he was soaking up anything I had to say last week and I enjoy that role."

The Jillaroos have also named two debutants for their Women's Rugby League World Cup clash with England on Saturday night.

Sydney Roosters premiership winner Sariah Paki will become a dual international, while Maroons forward Makenzie Weale has been named to make her debut from the bench in Perth.

Their first caps come after five-eighth Jocelyn Kelleher entered the international arena with a bang in round one, claiming player of the match honours against Samoa.

World.title: Aussie Opal's block fires Dream to WNBA finals win
World.content:
Australian rookie Izzy Borlase has helped the Atlanta Dream to their historic first WNBA finals victory, shining in a series-levelling 79–65 triumph over Golden State.

Dream superstar Angel Reese was a dominant figure in game two at San Francisco's Chase Center on Monday (Tuesday AEDT), posting a monster double-double with 30 points and 16 rebounds.

The Dream's win was their first in a title-deciding best-of-seven series, after being swept in their three previous appearances and losing game one against the Valkyries this year.

Coach Karl Smesko's team will enjoy home-court advantage in the next two games as they chase their first WNBA championship.

Borlase could play a key role after being entrusted with almost 17 minutes on court in game two, finishing with two points, one assist, one steal and one block.

The 22-year-old missed all four field-goal attempts in the first half, but sank a pair of free throws and made a huge play to help Atlanta to a 39–37 lead at the main break.

Borlase's block on Veronica Burton late in the second period led to an Allisha Gray (18 points) triple and forced the Valkyries to call a time-out.

It drew huge praise from Reese, who made a beeline for her teammate and celebrated with a chest bump and double-fist to the chest.

Atlanta seized control in a dominant third quarter and took a 60–46 lead after Jordin Canada (13 points) banked a long-range three on the buzzer.

Overrun after leading late in game one, the Dream held firm this time to record their breakthrough finals victory.

Reese became the third player in WNBA history to have at least 30 points and 15 rebounds in a finals game.

Another Australian Opals star, Miela Sowah, sat on the bench for the Valkyries and will remain there throughout the finals due to her restricted status as a development player.

World.title: Diamonds boosted by imminent return of vice-captain
World.content:
Diamonds vice-captain Kate Moloney is on track to return from injury and give Australia a much-needed boost for the Constellation Cup.

Moloney was forced to watch the netball world's number-one side suffer a shock 56–50 loss to the Silver Ferns from the sidelines after a finger laceration in the lead-up to the Auckland series opener.

The Diamonds were already without defender Jo Weston (managed), and the experienced duo were sorely missed against the Commonwealth Games champions.

Diamonds centurions forced to the bench in Constellation Cup loss It was defender Courtney Bruce's 100th milestone game to start the Constellation Cup but the brand new centurion and her captain Liz Watson were both sent to the bench in Australia's 56-50 loss to New Zealand in Auckland.

New Zealand stormed to a 15-goal lead in the first of four matches, forcing Diamonds coach Stacey Marinkovich to bench captain and midcourter Liz Watson alongside goalkeeper Courtney Bruce in her 100th game.

Jamie-Lee Price took over centre duties against New Zealand's Adelaide Lightning star Kate Heffernan, while Jessie Grenvold was tasked with containing Silver Ferns goalscoring superstar Grace Nweke on debut.

Australia cut the deficit to just six goals in the fourth quarter, but the damage had been done.

Georgie Horjus was the only Diamond who remained on the court for four quarters, finishing with a game-high 19 gains and 38 feeds as wing attack.

With the Diamonds set to name their squad this evening, Marinkovich said Melbourne Vixens captain Moloney's return was imminent.

"We'll definitely see her back in the series," Marinkovich said.

"It was a bit of a nasty laceration to her finger, so we had to wait till it pretty much stuck back together.

"It's just one of those innocuous things that happen at training, but she's been able to do all the running and the movement, and yeah, look forward to having her back."

But the midcourt will not be the only area of focus for tomorrow night's game in Christchurch.

Looking to end their five-year drought on Kiwi soil, the Diamonds will need to find a way past the towering defensive duo of Kelly Jackson and Karin Burger.

With goalkeeper Jackson standing at 192cm and goal defence Burger at 184cm, Australia's attacking roster of Kiera Austin, Cara Koenen, Sophie Dwyer and Sophie Garbin struggled to fire.

Marinkovich is urging her Diamonds to start with "immediacy" on the court.

"We were slightly off our pace [in game one], and our numbers would show that we weren't as aggressive as what we needed to be on the ball," she said.

ABC Sport will have live blog coverage of Game II between the Diamonds and Silver Ferns on Wednesday, October 21.

AAP

World.title: Jockeys cleared over Ohope Wins's fatal Caulfield Cup fall
World.content:
A Racing Victoria investigation into the fall at the Caulfield Cup that resulted in the euthanasia of Ohope Wins has finished, clearing all jockeys involved of any wrongdoing.

Ohope Wins, ridden by Jye McNeil, and Half Yours, ridden by Mark Zahra, both went down in the final straight at the 150th running of the famous 2,400-metre race.

Zahra and Half Yours fell first after getting tangled in the pack chasing eventual winner Kingswood, with Ohope Wins going over the top of the fallen gelding.

Loading...

Last year's Melbourne Cup winner Half Yours suffered superficial cuts and scrapes, but Ohope Wins was assessed on track as having a "serious racing injury" and was put down by on-course veterinarians.

Both jockeys were thrown from their mounts and taken to hospital, delaying the conclusion of the inquiry into the incident, which once again prompted calls for the racing industry to be made more accountable for racehorse deaths.

After hearing evidence from McNeil, Zahra and three other jockeys in the race, Racing Victoria stewards said they "could not attribute the incident to the careless actions of any one particular rider".

The hearing at Racing Victoria headquarters found contact between Kings Valley and Green Spaces with about 300m to go resulted in the latter becoming unbalanced.

Half Yours ran the rest of the course without a rider. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Green Spaces, ridden by Rachel King, then turned inward and made more contact with apprentice rider Jabez Johnstone's Kings Valley, who also turned inward, resulting in Half Yours being squeezed for room between Kings Valley and Zahrann.

"A short distance later, Half Yours subsequently fell," the stewards' report read.

"Ohope Wins that was trailing was subsequently brought down when unable to avoid the fallen Half Yours."

The incident has been referred to Racing Victoria's Veterinary Services Department, as is standard practice.

Trainer Tony McEvoy said Half Yours was recovering well from injuries and would be rested, while Zahra was meeting with doctors today about a timeline for his return to riding.

McNeil was cleared of any injury and is expected to ride at the Geelong Cup tomorrow.

World.title: Collingwood AFLW captain to leave at end of season
World.content:
Collingwood captain Ruby Schleicher will leave the struggling AFLW club to return to her native Western Australia.

Schleicher informed the Magpies of her decision on Tuesday after suffering a season-ending shoulder injury in their round 9 loss to St Kilda.

The 28-year-old inaugural Collingwood player is expected to land at West Coast, with the Eagles reportedly offering a four-year contract.

Do you have a story idea about women in sport? Email us abcsport5050@your.abc.net.au

A two-time All-Australian, Schleicher's departure is a massive blow to perennial competition strugglers Collingwood, who have only won one game after 10 rounds this season.

"This has been a really tough decision for me to make but one that is ultimately the best for where I am in my life and career," Schleicher said in a club statement.

"Collingwood has been my home for my entire adult life … I'll always consider myself a Collingwood person.

"I'm excited for my next chapter, but also for the club's next chapter."

Collingwood chief executive Craig Kelly expressed the club's disappointment in Schleicher's decision.

Schleicher reportedly turned down a one-year deal to remain at the Magpies after strong interest from the Eagles.

Joining the Magpies ahead of the inaugural AFLW season in 2017, the defender-turned-midfielder has played 82 games for the club and took over as captain from Bri Davey in 2025.

Schleicher was moved to the forward line this season under coach Sam Wright and kicked 10 goals before fracturing her shoulder against the Saints.

"While we are disappointed to see Ruby depart our Club, we respect her decision to return home," Kelly said in a statement.

"We thank Ruby for everything she has given to Collingwood and wish her all the very best for the next chapter."

Like Schleicher, Davey is among several senior leaders set to come off contract at the end of this campaign, while vice-captain Jordy Allen's contract runs until the end of the 2027 season.

AAP

World.title: NFL QB in hospital at 4am before London game due to blood clots
World.content:
Philadelphia Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts has blood clots in both lungs, according to his team and his agent, with media reports saying the former Super Bowl MVP is expected to miss the rest of the 2026 season.

Hurts was clinically stable but his treatment would involve blood thinners, which would rule him out of contact activities, the Eagles and agent Nicole Lynn said in a statement.

The 28-year-old was initially diagnosed with a left calf superficial vein thrombosis after an ultrasound in London before Philadelphia's 19-17 loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, which Hurts played in.

The current diagnosis is a deep vein thrombosis and bilateral pulmonary emboli. A bilateral pulmonary embolism is where a blood clot travels from a deep vein in the body, often the leg, and blocks an artery in both lungs.

"Jalen's prognosis is very good, and we expect a full recovery," the statement said.

"We anticipate that he will have the opportunity to resume contact football activities when off the blood thinners."

It said no long-term effects were expected.

According to an ESPN report, Hurts was in the hospital in London until 4am on the day of the game and did not sleep the night before the contest as a health precaution.

Speaking at a press conference on Monday, local time, Eagles head coach Nick Sirianni said the team cared about its players and he trusted the medical staff.

"I'm a football coach. I lean on our medical experts in every situation. I have full trust and full faith in them," Sirianni said.

"We get medical information from our guys, and we always put the players' health first and foremost in every situation. And, you know, that's where we were there."

The Eagles said in a statement on Thursday that their medical staff and doctors in London reviewed the ultrasound results and concluded that "activity and mobility were important" and that Hurts could safely play in the game against the Jaguars, adding that he "played without limitation".

Hurts guided the Eagles to the Super Bowl title in February 2025, throwing for two touchdowns and running in another against the Kansas City Chiefs to earn the game's Most Valuable Player trophy.

Reuters

World.title: Quick hits: Renshaw floored by miracle grab as Bavuma's six stops traffic
World.content:
Matt Renshaw has been shocked by his own miracle grab, while Temba Bavuma's soaring six has stopped the Gqeberha traffic on a day when a soggy outfield threatened to ruin it all.

Here are the quick hits from day two of the second Test between Australia and South Africa.

1. A soggy outfield almost ruins it all

Things did not look good as the scheduled start of play approached on day two. Dark skies and pouring rain meant a delay was inevitable.

But within two hours, the rain had ceased, and another hour after that, the sun was beating down in Gqeberha.

The St George's ground staff had a lot on their plate on day two. (Getty Images: Richard Huggard/Gallo Images)

The St George's outfield, however, just wasn't playing ball. Three surface inspections came and went, with the umpires and ground staff determining the soggy turf too treacherous for play on each occasion.

The two areas of particular concern, both deep in the outfield, were simply refusing to drain.

It was Test cricket at its exasperating, excruciating worst, and the threat of an entirely lost day loomed on the horizon.

But five hours after the scheduled start of play, and more than three since the last downfall, the officials finally determined the field fit for purpose.

By the time the Australian bowlers were going through their warm-ups, it was a glorious day in the Eastern Cape.

2. Hazlewood the latest to succumb to sickness

But when the Australians finally got on the field for a 30-over evening session, they were without one of their most dangerous weapons.

Josh Hazlewood was battling sickness and nowhere to be seen at St George's Park, leaving just the — admittedly serviceable — trio of Pat Cummins, Mitch Starc and Scott Boland for the South African batters to contend with.

A day earlier umpire Chris Gaffaney was forced to withdraw from the Test with a bout of food poisoning, the saga no doubt leaving those in attendance wondering if there might be a dish to avoid at the St George's canteen.

Hazlewood is expected to return on day three.

3. Carey poised for 200

Scott Boland picked up from where he left off as play finally got underway. (Getty Images: Richard Huggard/Gallo Images)

It was typically outstanding stuff from Boland as day two belatedly began.

The Victorian had Temba Bavuma swinging and missing dramatically with the first ball of the afternoon. He only had to wait until his second set of the day to claim his third wicket of the match, luring Marques Ackerman into a drive and nicking off the debutant for six.

Meanwhile, behind the stumps, Alex Carey was nearing a major milestone.

And when Mitchell Starc had Matthew Breetzke edging through to the Australian wicketkeeper only moments later, Carey was one take away from becoming the fifth Australian gloveman to take 200 catches in Test cricket after Adam Gilchrist, Ian Healy, Rod Marsh and Brad Haddin.

Carey will hope to join that group on day three.

4. Bavuma interrupts traffic with massive six

It was an absolutely massive six, and it came from absolutely nowhere.

Bavuma had been so composed and diligent in steadying ship after the losses of Ackerman and Breetzke, and looked set to defend his way to stumps.

But the South Africa captain absolutely exploded in hooking Cummins over the backward square leg boundary.

Temba Bavuma's six interrupted the Gqeberha traffic. (Fox Cricket)

The ball sailed over the rope, out of the stadium and then rolled onto the road, where a security guard was forced to weave through the Gqeberha traffic to collect it.

5. Renshaw stunned by own miracle grab

With only a matter of minutes remaining in the day's play, Australia was pushing for the one final wicket that would put them well on top in the game.

Shadows were lengthening, light was fading quickly, and Marnus Labuschagne had just put down a relatively simple catch at leg slip.

Visibility clearly wasn't great but, somehow, Matt Renshaw produced something remarkable.

Renshaw took a remarkable catch late on day two. (Fox Cricket)

It was definitely Carey's catch, but the Australian wicketkeeper was rooted to the spot as Ryan Rickleton edged towards the men behind the wicket.

The ball looked destined to fly between the keeper and slip, but there he was, Renshaw, diving at full stretch and managing to get his right hand between ball and turf.

Matt Renshaw was blown away by his stunning catch. (Fox Cricket)

The Queenslander looked absolutely stunned to have taken the catch that had South Africa rocking at 5-97 at stumps.

Tech.title: Meta pauses Muse sharing after researchers find AI chats on the web
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Meta says it paused a Muse feature that lets you share conversations with the AI assistant after researchers found the URLs publicly available on the web, as reported by Ars Technica. In a report published this week, researchers at the security firm Claroc say they found more than 6,800 Muse links through public DNS records.

“People have the ability to share specific Muse artifacts, which creates a page that can be accessed by those with the link,” Muse spokesperson Tracy Clayton says in an emailed statement to The Verge. “However, we’ve paused this functionality while we review this report and consider changes to how these links can be discovered.”

The feature in question allows you to share your Muse conversation with someone else through a link. But, as pointed out by Claroc, the way Meta designed these links made them easy to find. “Muse builds each share’s web address from the share’s title, a short phrase describing the conversation, then a random ID,” Claroc says. “The hostname usually gave away what a page held before we opened it, and since the link carries that same title and ID, a hostname pulled from DNS rebuilds the link.”

By searching public DNS records, which serve as a directory for web traffic, Claroc was able to view hundreds of Muse conversations, including some containing a marketing company’s revenue review, a small business owner’s loan application, a workplace’s full-year staff calendar, and notes for a job candidate’s call with an AI lab. This isn’t the first time AI sharing features made chats more public than intended, as conversations with OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Anthropic’s Claude, and xAI’s Grok have wound up on Google Search.

Tech.title: The $20,000 Voxel bot will help you find misplaced things around your home
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

Tuesday Labs, a New York City-based robotics lab and design studio, has opened reservations for Voxel, its new bi-pedal robot designed to learn and take over routine tasks throughout your home. Similar to other robots like Weave Robotics’ Issac 1 that are designed for household chores beyond mopping or vacuuming floors, Voxel features a pair of highly-articulated arms and an advanced vision system. If you’re interested in bringing home what Tuesday Labs describes as a “droid butler” you can reserve one now for $200 while full pricing is expected to be around $20,000 when Voxel ships sometime in 2028.

The model available for preorder is known as the Voxel Series-1 and features a mostly humanoid design with a few liberties. The bot primarily relies on a pair of articulated arms with seven degrees of freedom that end in a pair of grippers that are much simpler than the dextrous fingered hands on robots like Boston Dynamics’ Atlas.

Those arms extend out of the top of Voxel’s torso that also appears to double as its head with a small mouth and a set of pixelated, animated eyes located closer to the robot’s waist that sit well below a hidden pair of stereo RGB cameras that work alongside a secondary “wide-field” camera for monitoring an entire room.

Image: Tuesday Labs

The Series-1 navigates your home using a pair of Z-shaped legs with knees that bend in the opposite direction to ours. The design is intentional and allows the robot to bend its knees for balance and raise and lower its height while standing close to kitchen cabinets, tables, and shelving.

While Tuesday Labs’ website describes Voxel’s design and hardware in a lot of detail, it doesn’t go as in-depth when it comes to the robot’s capabilities and how it can benefit your household. The robot can carry out basic autonomous tasks like decluttering your home and putting things back where they belong, handling routine and mundane chores like watering plants, retrieving items like books, or helping you find a misplaced item like the TV remote by asking Voxel where it last saw it. At launch it’s not going to be making dinner or changing diapers, but if it can reliably remember where you left your keys, those of us with bad short term memories could have a good reason to justify its steep price tag.

Tech.title: Chrome will now show a warning before you visit ‘suspicious’ sites
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Google is launching a new browser safety feature for Chrome that aims to keep you better informed about how malicious a website might be before you open it. The new suspicious site warnings, available when Chrome’s Enhanced Protection is on, build on a similar two-stage system introduced for Chrome file downloads in 2024, which provides visually different notifications for blocked files based on whether they’re determined to be “suspicious” or “dangerous.”

For the Chrome site warnings, the feature will flag a website as suspicious if it detects that it has similar qualities to other sites associated with phishing, malware, and scams. Google describes this warning as having a “lower confidence verdict” with possible risk of user harm — meaning there’s a chance it could be incorrectly flagged, but you should only proceed to the site if you’re 100 percent confident that it’s safe to do so. The warnings on “dangerous” website have a higher confidence verdict and “high risk of user harm,” however, and should be avoided entirely.

It’s easy to distinguish between these warnings at a glance. The notifications for suspicious websites will appear as a pop-up window on both desktop and mobile, with the webpage visible but darkened underneath, and an option to “Mark as safe” if the site was flagged mistakenly. The already familiar notification for dangerous sites is much harder to ignore: the warning message takes up almost the entire screen and the website will be replaced with a solid red background.

Here’s a comparison between the two warning types on Chrome’s mobile browser. Image: Google

Google also improved Gemini-powered scam detection for Enhanced Protection users, alongside introducing the browser warning redesign.

Update, October 20th: Clarified that the suspicious site warnings appear when Enhanced Protection mode is on.

Tech.title: AMD is bringing FSR 4.1 to Xbox consoles and handhelds
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

AMD has just revealed that it’s bringing its latest upscaling technology, FSR 4.1, to the Xbox Series S and X consoles, as well as laptops, 6000-series GPUs, and handhelds like the Xbox Ally X devices. FSR 4.1 will start appearing for Radeon RX 6000-series GPUs today, as well as Ryzen AI Max 300 and 400 series devices, and Ryzen AI 9 300 and 400 series devices.

AMD launched its FSR 4.1 update for Radeon RX 9000-series graphics cards in March, and promised to bring the technology to older GPUs and handhelds this year. FSR 4.1 can improve performance in more than 300 supported games, including Cyberpunk 2077, Battlefield 6, and Assassin’s Creed Shadows.

FSR 4.1 arrives just weeks after Sony and AMD teamed up to bring Quick Spectral Super Resolution (QSSR) to the base PS5, based on Sony and AMD’s Project Amethyst work. “We want to bring that work to more gamers,” says Jack Huynh, senior vice president and general manager of AMD’s computer and graphics group. “We didn’t just bring it over, we made it better. We went back into the model, we tuned it and optimized the code path.”

While owners of Radeon RX 6000-series GPUs and Gorgon Halo- or Strix Halo-powered devices will get FSR 4.1 today with the latest Adrenalin Edition 26.10.1 drivers, Xbox console owners will have to wait a little longer.

“We’ve worked very closely with AMD to optimize this technology, giving developers another powerful tool for great performance and visual quality for players,” says Xbox CTO Scott Van Vilet. “Our teams are continuing to work together across hardware and software, and there’s even more ahead with Project Helix, leveraging FSR Diamond to power what comes next.”

FSR 4.1 could have a big impact on Xbox console games, particularly on the lesser powered Xbox Series S. Neither Microsoft or AMD will say when FSR 4.1 will arrive on Xbox consoles, with it simply listed as “coming soon.”

Tech.title: Arturia’s MiniFreak 49 makes its Freak synths more professional
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Arturia is adding to its Freak line of proudly weird digital synths with the MiniFreak 49. Under the hood, it’s almost identical to the current MiniFreak, but it adds a number of more professional features and some interface improvements.

The most noticeable change is that, rather than the MiniFreak’s 37 minikeys or the MicroFreak’s 25 “key” touchplate, the MiniFreak 49 has (as you may have guessed) 49 full-sized, semi-weighted keys. Though it’s somewhat disappointing that they feature only mono aftertouch instead of polyphonic aftertouch. It also trades the touchstrips of the other Freak instruments for proper aluminum pitch and mod wheels.

The MiniFreak 49 also has a larger LCD than its siblings and dedicated controls for its two sound engines, so you don’t have to switch between them. Like the MiniFreak, it offers over 30 digital oscillator types, each with analog filters. It also adds audio-rate filter FM for even freakier sounds and has 256MB of storage for user samples and wavetables, which were just added to the original MiniFreak in a firmware update last month.

Lastly, there’s a new XYZ touchpad that not only replaces the mod matrix’s intuitive but slow knob-based interface, but also adds performance features and speeds up preset browsing. You can swipe through presets, control macros, manipulate the filter, and more.

MiniFreak 49 is available now with an MSRP of $849, though the street price is likely to be lower.

Tech.title: The Gospel according to Peter (Thiel)
Tech.content:
It’s a time of apocalyptic worldviews in Silicon Valley. The latest AI doom cycle is driven by effective altruism (EA), a philosophy that has lurked around the fringes for years but recently burst into the mainstream because its adherents are embedded across the AI industry, from Anthropic to newly appointed AI safety watchdog METR. EA is a utilitarian approach to charity premised on doing the most good for the most people over the longest time, and EA advocates see halting an AI-induced doomsday as critical to saving as many humans as possible.

But EA has an important and equally apocalyptic rival in the crosscutting cosmologies of the tech titans — a strain of Christianity best represented by Peter Thiel, who believes EA will bring about the Antichrist. It’s an issue on which the billionaire techno-capitalist is a self-styled expert, and, somehow, Thiel has become America’s most provocative and visible Christian theologian.

Thiel’s current fixation on the End of the World as We Know It is in theological language called eschatology, the study of the “last things.” His specific bête noire is the Antichrist, the villain of these end times scenarios. Thiel’s riffs on the Antichrist began a little over three years ago, first in a 2023 talk at the Catholic University of America but then, starting in 2025, only in closed-door, invitation-only, multipart lectures out of San Francisco. While that secrecy is frustrating for those of us interested in how uber-rich and politically powerful tech titans see the future of our world, it’s also rather savvy — no surprise from the guy who started hugely successful ventures like PayPal and Palantir. “It’s a pretty good marketing shtick if you want everybody to hear about something, not to let anybody in the room,” Thiel reportedly told one San Francisco audience last fall.

In March, he traveled to Rome for another private, four-part series on the Antichrist. Taking his shtick to the doorstep of the Vatican was guaranteed to generate publicity, and it did.

Months ago, recordings of Thiel’s lectures were leaked to The Verge. We have listened to and read transcripts of all four of these lectures, which provide a window into Thiel’s dizzying religious and sociocultural philosophy. He comes off as an intellectual magpie who somehow combines disparate elements into grave warnings against the AI and general “safetyism” that he claims precedes the Antichrist.

“Peace and safety” — the slogan of the Antichrist, according to Thiel — trouble him throughout the lectures. In the first, he wonders if we’re headed toward World War III or Cold War II, and afterward, potentially, an unjust peace, the corollary to an unjust war:

Somehow, it’s very strange how the first Cold War from ’49 to ’89 ended. But it ended with roughly what I think of as a just peace. Where somehow you didn’t have a nuclear war. And somehow our side, which I think was more the good side, basically won. And you ended up not with a perfect peace, but more or less a just peace. And so if we have World War III, it will be an unjust war. If we have Cold War II, maybe it can end in a just peace or an unjust peace. Reflecting on this material and thinking about it, it’s obviously not written in stone and there’s a lot of different ways this stuff can go. But I keep thinking that, if you had to put odds on it, aren’t the odds that we’re trending towards the fourth quadrant this time? The fourth possibility is that Cold War II will end an unjust peace. And it’s because the Antichrist talks about Armageddon nonstop. We’re all scared to death that we’re sleepwalking into Armageddon. And then because we know World War III will be an unjust war, that pushes us very hard towards peace at any price. What I worry about in that sort of situation is you don’t think too hard about the details of the peace and it becomes much more likely that you get an unjust peace. This is, by the way, the slogan of the Antichrist: 1 Thessalonians 5:3. It’s “peace and safety,” the unjust peace. And then what Christ says in Matthew 24:6, the full verse: “And you shall hear of wars and rumours of wars, see that ye be not troubled.” If you’re too troubled, will we always end up with very unjust peace? Or something like this.

We are publishing an analysis of these lectures now because Thiel published a version of these same ideas in the conservative religious journal First Things in July. You can read along for yourself. Titled “The Pope and the Antichrist,” the essay fills in the huge gaps in Thiel’s thinking and allows us to better understand his ideas, such as they are.

The bottom line is that after sifting through all of the arcane references and esoteric exegesis, it turns out that Thiel — a Protestant who likes to describe himself as a “heterodox Christian” — offers a fairly standard-issue American evangelical worldview, and a rather fundamentalist one at that.

He’s less a coherent religious thinker than a repackager of recognizable ideas — dressing them up in the rhetoric of a tech nerd turned theological hobbyist — which he uses to promote his own ideology. He reads everything from the Bible to pre-papal writings of a future pope to Robert Hugh Benson’s 1907 novel Lord of the World to semi-obscure Scottish poetry with an eye toward his own, sometimes shockingly literal interpretation of the Antichrist’s arrival (ideally, he should make his mark, as it were, more quickly than Jesus, who died at 33 and a few months — although Thiel allows in his third lecture that perhaps “in our gerontocracy, 66 is the new 33”). While his mashup of religious concepts and authoritative assertions on dubious interpretations make him sound like an undergrad who just took his first philosophy class and then a few too many hits on the bong, the goal of his eschatology is the same as every apocalyptic visionary: to divide the world between the saved and the damned. And Thiel is, clearly, one of the righteous.

It’s notable here that Thiel is coming from the heart of what is arguably America’s latest, and most unexpected, religious revival — one concentrated among the Silicon Valley elite, like the ACTS 17 Collective, which is a reference to St. Paul’s preaching to the Greek pagans in the Acts of the Apostles and an acronym for “Acknowledging Christ in Technology and Society.” But that movement presents an upbeat message of self-improvement through Jesus, the kind that the clean-and-fit Bay Area crowd tends to embrace. Thiel’s worldview is quite unusual for Silicon Valley, and perhaps especially unexpected for a gay German billionaire; he’s right at home in the US tradition of apocalypticism.

The key to Thiel’s theological vision comes at the very opening of his most recent First Things essay, and it is his fixation on, and fear of, the Antichrist. The Antichrist has traditionally been associated with, as Thiel himself put it elsewhere, “an evil king or tyrant or anti-messiah who appears in the end times.” That is true, though Thiel says that the Antichrist interests him “mostly because nobody else is talking about it.” That would be news to anybody with even a passing familiarity with American Christianity.

In fact, the Antichrist and eschatology are arguably the central religious impulse running through American Christianity, and that focus distinguishes the US from most other churches and cultures around the globe. In America, biblical teachings tend to jump from the Ten Commandments at the beginning of the Old Testament to the Book of Revelation at the end of the New Testament. The Gospels, the Beatitudes, all that provides the key teachings of Jesus Christ is a footnote.

The enthusiasm for the end of the world has been fueled in large part by the series of sweeping revivals, or “Great Awakenings,” that have marked American religious history from the Colonial era up through the 1800s and, some would say, on into the 20th century. These revivals focused not only on personal conversion but on dark warnings about the “end times” as foretold in the New Testament, when Christ would return to gather believers up to Heaven and those who remained would be stuck facing various tribulations on their own.

For American Christians especially, the quest to save souls from eternal damnation was increasingly driven by the fear that the Second Coming was imminent, so you’d better repent now. New apocalyptic movements and sects and cults continued to flourish, from those early tent revivals through the more slickly branded televangelists and, later, the enormously popular Left Behind series of novels in the 1990s. Forecasters variously took snippets in the Book of Daniel and other prophets in the Hebrew Bible and joined them with the often phantasmagoric array of visions from the Book of Revelation, and eventually what had been a confusing jumble of end times scenarios solidified into a widely accepted timeline: increasing natural and human-made disasters, the Second Coming of Jesus, aka the Rapture of true believers, followed by the rise of the Antichrist and seven years of the Great Tribulation on Earth, ending with a final battle between good and evil and a thousand years of peace.

Peter Thiel on Bill Gates “One of my friends was telling me that I should not pass up on the opportunity to tell those people in San Francisco that Bill Gates is the Antichrist. I will concede that he is certainly a Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde-type character. The public Mr. Rogers, the neighborhood character — but I saw the Mr. Hyde version about a year ago, where it was just a nonstop Tourette’s, yelling swear words, almost incomprehensible what was going on. Certainly, of course, there are a lot of people who are wannabe Antichrists. They sort of want peace and safety. [He] definitely wants a Nobel Peace Prize. He would give his soul for that, no question about it.” Eliezer Yudkowsky “There is another book — I haven’t been able to get a copy of it because it’s coming out tomorrow, but we sort of downloaded it — that fits this thesis even better. It’s from the East Bay rationalist Eliezer Yudkowsky. I’m embarrassed about all the ways I was once affiliated with these various people and how deranged and crazy they’ve all gone. It started with these Baconian aspirations of transformative technology: We’re going to build it, it’s going to change the world. And then it’s somehow ended in some sort of blackpilled thing that’s probably more depressed and more Luddite than Greta.” Greta Thunberg “I think one of the ways these things always get reported is I denounce Greta as an Antichrist. And I want to be very clear, Greta is not, I mean, she’s maybe sort of a type or a shadow of an Antichrist of the sort that would be tempting, but I don’t want to flatter her too much.” Marc Andreessen “It’s not Andreessen, by the way. I think Andreessen is not the Antichrist. Because, you know, the Antichrist is popular.”

Phew. Now enter Peter Thiel. He is in effect the latest in a long line of apocalypticists, though his own spin is that anxieties over strange new technologies like AI will prompt demands for greater regulation and that would be a grave, almost apocalyptic, mistake. Given the latest warnings from AI leaders themselves that the new technology could risk human extinction within a decade, Thiel’s concerns run counter to what you’d expect from an apocalypticist.

Thiel’s theological justification for criticizing this instinct toward what he derides as “safetyism” rests on a verse in St. Paul’s first letter to the Thessalonians in which the apostle warns that many will promote “peace and safety” to lull people into a false sense of security and then POOF, Jesus returns and the Antichrist appears and unbelievers are doomed.

Thiel identifies promoters of this kind of peace and safety with a “restraining” force that will be a sign of the coming of the Antichrist and which will eventually pave the way for the Antichrist. He has pointed to Anthony Fauci as one example of such a “restrainer.” And now the apostles of effective altruism, with their concern for protecting as many people as possible, are in Thiel’s sights. Thiel uses the original Greek term for “the restrainer,” katechon, because of course he does. Deploying arcane terms is part of the mystery that gives apocalypticism its allure, and prophets their power.

So who is actually the Antichrist? Thiel at one point dismissed such speculations as “down-market” behavior, but he himself cannot resist weighing in. Viewing the Roman pontiff as the Antichrist or a collaborator with the Antichrist is a standard trope of end times theology, and in his First Things essay Thiel follows that tradition by suggesting that the late Pope Francis could have been the Antichrist. In previously leaked snippets of Thiel’s talks he has accused the current American pope, Leo XIV, of being a “Chinese communist agent” or, more recently, Beijing’s “useful idiot,” because he wants to regulate AI — all very Antichrist-adjacent behavior.

Thiel has a somewhat unusual relationship to the Catholic Church. True to the more anti-papist strains of his tradition, he worries that Pope Leo XIV is a “woke American pope” who will join with American liberals to create a tyrannical “Caesaro-Papist fusion.”

At the same time, the German-born Thiel’s record-breaking financial support propelled JD Vance, a relatively recent Catholic convert, to the US Senate and now a heartbeat away from the presidency. Thiel has also made a little-known Catholic literary theorist from France, René Girard, a spiritual guide for America’s political right — though only by completely inverting Girard’s famous teaching about the scapegoat mechanism by which a society eases internal divisions by blaming a single person or subgroup of people for their problems.

Thiel’s latest essay is also unusual, or inventive, in that rather than denouncing the papacy as the Whore of Babylon — a traditional fundamentalist Protestant trope drawn from a stark image in Revelation 17 — he tries to co-opt one pope, the late Benedict XVI, into his very American and Protestant worldview and against the papacy and the Catholic Church itself.

“I did not come to Rome to try to be more Catholic than the pope, but I did hope, even as a Protestant, to be more Catholic than the average Catholic,” Thiel says. His aim is to use Benedict — who resigned as pope in 2013 and died in seclusion in the Vatican in 2022 — as the one Catholic leader who understood the imminent threat of the Antichrist and the end times, the one Catholic who got it right.

Granted, Benedict is the one pope who provides Thiel with the kind of opening, however tiny, that Thiel could run with. Benedict was “a decided Augustinian,” as he wrote during his earlier days as Cardinal Joseph Ratzinger, and he shared St. Augustine’s rather pessimistic view of humankind. Thiel spends much time on the young Ratzinger’s dissertation on St. Bonaventure’s theology of history — a recondite topic in which the 13th-century Italian Franciscan rebutted the odd apocalyptic writings of Joachim of Fiore, an Italian abbot who lived a century before St. Bonaventure.

Thiel somehow reads Ratzinger’s endorsement of Bonaventure over Joachim of Fiore as a sign that Ratzinger saw the apocalypse coming rather than what Ratzinger actually wrote and meant. In his third lecture Thiel extrapolates wildly on this theme from a quote within a footnote, saying:

The TL;DR: My belief is that Benedict literally thought that the historic falling away from the church during his papacy was a sign of the end times. Is there evidence for this? There’s all sorts of subtle hints. Writing the 1959 professorial dissertation on Bonaventure, he uses all this colorful language on the Antichrist, the Whore of Babylon. What does one make of this? In a footnote, it’s sort of the most cryptic, esoteric way to write it. Not in his own words but quoting another professor, Ratzinger wrote — obviously before he’s Pope — quoting this other professor: “In the case of Bonaventure, we see how difficult it is to succeed in placing the proper limits on apocalyptic images. Apocalyptic images are like a torrent of water that overflows the banks and it’s difficult to keep in bounds. And regardless of all efforts to mollify the imagery, the apocalyptic tone predominates. Even a Mozart cannot make a trumpet forget to sound like a trumpet.” So it’s sort of like you are saying, if you think about this stuff, you can never, ever talk about it. If you talk about it even one peep, it will dominate everything and you can’t say anything else.

The proof that future Pope Benedict was as focused on the literal end times as Thiel? That he would never talk about it, of course.

What Ratzinger actually wanted was to avoid the idea that humanity could bring peace and justice to this world through our own efforts — a preview of his decadeslong campaign against what he saw as Marxist-influenced liberation theology, not on behalf of the Antichrist. Yet Thiel continues to pick out various comments on eschatology — “breadcrumbs,” Thiel calls them — from Ratzinger’s lectures and writings as the decades progressed and Ratzinger’s own theological vision admittedly grew darker and more conservative. He interprets Benedict’s resignation from the papacy — unprecedented in modern times — as one of Benedict’s “winks and hints” that the Antichrist is coming.

This ventriloquizing is as bizarre as it is morbid, but Thiel is convinced that when it comes to talking about the Antichrist “these apocalyptic paroxysms make Benedict sound like a fire-and-brimstone Southern Baptist.”

That comment shows Thiel’s basic problem, which is that he wants to view Roman Catholicism through an Evangelical Protestant lens that sees the end times as a global apocalypse where the “saved” will be rescued — and confirmed in their righteousness. Ratzinger, and later as Pope Benedict, was a thoroughgoing Catholic churchman who was less concerned about the end of time than he was “anxious about the end of a historical era of the Catholic Church,” as the Italian theologian Marcello Neri put it. Ratzinger saw Catholic liberals who would dilute church doctrine and dogma as the apocalyptic threat, and it’s a threat to the Catholic Church, not the planet. History will go on, Ratzinger believed. It’s the church’s fate that’s less certain, thanks to infiltration by modernist currents. Thiel is making a category error that undermines his entire argument. It’s typical Thiel.

At the end of the day, and of his essay, Thiel’s grandiose language and project is shown to be a rather ordinary ideological one. “Thiel is above all a political theologian operating at the very heart of the Silicon Valley ecosystem,” the Italian Franciscan Paolo Benanti wrote in a sharp riposte to Thiel’s Rome talks. As Benanti explains, this ideology includes the “pathological radicalization” of a handful of Western values — “competition, technology, the individual” — resulting in outcomes “radically divergent from the common democratic project.” Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor elaborate on that theme in their new book, End Times Fascism: And the Fight for the Living World.

If liberals want to “immanentize the eschaton,” as William F. Buckley once put it, by focusing on doing good in this life instead of being anxious about the world to come, conservatives tend to focus on personal salvation ahead of the apocalypse. That end times theology is a perfect match for them because it tends toward a libertarian ethos like Thiel’s; Jesus is coming back soon, let’s not get bogged down in overregulating or overthinking. “We moralize way too much,” as Thiel said in a podcast last month with Axel Springer CEO Mathias Döpfner. “If you’re evil, you’re at least competent. And if you’re evil, you’re not bad, and therefore you’re actually maybe kind of good because you’re at least getting something done.” Instead, Thiel suggests, let’s make hay — meaning, bushels of money — while the sun shines. Climate anxiety? Your worries about the future show a lack of faith! That’s why, in addition to the previous pope and the effective altruism movement, Thiel has also been reported as suggesting climate change activist Greta Thunberg might be the Antichrist.

Or maybe, he suggests in one lecture, it’s the system that’s the real Antichrist — specifically the financial regulatory system.

The Book of Revelation tells us, sort of, the Antichrist will abolish financial freedom. Revelation 13:16–17: “He causes all, both great and small, rich and poor, free and bond, to receive a mark in their right hand or in their foreheads, that no man might buy or sell save that he had the mark, or the name of the beast, or the number of his name.” There’s this whole constellation of things, where over the last 25 years — this uneventful, Groundhog Day 21st century since 2000 — under cover of relative peace and safety, an incredible machinery of tax treaties, financial surveillance, and sanctions architecture has been constructed. And all these tech fortunes are downstream of this vast system. You have the illusion of power and autonomy, but you have this sense it could be taken away at any moment. It’s become quite difficult to hide one’s money.

He admits that “this Antichrist-like system, this machinery” moves at a different speed than a human Antichrist (who, again, should probably be 33.5 or younger), but insists it was set up “not overnight but relatively quickly, and there’s a feeling it could be activated at the flip of a switch.” If that all seems like a definition of the Antichrist that only a billionaire could love, he assures his listeners it’s more than that.

And then, of course, it’s not just a financial system. It’s also, in some sense, an ideological system. The Antichrist won’t stop just at money. Money is not enough to stop the Antichrist and follows that he wants something more from you.

It’s also, per Thiel, the International Criminal Court and the way it has spooked Vladimir Putin, Benjamin Netanyahu, and erstwhile members of the George W. Bush administration, and it’s Germany’s strict laws around Nazi symbolism and libel online, and it’s Australian age verification laws, which all cobble together into a vision of the end of days that so transfixes him. It’s not exactly fire and brimstone, but to Thiel, it is.

For all of Peter Thiel’s prominence and brilliance — Vance called him “the smartest man I’ve ever met” — his spiritual preoccupations are ultimately quite mainstream. Vance recently spent part of a long podcast with a popular Evangelical influencer talking about the End Times and the Antichrist. It blew the mind of most Catholics, but as Vance’s friend conservative Christian commentator Rod Dreher said, this is “a very, very common belief.”

These beliefs are also very representative of an increasingly DIY religious culture in America that is disconnected from traditional practices and flesh-and-blood congregations. When it comes to religion, seemingly everyone now does their own research and generates their own social media ministry.

The difference is that Thiel is an uber-wealthy influencer with political power. The theological thrifting by which he has sewn together his own apocalyptic vision would at one level be seen as quirky but innocent if not for the fact that he is using that vision to set himself up as a godlike judge between the saved and the damned — one might almost say a kind of Antichrist. That’s what eschatology has always done, but few apocalyptic preachers have wielded the kind of power Peter Thiel does, and he doesn’t seem to view many of us outside his circle as worthy of salvation.

Additional reporting by Tina Nguyen

Tech.title: Over $963,000 worth of graded Pokémon and sports cards were stolen from FedEx
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

Last week over 200 packages of graded trading cards being shipped back to their owners were stolen from a FedEx truck parked outside the headquarters of Professional Sports Authenticator (PSA) in Santa Ana, California, according to a report by The Athletic. PSA is one of the largest third-party sports and hobby card grading companies in the world and it reported to the Santa Ana Police Department that the majority of the stolen packages had an approximate value of over $963,000, but that amount could further increase as PSA continues the process of confirming exactly which cards included in the shipment were taken.

In a statement shared to its website, Collectors Holdings, the parent company of PSA, acknowledged the theft and that it’s working closely with local law enforcement and FedEx as the investigation continues. In response to the incident the company says it has “notified marketplace partners so they can be on the lookout for rare and serialized items” to help prevent the stolen cards from being resold. All cards graded by PSA are assigned a unique certification number that the company has since deactivated for all the cards that have so far been identified as stolen.

Collectors Holdings also says it has contacted affected customers to arrange compensation based on the fair market value of their missing collectibles, but “up to the maximum insured value for each item selected by the customer prior to grading,” according to the report.

In a video posted over the weekend, YouTuber Sky-B Cards identified themselves as one of the victims of the theft and shared the response they were sent by PSA. They had paid $8,468 to have 104 collectible sports cards graded by the company, many of which are irreplaceable, and had opted to insure the order for up to $156,000. It is not yet known what compensation they have received. Other collectors affected by the incident have started to reach out to another YouTuber, Boston Card Hunter, who is working to compile a shared list of serialized cards that were stolen including detailed descriptions of each one in hopes it can help other collectors identify them.

Tech.title: Spotify pulled 50 million AI slop and spam tracks from its recommendations
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Spotify says it has removed more than 50 million songs considered AI-generated slop or spam from user recommendations over the past year. That’s according to an announcement on Tuesday that says Spotify has also made changes to its recommendation system to highlight more music made by human artists.

“Our editors hold the same standard and don’t program content identified as slop or spam,” Spotify says. “Since we made these changes, we’ve seen a marked decrease in listener concerns about this content showing up in recommendations.”

Spotify says it uses a combination of listener engagement and feedback, upload patterns, metadata, and third-party AI detection tools to determine whether a track may be AI-generated slop. Last year, the company said it took down more than 75 million songs identified as spam. It’s also partnering with Universal Music Group and the independent music publisher Believe to launch a tool for creating AI music remixes.

Tech.title: Eric Schmidt reportedly owns about half as much of Anthropic as CEO Dario Amodei
Tech.content:
In Brief

Eric Schmidt’s fortune is about to get even bigger. The former Google CEO is reported to own about 1% of Anthropic after investing tens of millions of dollars in the leading AI lab’s Series A round in 2021, according to Bloomberg. The startup was valued at $461 million at the time, according to PitchBook data.

If Bloomberg’s estimate is accurate, Schmidt’s stake is remarkably large compared with the 2% of the company that co-founder and CEO Dario Amodei holds. Anthropic is widely expected to go public before the end of the year, with top-end market estimates valuing the company at as much as $2 trillion. At that valuation, Schmidt would add as much as $20 billion to his net worth, which Bloomberg currently puts at $57.5 billion.

Schmidt has been an active tech investor since stepping down as Google CEO in 2011. He deploys capital through multiple entities, including Tomorrow Ventures, Innovation Endeavors Management, and his family office, Hillspire. His other AI bets include Mistral, General Intuition, and Reflection AI.

Schmidt and Anthropic didn’t immediately respond to our request for comment.

Tech.title: Meta’s Muse hits 10M U.S. downloads in 40 days, a milestone reached by only 11 other apps
Tech.content:
Meta’s AI companion, Muse, is now one of only a dozen mobile apps to have reached 10 million U.S. downloads in its first 40 days on the market. According to new data from market intelligence provider Sensor Tower, Muse has seen 10.9 million downloads since its September debut, 10.2 million of which were in the United States.

Only 11 other apps to date have reached this type of post-launch milestone, said Sensor Tower’s Senior Insights Analyst Kara Lee. The most recent of these was Meta’s Threads, back in July 2023.

Other apps that saw this kind of scale were largely mobile games, Lee noted, like Fortnite, PUBG Mobile, Pokémon GO, and others. Besides Threads, Disney+ was the only other non-game app to make it into the exclusive club.

Meta’s success is tied to the company’s ability to scale its new apps by marketing them across its other services, which it has done with both Threads and Muse. Threads was built on top of Instagram’s social graph, and its content has been integrated into both Facebook and Instagram. However, Muse isn’t only benefiting from Meta’s ability to market the AI agent across its family of apps, which today includes 3.6 billion daily active users; the company is also heavily investing in advertising to drive new users to Muse.

Per Sensor Tower’s data, Meta has allocated 39% of its total advertising spend to market Muse in October, up from 23% last month. In addition, Muse now ranks as the 21st largest brand in the U.S. by advertising impressions this month, up from 73rd in September.

Still, marketing an app and retaining users after the initial shine wears off are two different things. In this case, Muse is seeing better retention rates than its AI competitors like ChatGPT, Claude, and Grok.

In the U.S., the app had a 30% retention rate after 7 days and a 23% retention rate after 14 days. By comparison, its rivals saw an average of a 19% 7-day retention rate and a 16% 14-day retention rate, according to the firm’s data.

Muse also hit another milestone that demonstrates active engagement with the AI app. Its daily active users reached 2.5 million for the first time on October 16, a 15% week-over-week increase.

Meta’s latest AI app, which can handle various tasks on users’ behalf, has seen breakout success since its debut. It shot up to No. 1 on the App Store, and, at one point, even outpaced some of the metrics ChatGPT saw following its launch. Its latest milestone sees it topping its rivals again, as ChatGPT saw 3.7 million U.S. downloads in its first 40 days on the market. Grok and Claude saw only 500,000 and 200,000 U.S. downloads, respectively, in their first 40 days.

Globally, ChatGPT beat out Muse, having scaled to around 15 million global downloads in its first 40 days. But this isn’t a fair comparison, as ChatGPT benefited from a wider reach. Muse is only available in the U.S. and Canada for now, while ChatGPT’s app attracted attention from markets like Japan, Brazil, and Germany, too. (Japan, for instance, accounted for 25% of its global installs during its first 40 days.)

Since launching, Muse has retained its No. 1 rank on the U.S. App Store for all days except October 19, when streaming app Kick briefly beat it out. It has since reclaimed the top spot as of Tuesday. Muse has also been No. 1 on Google Play over the past 30 days.

Tech.title: Ex-Nvidia-turned-VC Amulya Vishwanath: ‘Physical AI is in it’s LEGO era’
Tech.content:
It’s the moment everyone is waiting for — the ChatGPT moment for robotics, Amulya Vishwanath explained to TechCrunch’s Equity.

She is the founder and managing partner of Techable Ventures, a VC firm focused on physical AI, which she started after spending nearly seven years as a product marketer at Nvidia.
