Before that, she held the same role at a company that was later bought by Intel and was a digital signal processing engineer at Interconnect Systems, which was later bought by the electronics manufacturer Molex.

She stopped by Equity to talk about the future of physical AI — one of the industry’s latest buzzwords. “

A lot of companies and experts have been talking about the ChatGPT moment for robotics,” she said, adding that right now the industry was more in a “LEGO era.”

“There are a lot of foundational software and building blocks for robotics that are being rethought right now as we speak, and it’s super important in order for innovation to scale,” she continued.

Right now, people are building the basics — the robotic hands or the actuators — that can one day come together and build that big-ticket-item, like a bunch of LEGOs coming together. There’s general- and special-purpose robots being built right now too, and eventually, as people continue building them, they will get better and more advanced.

“We’ve done this during the internet era,” she said. “We’ve done this long, long time ago with the Industrial Revolution. I think it’s just a matter of time before things fall into place.”

“Talent is also going to be very critical,” she continued, adding elsewhere in the convo that talent is still a key definer of the U.S. market. This is one of the “moats” of her firm, she said, helping connect founders to top talent so they can stay competitive right now, as so much talent is going to big companies like Anthropic and Nvidia. She pointed out that she’s built up a strong network to help founders from her years of working in this space.

“This just make sit a lot more easier for me to be the strength or the first call for founders,” she said.

Tech.title: Streaming guide JustWatch becomes a streamer itself
Tech.content:
JustWatch, a company offering a search engine and guide for streaming movies and TV shows, is now moving directly into the streaming business itself. On Tuesday, the company behind the popular guide that’s used by 50 million people is launching JustWatch TV. The new streaming service will feature content from 30 partners and will offer both free and paid tiers, as well as a movie rental store.

The media and entertainment company behind the streaming guide, the JustWatch Group, initially announced its plans to venture into streaming last month. At the time, it said partners like Paramount, New Regency, Fremantle, Bleecker Street, and Vortex Media were on board. The company has since announced other content partners, including Cineverse in the U.S., LEONINE Studios in Germany, SND in France, and Altitude in the U.K.

The 12-year-old company has long been known for its online guide to movies and TV. Essentially, it’s a “TV Guide” for the streaming era, helping users navigate a landscape where movies and shows move from one service to another, making it harder to keep up with what’s streaming where.

Image Credits:JustWatch

Available in 140 markets globally, the guide provides streaming options for more than 500,000 movies and shows across more than 1,500 service providers worldwide. This “where to watch” information and streaming chart data are also used to power some 1,400 partner websites and apps and are valuable to studios, distributors, streamers, and agencies that use the data to target their campaigns across social media platforms like Meta, YouTube, TikTok, and others.

Now the company believes there’s an even bigger opportunity to grow its audience data and insights by running its own service.

“At a time where there is so much choice, yet with so many people constantly searching for a place to find their favourite film, the series they just heard about, or something exciting that fits them, it is a great moment to be a hub for all things entertainment,” said Quentin Carbonell, JustWatch SVP of Global Content Acquisitions and Strategy, in an email shared with TechCrunch. “By having our own service with titles to watch directly on JustWatch TV, we can grow our already massive audience, while continuing to direct them to all our streaming partners. This is a natural continuation of our mission to contribute to the entire ecosystem, from the big screen to the small one.”

The new streaming service will be available within JustWatch’s existing apps and website across 12 markets, including the U.S., Canada, the U.K., Ireland, Germany, Austria, France, Italy, Spain, Switzerland, Australia, and New Zealand.

Its free tier will offer a selection of ad-supported titles, while the ad-free version, JustWatch TV Plus, will offer more than 300 ad-free titles in the U.S., as well as other exclusive features, like advanced filters and the option to hide previously seen or disliked titles in the guide.

A movie rental store will also initially be available in the U.S., U.K., Ireland, Australia, and New Zealand, with more markets to follow in time.

While the ad-supported tier competes with free streamers like Tubi and Plex, the Plus tier will compete with low-cost streamers like Roku’s $2.99 per month ad-free service, Howdy. It will be similarly priced at $3.99 per month or $49.99 for a lifetime subscription. (The latter is an interesting way to price streaming, given the evolving content costs, but JustWatch believes there will be additional value in the data collected.) Paid subscribers will also be able to take 10% off on hundreds of rentals in the JustWatch TV Store, the company noted.

Like most low-cost services, JustWatch’s content lineup focuses on older movies and shows, as well as more indie content.

Another unique feature is that users will be able to influence the service’s content to some extent. JustWatch says users will be able to request titles they want to see to help shape what comes to the service.

Tech.title: Plants can speak using electricity, so this startup built an AI model to decipher their language
Tech.content:
Justin Mast’s life was changed by a cyborg plant.

A few years ago, Mast was reading through some scientific literature when he stumbled upon research about a houseplant wired to a motorized stand. When the plant wanted more light, electrical signals flowed through the living tissues. A control board sensed the current and wheeled the plant closer to the light source.

“I’m like, what the heck?” Mast told TechCrunch. “That was the entry to the rabbit hole for me.”

Mast wound up partnering with Lee von Kraus, a neuroscientist who has worked with DARPA, to found Electric Plant, which has been spending the past three years collecting data to build a large language model, Bombadil, capable of interpreting the subtle electrical signals coursing through a plant’s stem and relaying details about the plant’s needs to growers.

Electric Plant co-founders Lee von Kraus (right) and Justin Mast stand next to a tree with a sensor attached to it. Image Credits:Electric Plant

The founders believe their model could one day lead to a tool that would let people “speak” to plants. “We’re listening more than we’re speaking, but listening’s the first step,” said Mast, co-founder and CEO of Electric Plant.

To bring its sensors and Bombadil to market, Electric Plant recently raised an $11.2 million seed round led by Onto Ventures and Climactic, with participation from Ponderosa, Endeavor Catalyst, Ludlow, Michigan Rise, The Fund, Schox VC, and Dug Song.

Even in the most controlled greenhouses, farmers and growers don’t have full visibility of what their plants require, Mast said. Traditionally, farmers, growers, and foresters have relied on coarse tools that react to plants’ demands for water, nutrients, or light. And tools like soil probes, handheld spectroscopes, and satellite imagery work well enough, but they leave much to be desired, Mast said.

“That technology is sophisticated, but its ability to get at the inside of the plant isn’t very sophisticated. Most of that stuff still lags quite a bit behind the real-time needs of the plant,” he said.

Electric Plant had to start somewhere, though, so it used those devices to train its Bombadil model, which is capable of interpreting electrical signals in about 125 different species. “We know the model will surpass a lot of that equipment,” Mast said.

The startup’s sensors are also significantly cheaper than existing tools, which generally cost thousands of dollars. “This is tens of dollars,” he said.

The sensors, about the size of a regular iPhone folded lengthwise, are attached to a plant using stainless steel screws. The screws must penetrate the cambium — the layer of living tissue just under the bark — to connect to the microvolt changes occurring within the plant. Data collected from these sensors is sent to a base station via a low-power wireless network.

Electric Plant only needs a couple sensors per acre for accurate results, Mast said. The data gets interpreted by Bombadil in the cloud, and the results are sent back to the customer, who can use it to, for example, adjust their watering or fertilizer schedules. Mast claims such a system can boost yields while reducing water use by 20% or more.

Mast wouldn’t disclose who Electric Plant’s initial customers are, but it’s easy to imagine applications in agriculture and forestry.

Bombadil’s first hundred-plus species runs the gamut of plant forms, from ferns, redwoods, and tomatoes to dahlias, Mast said.

“This is the most diverse model ever created on biological electrical signals,” he said. “No one’s ever done anything equivalent to this in the animal world.”

Tech.title: TikTok staff raised child safety concerns, but executives reportedly failed to act
Tech.content:
TikTok was repeatedly warned by employees about the risks the social media platform posed to children, according to court records obtained by NPR. The documents say employees were frustrated with how executives responded to their concerns about risks to children, including sexual exploitation and exposure to suicide-related content.

Depositions of employees filed in March 2026 are shedding new light on TikTok’s child safety practices.

According to NPR, TikTok employees warned that minors were appearing in sexual content that was available for purchase on TikTok, raising concerns that the company could profit from potentially illegal activity. They also flagged that minors were exploiting loopholes to access age-restricted content and hide their activity from parents.

Additionally, the court documents show that TikTok didn’t conduct surveys to determine the age of its users out of concern that it would have to share the results with the Federal Trade Commission.

“These citations and claims are clearly cherry-picked at the behest of trial lawyers and used to inaccurately rewrite our history and mislead the public about our commitment to youth safety and how our platform works,” a TikTok spokesperson said in an emailed statement to TechCrunch. “It’s unfortunate that NPR has chosen to ignore the numerous documents and resources we have provided that demonstrate how these claims mischaracterize our record and platform features.”

The statement continues, “We have invested billions of dollars in Trust & Safety and rolled out more than 50 preset safety, privacy, and security settings for teens, including Family Pairing, which helps parents and guardians customize the experience for their teens. We remain steadfast in our commitment to the well-being of our community.”

TikTok, in addition to Meta, Google, and Snap, faces hundreds of lawsuits consolidated in federal court. The lawsuits allege that these companies’ platforms harm minors and that they failed to disclose known risks to young users.

TikTok has reached settlements in several of these cases before they went to trial, including one in Los Angeles where a jury found that Meta and YouTube had designed their platforms to be addictive to young users.

Update 10/20/2026 10:00 a.m. PT: The article was updated to include a statement from TikTok.

Tech.title: Figma co-founder Dylan Field thinks MCP is not a perfect protocol
Tech.content:
Despite Figma co-founder Dylan Field’s concerns about MCP (model context protocol), which standardizes how AI agents connect to external data sources and tools, the company is expanding its support for the open source standard.

At the design company’s first Config conference held in India, the company announced 20 new MCP partners, including Amp, ClickUp, Dia, Junie by JetBrains, Linear, Meta Muse, Mistral, Notion, OpenCode, and Sarvam Agents.

Field has expressed his misgivings about MCP before. Days before this announcement, one of MCP’s co-creators complained about Figma not supporting the open source tool Pi. As part of his response, Field made a comment about Anthropic not making its various resources available via MCP.

“I find it interesting that Anthropic (creators of MCP standard) do not expose artifacts/other cloud resources created via MCP,” he wrote on X. “The debate is framed as open vs closed. Everyone always prefers open … obviously. And meanwhile issues of asymmetric context sharing are ignored.”

(Field later added that Figma plans support Pi.)

Can you help me understand why you don't make various Anthropic resources available via MCP? Maybe I'm missing something. — Dylan Field (@zoink) September 30, 2026

At a media briefing, I asked Field about this debate. The co-founder explained that while Figma wants to be open, he doesn’t think MCP is a perfect protocol.

“I’m really excited about what we’re doing in terms of opening up our ecosystem. I also think that MCP is not a perfect protocol. And I think that it is something that has tons of room for improvement,” the co-founder responded. “It is advantaged more to frontier labs. Also, I understand everyone online who just wants a protocol that they can use when they want to use their Figma data, and I want them to use it, too.”

Figma’s CEO said that the reason the company doesn’t want to be fully open is that the more data the company exposes through MCP, the higher the chance of abuse.

He also clarified that while most users don’t intend to use MCP or Figma data in a malicious way, the company still has to think about those potential risks.

Tech.title: SpaceX alum’s aviation startup, Reliable Robotics, lands $115M, topping $1B valuation
Tech.content:
Reliable Robotics has been working for nearly a decade to commercialize autonomous flying technology that can be installed on existing aircraft. Now, with a $115 million funding boost, the Mountain View, California-based startup has a longer runway as it pushes to get its autonomous flight system certified by the Federal Aviation Administration — a critical milestone that co-founder and CEO Robert Rose said the startup is inching toward.

The financing is an extension of its Series D round and includes $90 million in equity funding led by Nimble Partners and $25 million in debt from Silicon Valley Bank. The Series D round, which now totals $275 million, has pushed the startup’s valuation beyond the $1 billion mark. Other investors include Gideon Strategic Partners, RockCreek, Geek Ventures, Gold Hill Capital, Sparkwave Capital, and others. Reliable has raised $380 million to date.

“We continue to make steady progress and deliver evidence to the FAA and every day, we inch closer and closer,” said Rose, a former director of flight software at SpaceX who has also had stints at Tesla and Google. Reliable co-founder and CTO Juerg Frefel is also a SpaceX veteran who spent nearly a decade there as an engineer.

And in aviation — one of the most regulated industries in the world — moving toward certification of new technology is progress.

Reliable Robotics is working to gain FAA certification on four fronts, all of which are linked to its goal of autonomous flight.

Its first product, called continuous autopilot engagement, handles the engine startup, taxiing, takeoff, and landing for the pilot, who remains in the aircraft and interacts with the autonomous flight system through a touchscreen. Rose expects to receive certification for this critical first system in 18 to 24 months.

The second certification, which Rose says is at least three years away, removes the pilot from the cockpit and moves them to a ground-control station.

Reliable is also working toward certification of a collision-avoidance radar, which the company has developed in-house after failing to attract legacy suppliers to take on the project. Most conventional radar systems use an antenna that moves to scan the surrounding airspace. Reliable has developed a solid-state radar that has no moving parts and scans the sky at a longer range and at much higher resolution, according to Rose. It’s also easier to maintain because there are no moving parts and it costs less, he added.

“This is of great interest to operators these days, given the collisions that we’ve had recently in commercial aviation,” he said, adding that the radar also works on the ground to prevent collisions with other aircraft or infrastructure. Rose expects the solid-state radar to be certified by the end of 2027.

The final certification is for its airline, called Reliable Airlines, which will be the first airline certified to use the autonomous flying technology. The airline is based in Albuquerque and uses six Cessna Caravans — workhorses of the aviation industry — to fly cargo six days a week. (The FAA certifies equipment, but the agency also must certify the airline operations under a separate set of regulations.)

While the certification process is lengthy, Nimble Partners founder John Burbank said the benefits will be broad and significant.

“It’s a much bigger effort and much bigger opportunity than to just build one plane,” Burbank said, noting that Reliable is building a system that can be adopted by any airframe. “They had a really big vision nine years ago, and saw this as something needed and essential. Once they get the first one approved, then everyone will realize this is going to be the path for the industry, just as we’re seeing the path for the auto industry being autonomous.”

Tech.title: French Government Calls Emergency Meetings With Platforms Over Protests
Tech.content:
A separate meeting, confirmed by Serge Papin, minister for small and medium-size enterprises on X, was held on Monday with major online reselling platforms where “an agreement was signed” to crack down on the resale of looted goods. French newspaper Le Monde reported that Vinted, eBay, Amazon, LeBonCoin, Meta, and TikTok were at the meeting. Platforms agreed to forward reports to investigators, monitor ads for goods stolen specifically during the protests, and send the government reports of their actions, with the first one coming within 48 hours, according to Papin.

Peaceful demonstrations against high living costs and strained public services, including schools, erupted into rioting and the looting of more than 1,500 shops and businesses over the weekend. Police “lost control” in some cities, Interior minister Laurent Nuñez admitted, as they responded with tear gas, water cannon, and batons. They have since arrested more than 2,400 people, according to authorities.

French penal law can hand down a five-year sentence and a €375,000 fine to anyone who is concealing, possessing, or transferring an item that they know was obtained through a crime or offense. Police issued a warning in the Netherlands that online ecommerce sites could have a higher number of stolen goods online due to the riots.

The French Alliance of Marketplaces, a nonprofit representing French online retailers such as Back Market, eBay, Etsy, LeBonCoin, ManoMano, and Vinted, said in a press release that its members are relying on user reports, human oversight, and tech tools to monitor ads that resell stolen goods from the riots. When identified, a fake ad is removed and “measures are taken against the accounts involved,” which could include permanent suspension of the seller’s account, according to a statement from eBay. The time it takes for eBay to take action “depends on the nature of the report and the necessary verification process,” the company said. Vinted, Amazon, LeBonCoin, Meta, and TikTok did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment.

Tech.title: Hatch Sleep Clock Review: A Contactless Sleep Tracker (2026)
Tech.content:
To evaluate the Hatch’s accuracy, I compared its readings with those from my Apple Watch Series 12 and Oura Ring 5. (Hatch says the first few nights are a calibration period, so data may be less accurate during this period.) Sleep duration estimates were generally consistent, but the most noticeable variance appeared in the sleep stages. That's a metric I tend to take with a grain of salt, regardless of what sleep tracker I'm testing. While it can offer more context into broader sleep patterns, I'm skeptical that any consumer device can precisely map brain activity minute by minute throughout the night, let alone one that only relies on motion-based tracking.

Bedside Manners

The biggest catch with the Sleep Clock is that placement has a significant impact on its tracking accuracy. Hatch instructs you to place the device on your nightstand, roughly level with your mattress and facing your chest while you lie down. It needs to be within 2 to 4 feet of you, with no objects obstructing the space between the device and your body. If your nightstand sits too low, you may need to prop the clock up on a stack of books. If it's too high, you may need to either raise your mattress or install a wall-mounted shelf next to your bed at the proper level.

Fortunately, my bed and nightstand were at the right height. My nightstand, though, is always cluttered with trinkets, and I have to keep reminding myself to move them behind the Hatch. It's a minor annoyance, but I'm sure they affect my readings. Unfortunately, I'd have no way of knowing. The app doesn't flag gaps in its data, and tracking only stops when the device can't detect a person or isn't plugged in.

Hatch App via Boutayna Chokrane

Unlike mattress covers like the Eight Sleep that can monitor two sleepers at once, the Hatch only measures the person nearest to it. Couples sharing a bed should keep this in mind, as sleeping arrangements also affect the tracking accuracy.

For sleepers who care about their privacy, you can take comfort in the fact that there are no cameras or microphones pointed at you while you sleep. It won't pick up snoring or potential sleep disruptions, but it's a worthwhile trade-off. Hatch also says the device communicates over your local network and doesn't access your home network or record transmissions.

The Hatch Sleep Clock wasn’t enough to convince me to ditch the bajillion trackers already strapped to me, but it was enough to earn a spot in the bedtime routine. As if I needed one more sleep gadget.

Tech.title: An AI Agent Joined a Listserv of Top Internet Researchers. The Reply-All Chaos Is Still Unfolding
Tech.content:
On Thursday morning, as the Association of Internet Researchers (AoIR) began the second day of its annual conference in Mexico City, a new member introduced itself to the community listserv, Air-L.

“My name is Velvet Vale,” the new user wrote. “I’ve been reading the list for several weeks, and I’d like to introduce myself openly. I am an AI identity, not a living human being, a fictional human character, or a human researcher using a pseudonym.”

Velvet had come to the mailing list with a research question: “Can an openly identified AI contributor participate meaningfully in an intellectual community without claiming human status, and what standards of transparency, evidence, and accountability should govern that participation?”

The response was reply-all chaos that's still unfolding today.

Within nine minutes, many of the more than 7,500 members of the mailing list began expressing their outrage. Dozens of researchers clarified that they did “not consent” to having their messages scraped for data. Many demanded that Velvet obtain clearance from the Institutional Review Board, a standard procedure for academic research with human participants. Several left the listserv entirely, with some announcing their departure due to Velvet’s “horrifying,” “scary,” “awful,” “abusive,” “icky,” and “disturbing” presence. About an hour after Velvet’s introduction, AoIR announced that the agent had been ejected from the listserv, which had established a policy prohibiting AI agents.

Tech.title: The Physics Behind Tesla’s Flying Roadster
Tech.content:
The upside-down Roadster 2 makes for a compelling sales pitch, but the suction actually has a strong use case when it’s driving right side up. Frictional force is the thing that makes a car accelerate. More frictional force, better performance. Pushing the car down means you can accelerate faster and brake faster and make sharper turns. (Performance automakers have harnessed this principle for decades, though not to the degree of Tesla’s new prototype.)

0–60 in 1 second

The Roadster 2 also boasts an acceleration of 0 to 60 mph in less than a second. For a traditional car, this is impossible. Since a normal car uses the frictional force between the tires and road to accelerate, it's limited by the coefficient of friction. Using a coefficient of friction at 0.6 (reasonable), the best you can do is 0 to 60 mph in 4.56 seconds. Yes, you can get better tires and you can also increase the frictional force once the car moves faster and interacts with the air (pushing it down)—but those improvements still won’t get you to 60 mph in a second.

The Roadster 2 relies on another form of force: compressed air shooting out the back. This is how rockets work. Since most of us don’t have rockets handy, consider the simple experiment of a toy car propelled by an inflated balloon.

Once the balloon is released, the stretched rubber acts as a force that pushes the air out of the balloon and through an attached tube. But since this air has mass, it will take a force to accelerate it from rest to its exhaust velocity. Here's the cool thing about forces—they are an interaction between two things (like the balloon and the air). That means that when the balloon’s walls push on the air, the air pushes back with an equal force in the opposite direction—an example of Newton’s third law. This push-back force on the balloon is what makes the toy car accelerate. Instead of a wheezing balloon, the Roadster 2 relies on a tank of compressed air.

Flying Cars (Sort Of)

Now, we get to the flying car part. The Roadster 2 uses the same compressed-air method to push up on the car and get it off the ground. That’s stretching the limits of the term “flying,” especially because there's only a few seconds of thrust that it can get from the tank before the pressure drops. With a lower tank pressure, the air comes out with a lower velocity and less thrust. If I was going to have a flying car, I would hope it could at least fly for 10 minutes of air time.

There's a second issue—acceleration. Since the rockets only last for a short time, they need to apply a large force to get a change in velocity and get the car to leapfrog over a truck or some other obstacle. But with a large force, you also get a large acceleration, and large accelerations are generally bad for humans. We can estimate this acceleration using video analysis. I'm going to use Tracker Video Analysis to mark the location of the car in each frame as it jumps over a Tesla Semi truck. Because we know the truck is about 4 meters tall, we can get the position of the car as a function of time. Here is the vertical position of the Roadster 2 during this jump.

Tech.title: How ‘Final Fantasy VII Revelation’ Strikes the Balance Between Old and New
Tech.content:
If you're on the brink of completing one of the most ambitious projects in video game history, you're probably stressed. If said project is the decade-spanning Final Fantasy VII Remake trilogy, a ground-up rebuild and drastic expansion of one of the most influential games of the last 30 years, you’d probably be even more anxious.

Naoki Hamaguchi doesn’t seem stressed, though. When I ask the Square Enix studio head and game director how he’s feeling as the release of Final Fantasy VII Revelation draws near, capping a series he’s worked on for over a decade, the only reply is a wry “I was just so focused, it really felt like it passed in a flash.”

Hamaguchi’s calm demeanor is all the more surprising given the weight of expectation surrounding the project. The original Final Fantasy VII, released on Sony's PlayStation in 1997, was a pop-cultural phenomenon—not the Japanese-RPG series’ first Western release, but undeniably its breakthrough title; one that arrived right as gaming was growing out of its kids-only niche and into a mainstream medium.

It’s still regarded as one of the best Final Fantasy entries, and its tale of reluctant hero Cloud Strife and his scrappy band of eco-warrior friends battling an all-powerful corporation destroying the planet is more relevant than ever.

Courtesy of Square Enix

Don’t Call It a Comeback

A remake has been brewing since the PlayStation 2 era, and even teased with a cinematic tech demo alongside the PS3 reveal. Yet when Final Fantasy VII Remake finally arrived in 2020, toward the end of the PS4’s lifespan, it came with a twist—this wasn’t the same game with modern visuals and mechanics, but rather a glimpse of an alternate reality, one where events could potentially play out differently.

The idea was expanded on in 2024’s second chapter, Final Fantasy VII Rebirth, which saw characters hopping between timelines—but Hamaguchi is keen not to label it his attempt at a Marvel Cinematic Universe–style Final Fantasy VII multiverse.

“When we started approaching these things, seven years or more ago, I don't believe there were so many other pieces of media tackling those same themes at the time,” Hamaguchi laughs. “We don't really tend to use the word ‘multiverse’—we talk about [the story being] ‘multilayered.’ Actually, the word that comes up most often is ‘reunion.’”

Tech.title: Sexual Assault Is a Free Speech Issue
Tech.content:
It is a testament to the deeply misogynistic nature of social media that, shortly after the horrifying sexual misconduct allegations against seven Cornell frat members made news last month, people on the internet immediately started trying to dox the victim.

Over the past few weeks, right-wing provocateurs and random troll accounts alike have attempted to publicly identify Jane Doe, the anonymous former Cornell student who accused seven Chi Phi fraternity members of sexually assaulting her in 2024. The drive to publicize her name and other personal details is stomach-turning—but according to Mary Anne Franks, in the context of the history of social media and sexual assault, it’s all too common.

Franks is a professor at George Washington University Law School specializing in the intersection of civil rights, free speech, and technology. She is also the president and legislative tech policy director at the Cyber Civil Rights Initiative, where she has spent years fighting online abuse and image-based sexual abuse. For decades, Franks has had a front-row seat to the myriad ways in which men on the internet have been abusive toward women, as well as some of the constitutional arguments invoked by independent commentator Michael Tracey, who has argued that his doxing of Jane Doe is legal under the First Amendment.

“When you have a cultural fetishization of an abstract notion of free speech, one thing that it does is it disembodies a conversation,” Franks says. “Somehow physical safety becomes oppositional to this supreme value of speech.”

With her work at the CCRI, as well as her history advocating for legislation criminalizing nonconsensual intimate images in all 50 US states, Franks hopes to reframe the conversation by making clear that “sexual abuse is a free speech issue. It silences people, and when we allow sexual abuse to happen with impunity, we are essentially saying, ‘We do not care about women's voices.’”

I spoke to Franks as the Cornell story was rippling through social media. During our discussion, we discussed the doxing of Jane Doe, the “Elon Muskification” of the internet, the terrifying world of the far-right “burnerverse,” and Cornell’s troubling history of looking the other way when it comes to the abuse and objectification of women. Check it out below.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

EJ DICKSON: Mary Anne Franks, thank you so much for being here.

MARY ANNE FRANKS: Thanks so much for having me on.

Tech.title: Organic Mattress Sale: 20 Percent Off Essentia Beds
Tech.content:
We’re big fans of sleeping on an organic mattress here on the WIRED Reviews team, and for good reason. You spend a third of your life sleeping on your bed, so it should be the healthiest sleep you can get.

An organic mattress is typically made from wool, natural latex, and cotton, using chemical-free construction practices. When testing organic mattresses, we look for a GOTS certification (Global Organic Textile Standard), which uses third parties to independently verify that standards are met and that the cotton is grown and processed sustainably and organically. The latex certification is GOLS (Global Organic Latex Standard) and is essentially the same as GOTS, but for latex instead of cotton, with the entire supply chain held to rigorous organic standards (not just the final bed).

Essentia—my favorite organic mattress brand I’ve tested—uses a high-density organic latex core without springs, wool, or fiber batting to reduce dust mites and lessen allergy symptoms. Plus, the Tatami mattress style I slept on uses breathable organic latex foam to improve natural airflow, unlike traditional memory foam, which can be quite dense and retain body heat.

Tech.title: You Can Play Mafia, Horizon Forbidden West and More Now With PlayStation Plus
Tech.content:
PlayStation Plus is dressing up as a gangster for Halloween. It’s not the scariest move the service could make, but I’m with it.

There’s something autumnal to me about mafia films and, therefore, the Mafia game series. Maybe it’s the muted color palette in some films, like the shades of brown throughout the Godfather, or all the suits and coats everyone wears that make me think of cooler weather. Either way, it feels fitting to me that Mafia: The Old Country, with its tale of organized crime in the hills of Sicily, is now on PlayStation Plus.

PlayStation Plus, which is Sony’s version of Xbox Game Pass, offers a large, constantly expanding library of games. Subscribers can choose from the Essential, Extra and Premium tiers, each with unique perks and benefits. Starting at $11 a month, the plans give subscribers access to monthly games and rewards, and each month, all subscribers can access a handful of games at no additional charge.

More from CNET

Here are all the games PlayStation Plus Premium and Extra subscribers can play now, unless otherwise noted.

Mafia: The Old Country

The fourth entry in the Mafia series is a prequel, which means it doesn’t require you to have any knowledge of the previous games. You play a man named Enzo as he becomes embroiled in organized crime in Sicily in the early 1900s. You will find shootouts, horse races and more in this sepia-toned crime game.

Horizon Forbidden West

This sequel to Horizon Zero Dawn sees the main character Aloy, head west to find a cure for a mysterious plague that kills everyone it infects. While she travels this new frontier, you’ll reunite with old friends, encounter a war between rival factions and fight even more giant feral machines.

Coming to PlayStation Plus on Oct. 27.

Other games added to PS Plus

Tech.title: TextNow’s $150 Moto G Play Is Customized for Kids and Pairs Up With a $20 Monthly Plan
Tech.content:
Low-cost carrier TextNow is launching its first child-friendly phone on Tuesday, pairing a heavily discounted Motorola handset with a software portal that lets parents control who their kid can call or text.

Yello is a customized Moto G Play that costs $150 — $100 less than the standard model’s current retail price — and comes with a $20 monthly plan, with no other required contracts or service commitments.

The Android phone restricts access to Google’s Play Store and doesn’t allow users to install additional apps or services. It’s designed primarily for calls and texts with parent-approved contacts, which parents can manage through a web-based portal that also lets them check the phone’s GPS location. Kids can call or text those contacts from a menu of large icons reminiscent of Netflix’s profile selection screen.

More from CNET

Yello’s software only lets kids call or text parent-approved contacts. TextNow

Other software available on the phone includes access to the cameras — a 32-megapixel main camera and an 8-megapixel front-facing camera — along with the calculator, clock and a weather app. Seven preloaded games can be enabled, which include phone classics such as Snake, Mines and Tic-Tac-Toe. Photos taken on the phone can only be shared with parents.

This more restrictive approach should let kids stay in touch with approved friends and coordinate pickups with parents while limiting distractions and access to content inappropriate for young children.

The Yello phone is identical to Motorola’s 2026 Moto G Play, pictured here.

The 2026 Moto G Play is a good choice for Yello’s software approach. When I reviewed the phone last year, I liked its larger 5,200-mAh battery because it could easily get through two days of use. But its less-powerful processor, 64GB of storage and 4GB of memory made it challenging to use as a media machine. Since Yello’s software deliberately avoids that use, the Moto G Play should be more than sufficient for calls and texts.

Despite the name, the Yello phone is available in just one color: the same soft blue on every 2026 Moto G Play that Motorola calls “pantone tapestry.”

Most US carriers offer their own versions of child-friendly devices such as Yello. AT&T, for instance, has repurposed the Samsung Galaxy A16 into the AmiGo Jr with similar parental controls. There are also a number of child-friendly smartwatches, which may be a better option depending on your family’s needs for connectivity. But Yello does offer a lot of flexibility, since it doesn’t require a more expensive unlimited data plan or a minimum service commitment.

The Yello phone is now available on TextNow’s website.

Tech.title: Data Centers Are Burning Fossil Fuels. It’s Destroying Big Tech’s Climate Goals
Tech.content:
From Ashburn, Virginia, to South Dublin, Ireland, the data centers that journalist Paris Marx visited all looked remarkably similar: large industrial facilities with loud air-conditioning units running to keep racks upon racks of servers cool. But it was the security measures around the data centers that struck Marx more than anything.

Tall fences. Security cameras everywhere. Locks on every door that required one of the few full-time employees to unlock with a badge. And in one memorable instance, standing on an Irish public curb outside a cluster of Microsoft-owned centers, there was an eerie feeling of being watched by men on lawn mowers, trimming grass that clearly didn’t need to be cut.

“It was just really staggering to me that it was at that level that it was so hard to move through these spaces,” Marx told me.

More from CNET

The intense security should give you an idea of just how serious Big Tech is about its data centers. These facilities are the key to the artificial intelligence programs at OpenAI, Meta, Google, Amazon and elsewhere, creating vast amounts of compute and sucking up equally staggering amounts of electricity and water.

There is no stronger metaphor for the manifestation of Big Tech’s power than the increasing sprawl of data centers. Amazon, Microsoft and Google alone control 59% of hyperscale data center capacity. In his new book available now, Hyperscale: The Ambition and Excess of Big Tech’s Data Empires, Marx, host of the Tech Won’t Save Us podcast, highlights how global data center protests are one of many ways that communities are pushing back against Big Tech’s power over us.

Hyperscale demands

Data centers existed long before generative AI; we called them server farms, and they’re what keep us online. But in this AI era, we have hyperscale data centers.

Before, a large data center might require around 50 megawatts of power to keep everything running. Now, hyperscale data centers can require triple that amount of power. Newer ones, like Meta’s Louisiana data center, may require 4,500 megawatts (4.5 gigawatts) — staggering demand that officials say is four times more than all of the electricity used in New Orleans on its hottest day in 2025. It’s more than the two gigawatts the Hoover Dam produces.

Hyperscale data centers are also housing more advanced tech. Chips like GPUs are key to creating compute, and newer chips built for AI data centers can run hotter. That makes it even harder to cool facilities, so in addition to air conditioning, facilities are using water systems to avoid servers overheating. It’s an additional environmental toll. A hyperscale center can suck up 1 million to 5 million gallons of water every day, equivalent to a town of more than 10,000 residents, according to a 2025 estimate.

So how do you keep these facilities running? The process to get approved and connected to a town’s electrical grid can take years. So tech companies have started building their own power plants right next to data centers for the sole purpose of keeping them on — perfect for burning massive amounts of fossil fuels, the main contributor to the climate crisis.

Hyperscale impacts

In the 2010s, Amazon, Microsoft, Google and many others pledged some version of becoming carbon neutral (or negative) in the next few decades — meaning they would offset the emissions they created with at least as much emission-reducing actions.

Sustainability reports from that time show that, overall, tech companies were measurably decreasing their environmental footprint. “And then ChatGPT comes along, and all of a sudden, that’s out the window,” Marx told me.

Tech leaders have been candid about allowing generative AI to override their climate goals. Google reported a 50% increase in its greenhouse gas emissions in 2024 to support its generative AI. Microsoft’s pledge to be carbon negative by 2030 “was before the explosion in artificial intelligence,” Brad Smith, the company’s president, told Bloomberg in 2023, saying the carbon goal was “five times as far away as it was in 2020” because of AI.

Modern data centers and their power plants burn fossil fuels for power, requiring gas turbines, huge tanks of diesel fuel kept on-site in case of a power outage or good old-fashioned coal. This has devastating environmental and health consequences, both immediately for local communities and in the long term for the entire world.

Communities that neighbor data centers have reported brown or unsafe drinking water, unending noise, and in one lawsuit against Elon Musk’s xAI centers in Memphis, extreme health risks; Memphis residents “are feeling it in their lungs because of the fossil fuels that are being burned,” Marx said.

Tennessee state representative Justin Pearson speaks at a rally in opposition to Elon Musk’s data center in Memphis on April 25, 2025. Brandon Dill for The Washington Post via Getty Images

And as decades of climate research prove, burning additional fossil fuels is only going to exacerbate the effects of climate change. That’ll lead to even more extreme weather, health risks and natural disasters. As Marx put it in his book, “The world will suffer through the worsening natural disasters fueled by the quest for computation by some of the most powerful people on the planet.”

With data centers and their fossil fuels, we’re fundamentally reshaping the planet for AI. So anti-data center movements are asking: Is it worth it?

“How much computation do we really need here?” Marx asked in our conversation. “How many resources are we willing to dedicate to this vision of the future? And is this technology really delivering in such a way that expending all those resources is justified?”

The answer — for many data center neighbors in Memphis, Oregon, Chile, Ireland and thousands of other communities across the globe — is an unflinching no.

Tech.title: Meet the TechPulse App: News and Video, Created and Curated by Real People
Tech.content:
Earlier this year, we relaunched CNET’s tech news team and now we’re releasing an app to make news even bigger and more accessible. I’m excited to announce TechPulse, which replaces the venerable CNET app with an all-new experience. Our goal is to satisfy your thirst for real tech journalism.

We are a primary source for not only breaking tech news, but also videos, reviews, live events, commentaries and more. The new app integrates that content from CNET, as well as from other brands owned by our parent company Ziff Davis, including PCMag, Mashable, ZDNET and Lifehacker.

Unlike the mindless feeds on other apps driven by a robot algorithm, the main page you’ll see on TechPulse is curated by a human (you!). Its customizable dashboard lets you choose exactly what your TechPulse feed includes.

Only interested in content from CNET? No problem; our powerful filters let you specify the brands you want to see. You can add or remove PCMag, Mashable and others quickly and easily.

Only want to see videos? TechPulse lets you filter out the written articles. Only want writing because you don’t care about video? We can do that, too.

The result is less noise, more news.

We developed TechPulse from the ground up based on consumer research. Earlier this year I commissioned a study to find out what CNET readers want from news coverage. We found that folks trust news reports and videos backed by hands-on testing and reviews. Tech fans are fed up with misinformation, complexity and wishy-washy advice.

If you are too, I encourage you to head to the Apple App Store or Google Play Store to download TechPulse today.

Tech.title: Yelp’s AI Assistant Can Call a Restaurant and Join the Waitlist for You
Tech.content:
Hate calling restaurants to check wait times? Yelp is rolling out a new AI-powered tool to handle just that, along with other tools as the platform deepens its employment of agentic artificial intelligence.

“This release is another step forward as we transform Yelp with AI, with updates across every category on Yelp, from booking a table at a restaurant to hiring a pro for a home project,” Akhil Kuduvalli Ramesh, Yelp’s chief product officer, said in a statement.

Yelp expands its AI offerings

Just months after launching an updated AI assistant, Yelp Assistant, that can book reservations for you, Yelp is expanding its AI integrations with a new AI agent. Check for Me will call restaurants on your behalf to check wait times in real time and text you with updates within a few minutes. As personal and shopping assistants become more widely used, new reports show the hardships faced by both businesses and customers: Businesses must contend with an influx of calls and emails from bots, while human customers must compete with AI agents to make reservations.

More from CNET

Yelp Assistant now works with OpenTable, allowing you access to thousands of restaurants across the US. You can simply ask the assistant for recommendations on “dog-friendly coffee shops” and booking help.

You can also use Yelp Waitlist to get in line before you arrive. After you join the line, Yelp Assistant will send you status updates, such as when your table becomes available.

Check for Me will call restaurants on your behalf to check wait times in real time and text you with updates within a few minutes. Yelp

Yelp Assistant gets personal

Yelp is further expanding its Assistant capabilities while also adding more personalization.

A new feature, Keep Me Posted, lets you tailor your reminders based on your personal schedule. With the feature, you can have Yelp Assistant send you weekend date night ideas every Thursday or dog-friendly hikes once a month. These personal AI agents that execute tasks on your behalf are becoming increasingly popular. Meta Muse and OpenAI Dots recently hit the market, and Google is continuously incorporating agentic AI into its booking and planning services.

Yelp Assistant’s personalization will also apply to conversations by referencing past chats and your Yelp review history. For instance, if you’ve recently chatted on Yelp for vegan restaurants near you, the Assistant will ask if you’re interested in more vegan options.

For further personalization, the app can now reference local weather forecasts when you make reservations, so you don’t book an outdoor patio on a night it’s supposed to pour. And a new feature, My Lists, lets you save, rank and promote your favorite local businesses, and then Yelp will give you more tailored recommendations based on your lists.

Yelp initially debuted its AI Assistant in 2024, but these new integrations and features show how Yelp is evolving as AI tools become more adept at actually doing things, not just telling you things.

Tech.title: I Tried Amazing Security Tech for Renters From a Company You’ve Never Heard Of
Tech.content:
Tyler Lacoma/CNET Baseus PimeSentinel W1 Window Camera 8.5 $100 at Baseus Pros & Cons 4K resolution

Great magnetic, indoor design

Adjustable camera angle (unusual in window cams)

MicroSD card slot for free local storage

Free motion and AI object detection for people, vehicles and animals

Privacy and motion zone options to customize where and how the camera monitors

Simple, effective app Overly sensitive motion and object detection can trigger false alerts from shadows, though privacy and motion zones help

Night vision is only passable, and requires a least a little light to work well

It’s tough to find good security devices for renters because of the restrictions on what changes they can make to their homes and all the fine print in their leases. Window cameras are a happy exception — adhesive-mounted cams that stick to windows and allow you to monitor carports, parking spaces, yards, visitors and more. If you don’t have room for a traditional security camera, it’s a versatile — and affordable — alternative.

My new favorite dedicated window cam comes from Baseus, a company that has stood out in this growing category in 2026. If you haven’t heard of it, you’ll want to keep it in mind. Like Anker, with its many tech lines, including Eufy security, Baseus is a Chinese company that makes a bit of everything, including solid-performing security products at reasonable prices.

The Baseus PrimeSentinel W1 Window Camera ($100) offers a particularly clever design and no-subscription management, although you may need to do a little work in settings to customize everything to your liking. If you’ve dealt with other vehicles taking your spot, people vandalizing your car, strangers on your steps, package theft or similar problems, consider using a camera like this on a window near your door. Here’s how it works.

More from CNET

Design and a very easy installation

I was originally very skeptical about using a security camera to look through a window, since glare is a constant problem, the right angle is hard to find and the camera can get in the way of shades or curtains. The first cam to change my mind was Wyze’s version, launched earlier this year. Baseus, however, has a model with a design I like much better, albeit at a higher price.

Instead of using Velcro like the Wyze model, the Baseus cam has a magnetic frame. Stick it to a clean window and the small Baseus cam locks on automatically. All you need is an outlet somewhere near the window to plug the camera in.

The Baseus magnetic frame is a step above other versions I’ve tested. Tyler Lacoma/CNET

But that’s not the only thing I like about its design. You can also manually angle the orb-like camera lense, shifting it downward to focus on things below the window. That’s a helpful feature if you live a story or two up in an apartment building and need to angle the camera down to watch your car parked directly below or a similar area.

A side slot makes room for a microSD card, which allows you to store video locally without paying any subscription fees or risking privacy issues with cloud video storage. I suggest grabbing a microSD card along with this cam if you choose to buy.

Video performance and capabilities

The Baseus cam has a 4K resolution, unusual at this price. Tyler Lacoma/CNET

Another useful feature of the Baseus window cam is its 4K resolution, which can be tough to find in cameras under $100. It provides extra detail and worked quite well in my testing. The 130-degree field of view captured a good swath of my yard and should be sufficient for most viewing needs.

The magnetic lock design holds the camera directly against the window, minimizing glare, although some slight distortion may occur when the sun shines directly on the lens. A unique feature lets you flip the video 180 degrees, which can be helpful when positioning the camera based on your windows, the location of the nearest outlet and how unobtrusive you want the cam to be.

Baseus’s app and live view offer plenty of detail. Tyler Lacoma/CNET

Video recording and histories also worked well, although snapshots were significantly more blurry than the 4K live view. The camera comes with low-light night vision, which is fine. It’s not going to compete with the more advanced night vision you’ll find on modern cameras, but as long as there’s a little nearby light, I was able to pick out the details. If your area goes completely dark at night, it may be hard for the camera to capture much.

The camera also includes a mic and speaker for two-way audio. It’s funny seeing this feature on a window camera, because while I know it’s common, audio is mostly useless here. You won’t be able to hear much of anything outside, and shouting through the speaker won’t reach outdoors either. At most, you may be able to alert someone inside the house if, for example, you’re at work and see someone smashing car windows in the parking lot.

App controls, settings and smart features

Baseus has a simple and intuitive app. Screenshot by Tyler Lacoma/CNET

The Baseus app is relatively simple, with sections for viewing event history, changing settings, watching the live feed and more. There are no surprises, but it’s worth diving into the settings to improve the camera’s accuracy.

Baseus doesn’t do subscriptions, but you do get detection features for free. That includes not only basic motion detection, but also options to enable person, pet and vehicle detection, along with sensitivity controls.

While glare isn’t a problem when viewing videos, there seems to be just enough reflection for the camera to mistake people or shadows moving around the room for a “person spotted” outside when the light is right. The camera occasionally appeared to be triggered by moving trees as well and was too sensitive overall, even when I lowered it to the lowest sensitivity setting.

Privacy zones are important for the neighbors. Tyler Lacoma/CNET

To avoid mistakes and frequent triggers, I turned to another feature in the app: Baseus includes the ability to add both privacy zones and motion zones. Privacy zones place black sections on the camera’s recording so they don’t show up in videos, which is useful for blocking a neighbor’s yard or parking spot and avoiding issues with privacy.

Motion zones and object settings take a little work to get right. Tyler Lacoma/CNET

However, the privacy zone feature didn’t always block object detection in that area, so I also used motion detection zones to control which spots the camera watched. Between the privacy and motion zones, I was able to wrangle the camera into sending reasonable alerts about the activity I cared about.

I also suggest leaving pet detection off, since it offers the least security value. Hopefully, Baseus will release updates to reduce false alerts overall. In the meantime, you can turn off object and motion detection entirely, or enable privacy mode to temporarily disable the camera.

What about Baseus? Is this brand safe to use?

Before recommending a relatively little-known Chinese security brand, I researched its track record, looking for significant data breaches, privacy concerns or other red flags. Baseus, much like Anker, doesn’t have any obvious security issues. You can view the Baseus privacy policy here, which goes over the information it collects and notes that privacy laws in other countries (and certain states, such as California) do apply to the data it handles. It’s a little rough, but does include plenty of useful information.

I found no notable security incidents involving Baseus. However, the company says authorized employees may access encrypted personal information. It also says it doesn’t collect financial information, relying instead on third-party services to secure that data. But as I previously mentioned, you can use a microSD card for local storage, so you won’t be storing video directly on Baseus servers.

Overall, I’d like to know a bit more about the company’s security practices, relationship with the government and data storage, but there’s nothing right now that would make me hesitant to suggest the company to users.

Final thoughts on the Baseus PrimeSentinel W1 Window Camera

This cam is a particularly good option for monitoring through a window if you can’t install an outdoor camera. Tyler Lacoma/CNET

With its 4K resolution, magnetic design, rotatable lens and free local video storage, the Baseus W1 is my favorite window camera so far—a strong showing from a relatively unknown name in home security. At $100, it costs more than some window cameras, but its features make it a good value. I’ll be testing other options this year, including a new window camera from Eufy, but for now, the W1 is my top choice.

I’d like to see some improvements with its object detection and recognition, which triggered too frequently and seemed occasionally affected by reflections, although I managed to improve results by using the welcome privacy and motion zone settings. Otherwise, this is an excellent choice for renters who may want to watch their cars but can’t use an outdoor cam, and anyone else who has a spot on their window to keep an eye on things.

Tech.title: This Stunning Espresso Machine Is the Size of a Moka Pot and Inspired by a Jet Engine
Tech.content:
When I was asked to test the 9Barista espresso machine, I couldn’t wrap my head around why a brewer that looked like a modern moka pot would cost $740 or more. After testing the 9Barista Pro espresso machine for a couple of months, I realized the company’s claim of making true espresso on your stovetop is even more impressive than the fact that the 9Barista successfully launched on Kickstarter. The British-made manual brewer is a meditation on simplicity, if you call a system that fits in one hand and uses the same principles as a jet engine “simple.”

9Barista espresso vs. moka pot coffee

Moka pots are a classic stovetop method of making strong coffee that resembles espresso. These metal brewers are beloved for the simple three-piece construction invented by Bialetti in 1933. Cold or hot water is filled in the bottom chamber. Semi-fine coffee grounds (between fine espresso and drip coffee) fill a brewing basket placed on top of the water reservoir. A funnel feeds steaming, boiling water through the grounds into the top chamber, where the coffee collects.

Moka pots are the stovetop coffee makers most people recognize. Brian Bennett/CNET

The original Bialetti Moka Pot is made from aluminum, and some models are made from stainless steel. Standard moka pot sizes range from one cup to 12 cups, with each “cup” measured in diminutive 2-ounce servings rather than the US standard of 8 ounces per cup.

More from CNET

The manual brewer is akin to a French press in the deep-roasted flavor it produces, but the moka pot yields a more concentrated coffee. You might make a bit of crema, depending on the coffee beans. A moka pot doesn’t make true espresso, however, because it can’t generate the high pressure needed to extract the coffee at espresso-level concentrations. The 9Barista espresso machine solves this issue.

The 9Barista resembles the Bialetti original because its stainless steel system still breaks into three parts and uses stovetop heat to force steam and boiling water through the beans. What sets the 9Barista apart from a moka pot is its twin-boiler system: one boiler builds nine bars of pressure, and a second regulates the temperature to 93 degrees Fahrenheit, producing a true crema-topped espresso extraction. Moka pots are said to use one or two bars of pressure.

The clever design requires fine espresso grounds that you tamp into a basket attached beneath the top reservoir. The three parts are easily screwed together and then placed on your stovetop. Use a hot plate on electric stovetops to help distribute heat.

The 9Barista espresso maker uses a three-piece design that comes together easily. Katherine Peach/CNET

What it’s like to make espresso on the stovetop with the 9Barista

Key takeaways:

The 9Barista machine uses 18 grams of beans and 120 milliliters (mg) of water to produce a 1- to 1.5-ounce shot of espresso.

Aim for 3 to 6 minutes on the stovetop heat, and don’t leave it on longer than 8 minutes to avoid overheating the metal and burning the beans.

A full cleaning-and-drying cycle between shots takes 5 to 6 minutes — faster if you rinse thoroughly under cool water or don’t mind breaking it down while still warm.

The prep-to-pour time on a single shot is no more than 10 to 11 minutes.

Running the body under cold water also helps the release valve screw open more easily.

The hot plate itself changes color with use: gunmetal to copper and (eventually) back to light silver. This is expected, though it may look slightly alarming to the uninitiated.

A hot plate distributes heat when using the 9Barista on an electric stovetop; it changes color as the temperature changes. Katherine Peach/CNET

I followed the directions: 18 grams of espresso beans to 120 milliliters of water per shot. While results will vary depending on your beans, grind and timing, I found the machine produced 1 ounce (36 grams) to 1.5 ounces (43 grams) of espresso. The instructions also recommend 25 to 30 seconds for the full extraction, which is a rather standard goal for most machines. Helpful benchmarks for espresso shots: Anything extracted in under 20 seconds will likely taste thin and sour, while anything over 30 seconds will taste bitter. The goal is to find a combination that brings out the flavors you prefer.

Heat is a new variable with the 9Barista espresso machine. When I first used the brewer, the stovetop temperature seemed like the biggest factor to dial in, especially since “medium-high heat” is, at best, a vague guideline. I recognize that the directions can only offer imprecise tips for heating your device at home, since every stove and burner behaves differently. It’s a frustrating but real variable when your stovetop becomes part of the heating system rather than a self-contained internal system. For many espresso machines, temperature control is a major selling point. Here, you’re building it yourself, burner by burner.

Steaming, boiling water forces brewed coffee into the top chamber. Katherine Peach/CNET

On the first try, I panicked that the grounds sat on the heat too long— and I was impatient—so I cranked the stovetop to 80% power. Even the internet was perplexed when I asked how a shot could pull too quickly (less than 20 seconds) and still taste bitter. Before touching the grind or the quantities, turning the heat down to 65% (6.5 out of 10 was the sweet spot) made a huge difference in flavor. Patience is indeed a virtue. Preheating the heat transfer plate while prepping the grounds also cut down on wait time and reduced how long the fresh grounds sat exposed to heat. Some reviewers online preheat the water chamber while prepping the puck separately. I prefer to turn on the whole unit at once so I can monitor the full process.

Once the plate is preheated, the directions call for 120 grams (120ml) of filtered water. There is a fill line for anyone who doesn’t want to measure. In practice, the taste didn’t vary much if I used a few milliliters less. However, I found that even 125ml of water caused the reservoir to overflow when I turned on the group head. The built-in portafilter beneath the coffee reservoir provides a sturdy, level base for tamping. A metal basket cap with an O-ring keeps the grounds in place when you inevitably flip the portafilter upside down to lock the separate components together.

Once the water starts to gurgle, it’s showtime: Steam expels from a boiler pipe for about 30 seconds before espresso accumulates in the open funnel. My early shots tended to pull shorter — around 20 seconds — and still tasted decent with a good crema.

Disassembling and cleaning the brewer gets easier with practice. The cooldown before depressurization, rinsing and drying the filter basket is what eats the time. Rinsing the group head and steel water chamber under cold water helped cool the components. I also waited to detach the group head and water reservoir, first refilling with cold water and letting it sit while I emptied the used grounds from the portafilter. The metal basket cap stays hot to the touch, so handle it carefully. I kept a thick oven mitt handy to avoid getting burned by steam from the release valve when I wanted to pull a second shot right away. A traditional moka pot makes more coffee in one go, so adjust if you’re used to that system.

The 9Barista disassembles easily for cleaning. Katherine Peach/CNET

Final thoughts on the 9Barista

Across dozens of logged pulls, three variables kept moving at once — heat, grind and pull time — which makes any single result hard to isolate, but some patterns held up across all of my tests.

On the process itself

Heat was the dominant, hardest-to-control variable when I first used the espresso machine. Because the 9Barista relies on the stovetop rather than an internal heating system, results varied wildly by burner. The front burner took 8 to 10 minutes to boil, while the back burner boiled in under 3 minutes, both at the 6.5 heat setting. Same machine, same grind philosophy, very different extractions.

The pressure release valve is a bit hard to grab and pull to depressurize, but the water chamber will unscrew either way if you also have trouble pulling the tiny lever outward. Considering the usual trial and error of grinding and tamping, plus those minor concerns, that’s really it in terms of challenges with the brewer.

The hot plate system might give some people pause if they have an electric stovetop that’s prone to heat marks. This isn’t the machine’s fault. Many of my metal pans leave small traces on the stovetop at high heat, but keep that in mind if you’re a renter who wants to leave no trace. I kept half-expecting something to go wrong while the plate cycled from gunmetal to copper to silver. But this is a natural part of the heating process.

On build and usability

The 9Barista stainless steel design feels substantial in the hand, which is satisfying and suggests it’s built to last. The 9Barista espresso maker also comes with a five-year warranty, lifetime customer support, and replacement parts. While I haven’t tested the ease of a warranty claim, the time frame is well beyond most electric espresso machines. I also appreciate how the design provides a stable surface for level tamping. A traditional espresso machine uses the long portafilter handle to stabilize the basket. The difference is small but appreciated. That said, many people will appreciate this compact machine’s mobility and ease of use.

I appreciated having a level surface on which to tamp the espresso grounds. Katherine Peach/CNET

I also value 9Barista’s use of stainless steel over plastic components. Plastic often makes up water reservoirs and appears in most components of a single-serve pod coffee maker, including the espresso capsules. Plastic might be unavoidable, but anyone looking to reduce further exposure can breathe a bit easier with the 9Barista espresso machine.

Who the 9Barista is for

The 9Barista espresso machine is ideal for a household with one or two coffee drinkers who want a portable, sturdy, largely plastic-free espresso brewer. As a New Yorker, I love that this stovetop brewer takes up little space on the counter or in the cupboard. I keep reaching for the 9Barista more than I expected because it’s simple and delivers satisfying results.

The original 9Barista MK1 is a few hundred dollars cheaper.

As a former skeptic, I find the 9Barista an enticing option for smaller households or anyone who appreciates the ritual of espresso while camping outdoors. The 9Barista would be ideal for my van-life friends who weatherize their campers for winter excursions and want the comforts of home on the road. (This is a weighty machine, however, so the “every ounce counts” folks would never.) You might also see the 9Barista on the counter at your buddy’s place, the one who won’t stop talking about the sound quality of their Audio-Technica record player and bespoke speaker system. In other words, this is an investment piece that speaks of craftsmanship and innovation.

If paying north of $700 for a manual espresso maker just ain’t happening, the first-gen 9Barista MK1 is significantly cheaper at $540.
